## Dīgha Nikāya
## Mahāvagga-ṭīkā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Mahāpadānasutta-vaṇṇanā
## Pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttakathā-vaṇṇanā

A place well-covered by the dense leaves, branches, and twigs of naturally grown Kareri trees, appearing like a pavilion, is intended as the "Kareri Pavilion" (Karerimaṇḍapa). "Dvāre" means [situated] near the door. The phrase beginning with "Yathā" is spoken to show that similar names exist in other places due to trees standing at the door. One might ask: Why did the Blessed One not reside in the Great Fragrant Chamber (Mahāgandhakuṭi) but instead resided in the small Kareri hut at that time? To show that this small Kareri hut was also the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) where the Blessed One resided, the phrase beginning with "Anto Jetavane" (Inside Jeta's Grove) was spoken. "Salaḷāgāraṃ" refers to a dwelling constructed from pine wood. "Pakatibhattassa pacchato" means after the time of the monks' usual meal, or after midday. "Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṃ" means those who have departed from the place of eating alms-food. Therefore, the phrase beginning with "Bhattakicca" was spoken.

A sitting hall constructed in the form of a circular pavilion is intended as "Maṇḍalamāḷa"; to show this meaning, "Nisīdanasālāya" was spoken. In the Pāḷi term "Pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttā", the word "Pubba" refers to past lives. The word "Nivāsa" is used in the sense of "that which is inhabited" (kamma-sādhana). There is no "dwelled-in" state apart from the aggregates, and the aggregates occur only as a continuum. To show this meaning, "Pubbenivūtthakkhandhasantānasaṅkhātena pubbenivāsena" was spoken.
2:
“Yojetvā” means connecting in the sense of an object. “Pavattitā” means spoken or expounded (kathitā). Being associated with the Dhamma and not departing from it, it is called “Dhammī”. Therefore, it is said to be “Dhamma-saṃyuttā” (associated with the Dhamma).

“Udapādi” is an extraction of the term, which should be connected with the words “uppannā jātā” (arisen, born). The manner in which this [Dhamma talk] arose for Venerable Ānanda is shown only briefly in the Pāḷi; to show it in detail, the commentary begins with “Aho acchariyaṃ” and so on. Between the two phrases “Who can remember?” and “Who cannot remember?”, only the first is expanded upon in detail, not the other. Thus, to explain that first phrase through the distinction of persons, division of time, manner of remembering, and similes, it is said: “Heretics can remember,” and so on.

“Aggappattakammavādino” refers to those who are supreme proponents of the doctrine of Kamma, such as ascetics and wanderers who are established in the knowledge of the ownership of Kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa), believing that “there is kamma and there is the result of kamma.” They can remember only up to forty aeons (kappas), because the Blessed One has preached it as such in the Brahmajāla Sutta and elsewhere. The restriction that they cannot remember beyond that is because their knowledge, which supports wrong views, is extremely weak.

“Sāvaka” refers to the Great Disciples (Mahāsāvakas); for they fulfilled the preliminary requisites for one hundred thousand aeons. Ordinary disciples (pakati-sāvakas), however, remember for a period less than that. Since the period for the accumulation of the requisites of merit and knowledge, and the fulfillment of the perfections for the enlightenment of a Disciple or a Paccekabuddha, is respectively one hundred thousand aeons plus one or two incalculables (asaṅkhyeyyas), it is said: “The two Chief Disciples... one hundred thousand aeons...” and so on.

If it were argued that if the power of the supernormal knowledge (abhiññā-ñāṇa) of various Noble Ones is limited by the period of fulfilling the requisites for enlightenment, then the knowledge of the Buddhas must also be limited, [the commentator] says: “For the Buddhas, there is no such limit; they can remember as much as they wish.” This is in accordance with the saying: “As much as there is to be known, so much is the knowledge.” Just like the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), the supernormal knowledge of the Buddhas has no limit within its own scope. Therefore, whatever they wish to know, they know it indeed.

Alternatively, although there is a limit to the period of fulfilling perfections, the requisites for Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi-sambhāra) embraced by compassion and skill in means are so extraordinary that there is no limit to the power of the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramitā). How then could there be a limit to the supernormal knowledges that have that wisdom as their cause? Thus it is said: “For the Buddhas... there is no [limit].”
3:
## The Meaning of the Words Beginning with Khandhapaṭipāṭiyā

The succession of aggregates (khandhapaṭipāṭiyā) refers to the sequential occurrence of the aggregates as they arise according to their respective conditions. The occurrence of aggregates (khandhappavatti) refers to the arising of the aggregates starting with feeling (vedanā) and so on. The manner in which those non-Buddhist ascetics (titthiyas) recollect (the aggregates such as feeling, etc.) is indeed intense. However, while they proceed by grasping those various aggregates through the power of recollection in the realms where there is perception (saññā), when they reach the realm of a single constituent (ekavokārabhava, the mindless realm), they do not find the occurrence of aggregates and are thus said to "not see." The meaning is that they are like birds or fish caught in a net. "Kuṇṭhā viya" means like those who are dull or sluggish. "Paṅguဠā viya" means like those who are lame or crippled. "They take up a view" means they adopt the false view of fortuitous origination (adhiccasamuppannika micchādiṭṭhi), which assumes things arise without a cause. Because they cannot let go of the succession of aggregates, it is like having to follow someone ahead while holding onto the tip of a staff.

Even though this is the case, the disciples of the Buddha (Buddhasāvakas) also do not actually see the occurrence of mental aggregates in the mindless realm (asaññabhava). Nevertheless, those disciples of the Buddha are able to leap over the mindless realm and recollect the lives before and after it. The words beginning with "Vaṭṭe" are words that show the manner of recollection of those Buddha-disciples. "Standing in the method granted by the Buddhas" means standing in the guidance of the Dhamma taught by the Fully Enlightened Buddhas, such as: "That realm where there is only the occurrence of the material aggregate (rūpa) for five hundred great eons, and no occurrence of the mental aggregates (arūpa), is the mindless realm (asaññabhava)." By thus standing in the method, even though they do not see the death and rebirth within the interval of the mindless realm, they can recollect the before and after of that realm, just as the Venerable Sobhita did.

Venerable Sobhita, having become one who had mastered the practice of recollecting past lives, saw his own mindless rebirth (material rebirth) in the mindless realm while recollecting his places of birth in succession. Beyond that, having not seen death and rebirth for a duration of five hundred great eons, and seeing death at the end, he reflected, "What kind of death is this?" and through the method, he came to the conclusion, "It must be the mindless realm." Subsequently, the Buddha, based on that event, placed him in the foremost position (etadagga) among those who recollect past lives. The phrase "looking at death and rebirth" shows how the knowledge of the Chief Disciples and Paccekabuddhas transfers from one life to another by way of death and rebirth. This shows that even the Chief Disciples and Paccekabuddhas are unable to leap over without examining all lives in their entirety.

"They see that very matter" means, for example, just as an object is very clear to a man with good eyesight in a house of four cubits at noon during the autumn season; this is a well-known fact in the world. However, there might be objects that are too subtle or hidden for that man to see. But for the Buddhas, there is no knowable object (ñeyyadhamma) that they wish to know which is not within the range of their vision. Rather, illuminated by the light of knowledge, it is as clear and distinct as an emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) placed in the palm of the hand.
4:
This is because the obstruction to the knowable (ñeyyāvaraṇa), which prevents one from knowing the objects of knowledge, has been completely and perfectly abandoned. Therefore, the commentator said, "When the Buddhas recollect what has been seen, done, or heard by themselves or others, it is like the radiance of the sun's orb," and so on. Likewise, the disciples and Paccekabuddhas also recollect. Here, by the word "tathā" (likewise), it conveys the meaning that "they recollect only what has been seen, done, or heard by themselves." By conveying this, it indicates that the recollection of those disciples and Paccekabuddhas is only partial (sappadesa) and not exhaustive (nippadesa). Because the power of their knowledge is extremely small, the knowledge of non-Buddhist ascetics is like the light of a firefly. In the phrase "sāvakānaṃ," the knowledge of ordinary disciples (pakatisāvaka) is like the light of an ordinary lamp. The knowledge of the great disciples (mahāsāvaka) is like the light of a great lamp. Therefore, it is said in the Visuddhimagga, "It is like the light of a torch." "Osadhītārakobhāsasadisaṃ" means it is like the light of the star named Osadhī (Venus), so called either because it carries a great amount of light or because it provides strength to medicinal plants (osadhī). The Buddha's knowledge is like the radiance of the autumn sun because it completely dispels all darkness. Wavering in grasping an object due to a lack of sharpness is called "khalita" (stumbling). Non-penetration of an object due to dullness is called "paṭighāta" (obstruction). "Āvajjanapaṭibaddha" means it is dependent merely on reflection; the meaning is that the desired object is penetrated immediately upon reflecting. The same method applies to the remaining two terms.

To show that the Buddha's knowledge, which proceeds unattached and unobstructed (asaṅga-appaṭihata), is the same whether the object is very light or very heavy, two similes are given, starting with "dubbalapattapuṭa" (a weak leaf-basket). Because the Buddha is the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya), the words spoken concerning the Buddha's qualities are said to be "words arisen concerning the Buddha himself." "Taṃ sabbampi" refers to all the aforementioned matters related to past lives. Here, the recollection of past lives by titthiyas and disciples is mentioned by way of showing inferior examples in comparison to the Buddha's recollection of past lives. In this way, the greatness of the Buddha is specially revealed. "Saṅkhepato" means in brief. At that time, those monks summarized all the various modes of the occurrence of the knowledge of recollecting past lives that were the objects of their own knowledge, as described in the Pali, and said "itipi." Because of the manifold nature of that recollection, the word is repeated. The word "pi" has the sense of conjunction. To show that the word "iti" has the sense of "manner" (ākāra), as in "Iti kho bhikkhave sappaṭibhayo bālo" and so on, he said "evampi" to express that meaning.
5: 2-3. In the phrase "vuttameva" (already stated), the explanation given here in this Mahāpadāna Sutta Pāli is relevant to the Brahmajāla Sutta Pāli; it refers only to the meaning already stated in that Brahmajāla Sutta Commentary. Since the focus is on explaining new terms, explanations not relevant to the Brahmajāla Sutta are not intended. To show these new terms, he said "ayam eva hi viseso" (this indeed is the distinction), etc. The word "assosi" (heard) is said in terms of the completion of the act of hearing. This is because, starting with the hearing of the sound, the task of understanding its meaning is accomplished. In that Brahmajāla Sutta Pāli, however, it is only stated: "Having understood this well-spoken Dhamma." The connection should be made as: "How do these monks praise my virtues based on my knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa)?" "Nipphatti" means the successful completion of the act of recollecting. It means the accomplishment of the tasks that should be performed with that knowledge of past lives. The word "no" is an interrogative particle (nipāta) with the same meaning as "nu," as stated in "iccheyyātha nu" (would you wish?). "Naṃ" refers to the Blessed One. In the phrase "yaṃ bhagavā," the word "yaṃ" refers to the action, pointing to the delivery of the Dhamma talk as in "How will he deliver the Dhamma talk?" The meaning of the word "etassa" is "of this delivery of the Dhamma talk," thus he said "etassa dhammikathākaraṇassa." Out of respect, that meaning is stated twice.## 4. In the word "suṇātha" (listen), the word "iti" carries the meaning of "and so forth" or "in this manner." By this word "iti," the term "manasi karotha" (pay attention) is included. "Sotāvadhānaṃ" means lending an ear or the desire to listen. Because the path of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa) has been completely cut off, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas (Sammāsambuddhas) and other Arahants are called "chinnavaṭumaka" (those whose path is cut). Here, however, only the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas are intended. This is because their total recollection (anussaraṇa) is not within the scope of others. Therefore, he said "not shared with others." The word "yaṃ" is found in the nominative case (paccatta) because it indicates the object-meaning (kamma-attha). It is found in the accusative case (upayoga) because it indicates the object-meaning of the act of questioning. The word "taṃ" is also in the accusative case because the verb "pucchati" (asks) takes two objects. He stated that "yaṃ" is also found in the instrumental case (karaṇa) because it means "by which cause." It should be noted that the word "yaṃ" is not only in the nominative, accusative, and instrumental, but here it is also in the locative case (bhumma). "Dasasahassilokadhātu" refers to the ten thousand world systems which are the birth-field (jātikhetta) of the Bodhisatta. Because the arising of a Buddha is adorned with the appearance of many wonders, he arose making the ten thousand world systems resound.The auspiciousness (baddatā) of time refers to the abundance of virtues and prosperity of beings at that time. The arising of Buddhas is the supreme virtue and prosperity, and because of the frequency of such arisings, that aeon is auspicious; thus he said, "In the auspicious aeon adorned with the arising of five Buddhas." Likewise, by the power of excellent virtues...
6: After saying the word "sārakappe" (in the essence-aeon) as "He said this wishing to praise this aeon," he said "yato paṭṭhāya" (starting from when), etc., to show that such praiseworthiness of this aeon is a special quality not shared with other aeons. In that phrase, "yato paṭṭhāya" means starting from the time the initial aspiration (abhinīhāra), endowed with the eight factors such as being human, was made. Since saṃsāra has no beginning, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas who arose in the time before this Blessed One's initial aspiration are infinite and immeasurable. Excluding the aeons in which those Buddhas arose, he said "etasmiṃ antare" (in this interval). In fact, this Blessed One made his initial aspiration during the time of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. However, because the appearance of that Buddha Dīpaṅkara occurred before this Bodhisatta's initial aspiration, he said "amhākaṃ...pe... nibbattisuṃ" (to us... arose)."Asaṅkhyeyyakappapariyosāne" means at the end of an incalculable number of great aeons. This method should be understood for other similar terms that follow. By the phrase "ito tiṃsakappasahassānaṃ upari" (above thirty thousand aeons from here), he shows that in the interval between the Buddha Padumuttara and the Buddha Sumedha, there were sixty-nine thousand (one less than seventy thousand) aeons empty of Buddhas. By the phrase "ito aṭṭhārasannaṃ kappasahassānaṃ upari" (above eighteen thousand aeons from here), he shows that in the interval between the Buddha Sujāta and the Buddha Atthadassī, there were eleven thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine (one less than twelve thousand) aeons empty of Buddhas. By the phrase "ito catunavute kappe" (in the ninety-fourth aeon from here), he shows that in the interval between the Buddha Dhammadassī and the Buddha Siddhattha, there were seventeen thousand nine hundred and six aeons empty of Buddhas. By the phrase "ekatiṃse kappe" (in the thirty-first aeon), he shows that in the interval between the Buddha Vipassī and the Buddha Sikhī, there were sixty aeons empty of Buddhas. All those aeons, when combined with the aeons in which Buddhas such as Sumedha arose on this side of the Buddha Padumuttara, become one hundred thousand aeons. In those one hundred thousand aeons, persons such as the Great Disciples (Mahāsāvaka) accumulated the merit of perfections (pāramī), which are the strong supporting conditions for Nibbāna, the state free from the suffering of the round of rebirths. Even in the world during aeons empty of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas arise and serve as the cause for the increase of the flow of merit for those exceptional persons. The phrase "evamayaṃ," etc., is said as a conclusion to the meaning already mentioned.The phrase "kiṃ panetaṃ," etc., is begun to clarify the omens (pubbanimitta). In that phrase, "etaṃ" refers to the arising of Buddhas. "Kappasaṇṭhānakālasmiṃ" means at the time when the evolving aeon (vivaṭṭakappa) is established. The phrase "ekamasaṅkhyeyyaṃ" is said with reference to the incalculable aeon of dissolution-stability (saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī). "Ekaṅgaṇaṃ hutvā ṭhite" means existing clearly like a vast open space because of the absence of mountains, trees, bushes, etc., as well as clouds, etc.
7:
"In the world-dwelling" means the place situated within the okāsaloka (the world of space). Twenty yaṭṭhis, each being seven cubits, constitute one usabha. The word mattā (measure/extent) should be applied to each term, such as "the measure of one usabha, the measure of two usabhas," and so on. "Being of the extent of a thousand yojanas" means that the falling streams of water, by spreading and flowing through a thousand yojanas of space, become a thousand yojanas in extent. "Up to the indestructible Brahma realms" means—depending on the mode of world destruction—up to the Ābhassara Brahma realm, or up to the Subhakiṇha Brahma realm, or up to the Vehapphala Brahma realm.

"By the power of the wind" means by the power of the wind-sphere that supports the mass of water, which is nine hundred and sixty thousand yojanas in height. By the term "Great Bodhi Seat" (Mahābodhi-pallaṅka), the location where the Great Bodhi tree and the throne will appear is meant. Its being the last to be destroyed and the first to be formed and established should be understood as a natural law (dhammatā). "Therein" means in that place where the Great Bodhi Seat is situated. "Being a precursor" means being a preliminary sign of the appearance of the Buddhas. The lotus bush, which is the support for the precursor lotus flowers, is called a "precursor" by way of the name of the sign it supports. Therefore, it was said, "of that," and so on. "Being like a cluster of lotus pericarps" means those lotus flowers bloom like a formed lotus pericarp (kaṇṇikā). "The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, being joyful... depart" is the syntactical connection of the words. The Vehapphala realms are also included in the Subhakiṇha group and referred to as the "nine Brahma realms." This is because those Brahmas belong only to the fourth station of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti) (the realm of beings with unity of body and unity of perception).

"When departing" means when departing through the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana). Here, "birth" (abhijāti) is included in "descent into the womb" (gabbhokkanti) due to the commonality of being a form of birth (jāti). It is called a "sign" (nimitta—omen/cause) because the effect is inferred through this cause. In fact, upon seeing a causative sign that makes something known, one takes the effect as certainly accomplished due to the sign's unfailing nature. For example, the hermit Asita, upon seeing the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa) at the time of birth, took the Buddha-qualities as certainly accomplished due to the unfailing nature of those marks. An effect arising from such a sign is spoken of as if it were accomplished by the power of that sign, because the effect exists when the sign exists. Therefore, it was said, "By the power of those signs," and so on. Likewise, the Blessed One said, "Endowed with that mark... what does he gain as a King? What does he gain as a Buddha?" and so forth. "This meaning" means they knew the fact truly that five Buddhas would appear in this aeon.

## Explanation of the Birth-Limit and Others

5-7. "By way of the limit of the aeon" (kappapariccheda-vasena) means knowing by way of defining the respective aeons in which those respective Buddhas appeared, such as "ninety-one aeons from now." Indeed, knowing by defining and determining "this is that" is called pariccheda (definition/limit). Paritta means brief. Lahuka means very light; it means "short" because the lifespan is intended. Therefore, it is said, "Both of these are synonyms for 'little'."

The phrase "little or more" (appaṃ vā bhiyyo) is an expression without specific distinction of the lifespan. It is a determination according to what is obtained, without being fixed, such as "twenty or thirty years." To show that this method is not common, it is said, "However, such a long life is extremely rare." To show this specific determination by applying it to individuals, it is said, "Among them, Visākhā," and so on.

If that is so, why did our Blessed One not live for such a long time? Do not the Bodhisattas in their final existence take rebirth with an exceedingly sublime accumulation of merit (puññābhisaṅkhāra)? If asked, the answer is "That is true." To show the reason for this, it is said, "But Vipassī and others," and so on. Therein, because the birth (abhijāti) is the ground for loving-kindness, the karmic-formation consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa) is preceded by loving-kindness. The rebirth-consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) of those Bodhisattas is particularly in accordance with that. That rebirth-consciousness should be understood as being associated with joy (somanassa) because it has the strong dependence of the thought of safety (khema-vitakka), associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta) because it has the strong dependence of a special knowledge that is not shared with others and is independent of others' instruction, and as unprompted (asaṅkhārika). The incalculable lifespan is due to a cause of immeasurable power, arising from the distinction of the support, the distinction of the dependence, the remoteness from opposition, and the distinction in the mode of occurrence. Therein, the fact that the continuum has been saturated with the perfections for a very long time is the distinction of the support (ādhāra-visesatā). The accomplishment of inclinations such as the inclination toward non-greed is the distinction of the dependence (nissaya-visesatā). The suppression of evil states such as greed and stinginess is the remoteness from opposition (paṭipakkha-dūrībhāva). The striving for the sake of the liberation of all beings from the entire suffering of the round of rebirths should be understood as the distinction in the mode of occurrence (pavatti-ākāra-visesa).

And this method is common to the accumulation of kamma (kamma-āyūhana) that brings about the final existence of all Great Bodhisattas; therefore, by its result, which is likewise identical...
9:
When the commentator states, "Thus all Buddhas have an incalculable (asaṅkheyya) lifespan," it means they have a lifespan that lasts for an incalculable period. There exists accumulated wholesome kamma capable of sustaining life for an incalculable period. However, the Buddhas remain only for a duration consistent with the maximum lifespan (paramāyu) of humans at that time and then attain Parinibbāna. This is because there is no further purpose to be achieved by staying longer, or it should be understood as the natural law (dhammatā) of the Buddhas. In the Commentary, the reason for not staying longer is stated as "due to the corruption of climate and food (utu-bhojana-vipatti)." It cannot be said that this does not apply to the Tathāgatas born in the world, as it is common to the world. Indeed, they also experience illness, fatigue, and so on. "By the power of climate and food" (utu-bhojana-vasena) means that through the influence of deficient or abundant climate and food, the lifespan decreases or increases accordingly. "Lifespan" (āyu) refers to the maximum lifespan (paramāyu). What needs to be said there has already been stated in the sub-commentaries (ṭīkā) such as the Brahmajāla Sutta.

Now, to show this matter from its origin, the phrase "Tattha yadā" etc. is spoken. Those devoted to the Dhamma are called "dhammika" (righteous). Those not devoted to the Dhamma are "adhammika" (unrighteous), being engaged in unrighteous acts such as violence. They become unrighteous due to following the example of rulers and imitating the behavior of others. The "Uṇhavalāhaka" deities are devas who bring about the clouds that cause the hot season. It is said that as soon as a thought arises in them, they spread heat in the desired place and spread clouds that are not too thick, covering the sky. This same principle applies to the "Sītavalāhaka" (cold-cloud) and "Vassavalāhaka" (rain-cloud) deities. The "Abbhavalāhaka" deities should be understood as those who bring about only the mist/cloud layers without cold, heat, or rain.

In the word "tāsaṃ", the word "mittā" should be brought in and connected. Certainly, the seven types of deities mentioned below are only the Cātumahārājikā devas. However, having described them by their specific characteristics, the author now uses "Cātumahārājikā" to generally include other sensual-sphere devas of the first plane. "Tāsaṃ adhammikatāya" means the unrighteousness of those deities, which is rooted in the unrighteousness of kings and passed down through the unrighteousness of sub-kings and so on. "The moon and sun move unevenly" means that due to the power of the common evil kamma of beings, known as unrighteousness, which is the basis for undesirable results such as many diseases, the moon and sun, being oppressed by the wind blowing unevenly, revolve around Mount Sineru unevenly, not following their regular path.
10:
The moon and sun revolve around Mount Sineru unevenly. They do not follow their regular paths. Just as the uneven revolution of the moon and sun is caused by the agitation of irregular winds, so too the irregular occurrence of seasons and rain should be understood. Thus it is said, "The wind does not blow according to its regular path," and so on. "Of the deities" refers to the Sītavalāhaka deities and others. Therefore, it is said, "The season with its divisions of cold and heat," etc. When that season, which is the seed of rain as described, does not reach its proper state at the right time, the rain does not fall properly.

To explain in detail the meaning summarized as "The rain does not fall properly," the phrase "Sometimes" etc. is spoken. There, "Sometimes it rains" means it rains at a time when it should not rain. "Sometimes it does not rain" means it does not rain at a time when it should rain. "It rains in some places and not in others" distinguishes the places where it rains and where it does not. The passage starting with "Even when it rains" is an explanation of the meaning of the two phrases "Sometimes it rains, sometimes it does not rain." In the phrase "devoid of scent, color, taste, etc.", the word "etc." includes the lack of nutrients (nirojatā). "In one place" means on one side of the cooking pot. "Uttaṇḍula" refers to the presence of uncooked rice that has moved away from the heat. It cooks in three ways: completely uncooked, partially cooked, or poorly cooked. Such food enters the stomach (pakkāsaya). In the context of "having a short lifespan," it should also be said "and of poor appearance." Thus, lifespan decreases due to the influence of climate and food; even if the root cause (kamma) is not yet exhausted, it is because the supporting conditions of climate and food are very weak.

The meaning of the "bright side" (sukka-pakkha) starting with "But when..." should be understood as the opposite of what was said for the "dark side."

It should be understood that [lifespan] decreases after having increased and increased. Why? Because many Buddhas do not arise in a single intermediate aeon (antarakappa); only one arises. Now, to show this matter in detail, the phrase "How?" etc. is spoken. In the phrase "remaining in four," the word "four" is in the accusative case in the sense of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga). "In whatever lifespan proportions" means among humans who have such-and-such a maximum lifespan. For those Buddhas too, that very lifespan proportion becomes their lifespan. The reason for this is as already stated above.

## The explanation of the section on birth and lineage, etc., is finished.
11:
## Commentary on the Section on the Bodhi Tree

"Mūle" means in the vicinity of the part known as the root (implying: "He penetrated the Four Noble Truths there"). Since this vicinity is the area beneath the Bodhi tree, it is said, "under the Pāṭali tree." "Taṃdivasaṃ" refers either to the day of its own sprouting or to the day of the Blessed One's Enlightenment (Abhisambodhi).

That Bodhi tree, like a Sālakalyāṇī tree, grew within the earth even before the Buddha's Enlightenment. On the day of Enlightenment, it burst through the earth and stood one hundred cubits high. It remained filling the sky, spreading to a width of one hundred cubits. This manner of the Bodhi tree's existence is a unique feature, distinct from the Bodhi trees of other Buddhas. Because of its densely packed stems and stalks, it was covered all at once with flowers like bound clusters. "Ekasañchannā" means being covered all at once because the flowers were crowded together without any gaps.

"Samujjalanti" means shining brightly due to flower garlands hanging here and there, flower masses thrown here and there, and various loose flowers detached from their stalks scattered here and there. "Aññamaññaṃ sirīsampattāni" refers to objects endowed with mutual glory and beauty. "Buddhaguṇavibhavasirinti" refers to the beauty of the fulfillment of virtues that are to be approached by the Buddhas. "Paṭivijjhamāno" means penetrating (the Four Noble Truths) or attaining them.

"Setambarukkho" is a mango tree with white-colored fruit. "Tadeva" refers to a tree of the same dimensions as the previously mentioned Pāṭali tree. "Ekato" means (fruits hanging) on one side. "Surasāni" are fruits with an extremely sweet taste.

"Ekovo pallaṅko" refers to the place where the single throne for sitting cross-legged is situated. Each such tree is called "Bodhi" because the Buddhas penetrate the sublime Bodhi-dhamma beneath them.

## Commentary on the Section on the Pair of Disciples

"Sāvakaparicchede" means in the chapter defining the pair of disciples. To show that the words "Khaṇḍatissaṃ" refer to both Chief Disciples taken together as a single term, it is said, "Khaṇḍa and Tissa." Since Buddhas have no elder brother from the same mother or a different mother, he is called a "younger brother" (kaniṭṭhabhātā) having the same father. "Avasesehi puttehi" means with the remaining noble sons (disciples) of the Buddha. After stating "reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom," the words beginning with "Sikhinā Bhagavatā" are explained to show his extraordinary quality of reaching the pinnacle.

"Uttaro" refers to the exalted Elder. Again, "Uttaro" mentions the Elder by name. "Pāraṃ" means reaching the final pinnacle or limit. "Paññāvisaye" means being supreme in the sphere of wisdom. Indeed, it explains the sequence of events by way of the place of occurrence.
13:
Just as the Niddesa Pāḷi and Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi are included in the group of Dhamma learned from the monk Venerable Sāriputta (it should be understood that the method of Abhidhamma also originated from Venerable Sāriputta). Other teachers, however, say: Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, had the opportunity to ask questions of the Blessed One daily regarding the triads (tika) and dyads (duka) in the sequence of the Abhidhamma Pāḷi. The Blessed One also answered all the questions asked by Venerable Ānanda by providing the methods (naya). Thus, although the Abhidhamma teaching was delivered by the Blessed One in the absence of Venerable Ānanda, it was received by the Elder Ānanda as if in the presence of the Blessed One. All such statements should be noted after careful investigation.

'Aggupaṭṭhāka' (Chief Attendant) means the foremost attendant because of his respectful performance of major and minor duties for the Blessed One. Since the time he received the position of attendant, Venerable Ānanda served the Blessed One with two kinds of water (hot and cold), three kinds of tooth-sticks (large, medium, and small), by massaging the feet, and by sweeping the surroundings of the Gandhakuṭi (Fragrant Chamber), and so on. Thinking, 'At such a time, such an object is suitable for the Teacher; such a task should be performed,' he would accomplish those various matters. Holding a large torch, he would circumambulate the surroundings of the Gandhakuṭi nine times throughout the night. Venerable Ānanda thought: 'If sloth and torpor (thina-middha) should overcome me, I might not be able to respond when the Blessed One calls.' Therefore, he did not let the torch out of his hand all night. Thus, he is called 'Aggupaṭṭhāka'.

The passage defining the father, mother, and the city of birth is called 'Pitipariccheda' (Section on the Father) because it begins with the father.

'Entering the monastery' means entering the Gandhakuṭi. 'Having taught this much' means having delivered the teaching concerning the past lives (pubbenivāsa) of the seven Buddhas, beginning with Vipassī, adorned with the nine aspects such as the definition of the aeon (kappa), with these words. Why did the Blessed One teach the past lives of only these seven Buddhas, such as Vipassī, in this Sutta, and not the twenty-five Buddhas as in the Buddhavamsa, or even more? Because there was no specific request (adhikāra) and no necessity (payojana). In the Buddhavamsa teaching, based on the question: 'O Great Hero, O Supreme among Men, what was your aspiration (abhinihāra)? At what time, O Hero, did you aspire for the supreme Enlightenment (bodhi)?' and so on, the past lives consisting of the practices of the twenty-four Buddhas—starting from the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, at whose feet he made the great aspiration and from whom he received the prophecy (byākaraṇa) for Enlightenment, and then fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) under each—as well as his own practice, were taught. In this Sutta, however, there is no such specific request...
14:
...there is no such request starting from Dīpaṅkara or even earlier Buddhas to teach their past lives. Therefore, in this Sutta, the past lives are not elaborated as in the Buddhavamsa. Furthermore, the teaching of the Buddhas is in accordance with the intellectual capacity of the persons who are the vessels for the teaching, not in accordance with their own intellectual power. Therefore, in that (Buddhavamsa) teaching, the discourse was elaborated for the sake of the Chief Disciples, Great Disciples, and such devas and brahmās. But in this (Mahāpadāna Sutta), while teaching the past lives for the sake of ordinary disciples (pakati-sāvaka) and such deities, he taught the past lives of only seven Buddhas. Indeed, the Blessed One, having stimulated them by way of attraction but without bringing the discourse to a conclusion with an elaborate talk, entered the Gandhakuṭi. Moreover, following the sequence of this very teaching, discourses such as the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta were delivered.

Alternatively, the Blessed One taught the past lives of only the seven Buddhas, such as Vipassī, to include the subsequent teaching that clarifies his own visit to the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes). For only the disciples of those seven Buddhas resided in the Suddhāvāsa at that time and reside now; not the disciples of others, because they have attained Parinibbāna. It is said: 'The disciples of the Buddhas Siddhattha, Tissa, and Phussa, having been reborn in the Suddhāvāsa, attained Arahantship immediately upon rebirth, like Upaka and others in this Dispensation, and attained Parinibbāna shortly after; they did not remain there for the full lifespan.' Likewise, in this Sutta, the Blessed One taught the past lives of the Buddhas such as Vipassī according to the inclination of those to be tamed (veneyya), intending to mention only those Buddhas whose Dispensation of Realization (paṭivedha-sāsana) is certainly still present today and has not disappeared. The rule of 'Apubbācarimaniyama' (the non-simultaneity of two Buddhas) is desired only within a single world-system (lokadhātu) in terms of beings wandering from one existence to another; thus, it should be understood that it does not contradict this teaching. 'Nirantaraṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā' means bringing it to the culmination, from the conception until the recitation of the Ovāda Pātimokkha, which is the accomplishment of the Buddha's duties. The construction is: 'it has not yet been taught' until such Buddha-duties are completed.

'Tanti' means the Dhamma-tanti, the Pariyatti Pāḷi to be learned. The section (vāra) that proceeds by clarifying many meanings such as the son, the son's mother, the vehicle, the monastery, the wealth for the monastery, the donor of the monastery, and so on, is called Sambahulavāra.
15:
## Commentary on the Section on Many [Buddhas] (Sambahulavāra-vaṇṇanā)
Although this section on many Buddhas (Sambahulavāra) does not appear in the Pāḷi text, it is presented here because it appears in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). Desiring to show this, the teacher said, "Sabbabodhisattānañhi," and so forth. *Kulavaṃsa* means the lineage of the clan. *Paveṇī* means the succession. By the question "Kasmā" (Why?), the reason for the birth of the son is asked, and desiring to answer that question, the teacher said, "Sabbaññubodhisattānañhi," and so forth. By those words, it should be understood for certain that they are truly human beings through the clarity of the birth city and so forth of the Bodhisattas. Otherwise (if they were not truly human), the fulfillment of the intended Buddha-duties would not even be possible. This is because Great Beings (Mahāsattas) appear only in the human world in their final birth, and not in other worlds such as the deva or brahma worlds.

## Commentary on the Section on Various Distinctions (Sambahulapariccheda-vaṇṇanā)
He is called Rāhu because he causes the moon and so forth to abandon their special beauty; he is like the planet Rāhu. In this context, however, the son is called Rāhu because he is like Rāhu. The word "Bandhana" (bond/fetter) is also spoken with reference to it being a cause of disadvantage. Taking the very words spoken by the Bodhisatta regarding it being a cause of disadvantage, they named the prince "Rāhula." "Atha" is merely a particle. *Rocinī* means a queen who is naturally radiant and beautiful. *Rucaggatī* means one who has reached radiant splendor; it is said by inserting the letter "ga" in the middle. Because she is a woman-treasure (itthi-ratana), she is named "Bimbā" because she is as beautiful as a statue covered with cloth among all women in the human world.

"Jhānā vuṭṭhāya" means having risen from the fourth jhāna which is the basis (pādakajjhāna).

"Aṭṭhaṅgulubbedhā" means having a thickness of eight finger-breadths. "Cūḷaṃsena chādetvā" means covering the entire monastery area by placing it on its side (edge). "Suvaṇṇayaṭṭhiphālehi" means with gold bars the size of a plowshare. "Suvaṇṇဟတ္ထိပါဒါနိ" means gold pieces the size of a natural elephant's foot. "Vuttanayeneva" means just as said before, on the side/edge. "Suvaṇṇakaṭṭīhi" means with gold pieces. "Salakkhaṇānaṃ" means of the wheels with a thousand spokes and endowed with marks.

*Bodhipallaṅka* is the seat where the Buddha sat at the time of attaining Enlightenment by penetrating the Four Noble Truths. "Avijahito" means it is an unabandoned place because such sitting of the Buddhas does not occur elsewhere. Therefore, it is said, "It occurs in only one place." "Paṭhamapadagaṇṭhikā" is the place where the right foot is placed while standing on the last step of the stairs. Because that place is firm, stable, and cannot be destroyed by anyone, it is called "Padagaṇṭhi."
16:
In the ground where the Jetavana Mahāvihāra is now located, the couches (mañca) of all previous Buddhas were prepared in that very spot. Thinking thus, our Blessed One's couch was also prepared there; hence it is said, "The four locations of the couch legs are never abandoned." The size of the area for preparing the couch is not measured by the largeness or smallness of the couches themselves; rather, by the power of the Buddhas, that spot always remains the same size. Thus, it should be understood as "The four locations of the couch legs are never abandoned." The same applies to the statement "The monastery (vihāra) is also not abandoned." It means the previous location of the monastery is not given up.

A distinguished measure is called *Vimatta*; *Vimatta* itself is *Vematta* (variation/difference), meaning the state of being dissimilar. *Pamāṇa* means height. *Padhāna* means the practice of austerities (dukkara-kiriya) which are difficult to perform. *Rasmi* means the bodily rays.

Teachers say: "A middle-sized man is six cubits by the ordinary hand-cubit of beings; three times that is the measure of the Blessed One's body, so the Blessed One is eighteen cubits tall." Others say: "A middle-sized man is four cubits by the ordinary hand-cubit of humans; three times that is the measure of the Blessed One's body, so the Blessed One is twelve cubits tall in terms of the physical body (upādinnaka-rūpa). However, since the fathom-wide radiance (byāmapabbhā) spreads for one fathom all around, it rises six cubits above, and together with the dense radiance, it is eighteen cubits."

*Addhaniya* means a long time.

*Ajjhāsayapaṭibaddha* means it follows the desire that arose while fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) which are the requisites for enlightenment (bodhi-sambhāra); it means it is extensive or even more extensive according to such an aspiration. This meaning should be understood in the manner stated in the Cariyāpiṭaka Commentary. Here, although the body size, the practice of austerities, and the bodily rays differ among Buddhas, they do not appear in this Mahāpadāna Sutta Pāḷi. Therefore, due to the similarity in being "differences" (vematta), the life-span and clan (āyu-kula) are also brought in and shown here. "Paṭividdhaguṇesu" means in the qualities of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) that have been attained. If one asks, "Is there not no difference in the requisites for enlightenment and the measure of the beings to be tamed (veneyya)?" It is true there is no difference, but both are included by taking the "Buddha-qualities," so they are not separately extracted. To the extent that there is no difference in the Buddha-qualities of all Buddhas, to that same extent, there is no difference in their requisites for enlightenment (sambodhi-sambhāra). Why? Because it is in accordance with the cause.
17: Because it is consistent with the result, it has been clearly shown that there is indeed no difference in the quantity of veneyya persons (those to be guided). In truth, during the causal stage of fulfilling the perfections by the Great Bodhisattas, the veneyya persons—whose faculties such as faith and wisdom, which are the perfections accumulated as strong supporting conditions, have matured—reach awakening in their final birth for the attainment of Arahantship, just as lotus groves reach full bloom upon contact with the sun's rays, so too do they reach awakening upon contact with the power of the Tathāgata's virtues. Thus have the teachers of the Commentaries shown. 'Nidhikumbho' refers to the four great treasure pots. In the phrase 'jāto ca', by the word 'ca', the meaning 'having made the Great Resolve (mahābhinīhāra)' is also included. This should be noted. For it is said in the Buddhavamsa: 'The clusters of stars and constellations shine in the vast expanse of the sky; the Visākhā constellation is joined with the moon; surely he will become a Buddha.' (Bu. Va. 65). And they also say: 'By this very Visākhā constellation of all Buddhas, the Great Resolve takes place.' 13. 'Ayaṃ gati' means this natural course or mode of occurrence. It means that when persons other than the Buddha recollect the sequence of aggregates lived in the past, they recollect in this manner. Because the recollection from the time of death (cuti) up to the time of rebirth (paṭisandhi) occurs with the knowledge facing towards the past lives known as the preceding, further preceding, and most preceding births, it is called 'ascending' (ārohana). Therefore, the recollection from rebirth up to death is called 'descending' (orohana), and because the knowledge occurs with its face turned away from the past lives, it is said: 'sending forth the knowledge with its face turned backward.' 'Cutigantabbaṃ' means that which is to be gone to by the movement of knowledge towards death; it means knowing that going. 'Garukaṃ' means very heavy and difficult to do. Therefore, it is said: 'As if showing a footprint in the sky.' 'Aparampi kāraṇaṃ' means another wonderful and marvelous reason, which is the recollection of the path already cut by sending the knowledge with its face turned backward. The word 'yatra' is a particle in the sense of the nominative case, the word 'nāma' is a particle in the sense of wonder, and the word 'hi' is an expletive particle. Therefore, it is said: 'He who is called the Tathāgata.' By doing so, the separate taking of the word 'yatra' by the power of the particle is established. Because they expand the continuity of beings in saṃsāra, they are called 'papañca' (proliferation). The round of kamma (kammavaṭṭa) is spoken of because the round of defilements (kilesavaṭṭa) is taken by the name 'papañca' and the round of results (vipākavaṭṭa) is taken by the name 'dukkha'. 'Pariyādinnavaṭṭe' refers to the Buddhas whose round of rebirth is entirely exhausted. In the statement 'maggasīlena phalasīlena', this virtue of the path and fruit is preceded by mundane virtue.
18:
To show that the mundane virtue (lokiya-sīla) of the Buddhas is also unique (not shared with others) like their supramundane virtue (lokuttara-sīla), it is said, 'by mundane and supramundane virtue.' The same method applies to concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā). In the word 'samādhipakkhā', it should be noted that both concentration and the factors associated with concentration are treated as a single term through the grammatical device of ekasesa (leaving one word to represent others). Therefore, it is said, 'by path-concentration,' and so forth, and 'the dwelling (vihāra) is taken.' What are called the factors associated with concentration are energy (vīriya), mindfulness (sati), and so forth.

'Sayaṃ' means by oneself (personally). 'Nīvaraṇādīhi' means [liberation] from the hindrances, from the evil states associated with those hindrances, and from initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra), and so forth. By the statement, 'Because of being liberated, they are called liberation (vimutti),' the passive sense (kamma-sādhana) of the word vimutti is expressed. This is because that liberation has the eight attainments (samāpatti) and so forth as its object. The word 'vimuttattā' (because of being liberated) should also be understood in connection with 'because of being liberated by way of suppression (vikkhambhana),' and so forth.

'Tassa tassa' refers to the states such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). 'Paccanīkaṅgavasena' means by way of the opposing factors that are to be abandoned. 'Paṭippassaddhante uppannattā' means because it arises at the end of the subsiding of defilements, since that subsiding is the conclusion (pariyosāna). It means it arises by way of the subsiding of the defilements to be abandoned by the respective paths. To show that the escape and departure from defilements occur only because Nibbāna is secluded from those defilements, it is said, 'because of standing far away.'

'Dhammadhātu' means the nature of things. In meaning, it refers to the Four Noble Truths. 'Suppaṭividdhā' means that because the Buddha has abandoned all defilements along with their residual traces (vāsanā), he has thoroughly penetrated [the Dhammadhātu]. In this way, the Buddha attained all the Buddha-qualities, such as omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and the ten powers (dasabala-ñāṇa). Some teachers say that the fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) is called Dhammadhātu. Other teachers say that omniscience is called Dhammadhātu.

'Dvīhi padehi' means by two sentences. 'Ābaddhaṃ' means that the teaching preached above is connected because it is based on those two sentences. 'Devacārikakolāhala' should be understood as: while wandering in the celestial realms, showing the excitement and wonder that arose among the deities of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), he will investigate at the end of the Sutta, meaning he will make it clear. 'This teaching' refers to the teaching set forth in detail, beginning with 'Monks, from here [looking back],' and so forth. It refers to the brief teaching preached in the 'Section on the Origin' (Nidāna-kaṇḍa), and so forth. This is because that brief teaching stands in the place of the origin for this discourse; thus it is so stated.

## Explanation of the Nature of Bodhisattas

Having explained that 'Vipassī is the name of that Bodhisatta,' the phrase 'And that [name],' etc., is stated to show how that name is consistent with its meaning. 'In various objects' refers to objects that are hidden or obstructed, or located in distant places, and so forth...
19:
He is called 'Vipassī' because of his skill in seeing various meanings, such as various colors like blue and so forth, other objects that fall within the range of the five senses, things that have come into his presence, and the determination of legal affairs. 'Bodhi' is so called because it understands the knowable as it truly is; because he is associated with that Bodhi, he is called a 'Bodhisatta' (Buddha-to-be). That Bodhisatta is a wise being, a knowing being. There is no need to mention his being wise due to his excellent thinking and so forth. From the time he made the Great Resolve (Mahābhinīhāra), because he is definitely inclined towards the Great Bodhi, he is called a 'Bodhisatta', meaning one who is attached to Bodhi. The Omniscience which is the proximate cause of the Knowledge of the Path, and the Knowledge of the Path which is the proximate cause of Omniscience, are both called 'Bodhi'.

By the words 'mindful and clearly comprehending', it is shown that he descended by the fourth type of descent into the womb. There are four types of descent into the womb: in this world, some are unaware in all three stages—at the time of entering the mother's womb, while staying there, and at the time of leaving; some are aware in the first stage but not in the others; some are aware in the first and second stages but not in the third; and some are aware in all three stages. Among these, the first type refers to ordinary worldly people; the second to the eighty Great Disciples; the third to the two Chief Disciples and Paccekabuddhas. It is said that those in the third category, being pushed by the karma-produced winds with feet upwards and head downwards, like being thrown into a pit hundreds of man-lengths deep, and emerging through the narrow birth canal like an elephant through a keyhole, experience great suffering; therefore, they lack the clear comprehension that 'we are emerging'.

The fourth type refers to the Omniscient Bodhisattas. They are aware while taking conception, while staying in the womb, and at the time of birth. The karma-produced winds cannot turn the Bodhisattas upside down; they are born standing, with two hands extended and eyes open.

'Distinguishing by knowledge' means knowing by distinguishing with the five great observations in the preceding stage, with the knowledge of death (cuti) distinguishing 'now I shall pass away', and in the subsequent stage, with the knowledge of conception (paṭisandhi) distinguishing 'I have now taken conception in this womb'.

Although the five great sacrifices and the conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātatthacariyā) etc., are included within the Perfections (pāramī), they are mentioned separately to show them as special accumulations of requisites. Among them, the sacrifice of limbs, the sacrifice of eyes, the sacrifice of self, the sacrifice of the kingdom, and the sacrifice of wife and children—these five are called the Mahāpariccāga (Five Great Sacrifices). They are, in truth, the Perfection of Giving (dāna-pāramī).
20:
These are the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga). Among them, although the sacrifice of limbs and so forth are indeed only the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī), they are taken separately as great sacrifices to show the special nature of the sacrifice and to show how extremely difficult they are to perform. For that very reason, the sacrifice of eyes is taken separately from the sacrifice of limbs, and although the nature of sacrifice is the same, the sacrifice of the kingdom and the sacrifice of wife and children are also taken separately.

Conduct for the benefit of relatives is called ñātatthacariyā, and that conduct occurs by the power of compassion (karuṇā). Likewise, conduct for the welfare of the world of beings by way of their benefit in the present life, the future life, and the ultimate benefit (nibbāna) is called lokatthacariyā. The range of knowledge through mindfulness in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth, for oneself and others, by way of the knowledge of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-ñāṇa), by way of blameless occupations, crafts, and branches of knowledge, by way of the aggregates (khandha) and sense-bases (āyatana), and by way of investigating the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), is called buddhacariyā. Although this buddhacariyā is essentially the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī), it is taken separately to show the special accumulation of knowledge. By the plural expression 'buddhacariyānaṃ', it should be understood that the prior application (pubbayoga), prior conduct (pubbacariya), and the preaching of the Dhamma (dhammakkhāna) etc., are included.

Among those, pubbayoga is the accomplishment of higher knowledges (abhiññā) and attainments (samāpatti) along with the preliminary practice known as the duty of going and returning for alms. The practice of exceeding effort in giving and so forth is called pubbacariya. Some teachers say: 'The resolve (abhinīhāra) included in the Cariyāpiṭaka is pubbayoga; solitary practice by way of physical seclusion and so forth is pubbacariya.' Preaching that occurs by way of explaining the disadvantages and advantages of saṃsāra and nibbāna regarding giving etc., and fewness of wishes etc., and by way of establishing and maturing beings in the three types of Bodhi, is called dhammakkhāna (preaching of the Dhamma).

'Having reached the pinnacle' means having reached the furthest limit, the highest excellence. 'The seven great gifts' refers to: the gift given at the age of eight after generating the intention, 'I would give even my heart-flesh and so forth to beggars'; the gift of the auspicious elephant; the great gift of seven-hundreds given at the time of departure; the gift of horses, the gift of a chariot, the gift of a son, and the gift of a wife given while traveling on the road—having given these seven great gifts.

'Death by resolution' (adhimutti-kālakiriyā) is the act of dying after firmly resolving, 'Let my death occur right now'; this occurs only to Bodhisattas and not to others. It is said that when Bodhisattas are in long-lived celestial realms, they think, 'Staying here, the accumulation of the requisites of Bodhi is not possible for me,' and thus they become weary of living there. At that time, they enter their celestial mansion, close their eyes, and resolve, 'From this point on, let my life not continue,' and they sit down; immediately after the mental resolution, death occurs.
21:
The wishes of Bodhisattvas are fulfilled because their mental continuums are distinguished by higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti) in various existences for the sake of reaching the culmination of the perfections (pāramī), because of the thinning of the moisture of self-affection (taṇhā), because of the vastness of their great compassion (mahākaruṇā) toward beings, and because of the sharpness and purity of their resolution. Just as these Bodhisattvas have mastery over their minds, they also have mastery over their bodily and verbal actions. Therefore, they pass away and take rebirth in whatever realm where the perfections can be fully cultivated, according to the method mentioned. Thus, our Great Being, having undiminished jhāna in various births even in this Bhadda-kappa, was reborn in the Brahma world after passing away; after staying there for a short time, he passed away from there and was reborn in the human world, striving in the accumulation of the perfections. Therefore, it is said, "Only to Bodhisattvas, not to others." By the phrase "because of being completely fulfilled... in a single existence," it shows that there was no such thing as adhimutti-kālakiriyā (death by resolution) while staying in the Tusita heaven, as there was no purpose for it. Alternatively, it should be understood that staying for the full lifespan in the Tusita heaven is due to the power of the accumulated merit that was exerted, thinking, "After this final birth, there is no more experiencing of divine bliss for the Great Being," just as great prosperity similar to divine bliss arises preceded by the appearance of many great treasure pots in the final birth, and just as the arising of unique gains through incomparable giving occurs when becoming a Buddha. This is the natural law (dhammatā) in this matter.

Passing away will occur within seven days by human reckoning, not by divine reckoning. "Pubbanimittāni" refers to the portents of passing away. In the word "amilāyitvā" (without withering), by mentioning the withering of flowers, it should be understood that the non-destruction of the color, scent, and beauty of those divine flowers is shown. Because there is no smearing of external or internal dust or dirt, the clothes on the bodies of deities remain pure and radiant at all times; thus it is said, "The same method applies to clothes." "Neither too cold nor too hot" means it is not the kind of heat that causes sweating when one resorts to it excessively to counteract cold, nor is it the kind of heat that is naturally intense and overcomes the body to produce sweat. "At that time" means at the aforementioned time near death. "Drop by drop" means sweat flows out in drops like pearls falling from a broken string of pearls. The breaking of teeth is called "khaṇḍicca." The graying of hair is called "pālicca." By the word "etc.," it includes the wrinkling of the skin. The body takes on a weary appearance, but...
22:
"Khaṇḍicca-pālicca-ādi" (broken teeth, gray hair, etc.) is the meaning. "Ukkaṇṭhita" means dissatisfaction. That dissatisfaction does not exist [normally] because of the presence of various grand and subtle pleasures that are difficult to discern. "Nissasanti" means they breathe heavily with physical and mental distress. "Vijambhanti" means they stretch their limbs due to dissatisfaction.

"Paṇḍitā eva" means only the wise deities. Just as newly born deities reflect, "By what kind of meritorious deed was I reborn here?" and know, "I was reborn here by such and such a meritorious deed," similarly, those of great merit know the deeds they performed in past lives or certain deeds performed at other times; thus it is said, "Those of great merit," etc.

Because it is a very long time exceeding a hundred thousand years, old age and death are not apparent. "Aniyyānikaṃ" means it is not conducive to leading out [from suffering] because it is not a basis for the noble practice for beings. Beings cannot have extremely long lives because of the abundance of unwholesome actions; thus it is said, "At that time, beings have abundant defilements."

Here, it may be asked: "Why do Fully Enlightened Buddhas arise only in the human world and not in the deva or brahma worlds?" Firstly, they do not arise in the deva world because there is no opportunity for the living of the holy life (brahmacariya), and likewise, because there is no sense of the marvelous. Although the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess marvelous qualities, those marvelous qualities of theirs are not as apparent when they are in a divine state as they are when they are human. For, the world would regard the Buddha-power seen in a Fully Enlightened Buddha who is a deity as divine power, not as Buddha-power. In that case, they would not firmly resolve upon or gain confidence in the "Fully Enlightened Buddha," nor would they abandon the grasp of "creation by a lord" (issara-kutta). And because the divine state lasts for a long time, they would not be liberated from the view of eternalism (sassata-vāda) that "some things are permanent."

The same method applies to why they do not arise in the brahma world. For the purpose of liberating beings from such views, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, arise only in the human happy destination (sugati), not in the divine happy destination. Even when arising in the human world, they are not of spontaneous birth (opapātika). This is because if there were spontaneous birth, the aforementioned faults could not be avoided, and because it is desirable to establish bodily relics for those to be guided by relics (dhātu-veneiyya), just as the teaching is established for those to be guided by the Dhamma (dhamma-veneiyya). For, after the parinibbāna of those of spontaneous birth, no bodily relics remain.

Even the Great Bodhisattvas who arise in the human world, in their final birth, remain in the midst of the household life until they see the face of a son, even taking a spouse, in order to make their human state evident. Although they possess perfections such as virtue, renunciation (nekkhamma), and wisdom that have reached maturity, they do not yet go forth into homelessness.
23:
By reflecting on these causes and effects, he perceived: "It is the constant tradition and practice of all Buddhas to attain full enlightenment only as human beings, and not as deities." This is the natural order (dhammatā) in this matter. Indeed, the Great Aspiration (mahābhinīhara) for the sake of Buddhahood is fulfilled only in human beings, and not in deities.

Why do the Perfectly Enlightened Ones arise only in Jambudīpa and not in other continents? Some teachers say: "Because the Bodhimaṇḍa (the Seat of Enlightenment), which is the navel of the earth, endowed with the power of the Buddhas, and is an immovable and firm place, exists only in Jambudīpa; therefore, they arise only in Jambudīpa." Likewise, they say: "Because other indispensable places are also found only in Jambudīpa." In this matter, our view is as follows: Because the arising of previous Buddhas, Great Bodhisattas, and Paccekabuddhas, as well as the aspiration for the enlightenment of disciples (sāvaka-bodhi), the accumulation of the perfections of disciples (sāvaka-pāramī), and their maturation, can only be accomplished in Jambudīpa within this world system (cakkavāḷa), which is the field of the Buddha, and not elsewhere. Since the arising of a Buddha is for the purpose of taming those who are trainable (veneyya), Buddhas arise only in this Jambudīpa out of consideration for special trainable persons such as the Chief Disciples and Great Disciples, and not in other continents. This method is also the constant tradition and practice of all Buddhas. It should be understood that the arising of those Supreme Persons only in Jambudīpa continues successively, like the wheels of success (sampatti-cakka), through mutual strong dependence (upanissaya). For this very reason, taking this world system as the center, it is shown that only this world system along with ten thousand world systems is the field of the Buddha's arising. This is because no other place for the arising of Buddhas is found in the Word of the Buddha within the Tipiṭaka. Therefore, it was said: "He saw the continent, thinking, 'Buddhas do not arise in the three other continents; they arise only in Jambudīpa.'" In this same manner, the reason should also be extracted and stated regarding the fixed law of regions (desa-niyāma).

Now, he chose the Khattiya (warrior-noble) caste because it was then esteemed as the highest in the world and was worthy of honor even by the Brahmins. He inspected the family, thinking, "The King shall be my father," because the family must be designated by the power of the father.

He saw "seven days beyond ten months." By seeing this, he knew that there would be no danger to his own conception and that his mother would enjoy divine bliss in the Tusita heaven.

"Those deities" refers to the deities of the ten thousand world systems. How did those deities know at that time the state of the Bodhisatta's fulfilled perfections and how he would become a Buddha?
24:
They knew through the power of the deities of great authority (mahesakkha), and because most of those deities were destined to realize the Four Noble Truths. Indeed, during the distribution of the gift of Dhamma by the Blessed One, the assembly of deities from the ten thousand world systems occurred many times.

"I shall pass away"—he knows this because the proximity of death (cuti) is recognized by the javana consciousnesses associated with knowledge that occur near death. He does not know the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) itself, because the moment of death-consciousness is extremely brief. Indeed, it is beyond the scope even of the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings (cutūpapāta-ñāṇa). The same method applies to the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta). The "process of advertence" (āvajjana-pariyāya) refers to the sequence of advertence. Because it is impossible to determine an object by merely advertencing once, one determines it only after advertencing to that same object a second and third time. Here, the javana process is included under the heading of advertence. Therefore, it was said: "He will know only in the second or third thought-process." Because he knows "My death is near" starting from a few thought-processes prior to death, it is said: "Even at the moment of death, he knows 'I am passing away'." However, he does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness because there is no prior state to it. Only after the arising of attachment to existence (bhavanikanti-lobha) does he know: "I have taken rebirth in such and such a place." "At that time" means at the time of taking rebirth-linking. The reason for the shaking of the ten thousand world systems has already been stated below in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta. What should be said regarding the meaning will appear later in the commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta.

The Great Compassionate Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are mostly associated with joy (somanassa) because they are intent on providing for the welfare and happiness of beings. Therefore, the Commentary states that they take rebirth-linking with the first great resultant consciousness (paṭhama-mahāvipāka-citta). However, the Elder Mahāsīva said that although the Great Compassionate Buddhas are intent on providing for the welfare and happiness of beings, they take rebirth-linking with the fifth great resultant consciousness (pañcama-mahāvipāka-citta) because they have a strong inclination for seclusion, tend toward the unconditioned (Nibbāna), and are mostly equanimous toward all conditioned things.

"Starting from the seventh day before the full moon" means starting from the seventh day before the full moon day, which is the 9th day of the waxing moon. "On the seventh day" means on the seventh day from the 9th, which is the full moon day of Āsāḷha. "This dream" refers to the dream of the nature that will now be described. In the Majjhima Commentary, however, it says: "The four Great Kings took the Queen to Lake Anotatta and stood to one side. Then their queens came and, for the purpose of removing human impurities..."
25: In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, it is said, 'they caused to bathe.' In that context, 'their goddesses' refers to the goddesses of the Great Kings. 'Wandering' means wandering in the feeding grounds. 'Smeared with green cow dung' means on a smooth ground prepared with green cow dung. 'That conception is only a male conception, not a female; a noble son will be born to you'—the Brahmins reported only this much according to their dream-interpretation manuals. However, the matter starting with 'If he leads a household life...' was reported truthfully because they were possessed and controlled by deities. In the term 'dhammatā', the word 'dhamma' is a synonym for 'prakati' (nature), as in the Pali passages such as 'Monks, for beings who have the nature of being born...' Just as 'deva' is called 'devatā', 'dhamma' itself is called 'dhammatā'; thus it is said, 'this is the nature (sabhāva).' It means this is the natural state. Since that nature is a fixed state in its essence, it is said, 'this means it is a niyāma (fixed law).' Since there are many types of niyāma, in order to extract them all by the method of defining meanings and show only the niyāma intended here, it is said, 'what is called niyāma...' and so on. Among those, the fixed nature of kammas is called Kamma-niyāma. This same method should be understood for the three types of niyāma such as Utu-niyāma. The remaining fact of dhamma itself being a niyāma is called Dhamma-niyāma or Dhammatā. (It is the fruition) of wholesome kamma. It is clear like making a blade sharp while whetting. Because of seeing the distinction of seasons according to the distinction of regions such as parched ground, the taking of flowers and fruits of trees etc. which are produced by the distinction of seasons is specifically stated as 'in various regions.' 'In various times' means in various times such as the spring. It should be construed as 'from sweet seeds' and 'from bitter seeds.' Because it is appropriate to speak of what is near the present as if it were the present, it is said 'is descending'; therefore it is said, 'this is the very meaning: has descended.' 'It happens thus' means that the Bodhisatta's clear comprehension occurs in the manner stated. It is not (comprehension) at the very moment of descending because the moment of rebirth-linking consciousness is difficult to perceive. Therefore, it is also said, 'he does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness.' It is immeasurable because of spreading through ten thousand world systems. It is magnificent because of its extreme brilliance. 'The majesty of the devas' means the power of the devas' radiance. Indeed, that light [surpasses] the radiance of the devas...
26: The light surpasses (the radiance of the devas), but it does not surpass their authority. Therefore, it is said, 'of one clothed in a garment,' and so on. The gap or opening between the worlds or world-elements is called 'Lokantara'; that same term is expressed in the feminine gender as 'Lokantarikā.' They are called 'aghā' (unbounded) because they are not obstructed by anything such as trees or bushes. Therefore, it is said, 'always open.' They are called 'asaṃvutā' (uncovered) because they are not covered by anything below or above. Thus it is said, 'even below, there is no support.' In that context, by the word 'pi' (even/also), it is shown that just as the Lokantarika hell is uncovered because there is no earth below to block the water, so too it is uncovered and without support above because there are no celestial mansions as there are in the world systems. They are called 'andhakārā' (dark) because there is darkness in that place. Eye-consciousness does not arise because of the absence of light, not because of the absence of the eye-organ. For it is said, 'by that light, they recognize one another.' Just as at the time of midday in Jambudīpa, half of the sun's disk is perceived by the inhabitants of Pubbavideha as sunset and by the inhabitants of Aparagoyāna as sunrise, so too it is in the other continents; thus it is said, 'they appear in three continents at the same time.' At other times, they appear in only two continents at the same time. The dispelling of darkness for nine hundred thousand yojanas in each direction should also be understood by this same method. 'They are unable to shine with their own light' means they are not able to illuminate with their own radiance. Because of moving in the sky which is the size of Mount Yugandhara, it is said, 'they move in the middle of the world-system mountains.' 'Vāvaṭā' means they are exerting themselves to catch and eat. 'Viparivattitvā' means having turned around many times. 'Chijjitvā' means either falling from the place where they were staying due to fainting, or falling after being severed by the cutting of limbs. In the phrase 'in extremely caustic water' (accantakhāre), it might be said to mean 'extremely cold' because of the absence of the sun's heat. For that water which supports the world cannot be caustic like the water that destroys the world, which is produced by the great clouds at the end of an aeon. If it were so, even the earth would dissolve. Alternatively, due to the power of the evil kamma of those beings, just as water becomes like saliva and pus for petas, that water at that time becomes caustic; thus it is said, 'in extremely caustic water.' 'Even for the duration of drinking one ladle of rice gruel' means the time taken to take rice gruel from a vessel like an alms-bowl with a ladle and drink it. 'From all sides' means shaking in six ways from all directions.
27:
"By the power of the Four Great Kings" means by way of the status of the Four Great Kings, such as Vessavaṇa and the others. "Yathāvihāraṃ" means returning to their respective abodes. "Pakatiyā" means by her own natural disposition. Therefore, it is said, "by nature alone." Without receiving the precepts from others, they are endowed with virtue (sīla) by undertaking it themselves through their own nature. Our Bodhisatta's mother was also endowed with virtue in this way. Although she used to receive the precepts from the ascetic Kāla Devala on other occasions, when the Bodhisatta was conceived, she undertook the precepts by herself. Similarly, it means that the mother of the Bodhisatta Vipassī also took the precepts by herself.

This statement "manussesu" (among humans) is spoken by way of natural conduct. It is natural for human women to have lustful thoughts towards human men. However, in the Bodhisatta's mother, such a mind does not arise even towards devas. Just as lustful thoughts towards men do not arise in the Bodhisatta's mother due to the Bodhisatta's majesty, so too, by that same majesty, no man is able to overcome or violate her. To show this meaning, it is said, "their feet cannot move, as if bound by divine shackles."

Previously (in verse 21), it was stated that "a mind associated with sensual pleasure does not arise," and later it is said that "she enjoys herself, being provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure." One might ask how these two statements are not contradictory. Therefore, the passage beginning with "pubbe" is stated. "Vatthupaṭikkhepa" means the rejection of the mind associated with sensual pleasure (purisādhippāyacitta), which is the basis for unholy conduct. Therefore, it is said, "by way of lustful thoughts towards men." "Ārammaṇapaṭilābha" refers only to the acquisition of the five cords of sensual pleasure, such as visual objects and so on.

"Kilamatha" means weariness or fatigue. At that time, the mother's body does not experience heaviness, stiffness, or the like. The Blessed One taught, "She sees the Bodhisatta who has entered her womb." One might ask from what time she begins to see him; therefore, it is explained as "after passing the stage of the clear embryo (kalala), etc." The commentator himself explains the purpose of seeing. Since that purpose is not present during the stage of the clear embryo and so on, she does not see him then. (She sees him) just like a young, tender son lying on his back. The words beginning with "yaṃ taṃ mātu" are spoken by way of natural conduct. This is because the Bodhisatta's womb receives special care, even more distinguished than that of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), due to the extraordinary accumulation of merit. Therefore, the Bodhisatta's mother, having very suitable food and behavior, looks after the womb with great care. "Sukhavāsatthaṃ" means for the sake of the Bodhisatta's comfortable dwelling. "Puratthābhimukho" means (he sits) facing the front (of the mother).
28:
(The mother sits) facing the front direction of the mother. Now, to show the internal and external reasons regarding the visibility of the one who has reached the inside of the womb, the passage beginning with "*Pubbe katakamma*" is stated. "*Assā*" means of the queen (the mother). "*Vatthu*" refers to the womb. Because the skin of the Bodhisatta's mother's womb is very thin, like crystal or a film of clouds, there is no obstruction to the light; thus, just as the mother sees the Bodhisatta in the womb, one might ask if the Bodhisatta also sees the mother or other visible forms standing in front. To answer this, the passage beginning with "*Bodhisatto pana*" is stated. Why does he not see despite having eyes and light? It is said, "Because eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) does not arise inside the womb." Just as inhalation and exhalation do not occur there, eye-consciousness also does not arise, because there is no appropriate attention (*samannāhāra*) for the arising of that eye-consciousness.

While other women might die being overcome by such diseases due to childbirth, in the case of the Bodhisatta's mother, no disease caused by childbirth arises while the Bodhisatta is in the womb; she passes away solely due to the exhaustion of her life-span (*āyuparikkhaya*). This meaning has already been stated below. The passage beginning with "*Bodhisattena vasitaဋ္ဌာနံ*" is the statement of the reason for that passing away. "Others should not use it" means it is not to be used by others, or it is not suitable for use.
