If that is the case, the Bodhisatta's father should have another chief queen, but since it is not appropriate for another to be the chief queen while the mother is still alive, the passage beginning with "*Na ca sakkā*" is stated. "*Apanetvā*" means having removed her from the position of chief queen. Seeking external objects occurs only through the power of desire and lust (*chandarāga*) for oneself. To show that strong lust for one's own body is the powerful cause of beings' lust for other objects, it is said, "In beings, desire and lust for their own individual existence (*attabhāva*) is strong." "Cannot protect" means not properly maintaining the pregnancy. Therefore, the fetus often suffers from many ailments. "*Vatthu visadaṃ hoti*" means the womb is exceptionally pure and clear. The descent of the Bodhisatta into the womb during the third part of the mother's middle age is also included by observing the limit of her life-span, because it avoids the physical changes that occur according to age. The physical changes that occur according to the nature of women are also calmed by the majesty of the Bodhisatta.

"Seven-month-born" (*sattamāsajāta*) refers to one born in the seventh month after conception. Such a person cannot endure cold or heat because of being extremely delicate.
29:
A child born at eight months, although more developed in limbs than one born at seven months, has certain parts of the skin that cannot expand with growth and thus cannot withstand the impact; therefore, an eight-month-old child does not survive. Regarding a seven-month-old child, they say that the body is not yet large enough to suffer such impact.

With a sense of deep respect and honor, thinking, "We ourselves shall first receive the Great Being (Mahāpurisa), the Refuge of the World," the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, who have exhausted all taints (khīṇāsava), first receive him, expressing their own joy. "Sūtivesaṃ" means in the guise of nurses attending the birth. "Eke" refers to the residents of the Abhayagiri Monastery. They receive him with a cloth (white robe) having a color like a fish's eye. (The mother) remained standing; she did not sit or lie down. Therefore, it is said, "The mother of the Bodhisatta gives birth to the Bodhisatta while standing." Because she is free from pain, she gives birth while standing. Other women, however, because of the intensity of the pain, cannot endure it and give birth either sitting or lying down.

"Ajinappaveṇiyā" means a rug (or pouch) sewn from skins. "Mahātejo" means having great power and majesty. "Mahāyaso" means having a large retinue and widespread fame.

"Bhaggavibhaggā" means as if broken and fragmented due to emerging from a narrow place; by this word, the impurity (of others) is shown. "Alaggo hutvā" means emerging without sticking to any part of the womb or the birth canal; thus it is said, "like water coming out of a water-strainer." "Udakena" refers to the fluid in the womb. (The Bodhisatta) emerges without being smeared by such fluid or phlegm, because such fluid and phlegm do not exist there. Due to the power of the Bodhisatta's merit, from the moment of conception, that place is purer than before, and especially like a fragrant chamber (Gandhakuṭī), it remains filled with the scent of sandalwood. "Udakavaṭṭiyo" means masses of water (streams of water).

"Muhuttajāto" means the Bodhisatta who is only a moment old after birth. "Anudhāriyamāne" means while being carried appropriately. "Āgatāneva" means they have arrived at that place (where the seven steps are taken). "Anekasākhaṃ" means a parasol with hundreds of ribs (branches) made of jewels. "Sahassamaṇဍalaṃ" means the parasol situated above that, having thousands of circular parts. "Marū" refers to the devas and brahmas. However, it should not be understood that he looks after taking the seven steps, because even before the stepping...
31:
## 
“The ten-thousandfold world system trembles”—this sentence, although it appears in this Pāḷi text, is stated to show the fundamental cause of the wonders that will be described later. Other sentences of this nature should be understood in the same way. “Lutes bound with strings, drums bound with skin”—this phrase is merely an illustration of the fivefold musical instruments. Alternatively, the word “ca” (and) should be understood to include other types of musical instruments.

“Some teachers say: ‘Shackles, fetters, and other bonds were broken at the very moment of the Bodhisatta’s birth, and then became as they were before. Likewise, the sense-bases such as the eyes and ears of those born blind or deaf were produced at that very moment due to the kamma that causes such seeing and hearing, and then vanished at that same moment.’” “Chijjiṃsu” means they were broken at the places where they were bound to the feet. “Vigacchiṃsu” means they subsided. “Treasures situated in the sky” refers to gems and such located in various celestial mansions (vimāna). “Shining with their own power” means they were illuminated by their own extremely brilliant radiance. “Did not proceed” means there was no flow (of rivers). “Did not blow” means the harsh wind did not blow. Instead, a gentle, pleasant breeze that brings happiness to beings blew. Birds, unable to remain in the high sky, reached the ground. “Endowed with the season” means endowed with weather characterized by being neither too hot nor too cold.

The sound produced by striking the arms and palms is called “apphoṭana.” In terms of meaning, it is the act of making a sound by placing the left hand on the chest and striking the arm with the right palm. Making a sound with the mouth is called “usseḷana.” Releasing a sound is “seḷana” (whistling). There was a continuous mass of banner-like flowers because the beautiful banner-like flowers were joined together without interruption throughout the ten-thousandfold world system. Not only did these wonders occur, but others did as well: “A rain of exquisite and fragrant flowers fell; stars shone even while the sun was visible; clear, transparent water gushed from the earth; burrowing animals came out of their holes; lust, hatred, and delusion became thin; dust on the earth subsided; unpleasant odors vanished and divine scents blew; deities with form appeared to the eyes of humans in their own forms; and the passing away and rebirth of beings did not occur.” These and other such thirty-two precursors that appeared at the time of the Great Resolve (Mahābhinīhāra) all occurred without exception at the time of the Bodhisatta’s birth.

“Tatrāpi” means that in those events such as the earthquake, the nature of being a precursor should be understood in this way. The meaning is that it is not only a precursor for the standing and so forth of the newborn Bodhisatta. The earthquake is a precursor to the attainment of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), because it shakes all that is to be known and the views of the founders of other sects. The gathering of deities in this single universe without being urged by anyone is a precursor to the gathering of beings to hear the Dhamma without being urged at the time of receiving the Dhamma (the first sermon). The initial reception by the deities is a precursor to the attainment of the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra). The subsequent reception by humans is a precursor to standing [firmly] in that very place...
32:
The state of being motionless is the precursor (pubbanimitta) for the attainment of the imperturbable dwelling (āneñjavihāra, i.e., the immaterial jhānas). The spontaneous sounding of lutes without human instruction is the precursor for the attainment of the nine successive dwellings (anupubbavihāra). The sounding of great drums is the precursor for the proclamation of the Dhamma drum and the sounding of the drum of the Deathless (amatadundubhi), which are capable of informing the assembly as far as the limits of the world-system. The cutting of shackles and bonds is the precursor for the breaking of the bond of conceit (māna). The recovery of the great multitude from diseases is the precursor for the realization of the Four Noble Truths, which is the recovery from the disease of all the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭadukkha).

The phrase 'of the great multitude' should be applied and connected to various contexts such as 'the great multitude's attainment of the divine eye' and 'the great multitude's attainment of the divine ear element.' Intending to show the accomplishment of the excellence of the speed of transcendent knowledge through the development of the bases of power (iddhipāda), it is said: 'The attainment of speed by the lame is the precursor for the attainment of the four bases of power.' Reaching the port safely is the precursor for the attainment of the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), because of the ability to correctly understand the meanings and so forth in accordance with their nature. The shining of jewels with their own radiance is the precursor for the world being illuminated by the light of the Dhamma, as it will manifest that light.

The precursor for the attainment of the four divine abidings (brahmavihāra) by the great multitude is because those divine abidings completely appease all enmity. The extinguishing of the eleven fires is the precursor for Nibbāna, which is the extinguishing of fires that are otherwise difficult to quench. The vision of the light of knowledge is the precursor for seeing light in a place where there was no light. 'By the taste of Nibbāna' means by the function of the quenching of defilements. 'Having a single taste' means that the Dispensation (sāsana) has a single taste in all respects; this is achieved by making the world, which is not sweet, entirely sweet. The precursor for the breaking of the sixty-two types of wrong views is the removal of the wind of all wrong views. The birds descending to the earth, abandoning unstable and uneven places like the sky, is the precursor for beings abandoning such wrong views and taking refuge in the Triple Gem with their very lives.

'Being beloved by the great multitude' is the precursor for being cherished by the people like the moon. The sun having a season of pleasant temperature, free from heat and cold, is the precursor for reaching physical and mental bliss free from distress. The deities' rejoicing through clapping and other forms of play is the precursor for the manifestation of joy through inspired utterances (udāna), due to reaching the end of existence (Nibbāna) and understanding the nature of the Dhamma. 'Raining with the force of the Dhamma' is the precursor for the raining of the nectar of the Dhamma through the force of the knowledge of the teaching. The experience of the bliss of the path and fruit, produced by taking the jhānas obtained through mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) as a basis, is the attainment of the Deathless through mindfulness of the body. Furthermore, because that body brings about an insatiable bliss, the absence of oppression by hunger and thirst is the precursor.
33:
It has been said. In the Commentary, however, the precursor is stated by distinguishing between hunger and thirst. In that explanation, the distinction of the precursors should be understood through the division of the specific and the general (visesa-sāmañña), and by the logic of the 'ox and the bull' (gobalīvadda-naya). The word 'spontaneously' (sayam eva) should also be brought forward and connected to the phrase 'the opening of the door to the Eightfold Path,' as in 'spontaneously is the precursor for the manifestation of the path factors.' 'The state of being full' (bharitabhāva) means the state of being complete. Some teachers say that 'adorned with the garland of noble banners' means having a garland of banners in the form of saffron robes; however, it is truly the precursor for the world with its devas being adorned with the garlands of the banners of the Noble Path and the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). The commentary that is not explicitly extracted here is easily understood.

'Here' (ettha) refers to this section beginning with 'just born' (sampatijāta). Since it has already been answered, it means there is nothing new for us to add here. At that time, although the Great Being (Mahāsatta) was walking on the ground, he appeared to the great multitude as if he were traveling through the sky. This is the fixed natural law (dhamma-niyāma), the nature of Bodhisattas; this statement is made according to the doctrine of natural necessity (niyati-vāda). Because such meritorious actions and accumulations of merit were performed and gathered in previous births, he appeared thus to the great multitude; this statement is made according to the doctrine of past actions (pubbekata-kamma-vāda). Because it has the nature of presiding over these beings, one's own karma is called 'Issara' (the Lord/Controller). The 'creation' by that karma is the production of its own fruit. The Great Man (Mahāpurisa) was also produced by a noble meritorious karma capable of overcoming the world with its devas; thus, he is said to be 'created by the Lord' (karma). This excellence of creation is his great majesty, by which he appeared thus to the great multitude; this statement is made according to the doctrine of creation by a Lord (issara-nimmāna-vāda, here referring to karma).

Having spoken thus in various ways, the teacher finally answered directly, asking, 'What is the use of these figurative explanations?' How can one just born walk on the ground with his feet? By way of imagination, thinking 'one with such great majesty must be traveling through the sky,' it was as if he were traveling through the sky. Furthermore, because he moved very quickly, traversing seven steps, although he was visible, he appeared to the great multitude as if he were invisible. Since being naked and having a small body would be unsuitable for such a posture, it should be understood that through the miracle produced by the power of his karma, he appeared to the great multitude as if he were adorned and prepared, and as if he were sixteen years of age. This was merely an appearance at that time due to the power of the Great Being's merit. Later, he was just a young child and not like that (sixteen years old). Because the majesty of the Bodhisatta, which is suitable for the state of Buddhahood, was declared as it truly is, the assembly was delighted by his explanation, as if it were spoken by a Buddha... and so forth.
34:
Sabba-dhammatā means that all sixteen kinds of natural laws (dhammatā) mentioned above should be understood as occurring to all Bodhisattas. This is because these Bodhisattas are identical in terms of the manifestation of their accumulation of merit and knowledge (puñña-ñāṇa-sambhāra).

## Description of the Thirty-Two Marks of a Great Man

Dukūla-cumbaṭake refers to [placing the child] on a soft fine-cloth cushion folded many times, suitable for an infant's sleep. Khattiya, Brāhmaṇa, etc., are called caste (jāti). Koṇḍañña, Gotama, etc., are called clan (gotta). Poṇika, Cikkhallika, Sākiya, Koḷiya, etc., are called lineage (kulapadesa). By the word ādi (etc.), all forms of success (sampatti) such as physical appearance, sovereignty, and retinue are included. Mahantassa means extensive and grand (vipula, uḷāra). Nipphattiyo means accomplishments (siddhi). In the phrase gantabba-gatiyā, the word gati is said to express the sense of kamma-sādhana (the object of the action). This is because it is called gati (a specific state of rebirth/upapatti-bhava) as it is the destination reached by beings through well-performed good conduct (sucarita) or ill-performed bad conduct (duccarita). It is also called gati (inclination/ajjhāsaya) because it proceeds according to one's desire.

Paṭisaraṇe means a refuge or reliance (parāyaṇa, avassaya). For an Arahant who is disconnected from all conditioned things (saṅkhata), Nibbāna alone is that refuge. Tyāhaṃ is simply the word analysis of te ahaṃ (I to you).

He is called Dhammika (Righteous) because he is endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action and the blameless royal virtues. He is called Dhamma-rājā (Righteous King) because he gladdens the entire world with that Dhamma. Since a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch) attains kingship through Dhamma and the right method, and not through unrighteousness, it is said: "Dhammena laddha-rajjattā dhamma-rājā" (A righteous king because he obtained kingship through Dhamma). To show that he is the lord of the earth in various great islands called Caturanta (Four-ended) because they are bounded by the ocean in the four directions, it is stated: "Puratthima... pe... issaro" (Lord of the East... etc.). Vijitāvī means one who has conquered what was to be conquered. It means one who remains after conquering the internal enemies such as lust (kāma) and anger (kodha), as well as the external enemies who are rival kings. Although a Cakkavatti king never actually has to fight any enemy, he is called Vijita-saṅgāma (Conqueror of Battles) because of the accomplishment of victory that would otherwise be achieved through battle.

He is called Janapadatthāvariyappatta because, under this king who is endowed with the four wonderful qualities etc., the country (janapada) itself reaches a state of stability that cannot be shaken by any enemy, or a state of being firmly conquered and possessed. Alternatively, he is called Janapadatthāvariyappatta because he reaches a state of stability in the country through his own righteous practice. Those who act violently toward others, such as by placing a weapon at people's chests and taking desired wealth, are called Sāhasika (violent ones).

Ratijananatthena means [it is called a jewel, ratana] because it produces an insatiable joy and happiness (pīti-somanassa). According to the literal meaning of the word, it is called ratana because it causes delight. It is called cittīkata because it is worthy of being cherished in the mind, as in "Oh, how captivating!" Such cherishing in the heart...
35:
*Cittīkata* means the sense of being worthy of honor. Because it is worthy of being esteemed and honored in the heart, it is called *cittīkata*. Because it is of great, extensive, and immeasurable value, it is called *mahaggha*. Because there is no comparison or simile for it, it is called *atula*; it is something without equal. Because it arises only occasionally and is difficult to obtain, it is called *dullabhadassana* (rare to behold). Because it is fit to be enjoyed only by beings of noble and lofty qualities, it is called *anomasattaparibhoga*.

Now, after showing how these meanings such as *cittīkata* exist uniquely in the Wheel-treasure, the author begins with "Cakkaratanassa ca" etc., to point out how these meanings also apply to the other treasures. Because it is the cause for obtaining the fulfillment of sovereignty etc., which does not belong to others, and because it is the cause for beings to obtain their desired benefits, there is no other divine abode besides the Wheel-treasure. Because it is made of the seven treasures that are extremely noble and radiant, and because it possesses wonderful and great power, its value cannot be appraised as being this much or that much. To whatever extent it is precious, to that same extent it is incomparable and peerless.

Just as a clear time, when beings are free from the stains of unwholesome deeds by loathing evil and accumulating merit, is worthy for the arising of a Buddha, so too do Universal Monarchs (*Cakkavatti*) arise only at such a time; thus it is said with "Yasmā ca pana" etc. This statement is made by way of a simile; however, the simile and the thing compared are not entirely identical. Therefore, while Buddhas arise only once in a long while, and Universal Monarchs are not exactly like that, the arising of a Universal Monarch is also difficult because it is hard to fulfill the duties of a Universal Monarch. Because they are similar in this aspect of being rare to arise, it should be understood that Universal Monarchs are also called *dullabhadassana* (rare to behold).

Although the quality achieved through the power of the Wheel-treasure is shared with the retinue of the Universal Monarch, "Tadetaṃ" etc. is said because only the Universal Monarch is worthy of enjoying it as the owner according to his wish. That prosperity arises only for the benefit of the Universal Monarch. Since the aforementioned five (or six) meanings can also be found in the other treasures, it is said "Evaṃ sesānipi." He is endowed with the conquest of unconquered enemies through the Elephant-treasure, Horse-treasure, and the Steward-treasure (*parināyaka-ratana*); with the Wheel-treasure as an accompaniment; and with the remaining treasures as requisites for enjoyment. Alternatively, the Elephant, Horse, Gem, and Woman-treasures are joined as requisites for enjoyment, while the remaining Treasurer and Steward-treasures are joined as accompaniments.

"Catuṇṇam mahādīpānaṃ sirivibhavaṃ" means the attainment of glory and the fulfillment of wealth obtained in the four great continents. "Tādisameva" means having the same power as previously mentioned. By pervading an area of one league (*yojana*), it dispels the darkness of one league, and (the Woman-treasure) is free from the six defects such as being too tall.

The word "Surā" means having courage and being without fear, thus it is said "Abhīrukā." "Anga" means a cause. The cause for which one is called "Vīra" (heroic) is called *vīranga*. Therefore, it is said *vīrangaṃ*. Because of the power of the Universal Monarch's Wheel-treasure revolving... etc. By the word "Adandena," it means not killing and not inflicting physical torture. By the word "Asatthena," it means not waging war with an army. Not performing both types of punishment is called *adandena asatthena*. (He conquers) the earth bounded by the ocean. Because of the sense of attachment, it is called *rāga*; because of the sense of thirst, it is called *taṇhā*. Due to the difference in the manner of arising, greed (*lobha*) itself is taught in two ways as *rāga* and *taṇhā*. This statement is indeed true.
36:
“Vīriyassetaṃ nāmaṃ” means it is called vīraṅga because it is a limb of energy (vīriya). The Wheel Treasure of a Universal Monarch has the power to travel as far as the Cakkavāḷa mountains; thus, it is said, “the earth bounded by the Cakkavāḷa mountains and ending at the ocean.” By the word “adaṇḍena,” it means not committing murder or physical torture (punishment). By the word “asatthena,” it means not engaging in warfare with an army. To show both, the phrase beginning with “ye katāparādhe” is spoken. “The earth of such a nature” refers to the earth ending at the ocean.

It is called “rāga” (lust) in the sense of attachment, and “taṇhā” (craving) in the sense of thirsting. Due to the difference in the mode of occurrence, greed (lobha) itself is taught in two ways as lust and craving. This teaching is indeed correct; in both, the sense of “covering” (chadana) is certainly the same. As it was said: “When lust overcomes a man, then there is a mass of darkness (blinding the eye of wisdom),” and “Covered by the veil of craving (beings follow old age and death).” In this same way, the sense of covering in hatred (dosa) and other unwholesome states should be understood. By the word “kilesa” (defilements), the remaining defilements such as doubt (vicikicchā) are meant. Because all those evil unwholesome states, when they arise, cover and entwine the continuity of beings and prevent the arising of wholesome states, they are called “chadanā” or “chada” (coverings). “Vivatta-chada” is a designation made by changing the letter ‘o’ to ‘ā’ (from vivaṭṭacchado).

“Tāsaṃ” refers to the causes of reaching both peaks (becoming a Universal Monarch or a Buddha). “Nimittabhūtāni” means they are the indicating causes (ñāpaka-kāraṇa). Because the state of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa) is marked by these (thirty-two) signs, they are called “lakkhaṇā” (marks). He is called “suppatiṭṭhitapāda” (one with well-placed feet) because his feet are firmly and evenly placed on the ground when standing, walking, etc. To clarify the evenness of his feet through the method of contrast (vyatireka), the words beginning with “yathā” are spoken. In that context, “aggatala” refers to the forepart of the sole. “Paṇhi” refers to the heel. “Passa” refers to each of the two sides of the sole, or both edges.

The words beginning with “assa pana” clarify the meaning through the direct method (anvaya). Like the sole of a golden sandal, when placed down straight, the entire sole touches the ground at the same moment. Similarly, the entire sole rises from the ground at the same moment. Therefore, it is concluded that this Blessed One is “suppatiṭṭhitapāda.” As for the extraordinary results (nissanda-phala) mentioned here, such as the evenness of the ground, they will be made clear later in the commentary on the Lakkhaṇa Sutta.

“Nābi dissati” means the hub (nābhi) of the wheel mark, being circular in shape, is clearly visible and well-defined. “Nābiparicchinnā” refers to the circular lines that stand as boundaries within that hub. “Nābhimukhaparikkhepapaṭṭa” means...
37:
...it has the shape of a circular iron plate to be placed inside the face of the hub as a lining to avoid friction from the axle of an ordinary cart wheel; here, the plate covering that hub-face is intended. “Nemimaṇikā” refers to the jewel-like lines situated in a row on the rim (nemi). “Sambahulavāro” is the section explaining the many various parts and features. “Satti” is the spear weapon. “Sirivaccha” is the auspicious house (shrine of glory). “Nandī” is a golden vessel shaped like a right-turning flower. “Sovattika” is the wheel mark with the three-ringed neck emblem. “Vaṭaṃsaka” is a floral crest or earring worn on the head. “Vaḍḍhamānaka” is the figure of a man carrying a man, found in ancient examples. “Morahatthaka” is a peacock-feather fan or a special fan made by stitching peacock feathers. “Vāḷabီjanī” is a yak-tail whisk. “Siddhattha” and others are full pots and vessels filled with white mustard, sesame, etc. After mentioning “Cakkavāḷa” (the universe), the words “Himavā, Sineru... many thousands” are spoken to show the principal parts of that universe. “Together with the retinue of the Universal Monarch” is to show that the Elephant Treasure and others can also be found in that wheel mark. It should be understood that all the specific features mentioned, such as the spear, are merely the retinue of the wheel mark.

“Āyatapaṇhi” (long heels) is spoken with reference to being longer than the heels of others; it does not mean excessively long, which is why “paripuṇṇapaṇhi” (full heels) is said. To show the perfection of the heel mark through contrast, the words beginning with “yathā hi” are spoken. “Āraggena” means with a rounded chisel-tip. “Vaṭṭetvā” means having made it well-rounded. “Rattakambalageṇḍuka-sadisā” means the heel is like a ball made of red woolen thread.

“Makkaṭasseva” (like a monkey's) is spoken with reference to the length and evenness of the fingers and toes. “Niyyāsatelena” means with oil mixed with resin from trees like the chattirita, which is also called “surabhiniyyāsa” (fragrant resin). The use of resin-oil as a simile here is to show the firm, smooth, and pleasant appearance of a stick of yellow orpiment.

Just as a layer of cotton wool that has been beaten a hundred times becomes extremely soft when dipped in clarified butter, the hands and feet of the Great Man are similarly soft; to show this, the words beginning with “sappimaṇḍe” are spoken. “Talunā” means delicate and tender hands and feet.

“Cammena” means with the skin that wraps and connects the spaces between the fingers. “Paṭibaddha-aṅgulantaro” does not mean that the spaces between the fingers are fused together as one. “Ekappa māṇā” means they are of equal measure in length. “Yavalakkhaṇaṃ” refers to the barley-grain-shaped lines situated on the inner joints of the fingers. “Paṭivijjhitvā” means that because those various finger and toe joints are in the same positions, even when the fingers are extended, they remain touching as if they were piercing through one another.
38:
Ankles are called 'saṅkha'; because the ankles are situated above these feet, they are called 'ussaṅkhapāda' (feet with ankles above). 'Pitti-pāde' means near the back of the foot. With the word 'tena', it should be connected as: 'because of the state of the ankles being situated on the back of the foot, they are bound.' This word 'tena' should also be connected to both the preceding words: 'because they are bound in that way, they cannot turn at will; because they cannot turn at will, the soles of the feet of those who are walking are not visible.' 'Upari' means about two finger-breadths above the back of the foot; some also say four finger-breadths. The ankles are hidden, not appearing prominently like those of others. 'Tena' means because of being established above the ankles. 'Assa' refers to the Great Man (Mahāpurisa). Although there is movement to another place, the navel (nābhi) is taken to show that the upper body remains motionless. The phrase 'only the lower body moves' is the reason for the preceding sentence. Because only the lower body moves, from the navel upwards... it is motionless. The phrase 'the feet turn easily' is the reason for both the preceding and following sentences. Because the feet turn easily, only the lower body moves; because the feet turn easily, they are not invisible to those standing and looking from the front... or from the back.

Just as the calves of the antelope called eṇī have flesh that is even all around and gradually becomes full towards the top, so too are the calves of the Great Man; therefore, he is called 'eṇimigasadisajaṅgha' (one with calves like an antelope). 'Paripuṇṇajaṅgha' means one whose calves are full with the accumulation of flesh all around. Therefore, it is said beginning with 'not from one side' (na ekato) and so on.

'By this' (etena) means showing the comfort of the kneecaps by the words 'without bending' and so on. 'Remaining people' refers to those who lack these marks. Such people are either hunchbacked (khujja) because the upper body is shorter than the lower body, or they are dwarfed (vāmana) because the lower body is shorter than the upper body. By this, it is shown that, excluding the Fully Enlightened Buddha and the Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), other beings fall into the categories of the hunchbacked or the dwarfed.

Indeed, although all lotus pericarps are golden-colored, the pericarp of the golden lotus (kañcanapaduma) is superior to others because of its radiance. Therefore, it is said, 'with those like the pericarp of a golden lotus.' 'Ohita' means well-placed within. Because the male organ thus situated within is covered by a sheath, it is called 'paṭicchanna' (covered).

'Suvaṇṇavaṇṇa' here means one whose body has a color like the color of gold. Therefore, it is said 'jātihingulaka' (cinnabar) and so on. This meaning should be understood by the method of repetition (āvutti) of the word 'vaṇṇa'. Here, the word 'vaṇṇa' is intended as a synonym for the body (sarīra). After explaining the first conceived meaning, the word 'vaṇṇa' is used in the sense of 'body', but considering that it might not be possible to take it that way, the second meaning is stated by taking only the sense of natural color (vaṇṇa). Therefore, by the two words 'suvaṇṇavaṇṇo kañcanasannibhattaco', it means having a skin color like gold that is pure and without impurity. 'Rajo' refers to the collection of subtle dust that is the cause of uncleanness. Therefore, it is said that like water drops on a lotus leaf, the impurity of dust does not stick. If it does not stick, why does he perform acts such as washing hands and bathing? This is answered by the words 'washing hands and so on.' At the end of the whorl that occurs by way of a clockwise rotation, the body of Brahmā in the front...
39:
After explaining the first conceived meaning, considering that the word 'vaṇṇa' is not well-known as a term for the body (ruḷhī), the second meaning is stated by taking the word 'vaṇṇa' in the sense of the color element (vaṇṇadhātu). Therefore, by both words, it means having a skin color like gold that has been very purely refined. 

Dust (raja) means subtle dust. A collection of dust that brings about uncleanness is called grime (jalla). Therefore, it is said 'or grime.' If dust does not stick, why does he perform acts such as washing hands and so on? This is answered by the words 'washing hands and so on.'

'At the end of the whorl' (āvaṭṭapariyosāne) means at the end of the whorl that occurs by way of a clockwise rotation.

Just as the body of Brahmā rises straight upwards without bending to the front or the back, it is said, 'He has a straight body like Brahmā' (brahmaujugatta). This quality of having a straight body is to be seen when the limbs have reached full growth, not in the time of youth; thus it is said, 'He will be one with a tall and straight body.' In others, however, in these two places, 'the neck and the knees,' when they bend, they bend forward; this should be connected and viewed accordingly. 'Crookedness of the sides' (passavaṅka) means being crooked either on the right side or the left side. 'Like a spit' (sūlasadisa) means like the legs of a spit-base used in making clay figures.

Because the seven parts of the body, starting with the backs of the hands, have full and abundant flesh, he is called 'sattussada' (one with seven protuberances). It should be connected as: 'the ends of the bones are not apparent.' The phrase 'covered by a network of veins' is a description of the mark, and by that very phrase, it is already said that 'the ends of the bones are covered by flesh.' In the phrase 'by the backs of the hands and so on,' although the tops of the shoulders and the base of the neck are included by the word 'ādi,' to show them partially, it is said 'rounded... by the neck.' Alternatively, by the words 'like a stone statue' and so on, the state of having the tops of the shoulders covered by flesh is also made clear.

The front half of a lion's body is called 'sīhapubbaddha'. Because his entire body is full like the front half of a lion's body due to the completeness of the limbs, he is called 'sīhapubbaddhakāya'. Therefore, it is said, 'The whole body is full like the front half of a lion's body.' 'Just like a lion' means it is just like a lion. 'Not ill-formed or deformed' means that the body does not reach a state of being ill-formed or deformed due to the unsuitability or abnormality of various limbs. 'They stand' (saṇṭhanti) means they are well-established. 'With long limbs' (dīghehi) refers to the beauty of the fingers, nose, and so on. 'With short limbs' (rassehi) refers to the beauty of the neck and so on. 'With thick limbs' (thūlehi) means...
40:
He is also beautiful with full and sturdy limbs such as the thighs and arms. The term 'kisehi' refers to being beautiful with slender parts such as the hair, body hair, and waist. The term 'puthulehi' refers to being beautiful with broad parts such as the eyes and the palms of the hands. The term 'vaṭṭehi' refers to being beautiful with rounded parts such as the calves and hands.

Possessing a body marked by hundreds of merits, he has a physical form that has arisen exquisitely through various meritorious thoughts. It is said, 'Only a body of such nature is worthy of being the dwelling place of the Buddhas' Dhamma-body (Dhammakāya),' having been prepared and conditioned by the ten perfections (pāramī). According to the text 'dānacittena puññacittena,' it refers to the meaning of merit arising from thoughts of generosity (dāna), virtue (sīla), and so on.

'Dwiṇṇam koṭṭānam antaram' refers to the middle of the two back-arms, the upper part of the middle of the back (the space between the shoulder blades). It is called 'citaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ' (heaped and full) because it is full without any indentation. It is full because the surface is level with the two shoulder blades. 'Uggammā' means the flesh rises from the waist up to the shoulders and stays even without indentation. Therefore, it is said to be 'like a golden plate.'

'Nigrodhaparimaṇḍala' means the proportions of the body are rounded like a well-proportioned banyan tree. Although it should be said 'nigrodhaparimaṇḍalaparimaṇḍala,' one 'parimaṇḍala' word is elided to say 'nigrodhaparimaṇḍala.' Thus, it is described as 'a banyan tree with equal trunk and branches.' Not all banyan trees are rounded; because of the proximity to the word 'parimaṇḍala,' only the rounded banyan tree is to be taken. Alternatively, this meaning can be obtained even without eliding one 'parimaṇḍala' word. Thus, it is said 'rounded like a banyan tree.' In the phrase 'yāvatako assa,' the 'o' is changed to 'va' to become 'yāvatkwassa.'

'Samavaṭṭitakkhandho' means having a neck that is evenly and well-rounded. The neck is not long like a crane's, nor crooked like a heron's, nor thick like a pig's, but is like a small drum (muriya) made of gold.

'Rasaggasaggī' refers to having excellent nerves called 'rasaggasa' that carry various tastes like sweetness into the body. Because of these excellent nerves, he is called 'rasaggasaggī.' In others, the essence of nutrition (ojā) does not spread, leading to a deficiency in elements and frequent illnesses.

'Hanu' is the name for the jaw, which is the support for the teeth. Because the Blessed One's jaw is like that of a lion, he is called 'sīhahanu' (lion-jawed). In this regard, it is stated 'tattha' etc., to show that for the physical body (rūpakāya) and the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya) of the Buddhas, there can only be inferior metaphors (hīnūpama); there are no equal metaphors (samānūpama), let alone superior ones (adhikūpama). Since the upper jaw of the Great Man is situated in accordance with the lower jaw...
41:
It is said, 'Both jaws are full.' This fullness is not because they are rounded in every part, but because they are rounded in three parts (about three-quarters), and thus it is said, 'They are like the moon on the twelfth day of the waxing fortnight.' 'Sallakkhetvā' means considering and comparing in accordance with one's own science of marks (lakkhaṇa-sattha). The height and depth of the teeth are to be known not only by the tips of the teeth but also by the inner and outer sides. Therefore, it is said, 'Like a layer of conch shell cut with an iron plate.' 'Iron plate' refers to a saw. It means the teeth will have an even shape, not uneven.

Because he possesses qualities such as softness, length, and breadth that surpass others, it is called 'pabhūta.' By changing the letter 'ba' to 'ha,' it becomes 'pahūta.' Because he has such a tongue, he is called 'pahūtajivha' (large-tongued).

Due to a voice that occurs in broken intervals, it is 'chinnassara' (broken voice); due to various modes, it is 'bhinnassara' (cracked voice); and due to an unpleasant sound like a crow, it is 'kākassara' (crow-like voice). 'Apalibuddhattā' means having a base that is not obstructed by bile or phlegm. The 'base' (vatthu) should be understood as the places where syllables arise, such as the throat. In the term 'aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgata' (endowed with eight factors), the eight factors will appear in the suttas to follow. 'Mañjughosa' means having a sweet voice.

'Abhinīlanetta' means having intensely blue eyes. This intensity is to be known by the exceedingly blue color, not by the entire eye being blue. Therefore, it is said, 'The whole eye is not blue,' etc. The yellow and red colors arise due to the streaks in the white circle. The blue, white, and black colors should be known according to their respective circular areas.

'Cakkhubhaṇḍa' means the eyelid, according to some teachers. Others say it is the eye-socket. In fact, it should be understood as the entire orb of the eye along with the eyelids. Only then is the description of protruding or sunken eyes logical. By the word 'adhippeta,' it shows the method of synecdoche (ekadesūpacāra-naya), where mentioning a part (the eyelashes) represents the whole (the eye). Since the word 'pakhuma' is commonly used for eyelashes in the world, it is said, 'Eyes covered with soft, smooth, blue-black, and delicate eyelashes.'

Although the word 'uṇṇā' is a general synonym for hair in the world, here it refers to a specific type of hair, and thus it is said 'uṇṇā loma.' 'Born in the middle of the forehead' means it has arisen reaching the center of the forehead. This is a metaphor for its whiteness, not...
42:
Because it is soft. The uṇṇā hair is especially superior and softer even than silk-cotton or vine-cotton. Therefore, it is said "sappi maṇḍe" and so on. Rajata-pubbuḷaka refers to a flower in the shape of a star made of silver.

It is spoken with reference to two reasons. The Buddhas and Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti) are called "uṇhīsa-sīsā" because they have a full forehead and a full head-circle. Therefore, "uṇhīsa-sīso" is spoken based on these two reasons. Now, to show how both these meanings are well-established in the Great Man (Mahāpurisa), it is said "mahāpurisassa hi" and so on. Because of its delicacy, golden color, radiance, and fullness, it shines like a royal headband (uṇhīsa-paṭṭa) bound on the king's head. Kapi-sīsā refers to those with heads split into two. Phala-sīsā refers to those with heads like ripe fruit. Aṭṭhi-sīsā refers to those whose heads consist merely of bone wrapped in skin, either because the bone is very prominent due to the absence of flesh, or because of being very small. Tumba-sīsā refers to those with heads like a gourd. Pabbhāra-sīsā refers to those with heads hanging down at the back. Purima-nayena means by the factor of having a full forehead. Uṇhīsa-veṭhita-sīso viya means like the area of the head wrapped with a headband. Uṇhīsaṃ viya means like a headband circle fashioned by a skilled artisan.

## Explanation of the Name Vipassī

"The detailed account" refers to the detailed talk of satisfying the fortune-tellers during the examination of the marks. It has already been mentioned in the context of satisfying the brahmins who interpreted the dreams that were omens of the descent into the mother's womb. Niddosena means with (milk) free from defects such as saltiness and so on. Dhātiyo refers to the wet-nurses who give milk. These women are called dhātiyo because they make (the child) drink milk (dhāpenti). With the word "tathā", the word "saṭṭhi" (sixty) is included. The remaining nurses are of three types: those who bathe, those who carry, and those who look after. They are also called "dhātiyo" because they arrange the bathing and perform the carrying. Among them, dhāraṇa means holding for a long time with the chest, thigh, or hands. Pariharaṇa means taking and carrying from another's bosom to one's own, or from another's arm to one's own.

Mañjussara means having a gentle voice. Since a gentle voice is not harsh, it is called "akharassara". Vaggussara means having a pleasant voice. The pleasantness of that voice is due to being associated with skill and proficiency, so it is called "cheka-nipuṇassara". Madhurassara means having a voice that is pleasant to the ear. The pleasantness of that voice to the ear is due to being extremely desirable, so it is called "sātassara".
43:
Pemanīyassara means a lovely voice. Because it can inspire devotion in those who hear it, it is called "pemajanaka-ssara" (love-producing voice). Karavīkassara means that when the sound of the Karavīka bird reaches the ears of beings, those beings abandon their natural state of being endowed with their own voices and, without their own will, follow the will of the Karavīka bird. To show how sweet it is, "tatridaṃ" and so on is said. In that passage, "karavīka-sakuṇe" and so on is a description of the bird's nature. Laḷitaṃ refers to the playfulness (līḷhā) arising from the force of joy (pīti). Chaḍḍetvā means removing the grass because even the act of chewing can interfere with hearing the sweet sound. Anikkhipitvā means staying in the air without dropping to the ground. Animals pursued by fierce beasts even disregard the fear of death because of that sound. They stand still without falling, keeping their wings spread as they were.

He released the golden cage into the sky, which had the extent of a league (yojana), because it could be maintained by his own authority. Therefore, the words "so rājāṇāyā" and so on are said. Laḷiṃsu means they began to play. Taṃ pītiṃ means that Queen Bandhumatī, having repeatedly generated that joy based on the Buddha's qualities without letting it go, and having suppressed the defilements, attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) together with seven hundred ladies of the court, because she had the suitable condition of hearing the Dhamma from the elders and possessed a mature wisdom with strong supporting conditions (upanissaya). It is said "together with seven hundred legs" (sattahi jaṅghasatehi saddhiṃ) because she went to the presence of the elders on foot with the seven hundred ladies. Tato means it should be understood that the voice is a hundred times, a thousand times sweeter than the sound of the Karavīka bird. This is because Prince Vipassī's voice is the perfection of the physical basis (vatthu-rūpa) arising from the accumulation of merit (pāramī) cultivated for many hundreds of billions of aeons.

39. Kamma-vipākajaṃ refers to the sensitive eye (pasāda-cakkhu) produced by exceptionally wholesome karma, not obstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., capable of receiving even distant objects, and arising together with the result of wholesome karma (or arising as the result of karma). The divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) is of two kinds: kamma-maya (made of karma) and bhāvanā-maya (made of meditation). Here, the Bodhisatta Vipassī's eye is kamma-maya, so it is said "not bhāvanā-maya". The bhāvanā-maya divine eye will arise at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Although the recognition that "this is that" occurs through mind-consciousness (mano-viññāṇa), because that object has been clearly seen by eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa), the mind-consciousness also arises in that way. Therefore, it is said "yena nimittaṃ... sakkoti".

## Explanation of the Old Man (Jiṇṇapurisa-vaṇṇanā)

'Bent like a rafter' means being like a curved rafter (gopānasī). To illustrate the nature of being bent, even a non-bent rafter is taken as a comparison. 'Bent, rising from the beginning' means being bent due to having a body that is curved and rising from the start. Therefore, the words beginning with 'khandhe' were spoken. One who goes by making the holding of a staff a priority, or one for whom a staff is the cause of movement, is called 'daṇḍaparāyana'. Because a staff is the basis and support for standing, etc., and because one cannot proceed without it, one is called 'daṇḍagatikā'. Alternatively, it means 'daṇḍagatikā' because one must go with a staff, or the staff is the cause of movement. In the word 'daṇḍapaṭisaraṇa', the method is the same. 'Jarātura' means one who is weary due to old age and cannot act according to one's will.

'When the chariot was in front' means when reaching a fork in the road, the chariot ridden by the Bodhisatta, amidst the troops going ahead, took another path and arrived in front of the army. At that time, all the troops remained behind the Bodhisatta's chariot. 'In such a place' means in the aforementioned section of the road. 'That man' refers to that old man. 'Suddhāvāsa Brahmas' are the Brahmas who, after practicing the holy life (brahmacariya) under the dispensation of the three Buddhas beginning with Siddhattha, were reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm. Those Brahmas were residing in that realm at that time.

The question 'What is this called an old man?' is intended to show: 'What is the meaning of that old man you speak of? Identify and tell me.' Since the specific nature of that old man had not yet been determined, the Bodhisatta asked using the neuter universal pronoun 'kiṃ' (what). For example, although mostly only a woman or a man is born in the world, people ask 'What was born to you? (kiṃ te jātaṃ)' using the neuter pronoun; this speech should be understood in the same way. The words beginning with 'What is meant?' also clarify that the specific nature of that old man was not yet clear.

The words beginning with 'If so' illustrate the Great Being's (Mahāsatta) state of being stirred (saṃvega), thinking: 'This state of aging, being common to all, will surely come upon me as well.' He is called 'sārathi' (charioteer) because he drives the chariot. It is called 'udyāna' (park) because it is a place where people go for the purpose of enjoyment. 'Alaṃ' is a word of prohibition. 'Nāma' is a particle used in the sense of reproach, as in 'kathañhi nāma' (how indeed), etc. To see the disadvantage of birth (jāti) is like uprooting the cause of birth. Since the cause of birth must certainly exist, it was said: 'He sat searching for the cause of birth.'
46:
Because the cause is accomplished, the effect is also accomplished. Therefore, there is the nature of not being able to abandon (that arrow). Having caused affliction and by the power of internal piercing, because it remains having entered the heart before all else, it should be construed as: "He sat as if pierced in the heart by the first arrow."

## Description of the Sick Man (Vyādhipurisa-vaṇṇanā)
"By the method previously mentioned" means by the method previously mentioned starting with "The Suddhāvāsa deities, it is said," and so on. "Ābādhika" refers to a person who has an illness. "Dukkhita" refers to a person who has reached suffering or has suffering. "Ajāta" refers to the state of non-arising (the non-arising of mind and matter) or Nibbāna.

## Description of the Dead Man (Kālakata-purisa-vaṇṇanā)
Because it is carried after making various decorations such as butterfly figures with moving eyes and lotus paintings, the covered cart and palanquin are called "vilāta"; therefore, the commentator says, "vilāta means a palanquin." Having seen a palanquin before, the Great Being called the pile of wood for the funeral pyre a "palanquin (sivikā)." "Ito paṭigata" means departing from this life. "Katakāla" means the completion of the period of living. Therefore, he said "yattaka" and so on.

## Description of the Renunciant (Pabbajita-vaṇṇanā)
Because one practices the Dhamma (the ten wholesome courses of action), one is called "dhammacaraṇa"; the state of such a person is "dhammacaraṇa-bhāva"; thus, it refers to "dhammacariya" (Dhamma practice) itself. Just as it is construed as "One is a renunciant because of practicing the Dhamma well," so should the construction of each word be understood as "One is a renunciant because of practicing equanimity well," and so on. "Sabbāni" refers to all the words Dhamma, Sama, Kusala, and Puñña that appear in the phrases such as "sādhu dhammacariyā." "Dasa-kusalakamma-patha-vevacanāni" are the synonymous terms for the ten wholesome dhammas, such as giving (dāna).

## Description of the Bodhisatta's Renunciation (Bodhisatta-pabbajjā-vaṇṇanā)
It should be construed as "having heard the Dhamma-talk of the renunciant." It should be construed as having also heard the Dhamma-talk preached by the renunciant (who was a Suddhāvāsa Brahma) at that time, which was not included in the Recital (Saṅgīti). By the three words "vaṃso vā" and so on, it shows that such renunciation is the nature of things (dhammatā). Because of the long lifespan, they see (the four great omens) only after a long time. Therefore, he preached "after many years... had passed," and so on. "Teneva" means precisely because of seeing the great omens not long ago. Desiring to show the preceding action with no long interval of time, he said, "Having seen the old man... having seen the renunciant, therefore, O Great King, I shall renounce."
47:
For example, the Great Being spoke as if saying, "Having bathed, having dressed, having anointed with perfumes, having worn flowers, I have eaten."

## Description of the Great Multitude Following into Renunciation (Mahājanakāya-anupabbajjā-vaṇṇanā)
By the words "Why in this place?" and so on, he shows the state of those eighty-four thousand beings being well-devoted to the Great Being and their state of having much spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Standing right at the place where they heard of the Great Being's renunciation, without informing relatives, friends, and so on of anything, they cut the firm bond of sensual pleasures and entered renunciation, just as a rutting bull elephant breaks a bond made of iron.

He wandered for four months because his knowledge was not yet mature.

When his knowledge matured, desiring to show that maturity, he said "But this person," and so on. The intended meaning is: "All these renunciants will know of my departure, and if they know, they will follow me continuously." "Sannisīvesu" means when they had settled down quietly. "Saṇateva" means as if making a sound, as if producing a sound.

"Avivekārāmānaṃ" means of those who do not delight in seclusion. "This is the time" means this is the time when those renunciants cannot know of my departure. "Having left" means leaving the leaf-hut; as for the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana), he had already departed earlier. Although it was well-prepared by deities with divine rugs above due to the power of his perfections (pāramīs), because it was accomplished by the power of the Great Being's merit, it is said, "having prepared the throne." Having resolved upon the fourfold effort (caturanga-vīriya) which proceeds in the manner of "Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain," and so on, he dwelt in seclusion.

"By another way only" means toward a direction other than where the Great Being was then residing. Although the Bodhimaṇḍa is situated at the center-point of Jambudīpa, at that time it stood as a great forest, secluded and suitable for the solitary retreat of yogis. Other regions of Jambudīpa were mostly crowded with many people and were prosperous and flourishing. Therefore, because those people went aiming for various provincial regions, it is said, "They set out wandering facing the interior of Jambudīpa." The meaning is that they did not go facing the mountain ranges such as the Himālaya.

## Explanation of the Bodhisatta’s Application of Mind

Although the Blessed One, after becoming Buddha, actually stayed in that very place (the Bodhimaṇḍa) for seven weeks, the statement "having come to stay for a single night" is said with reference to the first day, the full moon of Visākha, among all those days. "Raho-gatassa" means to one who has gone to a place secluded from people. By this, the Great Being’s (Bodhisatta’s) kāya-viveka (physical seclusion) due to the absence of social mingling is expressed. "Paṭisallīnassa" means to one whose mind is withdrawn from wandering among various objects and is well-settled, with a mind that is not distracted among those objects. By this, the citta-viveka (mental seclusion) of the preliminary stage of the path, due to the absence of mental mingling, is expressed. "Dukkha" refers to the suffering rooted in birth and so forth. Indeed, passing away and rebirth are themselves just birth and death. However, having said "is born, dies" (jāyati mīyati) for birth and death, the phrase "passes away, is reborn" (cavati upapajjati) is used not to take the death and rebirth belonging to a single life, but to show the taking of death and rebirth belonging to various lives together; thus it is said, "These two... pe... are stated." As to why, when reflecting on the world's falling into distress, the determination was made by way of aging and death as "of aging and death" (jarāmaraṇassa), it is said "Because..." and so forth. The meaning is that aging and death alone appear prominently at the beginning of reflection. "Abhiniviṭṭhassa" means to one who is reflecting and striving. In the beginning of insight (vipassanā) by way of Dependent Origination, the Bodhisatta’s application of mind starting from aging and death is like descending from the top down to the root; thus it is said, "Like one descending from the peak of existence."

"Upāya-manasikārā" is because of the occurrence of attention through the application of a method. Now, to show that yoniso-manasikāra (wise attention), which is a synonym for that upāya-manasikāra, in terms of its essence and mode of occurrence, "Aniccādīni hi" and so forth is said. It is called yoniso-manasikāra because it is attention according to the truth. In the term "aniccādīni," the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes suffering, non-self, foulness, etc. "Ayaṃ" refers to the attention that proceeds in the manner of "When what exists...?" which is stated as "this reflection arose." "Tesaṃ aññataro" means one among those reflections on impermanence and so forth. Which one is that? It is specifically the attention to impermanence (anicca-manasikāra). The reason for this is stated as "because it proceeds by way of the contemplation of rise and fall." For whatever arises and passes away is impermanent (anicca), being transient because it is delimited by rise and fall. Seeing its nature as such is yoniso-manasikāra because it is attention according to the truth. In the phrase "Ito yonisomanasikārā," the ablative case is in the sense of cause. Therefore, the meaning of that term is explained in the sense of cause by the instrumental case "upāyamanasikārena." The meeting...
49:
...was (ahosi) means there was a meeting (with knowledge) by way of penetration according to the truth. To the question "What then is the cause of that aging and death?" he said "Birth" (jāti). In the passages beginning with "Jātiyā kho," this is the summary of the meaning: To the Bodhisatta who was discerning the cause of aging and death, "When what exists does aging and death come to be? Due to what condition does aging and death come to be?"—discerning the invariable cause thus: "When this exists, that comes to be; when this is absent, that does not come to be"—the wisdom discerning the cause of aging and death arose: "When birth exists, aging and death come to be; due to the condition of birth, there is aging and death." It means there was a meeting with that arising wisdom. "Sabba-padāni" refers to the nine terms beginning with birth and ending with consciousness that appear in the manner of "When what exists does birth come to be?" and so forth.

In the twelve-linked Dependent Origination, regarding the two terms (ignorance and formations) that are not taken here, desiring to ask and answer the reason for not taking them, he first shows the manner in which they should be taken, saying "But here..." and so forth. Having first taken the present life which is manifest, and then the future as the second, the past becomes the third; thus he said, "For ignorance and formations are the past life." Is it not the case that here the taking of the future life is also not possible, because the application of mind is shown by way of the present? That is true, but it should be understood that when the cause is taken, the result is already taken. Furthermore, here the future period is also included in meaning, because later the teaching that includes the future period proceeds as "with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases," and so forth. "Tehi" means by those ignorance and formations which are the objects. It does not connect; it does not unite. He states the reason for the non-connection as being that the Great Man was applied by way of the present. "Adiṭṭhehi" means by those ignorance and formations that were not penetrated. Here the instrumental case is in the sense of a characteristic state (itthambhūta-lakkhaṇa). Intending to show that when there is anubodha (insight), there must be paṭivedha (penetration), he said, "He is not able to become a Buddha." By this [Great Being], those ignorance and formations were seen only by way of existence, clinging, and craving. This is because they have the same nature as those and are capable of being associated with them. Since this has already been told in the Visuddhimagga, the intention is that it should not be told here.

"Paccayato" means from a cause; the meaning is from a formation (saṅkhāra). For, by way of the sequence of causes, in the manner of "When what exists does aging and death come to be?" and so forth, [the sequence] of the succession of results...
50:
In the reflection, "When what exists does consciousness come to be?", if one does not take volitional formations (saṅkhāra)—which are the specific cause of consciousness—as the cause, then consciousness is said to "turn back" from those formations, but not from all conditions. For this very reason, it was said, "When name-and-form exist, consciousness comes to be" (D. ii. 58). Here, "name" (nāma) is intended as a cause only by way of conascence (sahajāta) and so on, and not by way of the decisive support of kamma (kammūpanissaya), because it is shown as a firm reflection on the presently occurring state. "By way of the object" means turning back from the object known as ignorance (avijjā) and volitional formations, or from the object known as the past existence. For ignorance and volitional formations are included in the past. When consciousness turns back from that past ignorance and volitional formations, it is also said to turn back from the past existence. "Both" refers to both rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa) and insight consciousness (vipassanāviññāṇa). "Does not go beyond name-and-form" means it does not transcend name-and-form as cause and name-and-form as object, because it cannot occur without that name-and-form. Therefore, it was said, "It does not go further than name-and-form."

"When consciousness is the cause of name-and-form" means when consciousness is the cause of name, of form, and of name-and-form. "When name-and-form is the cause of consciousness" likewise means when name, form, and name-and-form are the cause of consciousness; the application should be understood as appropriate by way of four-constituent (catuvokāra), one-constituent (ekavokāra), and five-constituent (pañcavokāra) existence. However, the phrase "when both are mutual conditions" refers only to the five-constituent existence. "By this much" means by the occurrence of consciousness and name-and-form through mutual support in this way. "Whether it is born... or whether it arises" means the designation "a being is born... or arises" occurs because there is no state that is the basis for the concept of a "being" (sattapaññatti) apart from consciousness and name-and-form. Therefore, it was said, "From this..." and so on. "Only this" refers only to these two: consciousness and name-and-form.

"The five terms" refers to the five terms beginning with "whether it is born." Since one might ask whether the first and third terms are not distinct in meaning from the fourth and fifth terms among those five, it was said, "together with other deaths and rebirth-linkings." Again, wishing to present and demonstrate the meaning already stated by the word "by this much" (ettāvatā) through the words "namely this" (yadidaṃ) and so on, he spoke again. "By way of the mode of conditions in forward order" (anuloma-paccayākāra) means by way of showing the result preceded by the showing of the causal state. For of the causal states, their own...
51:
The state of being a cause for a result is the mode of conditions of "this-conditionality" (idappaccayatā), and that mode of conditions was stated as "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [come to be]," and so on. Because it is in accordance with the forward occurrence of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra), it is called the "forward mode of conditions" (anuloma-paccayākāra). Taking all the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha), such as birth and so on, together as a mass by means of the mind, it was stated in the Pāḷi as "of this mass of suffering" (dukkhakkhandhassa); thus he said, "birth... [pe]... of this mass of suffering."

Because consciousness occurs by way of seeing the origin of the mass of suffering many times, the reiterated word "Origin, origin!" (samudayo samudayo) was spoken. Alternatively, this phrase "Thus is the origin" is not merely a term showing the production; rather, just as the word "dependent origination" (paṭiccasamuppāda) speaks of the state of being a condition by way of "origination" (samuppāda), here the word "origin" (samudayo) speaks of the state of being a condition by way of "production" (nibbattimukhena). In this context, consciousness and so on are pointed out as causal states; taking them in a general sense with the desire to encompass them all, he said, "Origin, origin!" By doing so, the statement to be made later—"It is said merely as the recognition of the condition: 'When this exists, this comes to be'" (DA. ii. 59)—will be well-established. If so, how is the statement "This is the wisdom of seeing the arising" (udayadassana-paññā) appropriate? This is not a fault, because the seeing of the characteristic of production is possible by way of seeing the arising from the cause.

It is called "eye" (cakkhu) because it is like an eye in the sense of seeing, by way of seeing the origin (samudaya) directly. It is called "knowledge" (ñāṇa) in the sense of making known, just as the origin is rightly known and understood. It is called "wisdom" (paññā) in the sense of knowing distinctly, as in "Through those respective conditions such as consciousness, the origin of this mass of suffering comes to be." It is called "true knowledge" (vijjā) in the sense of piercing and penetrating; having pierced through the opposing states with the wisdom of seeing the arising which had not been pierced before, it arises by way of penetrating "This is the origin" from the standpoint of cause, moment, and intrinsic nature; thus it is said to be "true knowledge" in the sense of piercing and penetrating. It is called "light" (āloka) in the sense of illuminating, by way of being an illuminator through the dispelling of the darkness of delusion (moha) and the darkness of defilements (kilesa) which cover the nature of the origin.

Now, to explain the aforementioned meaning in sequence, the phrase "As he said" (yathāha) and so on was spoken. Therein, "The eye arose" (cakkhuṃ udapādi) is the extraction of the term from the Pāḷi. As to how it arose, he said, "In the sense of seeing." The meaning "by way of seeing the origin directly" has already been stated. In this way, the meaning in the remaining terms should also be understood. "Cakkhu-dhammo" is the Pāḷi term "cakkhu." "Dassanaṭṭho attho" is the meaning which is the nature of seeing.
52:
This is the meaning indicated by that term. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. 'By so many terms' means by these five terms. 'What is taught?' asks for the summary meaning (piṇḍattha). 'Just the recognition of causes' means the mere recognition of the causal nature of the resultant phenomena (paccayuppanna), such as mind-and-matter and so on, in relation to the causal phenomena (paccaya), such as consciousness and so on. This is taught because it illuminates the marking of the causal nature without distinction. Because it illuminates the proper vision of the arising of formations (saṅkhāra), it is said: 'Tender insight (taruṇa-vipassanā) that has entered the cognitive process (vīthi) is taught.'

Because it is attained by oneself and is an immediate perception, it is called 'this' (ayaṃ). It is called 'path' (magga) in the sense of seeking the Noble Path (ariya-magga) and so on. This is insight belonging to the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga-vipassanā). Therefore, it is said: 'For awakening' (bodhāya). With reference to the state of being the means of awakening (bhāvasādhana) of the term 'bodha', it is said: 'For the purpose of awakening to the Four Truths.' The realizations of full understanding (pariññā), abandoning (pahāna), and development (bhāvanā) have the realization of witnessing (sacchikiriyā) as their benefit. Because the practice of the holy life (brahmacariya) has the benefit of attaining Nibbāna, it is said: 'Or rather, for the purpose of awakening to Nibbāna.' For it is said: 'Nibbāna is the highest happiness.' 'One awakens' means one penetrates the Four Noble Truths with a single penetration; thus, the agent-state (kattusādhana) of the word 'bodha' is stated. 'By the terms in the nominative case' (paccattapadehi) means by terms indicating the first grammatical case. Only Nibbāna is taught here, because consciousness and so on cease in this Nibbāna. 'Non-arising cessation' (anibbattinirodha) means the absolute cessation, the cessation of non-production through the total cessation of causes.

In saying 'just the recognition of cessation' by these five terms such as 'eye' and so on, only the mere recognition of cessation is taught by phrases like 'Cessation, cessation,' because it is the initial endeavor. It does not mean the direct perception by way of penetration, as the Noble Path has not yet been attained. Because the proper vision of the cessation of formations is desired through insight that has reached its peak, it is said: 'Strong insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī balava-vipassanā) is taught.'

'Having known' means knowing with the knowledge belonging to the preliminary stage. 'Thereafter' means after the knowledge of the cessation of causes according to the method stated. 'In the things that are causes of clinging' means in the things that are objects of clinging (upādāniya), which are the causes of the four types of clinging by way of object-condition and so on. 'Carrying' means proceeding. This statement, 'at another time' and so on—why is it said? It is a question asked with the desire to say: 'By whichever path of practice all Great Bodhisattas practice for awakening in their final birth, the Great Bodhisatta practiced in that very same way through insight.'
53:
Therefore, He said the words beginning with 'Sabbeyeva hi.' In that text, the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana) on the day of the son's birth and the application of exertion (padhāna) should be understood as the natural order (dhammatā) of the Bodhisattas. Other duties, however, should be understood through the knowledge of 'what ought to be done' (itikattabbatā).

Even in those matters to be known as 'what ought to be done,' the mind is urged by Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) gained through long-term cultivation. Thus, starting with 'Alas, this world has fallen into suffering,' and taking the vision of the suffering of the world of beings whom He wishes to liberate from the suffering of saṃsāra as the starting point, the contemplation of the structure of conditions (paccayākāra) starting from aging and death is also a natural occurrence (dhammatā). Similarly, the application to the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) is also a natural occurrence because of its dependence on oneself, because it is not disturbed by anything, because it is a dwelling in unadulterated happiness, and because it is associated with the fourth jhāna.

'Having entered into the five aggregates' means having entered by way of the application of insight into the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), which are taken by way of the varieties of consciousness, mind-and-matter, and so on, and thus beginning the practice of insight. 'Anukkama' (sequence) refers to the gradual practice (anupubbapaṭippatti) because it is to be followed or practiced step by step. 'Having done' means having practiced.

In the phrase 'iti rūpaṃ' (thus is form), the second 'iti' has the sense of pointing out (nidassana). Therefore, the first 'iti' indicates the specific nature (sarūpa) and the extent (parimāṇa) of form, as particles (nipāta) have multiple meanings. Or, the meaning should be understood as being for the sake of emphasis by way of repetition (āvutti) and so on. Desiring to show a sentence that includes the sense of limitation (avadhāraṇa), He said: 'This is form, form is only this much, there is no form beyond this,' and so on.

In that statement, by the term 'the nature of being deformed' (ruppana-sabhāva), the general nature of form is shown. By the terms 'the distinction of the primary elements and derived form' (bhūtupādāyabheda) and so on, the specific nature is shown. By both of these, the meaning of the term 'this is form' (idaṃ rūpaṃ) is indicated. Therein, 'characteristic' (lakkhaṇa) is the unique nature of each specific form that is not shared with others. 'Function' (rasa) is its causal state toward its own result. 'Manifestation' (paccupaṭṭhāna) is its state as an object of correct knowledge because it exists in the ultimate sense. 'Proximate cause' (padaṭṭhāna) is the immediate cause; by this, its existence dependent on conditions is shown.

By this phrase, 'the comprehension of form without remainder' (anavasesarūpapariggaho), the meaning of both terms—'form is only this much' and 'there is no form beyond this'—is indicated, because form is limited by way of total exhaustion. In the phrase 'iti rūpassa samudayo' (thus is the arising of form), the word 'iti' has the sense of 'manner' (pakāra), as in the passage 'iti kho bhikkhave' and so on; thus He explained it as 'iti means in this way' (itīti evaṃ).

'Due to the arising of ignorance' (avijjāsamudayā) means because of the production or the existence of ignorance. For 'arising' (uppāda), which is the opposite of 'cessation' (nirodha), also signifies 'existence' (atthibhāva). Therefore...
54:
It means that when there is ignorance (avijjā) accomplished in a previous life, there is the arising of matter (rūpa), which is the cause of matter in this life. The same method applies to terms such as 'arising due to craving' (taṇhāsamudaya). In the context of 'arising due to nutriment' (āhārasamudaya), among the causes that produce the continuity of matter, edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) is taken because it is predominant. Even though only nutriment is mentioned, it should be understood that temperature (utu) and consciousness (citta) are also included, as they are similarly causes for the continuity of matter. Thus, it should be known that the arising of matter through its four causes has been clarified.

By the words 'characteristic of birth' (nibbattilakkhaṇa) and so on, the seeing of arising in terms of time is stated. In that context, 'characteristic of birth' refers to the conditioned characteristic (saṅkhatalakkhaṇa) known as the arising (uppāda) of matter. 'While seeing' means seeing not only the arising through causes but also the arising in terms of moments (khaṇa). Indeed, having first seen the arising in terms of duration (addhā), and then in terms of continuity (santati), one gradually sees it in terms of moments.

'With the cessation of ignorance, matter ceases' means that due to the non-arising cessation of ignorance through the Path of Arahantship, there is the non-arising cessation of future matter. This is because when the cause is absent, the effect is absent. The same method applies here to 'with the cessation of craving, kamma ceases.' 'With the cessation of nutriment' means due to the absence of edible food, which is the producing cause. 'Matter ceases' means the absence of matter produced by that nutriment. The remaining words follow the same method already described.

'Characteristic of change' (vipariṇāmalakkhaṇa) refers to seeing the passing away in terms of the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga). Therefore, having first seen that dissolution in terms of duration, and then in terms of continuity, one gradually sees it in terms of moments. This method is stated in terms of ordinary practitioners of insight (vipassanā). For Bodhisattas, however, there is no such seeing in terms of duration and continuity. This same method applies to the seeing of arising.

In terms such as 'Thus, feeling' (iti vedanā), the meaning should be understood according to the method stated below for matter. Therefore, it was stated: 'This is feeling, this much is feeling,' and so on. In that context, in the phrase 'the nature of feeling... etc.', the word 'nature' (sabhāva) should be applied to each, as in 'the nature of feeling... etc... the nature of cognizing.' 'The nature of feeling' means the nature of experiencing the object. 'The nature of perception' means the nature of noting the object as 'blue, yellow,' and so on. 'The nature of mental formations' means the nature of striving and arranging. 'The nature of consciousness' means the nature of cognizing the object. In the term 'pleasant' (sukha), the word 'etc.' (ādi) includes painful, mentally pleasant, mentally painful, and equanimous feelings. In the term 'perception of forms' (rūpasaññā), the word 'etc.' includes perception of sounds and so on. In the term 'contact' (phassa), the word 'etc.' includes volition (cetanā), initial application (vitakka), and so on. In the term 'eye-consciousness' (cakkhuviññāṇa), the word 'etc.' includes all mundane consciousness. Just as with consciousness, the same method applies to feeling and the others.
55:
'Of them' refers to the meaning of the states called 'arising' (samudaya). 'In the three aggregates' refers to the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), and the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). According to the words, 'Touched, one feels; touched, one perceives; touched, one wills,' it is called 'arising due to contact' (phassasamudaya). According to the words, 'With name-and-form as condition, consciousness arises,' it is called 'arising due to name-and-form' (nāmarūpasamudaya) in the aggregate of consciousness. 'Of them indeed' means that the term 'passing away' (atthaṅgama) should also be applied in terms of contact for the three aggregates, and in terms of name-and-form for the aggregate of consciousness. The meaning is that ignorance and so on are just the same as what was stated regarding the aggregate of matter.

'By way of the fifty characteristics' means by way of exactly fifty characteristics of arising and passing away: twenty-five characteristics of arising (udaya)—consisting of twenty characteristics due to causes and five characteristics in terms of the moment (of arising)—and twenty-five characteristics of passing away (vaya)—consisting of twenty characteristics due to the cessation of causes and five characteristics in terms of the moment (of dissolution). Among those fifty characteristics, because the arising of the five aggregates is marked by these signs, the arising of ignorance and so on are called 'characteristics.' Similarly, because the non-arising cessation of those aggregates is known by these signs, the absolute cessation of causes such as ignorance and so on are called 'characteristics.' The characteristic of birth (nibbatti) and the characteristic of change (vipariṇāma) are merely conditioned characteristics (saṅkhatalakkhaṇa). Thus, these fifty characteristics should be known in their specific nature.

'Developed in due order' means when the aforementioned knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbayañāṇa) has arisen as sharp, courageous, and clear, and thereafter, through the sequence of the arising of the knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅgañāṇa) and so on, insight knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa) reaches growth and attains the summit.
