Even beforehand, the knowledge of purification by way of the path (paṭipadāvisuddhiñāṇa)—which possesses the power accumulated through the knowledge of comprehension (sammasanañāṇa) known as the Great Vajira Knowledge, occurring in 3.6 trillion ways and being suitable for Omniscience, and which reaches maturity while bearing the 'embryo' (of a person with mature perfections)—reaches the stage of supreme perfection through the power of the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī) accumulated over an immeasurable time. Having gradually reached the state of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā), when it connects with the Noble Path, at that time the consciousness of the Noble Path is liberated from all defilements through the sequence of the paths. And when it is liberated, it is liberated in such a way that it results in the abandoning of defilements that shroud all knowable things.

That abandoning of defilements, called 'abandoning along with residual traces' (savāsanappahāna), is in meaning the cessation of non-arising (anuppattinirodha); therefore, it is said, 'by the cessation of non-arising' (anuppādanirodhena). 'By the defilements called taints (āsava)' means [liberated] by these defilements—lust (rāga), wrong view (diṭṭhi), and delusion (moha)—which are called taints because they flow and occur as far as the peak of existence (bhavagga) in terms of life, and as far as the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) in terms of states. This phrase in the Pali text, 'from the taints' (āsavehi), is merely a figurative expression (lakkhaṇavacana) indicating a part. However, by being established in a single consciousness with those taints...
56:
The mind is liberated from all defilements and from all evil unwholesome states. "Without grasping" (aggahitvā) means without taking even a trace of those defilements.

In the moment of the Path (magga), it is said to be "being liberated" from the defilements to be abandoned by that respective Path; in the moment of Fruition (phala), it is said to be "liberated." Alternatively, in the moment of a higher Path, it is both "liberated" from the defilements already abandoned by the lower Paths and "being liberated" from the defilements to be abandoned by itself as appropriate. However, in the moment of Fruition, throughout all moments of Fruition-consciousness, it is only "liberated" and is not called "being liberated."

"From all bonds" (sabbabandhanā) refers to [the Bodhisatta] who is liberated from all fetters of existence, comprised of the lower and higher fetters, especially in various ways. "One whose mental continuum is well-blossomed" (suvikasitacittasantāno) refers to [the Bodhisatta] whose mental continuum is thoroughly and properly blossomed due to the touch of the extraordinary radiance of Path-knowledge. The phrase "the four Path-knowledges" and so on shows these knowledges, by which the mental continuum is well-blossomed, in part. The complete presentation will come later; therefore, those knowledges will be analyzed in those specific suttas. "And all the qualities of the Buddha" (sakale ca buddhaguṇe) refers to all the qualities of the Buddha, such as unimpeded knowledge regarding the past. Indeed, when the Lord of the World attains the Path of Arahantship, he is said to have brought all qualities into his hand. Thereafter, he is said to "stand having brought them into his hand."

Having said "one of fulfilled intention" (paripuṇṇasaṅkappo), the inspired utterance (udāna) beginning with "Through many a birth in saṃsāra" (aneka jāti saṃsāraṃ) is spoken to show the state of having fulfilled intentions. Among those, the meaning of the first two verses has already been explained below in the commentary on the introduction to the Brahmajāla Sutta. Later, "struck by an iron hammer" (ayoghanahatassa) refers to [an iron bar] struck by a blacksmith's iron hammer or iron fist, where "ayoghana" means that by which iron is struck. Here, the word "eva" is merely a particle. "Of the blazing fire" (jalato jātavedaso) refers to the meaning of a burning fire; or, the suffix used in the word "jalato" is the genitive case used in the sense of disregard (anādara). "Gradually extinguished" (anupubbūpasantassa) means [a fire] that is gradually calmed, removed, and ceased. "As its destination is not known" (yathā na ñāyate gatī) means just as the destination of that fire is not known. The intended meaning is this: when a blazing fire clinging to an iron bar or a bronze vessel, because of being struck by an iron fist or hammer, is gradually extinguished, its destination in the ten directions is not known or manifest. This is because it has ceased without further rebirth due to the cessation of its cause, the fuel. Thus, "of those who are rightly liberated" (evaṃ sammāvimuttānaṃ) means by the right cause, by the right method...
58:
It is said to be profound because there is no other Dhamma to be penetrated and known apart from these Four Noble Truths. *Gambhīra* (profound) means that just as the great ocean cannot be fathomed by a mosquito's proboscis, this Dhamma cannot be fathomed by the wisdom of others, except for those who have accumulated and matured the requisites of wisdom. Therefore, it is said, "This is a statement rejecting the state of being shallow." Because it cannot be fathomed and thus cannot be entered into, and because it cannot be seen either in its essence or in its specific characteristics, it is said, "Because it is profound, it is hard to see." *Duddasa* (hard to see) refers to a Dhamma that is seen only by some, with difficulty, and only at certain times. If it is not even possible to see a Dhamma, there is no need to speak of entering into it and understanding it repeatedly; thus it is said, "Because it is hard to see, it is hard to understand." Because understanding it repeatedly is difficult, it is a Dhamma that must be understood with difficulty. In this context, the Sutta passage should be cited: "Monks, what do you think? Is it more difficult to do, or more difficult to achieve?"

It is called *santa* (peaceful) because it has a peaceful object (or because it has the peaceful object of Nibbāna). It is called *nibbuta* (extinguished) because all the fevers of defilements have been extinguished. It is called *paṇīta* (sublime) because it has reached the state of being noble (preeminent). It is called *atappaka* (not satiating) in the sense of being insatiable (extremely delightful), just as delicious food does not lead to satiation. Here, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-sacca*) is called *santārammaṇa* because it is a peaceful object. The Truth of the Path (*magga-sacca*) is called *santārammaṇa* because it is both peaceful and has the peaceful object of Nibbāna. It is called *santa* because of the absence of defilements and conditioned things (*saṅkhāra*) which are unpeaceful by nature. It is called *nibbuta* because all the fevers of defilements have been extinguished. It should be understood as *atappaka* because, due to its peaceful and sublime nature, it is "without dregs" (*asecanaka*) for that purpose. Therefore, it is said, "These two dhammas are spoken of with reference only to the supramundane (*lokuttara*)."

Because it is the domain of noble wisdom, it is not a Dhamma to be reached or explored by mere reasoning (*takka*). Precisely because it cannot be known by reasoning, it is the sphere of subtle wisdom; and because it is fine and subtle in nature, it is called *nipuṇa* (subtle). Because it is not within the range of fools, it is a Dhamma to be known only by the wise; thus it is called *paṇḍitavedanīya* (to be experienced by the wise). *Ālaya* (attachments) refers to the five cords of sensual pleasure because they are resorted to as things to delight in. *Ālaya* also refers to the movements of craving (*taṇhā-vicarita*) because they resort [to objects] by way of delighting in them. *Ālayarata* means those who delight in attachments. They are those who are exceedingly joyful because they do not grow weary [of them]. *Ramati* means one finds delight, plays, and frolics. It is said, "In both ways," etc., meaning that just as these beings relish the cords of sensual pleasure, they likewise relish and delight in lust (*rāga*).

"With reference to the state (*ṭhānaṃ sandhāya*)" means speaking with reference to the word *ṭhāna*. In terms of meaning, however, by "state" (*ṭhāna*), only dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is intended. It is called *ṭhāna* because the effect stands in this cause, depending on it; [these are] ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth, which are the causes of the effects such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). Because they are the causes of these effects like volitional formations, ignorance and so forth are themselves called *idappaccaya* (having this as its condition). *Idappaccaya* itself is called *idappaccayatā* (specific conditionality), just as a deva is called *devatā*. Or, [it is called so] because ignorance and so forth, which are *idappaccaya*, [depend on] their own effects...
59:
The state of being a cause, the power to produce an effect, is called specific conditionality (idappaccayatā). By this statement, Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), which has the characteristic of a cause in the ultimate sense, is shown. Because an effect arises depending on (paṭicca) this cause (i.e., the harmony of causes), it is called Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). By these two words, only the causal meaning of phenomena is clarified. Therefore, it is said, 'This is a designation for ignorance (avijjā) etc., which are the causes of formations (saṅkhāra) etc.' This is just a summary here. The detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the commentaries of the Visuddhimagga.

In the words beginning with 'sabbasaṅkhārasamatha' (the stilling of all formations), 'sabba' (all) refers to the entire meaning denoted by those words, which in essence means Nibbāna alone. Now, to show the nature of that Nibbāna, the passage beginning with 'yasmā hi' is stated. 'Taṃ' (that) refers to Nibbāna. 'Āgamma' (having come to/depending on) means depending on it as the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) of the Noble Path. 'Sammanti' means they are stilled by way of cessation without further rebirth. Because they are thus stilled and are exceptionally peaceful, it is said 'vūpasammanti' (they are fully stilled). In this way, because all formations are stilled in this Nibbāna, Nibbāna is shown as 'sabbasaṅkhārasamatha'. Indeed, in Nibbāna, which is dissociated from all formations, the variety of ways in which all formations are stilled is logically established. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

Because it carries suffering closely within it, it is called 'upadhi' (acquisition/clinging); these are the aggregates (khandha) and so on. 'Paṭinissaṭṭha' means they are relinquished by way of total eradication. 'Sabbā taṇhā' refers to all cravings, which are of 108 varieties. 'Sabbe kilesarāgā' refers to all lustful defilements, such as sensual lust (kāma-rāga) and lust for fine-material existence (rūpa-rāga). Alternatively, all defilements should be understood here as 'kilesarāga' because they cause the mind to become perverted, not just specific types of greed. As it is said: 'A lustful mind is perverted, a hateful mind is perverted, and a deluded mind is perverted.' 'Virajjanti' means they abandon their own nature. 'Sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ' refers to the entire suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha), such as aging (jarā) and death (maraṇa). 'Bhavena bhavaṃ' means from one existence to another existence. It is bound together by craving for existence. Alternatively, it binds kamma together with its fruit because, for one with craving, it causes future rebirth. It is the escape from that craving called 'vāna', because that craving is entirely absent in that Nibbāna.

Physical fatigue and physical distress should be understood as the aching of the back and the dryness of the palate and throat due to sitting for a long time and speaking for a long time. However, that physical fatigue occurs only in relation to those who do not know the meaning of the teaching and those who do not practice it. For those who know and practice, the physical exertion in teaching is actually no exhaustion for the Teacher. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'The occasion of teaching the Dhamma does not weary me.' It is also said, 'Teaching to those who do not know would be my weariness.' 'Ubhayaṃ' (both) refers to mental fatigue (and mental distress).
60:
Both mental fatigue and mental distress do not exist for the Buddhas, as they were completely eradicated at the very foot of the Bodhi tree.

'Anubrūhanaṃ' means combining (sampiṇḍanaṃ). 'So' is the particle 'apissu'. 'Vipassi' is an accusative case used in the sense of the possessive (sāmī) due to its association with the prefix 'paṭi'; thus it is explained as 'vipassissa'. Whether the verses that have reached greatness are marvelous or not marvelous, the letter 'a' can also exist in the sense of growth (vuddhi-attha). For example, as in 'asekkhā dhammā'. It should be understood that after fulfilling the perfections (pāramī) for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons solely for the purpose of distributing the Dhamma to the world including the devas, the Buddha, having now rightly attained the status of the King of Dhamma (Dhammarāja), shows his reluctance (appossukkatā) therein; the marvelous nature of the meaning of the verses, and the growth of that meaning. By way of the literal meaning, the non-marvelous nature of the verses should be understood. 'Gocara ahesuṃ' means they became apparent (upaṭṭhahiṃsu). Since becoming apparent is the state of being reflected upon, it says 'parivitakkayitabbataṃ pāpuṇiṃsu' (they reached the state of being reflected upon).

If the practice of the path is indeed an easy practice, why is it said to be difficult? To answer this, it is said, 'During the time of fulfilling the perfections,' and so on. This refers to the practice of the Bodhisatta who gives away things that are difficult to give up. Some say the word 'ha' is a particle meaning 'evident' or 'certainly'. The construction is: 'It is evident, or certainly, not worthwhile (alaṃ nippayojanaṃ) to teach the Dhamma attained with such difficulty.' 'Halaṃ' is a word with the same meaning as 'alaṃ', as in the passages 'halanti vadāmi' and so on. 'Rāgadosaphuṭṭhehi' refers to beings who are oppressed and overwhelmed by lust and hatred, just as one is struck by a poisonous snake. 'Rāgadosānugatehi' refers to beings who are followed by lust and hatred.

'Niccādīnaṃ' is the opposite of the clinging to permanence and so on. 'Evaṃ gataṃ' means occurring in this way, occurring by way of impermanence and so on. The term 'catusacca-dhamma' (the Dhamma of the Four Truths) should be taken as applicable to the aspects of impermanence etc., and to the Four Truths. Alternatively, 'evaṃ gataṃ' means the Dhamma that has been reached, known, and penetrated by me and by other Fully Enlightened Buddhas through firm attention to 'impermanence' and so on. Because they are enamored by sensual lust and lust for existence, their minds are obstructed by the hindrances (nīvaraṇa); and because they are enamored by the lust for views, they have perverted inclinations; thus they will not see this Dhamma as it really is, they will not penetrate it. (Who would be able) to make them know the Dhamma as it really is, by way of its nature such as 'impermanence' and so on? Their being overwhelmed by lust and hatred is also due to their state of intense delusion; thus it is said 'tamokhandhena āvuṭā' (enveloped by the mass of darkness).

To clarify the reason for being reluctant (appossukkatā) to teach the Dhamma, he himself raises the objection (codanā) with the words 'kasmā pana' and so on. In that passage, just as now...
61:
## Explanation of the Account of Brahmā's Request

Reaching the state of being unconcerned (appossukkatā) regarding the preaching of the Dhamma is a practiced tradition of all Buddhas. At the beginning of the aspiration for Buddhahood of all Bodhisattvas, the act of greatly encouraging one's own mind in the Great Resolve (Mahābhinīhāra) with thoughts such as "Why should I live in an unknown form?" and so on, is also a practiced tradition. Thus, it is said, "Kiṃ me," etc. In that passage, "aññāta-vesena" means being in an unknown form merely by attaining the state of a disciple of the Buddhas, without becoming a Buddha who makes the world, including the devas, resound.

There are three reasons for reaching the state of being unconcerned: the strength of the opposing defilements (kilesa), the extreme profundity of the Dhamma, and the Buddha's supreme respect for that Dhamma. To show these reasons, the passage "Tassa hī," etc., was undertaken. In that context, "opposing" refers to defilements such as lust (rāga), because they create obstacles to right practice. Because these defilements are powerful and difficult to cleanse from the continuum (santāna) of beings due to long-term cultivation, they overpower and oppress beings—like wild elephants overpowering a weak man—leading them to ruin and causing them to dwell in or cling to even a dense thicket of thorns that is hundreds of leagues in length and breadth, extremely compact and thick.

To show the difficulty of cleansing because they are far-reaching and difficult to cut off, the passage "Athassā," etc., was spoken. In that context, it is like an old gourd filled with medicinal sour gruel that is not smooth inside, a pot filled with buttermilk that has been soaked for a long time, a worn-out cloth that has absorbed fat because it is weak and soaked with oil, or hands smeared with eye-ointment because they are mixed with oil—all of which are difficult to cleanse. These metaphors are inferior (hīna) because they pertain to the physical continuum and their impurity is of a short duration. Only the corruption of defilements (kilesa-saṅkilesa) is especially difficult to cleanse, because it has existed since a beginningless time and is latently inherent in the continuum of beings. Therefore, it was said, "atisaṅkiliṭṭhā" (extremely corrupted). Just as they are difficult to cleanse, the aforementioned metaphors are also inferior in terms of being profound, difficult to see, and difficult to understand.

Even the profound Dhamma can become very clear through the suppression of opposing defilements. The suppression of the opposing factors is connected to right practice. That practice is dependent on hearing the True Dhamma. That hearing of the Dhamma is dependent on faith in the Teacher and the Dhamma. That faith, in particular, has the request of a person who is esteemed and respected in the world as its cause. Desiring to show that cause, the request of Brahmā, which is the cause for beings to approach the Dhamma through the act of paying homage with joined palms, was spoken with "Api ca," etc.

Although the word "aññataro" was spoken as if referring to an unknown Brahmā, in truth, to show that he is a famous and well-known Brahmā, it was said, "the Great Brahmā (Mahābrahmā) who is the chief in this universe." He is the Great Brahmā who is the chief in the Mahābrahmā realm. That Mahābrahmā is very famous and well-known in the Brahma world, just as Sakka is in the sensual deva world. In this eye of wisdom, there is the dust of lust, etc., which is a minor impurity. Because of having such little dust, it is called "apparaja." Those beings who have an eye of wisdom with little dust of lust are called "apparajakkhajātika." To show that meaning, the explanatory words "paññāmaya," etc., were spoken. Those whose nature is to have little dust of lust, etc., are "apparajakkhajātika"; thus should the meaning be understood here. Those beings whose dust of lust, etc., is little, who are of such a nature with little dust...
62:
Just as Sakka is famous in the sensual deva world, that Mahābrahmā is also very famous and well-known in the Brahma world. To show that "apparajakkhajātika" refers to those whose nature is to have an eye of wisdom with only a small amount of the dust of defilements such as lust, the passage "paññāmaya," etc., was spoken. Those whose nature is to have little dust of defilements such as lust should be understood as "apparajakkhajātika." In the word "assavanatā," the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental, as in the words "sayaṃ abhiññā," etc.; therefore, it was explained as "assavanatāya." By means of the bases of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu) that ripen the ten factors of liberation such as giving (dāna), etc., it was said, "katādhikārā," etc. In the Papañcasūdanī Commentary, however, it is stated as "twelve bases of meritorious action," which is said by including the two factors of taking refuge and the dedication of merit for the benefit of others into the ten factors such as giving.

The request and invitation to hear the Dhamma with respect toward those worthy of honor is called "ajjhesanā." In terms of its essential meaning, it is indeed a petition (yācanā). Because these two knowledges are not a vision of knowledge that is limited to a certain area but are the unique property (āveṇika) of the Buddhas alone, they are called the "Buddha-eye" (Buddha-cakkhu). (These two are the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings and the knowledge of their dispositions and latent tendencies). The three lower path-knowledges are called the "Dhamma-eye" (Dhamma-cakkhu) because they involve merely seeing the Four Noble Truths. Since those knowledges are like a flash of lightning, they are called "vijjūpama." The knowledge of the highest path (Arahattamagga-ñāṇa), however, is not called the "Dhamma-eye" because it is not merely a seeing, having reached the peak of the function of knowledge. Thus, it is called "vajirူpama," having the metaphor of a diamond. Just as those with few defilements are called "apparajakkha," those with thick defilements should be known as "mahārajakkha." Because they are capable of destroying opposing unwholesome states, they are sharp (tikkha), brave, and clear; if they are the opposite of this, they are soft (mudu). The aspects such as faith (saddhā) are called "ākāra." In the Sammohavinodanī Commentary, it is said that those whose portions such as dispositions (āsaya) are good are "svākāra"; this should be understood as being in agreement and consistent with the explanation in this commentary. Due to being endowed with faith, etc., the disposition is good; if it is the opposite, it is bad. "Cause" (kāraṇa) refers to the mode of conditions (paccaya-ākāra) or the Four Noble Truths. The "next world" (paraloka) should be seen as a fearful danger like a fault that brings suffering; thus it was said, "they see the next world and faults as danger." Alternatively, a state of ruin (vipatti) other than a state of success (sampatti) is called the "next world," as in "they see the next... (pe)... as danger."
63:
In this context, in distinguishing the meaning of the terms 'apparajakkha' (those with little dust in their eyes) and so forth, this is the Pali text that proves that such is the case. Indeed, the strength of the qualities that mature liberation, such as faith (saddhā), occurs only through the weakness of the unwholesome qualities that are their opposites. The strength of those unwholesome qualities occurs through the weakness of faith and the other qualities. Thus, by way of the presence or absence of the specific qualities that mature liberation, the categories 'apparajakkha, mahārajakkha,' and so forth are shown by way of classification in the Pali (Paṭisambhidāmagga). In this way, there are five types of 'apparajakkha' by way of the five qualities such as faith, and five types of 'mahārajakkha' by way of the five qualities such as lack of faith. In the same manner, fifty types of persons are distinguished, such as those with keen faculties (tikkhindriya) and those with dull faculties (mudindriya). It should be understood that there are many divisions due to the internal variations of faith and the other qualities. The aggregates (khandha) and so forth are called 'loka' (world) in the sense of breaking and disintegrating. A world that is a successful existence is called 'sampatti-bhava-loka'; it is the rebirth existence (upapatti-bhava) known as a happy destination (sugati). Because success arises through this quality, it is called 'sampatti-sambhava-loka'; it is the karmic existence (kamma-bhava) that leads to a happy destination. The rebirth existence known as an unhappy destination (duggati) and the karmic existence leading to an unhappy destination are called 'vipatti-bhava-loka' and 'vipatti-sambhava-loka.'

Again, to show the world by way of groups of one, two, and so forth, it is said 'eko loko' (one world) and so on. Indeed, nutriment (āhāra) and so forth are called 'loka' in the sense of breaking and disintegrating. In that Pali, by the statement based on the person, 'The world is one; all beings subsist on nutriment,' the dependence on conditions of all formations (saṅkhāra) is taught. Because of that dependence on conditions, the entire world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka) is a single world, being of only one kind, as there is no other mode. In the Pali passages 'dve lokā' (two worlds) and so forth, the meaning should be understood in this same way. In this context, Nibbāna is not included when taking 'nāma' (mind/name), because Nibbāna does not have the nature of the world, which is disintegration. One might ask: 'In the statement "subsisting on nutriment," since they are dependent on conditions, would the Paths and Fruits (magga-phala) also not fall under the category of "world"?' They do not. This is because only the phenomena of the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca), which are to be fully understood (pariññeyya), are intended here as 'loka.' Alternatively, the nature that does not break or disintegrate is what is taken [as non-world]; it is not like that [for the world], for only that which disintegrates is the world. Therefore, the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma), being free from that nature of disintegration, are not called 'loka.' The aggregates that are the objects of clinging are called 'upādānakkhandha.' Gain and so forth, which are the bases for attraction and so on, are called the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma). 'Dasāyatanāni' refers to the ten material bases (rūpāyatana). This is because the intention is for one who has an inclination toward the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭajjhāsaya). To such a person, all karma produced in the three planes appears as something to be blamed and avoided. Thus it is said: 'All volitional constructions (abhisaṅkhāra) are a fault; all karmas leading to existence are a fault.'
64:
Those individuals whose faith and other faculties are dull (manda) are referred to here in the section on the Knowledge of the Degree of Maturity of the Faculties (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) as 'faithless' (asaddhā) and so forth. However, this does not mean a total absence of faith and other faculties in every respect. In each of the five dyads (duka) such as the 'apparajakkha' dyad, ten types are made, and it is said: 'He knows these five faculties through fifty modes.' Alternatively, it is said thus because he knows the degree of maturity (paropariyatta) of the faculties such as faith by way of both presence (anvaya) and absence (vyatireka). In this context, to the Blessed One who contemplates by way of 'apparajakkha' and so forth, those beings appear in groups and clusters, not individually.

Because there are lotuses here, it is called 'uppalinī'. This can refer to a thicket or a pond, but here a pond is intended; thus it is said: 'in a grove of lotuses' (uppalavane). Those lotuses that grow and thrive while remaining submerged within the water are called 'antonimuggaposīnī'. 'Dīpitāni' means those meanings explained in the Commentary, or those explained right here with 'others also' (aññānipi) and so forth.

'Ugghaṭana' means the opening of knowledge. One is called 'ugghaṭitaññū' because one understands as soon as knowledge is opened. One is called 'vipañcitaññū' because one understands the meaning of what is elaborated (vittāra). One is called 'neyya' because one is to be led (netabba) by means of recitation (uddesa) and so forth. 'Saha udāhaṭavelāya' means together with the time the Dhamma is proclaimed (even when just the heading is given). 'Dhammābhisamaya' is the penetration of the Truth of the Four Truths together with knowledge. An individual is called 'ugghaṭitaññū' if, while a summary (mātikā) is being shown in brief by way of 'the four foundations of mindfulness' and so forth, he is able to send forth his knowledge in accordance with the teaching and attain Arahantship. An individual is called 'vipañcitaññū' if, after the summary is set forth in brief, he is able to reach Arahantship while the meaning is being analyzed in detail.

'Uddesato' means because of recitation (for one who recites or causes another to recite). 'Paripucchato' means for one who inquires about the meaning. An individual who attains the penetration of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) and reaches Arahantship gradually is called 'neyya'. An individual who is unable to produce the path, the fruit, or even jhāna or insight (vipassanā) in that very life is called 'padaparama'. This individual is called 'padaparama' because the words of the text (byañjana-pada) are the maximum (parama) for him.

'Ye' refers to the two types of individuals (neyya and padaparama). 'Kammāvaraṇa' (karmic obstruction) refers to the five types of heinous kamma (ānantariya-kamma). 'Vipākāvaraṇa' (resultant obstruction) refers to rootless rebirth (ahetuka-paṭisandhi). Since those with double-rooted rebirth (duhetuka) also lack the penetration of the Noble Path...
65:
Double-rooted rebirth (duhetuka-paṭisandhi) should also be understood as "the obstruction of resultants" (vipākāvaraṇa). "By the obstruction of defilements" (kilesāvaraṇa) refers to the obstruction caused by fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi). "Faithless" (assaddhā) refers to those devoid of faith in the Triple Gem, such as the Buddha. "Lacking desire" (acchandika) refers to those devoid of wholesome desire, the desire to act (kattukamyatā-kusala-chanda). The people of Uttarakuru enter a state where there is no wholesome desire. "Lacking wisdom" (duppaññā) refers to those deficient in life-continuum wisdom (bhavaṅga-paññā). Even if one is complete in life-continuum wisdom, if that life-continuum does not serve as a condition for the supramundane state, that person is also called "lacking wisdom." They are incapable of entering (attaining) the Noble Path, known as the certainty of rightness (sammattaniyāma) in wholesome states. The phrases beginning with "na kammāvaraṇena" should be understood by the reverse of the meaning already stated.

Regarding the meaning of terms like "lustful temperament" (rāgacarita), it should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the Visuddhimagga called Paramatthadīpanī (it should be the Paramatthamañjūsā Ṭīkā, which is the explanation of the Visuddhimagga, as it is stated in the conclusion of the Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā itself: "This work is named Paramatthamañjūsā").

"Having started" (ārabbha) means with the intention of making the Buddha aware of one's desired meaning. A rocky mountain is high and firm. Since it is not a mountain of earth or a mixed mountain, it says, "sele yathā pabbatamuddhanī" (as on a crag on a mountain peak). "A palace made of Dhamma" (dhammamayaṃ pāsādaṃ) refers to the supramundane Dhamma. For it is like a mountain in the sense of transcending all things and being elevated, and like a palace in the sense of being lofty. Alternatively, the word "Dhamma" here is a synonym for wisdom (paññā). That wisdom is described in the Abhidhamma as a palace because of its loftiness. Thus it is said:

"Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the wise one, free from sorrow, looks upon the sorrowing folk. As one standing on a mountain peak looks down upon those on the ground, so the wise one looks upon the fools."

In the phrases beginning with "yathā hi," just as a person standing on a mountain and looking down in the darkness of night cannot clearly see the fields, embankments, huts, and the people sleeping there because of the lack of light, but a flame in the huts is visible because of its brightness; in the same way, for the Buddha who has ascended the palace of Dhamma and looks upon the world of beings, those who have not performed meritorious deeds do not come into the range of His knowledge because they are not illuminated by the fire of knowledge and are not noble. Like arrows shot at night...
67:
After speaking of the cause for the attainment of wealth and possessions, He taught the discourse on virtue (sīla-kathā) immediately after the discourse on giving (dāna-kathā) in order to teach the cause for the attainment of a good rebirth. If that giving and virtue are dependent on the round of rebirth, this attainment of rebirth is the result of that giving and virtue. To show this, and to show that through these bases of meritorious action (puññakiriya-vatthu) consisting of giving and virtue, which are distinguished as noble and more noble, there arise immeasurable divine wealth and attainments of rebirth in the Cātumahārājika heaven and so forth, He taught the discourse on heaven (sagga-kathā) immediately after that. After speaking [of heaven], He taught the discourse on the Path (magga-kathā) immediately after the discourse on heaven to show that 'This heaven is defiled by lust and so forth, but the Noble Path is forever undefiled.' In teaching the Path, to show the means of its attainment, He taught the danger (ādīnava) of sensual pleasures—that even those sensual pleasures included in heaven, let alone others, are full of disadvantages, impermanent, unstable, and subject to change. He also taught the lowliness (okāra) of those sensual pleasures—that they are inferior, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and not connected with benefit. He taught the defilement (saṅkilesa) therein—that all states of existence are the basis for defilements. And He taught the advantage of renunciation (nekkhamma)—that Nibbāna is completely free from defilements. This meaning should be understood as being indicated by the word 'iti' in the phrase 'magganti,' which highlights the beginning [of the sequence].

'The source of happiness' (sukhānaṃ nidānaṃ) means the cause of all happiness, including that of the present life, the future life, and that connected with Nibbāna. Whatever worldly happiness of possessions there is, it is well-known that it all has giving as its source. Even for the happiness connected with jhāna, insight (vipassanā), the Path (magga), the Fruit (phala), and Nibbāna, giving is certainly a strong dependence-condition (upanissaya-paccaya). 'The root of attainments' (sampattīnaṃ mūlaṃ) means that this giving is the root cause of all human attainments, such as regional kingship, sovereign wealth, and the attainment of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) shining with the seven jewels, as well as divine attainments such as those of the four Great Kings of the Cātumahārājika heaven, and any other attainments. It is called 'support' (patiṭṭhā) because it is the basis for the pleasant objects like sights and so forth, which are called 'possessions' (bhoga) in the sense of being enjoyed, and for the happiness of enjoyment dependent on them. It is called 'protection' (tāṇa) because it protects and guards one who has reached ruin. It is called 'shelter' (leṇa) because it is a place of hiding for one being oppressed by misfortunes. It is called 'destination' (gati) in the sense of being a place to go to. It is called 'refuge' (parāyaṇa) because it is a resort. It is called 'support' (avassaya) because it is a dependence that does not allow one to fall into ruin. It is called 'object' (ārammaṇa) because it is an object to be grasped and relied upon.

It is like a great Lion Throne (Sīhāsana) made of seven jewels because, being very costly, it prevents one from falling into ruin in every way. It is like the Great Earth (Mahāpathavī) because it allows one to find a footing wherever one goes. Just as a rope supports a weak man when he rises from sitting or when he stands, giving is like a rope to be grasped because it is the cause for the nobility and stability of beings' lives. It is like a boat because it enables one to cross over the suffering of the states of woe (apāya). It is like a hero because it provides great relief from the dangers of enemies such as greed and stinginess. It is like a well-planned city because it protects against the danger of poverty. Because of the state of not being smeared by the mental stains such as stinginess, greed, anger, envy, doubt, and wrong view...
68:
...it is like a lotus (because it is undefiled). [It is like the earth] because it provides a foundation wherever one goes. 'Like a supporting rope' (ālambanarajju-sadisaṃ) means that just as a supporting rope is an aid for a weak man when rising or standing, giving is like a supporting rope because it is the condition for the arising and stability of beings in a state of success. [It is like a boat] in the sense of crossing over the suffering of the woeful planes. [It is like a hero] in the sense of providing proper relief from the danger of opposing enemies such as greed and stinginess. [It is like a well-planned city] in the sense of protecting from the danger of poverty. [It is like a lotus] in the sense of being unsmeared (undefiled) by the stains of the mind such as stinginess, greed, anger, envy, doubt, and wrong view. It is like fire because it burns away the rubbish of stinginess and so forth. It is like a poisonous snake because those very defilements cannot approach it. It is like a lion because of the absence of fear due to being unconquerable. A donor who is a master of giving (dānapati) does not fear anything even in the present, let alone in the future. Here, the person is referred to by the head of the Dhamma (the quality of giving). It is like an elephant because of its great strength. A donor who is a master of giving is strong in the present through the strength of his retinue, and in the future even through physical strength and so forth. It is like a noble bull because it is highly regarded as the 'cause of prosperity'. It is a bringer of safety because it leads from a state of ruin to a state of success, brings one to a safe ground, and brings one from the battle of existence to the security from bondage (yogakkhema/Nibbāna).

Now, to show the virtue of giving as a practice for enlightenment (bodhicariya), demonstrating that giving fulfills attainments that have reached the pinnacle within the cycle of rebirth as well as those beyond the cycle, the passage beginning with 'Dānañhi' is stated. In that context, the attainments of Sakka, Māra, and Brahmā are for one's own benefit only, but the attainment of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) is for the benefit of both oneself and others; to show this, the Cakkavatti's attainment is mentioned after them. To show that these are mundane while the 'Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection' (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa) and so forth are supramundane, the passage beginning with 'sāvakapāramī-ñāṇaṃ' is stated after that. Even among the supramundane, the three types of knowledge are stated in order to show them as noble, more noble, and most noble. That giving is a condition for them has already been stated above. By this, it should be understood that giving is also shown to be the condition for the attainment of the Brahma-world.

Giving (dāna) is the relinquishing of one's own property to others, either with a mind of welfare or a mind of worship toward the recipients (dakkhiṇeyya). Therefore, a donor is a person who has an exclusively benevolent mind toward beings. It is impossible to say of such a person that 'he harms others' or 'he takes the property of others'. Therefore, it is said, 'One who gives can undertake virtue (sīla)'. There is no ornament like virtue, because it is not artificial and brings a special beauty at all times. There is no flower like the flower of virtue.
69:
Here too, the same method applies. In this passage, "There is no flower like the flower of virtue," it should be understood in this same way. In the passage, "There is no scent like the scent of virtue," the verses beginning with "Candanaṃ tagaraṃ vāpi" (Dhp. 54) and "The scent from the bodies of sages who have long practiced asceticism, carried by the wind, goes against the wind," etc., should be mentioned. Virtue is an adornment for beings, a decoration, an ointment of perfume, and a cause for being pleasing to others. Therefore, the Blessed One taught, beginning with "Sīlālaṅkārena hi," and so forth.

The statement, "This heavenly bliss is obtained," is said with reference to virtue undertaken with middling desire (chanda) and other wholesome qualities. Therefore, Sakka, the king of devas, said:
"By inferior holy life (virtue), one is born among the Khattiyas;
By middling, one attains the state of a deva;
By superior, one is purified (from defilements)."

Iṭṭha means pleasant; kanta means desirable; manāpa means that which increases the mind's delight. To show that state of being pleasant and so forth for that deva, the words beginning with "Niccamettha kīḷā" were spoken. Niccaṃ means at all times. Kīḷā refers to happy dwellings (playful enjoyment) associated with sensual pleasures. Sampattiyo means the attainment of wealth (bhoga-sampatti). Dibbaṃ means that which arises in the celestial realm, belonging to the world of devas. Sukhaṃ means bodily happiness and mental happiness. Dibba-sampatti means the attainment of celestial longevity, beauty, retinue, sovereignty, and the fulfillment of sensual pleasures such as visible forms and so forth. In the phrase "evamādī," the word ādi refers to the celestial attainments to be experienced in the Yāma heaven and so forth.

Appassāda means having little gratification, because the wise who see things as they really are do not see any gratification to be enjoyed there in those sensual pleasures. Bahudukkha means having much suffering, because great suffering follows both in the present and in the future. Bahupāyāsa means having many kinds of tribulations. "Ettha" means in these sensual pleasures. Bhiyyo means much. Dosa (fault) means the state of being corrupted by impermanence, lack of gratification, and so forth; therefore, those sensual pleasures do not satisfy the minds of the wise. Alternatively, it is called ādīnava (danger) because extreme misery arises, as it is said: "ādīnaṃ vā pavattatīti ādīnavo." Sensual pleasures appear as such to those who contemplate them truly in the manner of extreme misery. Lāmaka-bhāva means a low state, because it is practiced by the ignoble and not practiced by the noble. Saṃkilissana means being oppressed and tormented. In the phrase "nekkhamme āniśaṃsaṃ" (the benefits of renunciation), however many dangers there are in sensual pleasures, there are just as many benefits in renunciation, as it is the opposite of those dangers. Furthermore, the benefits of renunciation are shown in this way: "This renunciation is free from confinement, free from defilement, departed from sensual pleasures, departed from the perception of sensual pleasure, departed from thoughts of sensual pleasure, departed from the fever of sensual pleasure..." and so forth. He clearly showed and praised the virtues in monkhood, as well as in longevity, beauty, and so forth. It is just as the method already mentioned.
70:
By the method starting with "escape from ill-will" (from the Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Mahāvagga), he showed the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma). He revealed and praised the virtues in monkhood, the jhānas, and so forth.

In the phrase "by the method already mentioned," there is a collection of words such as "kallacitta" (ready mind) which have not yet been explained. In this context, "kallacitta" means having a mind fit for the task (of understanding the teaching). Because the mental stains such as lack of faith have been removed by the teaching previously given, the mind reaches a state capable of receiving the higher teaching; thus, it is said to be a mind fit for the task. Since things like lack of faith, which are like diseases of the mind, have disappeared at that time, it means having a mind free from disease. Due to the disappearance of defilements such as wrong view and conceit, it is a "soft mind" (muducitta). Due to the disappearance of sensual desire and so forth, it is a "mind free from hindrances" (vinīvaraṇacitta). Due to being associated with lofty joy and happiness in the right practice, it is an "exultant mind" (udaggacitta). Due to being endowed with faith in that Dhamma, it is a "clear mind" (pasannacitta). The connection should be made as: "When the Blessed One knew [this]..."

Alternatively, "kallacitta" means a mind free from disease due to the absence of sensual desire. "Muducitta" means a mind that is not harsh due to the power of loving-kindness through the absence of ill-will. "Vinīvaraṇacitta" means a mind that is not covered because distraction is absent due to the absence of restlessness and remorse. "Udaggacitta" means a mind that is not shrinking because it is well-exerted due to the absence of sloth and torpor. "Pasannacitta" means a mind that is inclined toward the right practice due to the absence of doubt. Thus should the meaning be understood.

With the words starting with "Seyyathāpi" (Just as), he showed by way of a simile the abandoning of their defilements and the arising of the Noble Path. "Apagatakāḷakaṃ" means (a cloth) free from black spots and stains. "Sammadeva" means "perfectly well." "Rajanaṃ" means dye such as blue, yellow, etc. "Paṭiggaṇheyya" means it would take up or the color would come out. By the phrase "on that very seat," he showed their ability to practice insight (vipassanā) quickly, their sharp wisdom, their easy practice, and their swift direct knowledge. "Virajaṃ" means "stainless" because of the absence of the dust of lust, etc., which leads to the lower realms. "Vītamalaṃ" (free from impurity) is because of the absence of the impurities of wrong view and doubt without remainder. Or, "virajaṃ" is because of the absence of the dust of defilements to be abandoned by the first path. "Vītamalaṃ" is because of the absence of the impurity of lacking the five precepts. By the term "Dhamma-cakkhu" (the Eye of Dhamma), in the Brahmāyu Sutta, the lower three paths are meant; in the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, the destruction of taints (Arahattamagga) is meant; but in this sutta, the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpattimagga) is intended. The sentence "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease" shows the mode of the arising of that Path. A question may arise: Does not the Path-knowledge take only the unconditioned (Nibbāna) as its object, and not the conditioned? This is true. However, because that Path-knowledge arises by taking Nibbāna as its object and penetrating all conditioned things by way of its function, it is spoken of in that way.

In the simile pointed out as "a clean cloth," this is the comparison of the simile. The mind should be understood as being like the cloth. Just as the cloth is soiled by adventitious stains, so the mind is [soiled] by the stains of lust and so forth...
71:
The defilement of the mind by lust (rāga) and so forth is like the defilement of cloth by adventitious stains. The Dhamma taught in sequence is like a washing stone, and the Dhamma is like water. Just as one soaks cloth in water and washes it by thoroughly kneading the dark spots with sand-soap and cow-dung ash, so too, one must exert effort to cleanse the mind through the sequence of hearing the Dhamma and so forth, sprinkling the mind with the moisture of faith (saddhā) and weakening the defilements (kilesa) with mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā). Through that exertion, just as various dark stains are removed from the cloth, the defilements are abandoned. The Noble Path (ariya magga) is like dye. Just as cloth dyed with dye becomes brilliant, the mind from which defilements have been removed is purified by the Noble Path.

When it is said 'diṭṭhadhamma' (one who has seen the Dhamma), since there can be other types of seeing (dassana) besides seeing with knowledge (ñāṇa), the term 'pattadhamma' (one who has attained the Dhamma) is used to exclude those other types of seeing. Since 'attainment' (patti) can also exist other than attainment through knowledge, the term 'viditadhamma' (one who has known the Dhamma) is used to show a special kind of attainment. Since such 'knowing' could be partial, the term 'pariyogāḷhadhamma' (one who has plunged into the Dhamma) is used to show knowledge without remainder. By this term, their realization of the Truths (sacca-abhisambodhi) is clearly shown. For Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), while accomplishing tasks such as full understanding (pariññā) through a single realization, penetrates and plunges into the four Truths from all sides without remainder. The rest is as explained below.

'Cīvaradānādīni' refers to the offering of requisites such as robes. If a person offers the eight requisites, or just the bowl and robes, to a Noble One (ariya) such as a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), or to a worldling (puthujjana) endowed with virtue, and makes the aspiration, 'May this gift of requisites be a support for becoming an "Ehi Bhikkhu" in the future,' then when their merit reaches fulfillment and they meet the Buddhas face-to-face, it will lead to obtaining requisites created by psychic power (iddhimaya-parikkhāra). The meaning is that they become endowed with proper conduct like elders of a hundred years.

'Sandassesi' means showing clearly as if before one's eyes. 'Idhalokattha' refers to the meaning of the five aggregates existing in this world. The same method applies to 'paralokattha'. He showed it by way of common characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa) and specific characteristics (sa-lakkhaṇa). Therefore, He said 'anicca' and so forth. Therein, He showed 'anicca' (impermanent) because of non-existence after having come to be. He showed 'dukkha' (suffering) because of being constantly oppressed by rise and fall. He showed 'anattā' (non-self) because of not following one's will. He showed the five aggregates, which have characteristics such as being deformed (ruppana), as 'khandha' in the sense of a heap (rāsa). He showed the eighteen 'dhātu' (elements), such as the eye and so forth, in the sense of being non-sentient and soulless. He showed the twelve 'āyatana' (bases), which are the doors and objects such as the eye and so forth.
72:
He showed that these twelve causal factors starting with ignorance (avijjā) and ending with aging and death (jarā-maraṇa) are Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Under the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), He showed these five characteristics: four by way of cause and one by way of the moment, as mentioned before. By the word 'tathā', the phrase 'pañca lakkhaṇāni' is drawn in. In the word 'dassento', the word 'iti' has the sense of pointing out; it means 'thus'. By the word 'nirayaṃ', He showed all hells, including the eight great hells and the sixteen prominent (ussada) hells. By the word 'tiracchānayoni', He showed the various animal worlds, divided into those without feet, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, etc., and categorized as deer, beasts, birds, land creatures, water creatures, etc. By the word 'petti-visaya', He showed the various worlds of ghosts (peta), divided into those consumed by hunger and thirst, those who eat vomit, those who live on what is given by others, those with thirst like a burning fire, etc. By the word 'asurakāya', He showed the host of Kālakañjika Asuras. Having thus spoken of the meaning of the other world in the woeful planes (duggati), He now spoke 'tiṇṇam kusalānaṃ vipākaṃ' etc., to show the world in the happy planes (sugati). Having included the Subhakiṇṇa Brahmas within the Vehapphala Brahmas, He said only 'navannaṃ brahmalokānaṃ' (nine Brahma worlds) because there is no prosperity to be shown in the non-percipient (asañña) and formless (arūpa) realms, and because they are difficult to understand. 

The word 'gaṇhāpesi' means He made them properly undertake (practice) those dhammas. Encouragement (samuttejana) means causing them to exert effort so that the unhelpful dhammas among those properly undertaken decrease and are abandoned, while the helpful dhammas increase and are purified; thus He said 'abbhussāhesi' (He roused them). To show how that rousing of effort occurs, He said 'idhalokatthañceva' and so forth. The phrase 'tāsetvā tāsetvā' means sharpening or making them keen by bringing them to a state of clarity. The phrase 'adhigataṃ viya katvā' means making it as if those to whom He preached were experiencing that meaning directly. For those who are teachable (veneyya), the meaning revealed by the Buddhas appears clearly, even more distinct than if seen directly. Indeed, the Blessed One is praised thus:

'Though this world is ablaze with the eleven fires, it does not reach spiritual urgency (saṃvega) because it is enveloped in delusion (sammoha). Having heard the words of the Great Sage connected with the perception of danger (ādīnava), just as one reaches spiritual urgency, the words of the Buddhas are very clear, as if seen directly.'

Therefore, He said 'dvattiṃsakammakāraṇapañcavīsatimahābhayappabhedaṃ' and so forth. The thirty-two types of torture are mentioned in the Dukkhakkhandha Sutta as 'they even cut off hands' and so forth...
73:
They should be understood according to the method presented. The twenty-five great fears, such as the fear of birth, the fear of aging, the fear of sickness, and the fear of death, should be understood according to the method presented in the Cūḷaniddesa and various suttas. Āghātanabhaṇḍikā refers to an executioner's block or a great hell, and it is also called accādhāna.

"Paṭiladdhaguṇena codesi" means that by the attainment of various virtues, [the Buddha] showed them clearly, saying, "You have also attained this benefit, this advantage," as if asking and exhorting, "Has there ever been such a benefit before this?" Therefore, it is said, "He spoke making it a great advantage."

"Tappaccayañca kilamathaṃ" refers to the fatigue, distress, and affliction that arise in the continuity of various beings due to the cause of the arising of formations (saṅkhāra). In this context (in the discourse taught for the sake of attaining the first path), it is "peaceful" (santa) because it is the subsiding of all formations. It is "sublime" (paṇīta) because it is the supreme happiness that never satiates. It is "protection" (tāṇa) in the sense of protecting from all the suffering of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra). It is "shelter" (leṇa) because it is the place of hiding for those whose hearts are weary of the round of rebirth. By the word "etc." (ādi), terms such as destination (gati), refuge (patiṭṭha), and supreme solace (paramassāsa) are included.

## Mahājanakāyapabbajjāvaṇṇanā

Because there were no monks sufficient to be called a Saṅgha, it is said, "because the Saṅgha was not complete." At that time, there were only the two chief disciples.

## Cārikāanujānanavaṇṇanā

To the question "When did it arise?", after answering briefly with "Since the Enlightenment," etc., the phrase "The Blessed One, it is said," etc., is stated to show the matter in detail. Desiring to favor his father, he stayed for seven years, seven months, and seven days since his Enlightenment—this should be understood in connection. This stay was because there were no beings to be converted (veneyya) at that time. He had the exterior covered with coarse mats, the interior covered with cloths, and the top also covered with cloths; beneath that, he had a ceiling decorated with golden stars, etc., made. "Mālāvacchake" refers to things entwined with flower garlands in the shape of small flowering trees. "Gandhantare" means in the midst of perfumes filled in jars. "Pupphāni" refers to aquatic flowers filled in jars, etc., and terrestrial flowers filled in baskets, etc.
74:
Although this King Bandhuma was indeed the father of the Buddha Vipassī, Buddhas are the teachers of the world. They cannot be made to follow anyone's will; rather, they make others follow their own will. Therefore, the King said, "I cannot give the Saṅgha of monks [to you]." Dānamukha means the objects of giving which are the means of performing an act of charity. "Now they do not allow me to give" means that now the citizens of Bandhumatī no longer give me the opportunity to perform charity. Paritassanajīvita means poverty, which is living a life of suffering and distress. "Sufficient for all the monks" means it was sufficient to offer to the Blessed One and the 168,000 monks when they arrived at the refectory; it does not mean it was insufficient for all monks to eat to their fill. Therefore, it was said, "The general also gave his own gift." Jeṭṭhikaṭṭhāne means in the place of the chief queen. Tatheva katvā means having placed spies. Suci means pure. Paṇīta means sublime food; this word paṇīta is a neuter gender used as an adverb, as in "ekamantaṃ," etc. Bhañjitvā means having pressed or squeezed. Jātisappikhīrādīhiyeva means only with ghee, milk, etc., produced within the house or obtained from one's own cows.

Enduring, overcoming, and tolerating the insults of others, the harm done by others, and the afflictions caused by cold, heat, and so on, is called khanti (patience). Because that patience specifically burns and destroys the states opposite to virtue (sīla) and so on, it is called the supreme ascetic practice (tapo). Therefore, it is said, "Patience known as endurance (adhivāsanakhanti) is the supreme ascetic practice." By the term "adhivāsanakhanti," it is distinguished from the patience of reflecting on the Dhamma (dhammanijjhānakkhanti). Titikkhanaṃ and khamanaṃ are simply titikkhā (forbearance). Grammarians explain the word titikkhā in the sense of patience. For that very reason, it is said, "It is a synonym (vevacana) of khanti," and so on. Sabbākārena means by all modes, such as being peaceful, sublime, subtle, secure, and safe. One is not called a "gone forth" (pabbajita) if there is no banishing of the states that should be banished. The third line of that verse is merely a synonym because there is no difference in meaning. By the words "na hi," etc., that very meaning is clarified. Parama is called "supreme" in the sense of the highest, as the word para denotes excellence, as in "puggalaparoparaññū," etc. Para means "another." Now, to show the meaning by taking the word para as a synonym for "another," the phrase "atha vā," etc., is stated. Malassa means of the stain of evil. Apabbājitattā means because of not being removed or not being banished.
75:
Because it is not discarded, it is called 'anirākata'. Because those evil unwholesome states are calmed, it is called 'samita'. It has been stated (in the Dhammapada): "Because evil unwholesome states are calmed, one is called a 'samaṇa'."

In another way, when the Blessed One was expounding the Ovāda Pātimokkha to the monks, since the Pātimokkha discourse has virtue (sīla) as its foundation, and since anger (dosa) is the specific opposite of virtue, he first said, "Patience (khanti) is the supreme austerity (tapo)," in order to show the method of subduing it. By that statement, he taught patience as the means to abandon anger arising from undesirable objects (aniṭṭhārammaṇa). By the word 'titiṭṭhā' (endurance), however, he taught the means to abandon greed arising from desirable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa). By both of these, he showed the meaning of living by overcoming the lack of delight (rati) that has arisen. The Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme because it is the cessation of the 'weaving' of craving (taṇhā).

In that teaching, by the word 'khanti', he showed the absence of failure in conduct (payoga-vipatti), and by the word 'titiṭṭhā', he showed the absence of failure in intention (āsaya-vipatti). Likewise, by the word 'khanti', he showed the endurance of the wrongs of others, and by the word 'titiṭṭhā', he showed the non-committing of wrongs against others. 

Having thus shown the Pātimokkha through the affirmative method (anwaya) by way of the initial causes, he now spoke the words beginning with "Na hi" to show that Pātimokkha through the negative method (vyatireka). By that statement, just as depriving beings of life and harming them with hands, clods of earth, sticks, and so on are called 'harming others' (parūpaghāta) and 'oppressing others' (paraviheṭhana), so too are stealing the capital and property of others, committing sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech to cause discord, attacking others by exposing sensitive personal flaws with harsh speech, frivolous and useless talk, coveting the property of others (abhijjhā), planning to kill or oppress (byāpāda), and wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) also considered 'harming' and 'oppressing'. Therefore, he showed that by performing any unwholesome course of action (akusala-kammapatha) or unwholesome deed, one cannot be called a 'pabbajita' (renunciant) or a 'samaṇa' (ascetic).

'Sabba-akusalassa' (of all unwholesome) refers to all blameworthy states included within the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness. 'Doing' (karaṇa) means the arising of those unwholesome states within one's own mental continuity. Therefore, 'not doing' by way of rejecting those unwholesome states is called 'anuppādana' (non-arising). Because the word 'kusalassa' (of the wholesome) will be followed by "This is the teaching of the Buddhas," it makes known the states of the Noble Path (ariya-magga) as well as the wholesome states of the three planes (tebhūmaka-kusala) which are the requisites for those Path states. Therefore, the teachers say 'catubhūmaka-kusalassa' (of the wholesome states of the four planes). 'Upasampadā' means fulfillment; since that fulfillment is the thorough acquisition of that wholesome state, it is called 'paṭilābha' (attainment). 'Citta-jotana' (making the mind radiant) means making the mind luminous, which is the total purification (pariyodapana).

This is because the mind of one possessed of the Highest Path (arahatta-magga) is said to be totally purified; however, at the moment of the Highest Fruition (arahatta-phala), it is already purified as there is no further need for purification. Thus, referring to the completed purification, he said, "That occurs through Arahatship." The intention is that all evil is abandoned by way of abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna) and so forth. By the words 'sīla-saṃvarena' (through restraint of virtue), when the wholesome states of the three planes are included, the abandonment of the remaining unwholesome states is also included. By doing so, the use of the word 'sabba' (all) is firmly established.
76:
It is (accomplished) through mundane and supramundane tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā). 'Sampādetvā' means having accomplished or having fulfilled. Here, accomplishment should be understood as occurring through the causal states for the resultant state, either as conascent (sahajāta) or as previously established (purimasiddha).

'Kassaci' (to anyone) refers to any kind of blame or insult toward any being, including those of low status. By saying this, he prohibits insulting even in jest. In the phrase 'upaghātassa akaraṇaṃ' (not harming), the word 'kassaci' should also be brought in and connected. 'Kāyena' (by body) is merely an illustration. This is because harming others through the mind, such as by planning their misfortune, must also be avoided. Alternatively, the word 'kāyena' here should be understood to include the immaterial body (arūpa-kāya), not only the physical body (karaja-kāya) and bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti).

'Atimokkha' refers to the virtue (sīla) that is exceptionally principal among the various types of virtue. The same term is also expressed as 'atipamokkha' by changing the prefix. Having thus explained the term by its variations, he states its true meaning as 'noble virtue' (uttama-sīla). By the words 'pāti vā' and so forth, he shows that it is called 'pātimokkha' because it guards (pālana), protects (rakkhana), and exceptionally liberates (mokkhana) or causes liberation (mocana). It is called 'atimokkha' because it exceptionally liberates one from evil; here, the virtue which is the cause is metaphorically referred to as the agent (kattar).

'Yo vā naṃ' means whichever person undertakes that Pātimokkha restraint virtue (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) and guards it without breaking it. Because it liberates that person who is called 'pātī' (the guardian) and who stands in the Pātimokkha restraint virtue, it is called 'pātimokkha'. This is the summary here; the detailed meaning of the word 'Pātimokkha' should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā.

'Mattaññutā' means moderation in eating. Since that moderation is specifically to be taken by way of the virtue related to the use of requisites (paccayasannissita-sīla), he said, "knowing the measure by way of acceptance and consumption." If it is taken by way of the virtue of purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla), it should be said, "by way of seeking and distributing."

'Saṅghaṭṭana-virahita' means free from contact with people; the meaning is 'secluded', being free from the congestion of people. 

He shows contentment with the four requisites (catupaccaya-santosa). This is because by the general mention of contentment with requisites, the other two are also illuminated through the method of the 'characteristic' (lakkhaṇa-hāra-naya). By the phrase 'aṭṭhasamāpatti-vasībhāvāya' (for the mastery of the eight attainments), he shows the purpose for which the resort to secluded dwellings is desired, namely, the devotion to the higher mind (adhicitta-anuyoga). Here, the eight attainments are intended as those that serve as the basis for insight (vipassanā-pādaka); it is not just any attainment. Thus, it should be understood that the entirety of the devotion to the higher mind is illuminated.
77:
## Commentary on the Announcement of the Deities

'Ettāvatā' means 'by this much of the sutta portion.' In that sutta also, it should be connected as 'showing the state of being well-penetrated by speaking thus.' The word 'ca' has the sense of distinction (vyatireka); by that word, it connects the meaning that is about to be spoken. 'Ekamidāhaṃ' is 'ekaṃ ahaṃ.' The word 'idaṃ' is merely a particle (nipāta). By the word 'ādi,' the text beginning with 'bhikkhave samayaṃ' should be taken. In this context, the words should be connected as 'Monks, I at one time...'

'Subhagavane' means it is called 'Subhaga' because it possesses beauty (subhaga); it is called 'Subhaga' either because of its beautiful glory or because it has beautiful desired objects. That forest is called 'Subhaga' because it is endowed with glory and because humans desire beautiful sensual pleasures in that forest. It is also called 'Subhaga' because it is liked by many people. It is called 'Vana' because it 'vanayati' (causes love); it means it causes love for itself through its own perfection. Alternatively, it is called 'Vana' because it 'vanute' (begs); it means that because of its own perfection, it is as if it begs beings, saying 'Enjoy me.' Because it is a forest that possesses beautiful glory and causes love, it is called 'Subhagavana'; (He dwelt) in that Subhagavana. In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, considering 'What is the use of this elaboration?', it is simply stated as 'in the forest of this name.' Indeed, the Sal tree is called 'Sāla,' and any tree or the lordly tree of the forest (vanappati) is also called so. Here, since only the last one (the lordly tree of the forest) is intended, it says 'at the foot of the lordly tree of the forest.' 'Mūlasamugghātavasena' means by way of completely uprooting the latent tendencies (anusaya).

'Na vihāyantī' means they do not leave (their prosperity and special attainment) because of their unshakable nature (akuppa). The statement 'They are called Atappa because they do not cause any being to burn (suffer)' is said because that name is established as a conventional name (rūḷhī) for those Brahmas. Otherwise, all inhabitants of the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) would be called Atappa as they do not cause any being to burn. In the definitions starting with 'Na vihāyantī,' the same method should be understood. 'Sundaradassanā' means they are beautiful to look at, so it says 'abhirūpā' (handsome/beautiful), etc. Their sight is beautiful; meaning, seeing with the eye and perceiving with consciousness are beautiful. All those Brahmas are great, because in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhava), there are no Brahmas superior to those Akaniṭṭha Brahmas.

'Sattannaṃ buddhānaṃ vasena' means by way of the life stories (apadāna) of the seven Buddhas. Even if one Aviha Brahma requested by the Aviha inhabitants speaks, it is considered as spoken by all of them; thus it is said 'Likewise, the Aviha deities.' The same method applies to the rest of the text. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'The deities said this to me.' As for the statement in the Pali 'many hundreds of deities,' it is because all those Brahmas are those who arose in that Suddhāvāsa after attaining the special distinction in the Dispensation (Sāsana) in later times.
78: It is spoken by way of the Brahmas who arose in that Suddhāvāsa after attaining the special distinction in His Dispensation. 'Anusandhidvayaṃ' means the two types of connection: the connection related to the term 'dhammadhātu' and the connection related to the term 'devatārocana.' 'Niyyātento' means concluding (ending). If there is any statement in this Mahāpadāna Sutta that has not been analyzed in terms of meaning, that statement is easily understood. ## The Līnatthappakāsanā Ṭīkā, the sub-commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta, is finished.
79:
## 2. Mahānidāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā
## Nidāna Vaṇṇanā

'Janapadino' means the princes who have a country (janapada) or are the lords and masters of a country; they are called Kuru by lineage. If the country where those princes live is one, why is it used in the plural? It is said that it is used by way of conventional usage (rūḷhī). Grammarians who contemplate syllables and words desire such genders and numbers as appropriate in such places. This is a conventional usage here, just as in other Pali texts: 'He dwells among the Angas, he dwells among the Mallas.' However, in the words 'janapada' and 'jāti' which distinguish that country, only the singular is used.

In the phrase 'Aṭṭhakathācariyā pana,' the word 'pana' shows a special meaning. By that word 'pana,' it highlights the special meaning to be spoken later, such as 'bahuke pana,' etc., meaning 'it is plural only because there are many objects of meaning.' 'Sutvā' (having heard) is due to hearing the successive reports following the sight of King Mandhātu's power. 'Anusaṃyāyantena' means by wandering along in order. By the phrase 'etesaṃ ṭhānaṃ' (their place), it refers to the Cātumahārājika celestial mansion, starting with the moon and the sun. Therefore, it is said 'he went to that heaven,' etc. 'So' refers to King Mandhātu. 'Taṃ' refers to the state of being a Cātumahārājika king. 'Gahetvā' means having accepted. That king asked the Counselor-gem (pariṇāyakaratana) again.

They stand in the gate-keeper's level because they have obtained the guardianship at the four gates of the celestial city and in the Sudhammā assembly hall. The phrase 'adorned with a thousand divine trees' should also be applied to places like 'Cittalatāvana,' etc.

'Stood on the ground' means falling (from heaven) and standing in a place near the ground. The Wheel-gem (cakkaratana) does not fall on the ground. Soon after standing thus, it disappeared because there was no longer the sovereignty of a Wheel-turning Monarch in that existence. Other teachers say, 'It disappeared after standing for a long time.' The king went alone by his own power. 'Manussabhāva' (human state) means the human state such as the human smell and the physical effects of the body. 'Pāturahosi' (became manifest) means because the kamma to be experienced in a subsequent life (aparāpariyāyavedanīya kamma), which gives results in the deva world, found an opportunity, the divine state such as always being sixteen years old and the flowers not withering became manifest. At that time, since humans had an incalculable lifespan (asaṅkheyyāyuka), after ruling as Sakka, he became dissatisfied due to great greed, thinking 'What is the use of this half-kingship to me?' Then, due to the harshness of the season in the human world, being touched by hot wind and hot sun, he passed away.
80:
Because a specific meaning established in parts characterizes the meaning of the whole, even a single country is referred to in the plural.

According to the method of Nirutti (etymology), the meaning is explained by the letter 'da'. Just as 'rūpabhava' is called 'rūpa' by the method of dropping the subsequent word, 'Kammāsapāda' is called 'Kammāsa'. As to why he is called 'Kammāsapāda', it is stated starting with 'Tassa kira', etc. In the word 'damito', what kind of taming is intended? It means being restrained from the state of being a man-eater (porisāda). Regarding the phrase 'Ime pana therā', some teachers say they are the Majjhima-bhāṇaka elders. Others say they are the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariyas) or the Dīgha-bhāṇaka elders. In both cases, they say so with reference to Cūḷakammāsadamma. Kammāsapāda, the son of an ogress, was tamed there by the Bodhisatta when he was Prince Alīnasattu. However, the place where the King of Bārāṇasī was tamed by being restrained from man-eating during the time of Sutasoma is called Mahākammāsadamma. Saying 'atruja' after 'putta' is to show that he is a biological son (born of the breast).

The region where those people lived acquired the name 'Kuru country'. Those people, having come from Uttarakuru, observed the five precepts according to the rules they had kept there. Because later generations followed their example, it became known as the 'Kuruvatta-dhamma' (Kuru practice), which continued uninterruptedly by the power of the local custom. This meaning should be understood through the Kurudhamma Jātaka. To show where that Kurudhamma first became defiled in later times, it is said starting with 'Kururaṭṭhavāsīnaṃ', etc. In a place where there is no monastery for the Blessed One to reside, it is the nature of the introductory discourse (nidānakathā) to mention only the alms-village. It is like the statement: 'He was staying among the Sakyans at a Sakyan town named Devadaha.' To show this meaning, it is said starting with 'Avasanokāsato', etc.

Addressing as 'Āyasmā' (Venerable), 'Devānaṃ Piya' (Beloved of the Gods), or 'Tatra bhava' is an endearing form of address. Therefore, it is said that 'Āyasmā' is a pleasant word. Since this pleasant word is spoken out of great respect, it is said to be a word of reverence.

By avoiding being too far or too close, 'neither too far nor too close' is taken. This should be known as the distance where two people can touch each other by extending their hands at the minimum. Looking eye-to-eye is also considered disrespectful. 'Gīvaṃ parivattetvā' means stretching the neck by turning it.
81:
'Kulasangahatthāya' means for the sake of favoring families out of compassion; by accepting alms, it generates a great flow of merit for those donors, like dropping a bag of a thousand coins for them. 'Paṭisammajjitvā' means having swept again even a place already swept by resident pupils, out of a desire to act with thoroughness. 'Tikkhattuṃ' (three times) refers to three rounds associated with the four modes mentioned as 'from the beginning to the end,' etc. By this, it means he contemplated twelve times.

Because our Blessed One taught with such profundity, it is said, 'All Buddhas... have taught thus,' staying within the lineage of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya). 'Sālindaṃ' refers to the open terrace along with its surroundings. By the phrase 'as if lifting Mount Sineru,' the extreme difficulty of such a discourse is expressed. The Sutta itself is called 'Suttantakathā' because it is a category of the Dhamma (dhammakkhandha).

Just as knowing the various occasions and locations of the Vinaya regulations is the exclusive domain of Omniscient Knowledge, so too is the analytical explanation of Dependent Origination (paccayākāra), which is free from the two extremes and devoid of a 'doer' or 'experiencer' (atta). To show this, the passage starting with 'Buddhānañhi' is begun. In that context, 'ṭhānāni' means causes. 'The roar is great' means that because the Dhamma to be taught has many aspects and is difficult to understand, the roar of the teaching proceeding through various methods is grand, extensive, and has many divisions. 'Knowledge penetrates' means that because it is so extensive, the knowledge of the teaching repeatedly enters into the Dhamma to be taught, dividing it into parts; it is as if it stands having entered into it. 'The greatness of the Buddha's knowledge is manifest' means that the nobility of the Buddhas' knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa) and knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa) becomes clear as the teacher and penetrator of such Dhamma.

Furthermore, according to the saying, 'Every verbal act of the Blessed Buddha is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge,' there is no discourse of the Blessed One that is devoid of knowledge. Due to his lion-like conduct, it proceeds uniformly everywhere. However, by the power of the Dhamma to be taught, the discourse is specifically penetrated by knowledge and is exceedingly profound.

How can a discourse, upon reaching the Vinaya regulations, be one that strikes with the three characteristics and is connected with emptiness (suññata)? Even in that Vinaya, the discourse proceeding according to the inclinations of the assembled audience explains the impermanence of formations, etc., and reveals the state of all phenomena as being non-self and not belonging to a self. Therefore, it is said: 'Having given a Dhamma talk in many ways' (anekapariyāyena dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā), etc.
82:
"Āpajjāti" means having reached. Just as one reaches the presence of the Great Elephant, the Buddha, and he emits the crane-like cry of the Dhamma teaching spoken through his wisdom, so too, having reached [that state] (one might listen).

"Pamāṇātikkameti" is used in the sense of "immeasurable," as in the Pali passages beginning with "yāvañcidaṃ tena bhagavatā." This word "yāva" indicates an incomparable and immeasurable state. Therefore, it is called "extremely deep meaning."

"Avabhasatīti" means it is evident or it appears. It is said as "dissati" (it is seen), referring to how it appeared to the wisdom of the Venerable Ānanda. If this Dependent Origination is indeed absolutely deep, why is it shown as "appearing deep" (gambhīrāvabhāsatā)? It is true; however, the use of "appearing deep" regarding this Dependent Origination is only for the purpose of showing its absolute depth. Therefore, by showing the fourfold aspects found in other things through the method of negation, the phrase beginning with "ekañhi" is stated to make its absolute depth clear.
