"Etaṃ natthi" means that these two—being not deep and not appearing deep—do not exist. Thus, it shows that the last of the four categories previously mentioned is obtained. Therefore, the phrase beginning with "ayañhi" is spoken.

To point out the depths by which Dependent Origination is called "deep" through four metaphors, the phrase beginning with "bhavaggaggahaṇāya" is spoken. Just as the highest plane of existence (bhavagga) cannot be reached by stretching out one's hand because of its distance, the meaning of how effects such as formations (saṅkhāra) arise from causes such as ignorance (avijjā) cannot be grasped by ordinary knowledge. Just as an ordinary person cannot split Mount Sineru to extract the essence or the mountain's flavor, the Dhamma and the meaning (attha) contained in Dependent Origination cannot be known by splitting, analyzing, and penetrating them with ordinary knowledge. Just as an ordinary person cannot cross the Great Ocean by swimming with both arms, the Dependent Origination, which is like the Great Ocean in its vastness, cannot be fully taught according to the sequence of the teaching by ordinary knowledge. Just as an ordinary person cannot overturn the great earth to take the essence of the earth, the causal state of those causes—how ignorance and so on become causes for formations and so on—cannot be extracted and grasped by ordinary knowledge.

In this way, the four metaphors should be applied according to the four kinds of depth. This explanation of the meaning is made from the perspective of ordinary knowledge; for the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who have seen the Four Noble Truths have the nature of penetration into that Dependent Origination. Nevertheless, because the knowledge of the disciples (sāvakas) and Paccekabuddhas regarding that Dependent Origination is only partial, while only the knowledge of the Buddhas is complete, the phrase beginning with "buddhavisayaṃ pañhaṃ" is spoken.
83:
"Ussādento" means uplifting or learning through wisdom. "Apasādento" means rebuking or restraining.

## Ussādanāvaṇṇanā

"Tena" means by that state of possessing great wisdom. In that [Dependent Origination], although it was clear to the Elder Ānanda, and although Dependent Origination is deep to others, [the Buddha uplifted him]. "Subhojanarasapuṭṭhassa" means [the meaning of] one who is nourished by the taste of good food. "Katayogassa" means [the meaning of] one who has familiarity through constant practice. "Mallapāsāṇaṃ" refers to a stone that can only be lifted by powerful wrestlers. "Kuhiṃ imassa bhāriyaṭṭhānaṃ" means "In which part of this stone is the heaviest portion?"—this is said to show the lightness of that stone [to the strong person].

The metaphor is shown only by the Timirapiṅgala fish because of its extremely vast size. Therefore, the phrase beginning with "tassa kira" is spoken. "Pakkuthati" means turning around and whirling in circles as if boiling. This is a description of a specific characteristic. On the back of the great fish, some parts remain along with the scales. "Kāyūpapannassa" means one endowed with a great body, meaning one who has a massive frame.

"Piñchavaṭṭi" means a bundle of tail feathers. "Supaṇṇavātaṃ" refers to the wind created by the flapping of wings in such actions as catching Nagas.

## Pubbūpanissayasampattikathāvaṇṇanā

The phrase beginning with "ito kira" is spoken to explain in detail the causes indicated by the words "pubbūpanissayasampattiyā" and so on. Therein, "ito" means from this aeon (kappa). "Satasahassime" means in the hundred-thousandth aeon. The city named Haṃsāvatī was the birthplace [of Padumuttara Buddha]. "Dhurapattānī" refers to the very long lotus leaves on the outer side.

"Kaniṭṭhabhātā" refers to a younger half-brother, like the Elder Nanda is to our Buddha. For the Buddhas, there are no full brothers. How could there be elder brothers? Even younger brothers do not exist [in the same womb]. "Bhogaṃ" means wealth and possessions. "Upasanto" refers to a peaceful countryside where the dangers caused by thieves and robbers have been quelled.

"Dve sāဋကေ nivāsetvā" means having used only two garments for one's own body and having discarded all other requisites from oneself.

"Pattaggahaṇatthaṃ" is for the purpose of holding the bowl of the Venerable one who was shifting it from hand to hand because of the hot food placed inside. "Uttarisāဋကံ" means one's own upper robe.
84:
These manifest places refer to the well-known locations of the meritorious deeds of the Venerable Ānanda within the teaching of the Blessed One mentioned above. 'Having taken rebirth' refers to taking rebirth on the very same day our Great Bodhisatta took rebirth.

## Description of the Stay at the Ford, etc. (Titthavāsādivaṇṇanā)

Learning (uggahaṇa) is learning the Pali text. Hearing (savana) is hearing the meaning. Inquiry (paripucchana) is inquiring about the meaning of difficult points. Retention (dhāraṇa) is keeping both the Pali text and its meaning in mind. All this should be understood here by way of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).

For the Stream-enterers... (and so on). Because of the destruction of delusion (moha), it becomes manifest through direct personal experience that 'whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.' Thus, [Dependent Origination] becomes manifest. Discerning mentality and materiality (nāmarūpapariccheda) is the penetrative understanding of mentality and materiality along with their causes.

## Description of the Profundity of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādagambhīratāvaṇṇanā)

To elaborate on the meaning briefly stated as 'profundity of meaning' (atthagambhīratā), etc., the passage beginning with 'Therein' is commenced. The meaning of arising and coming into existence due to the condition of birth (jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭha) refers to the meaning of the successive arising of aging and death, which arises from birth as its condition and conforms to its own cause. Alternatively, it is the combination of the meaning of arising (sambhūtaṭṭha) and the meaning of coming into existence (samudāgataṭṭha). Aging and death do not fail to arise from birth; nor do they arise from any other cause besides birth. Thus, it is called the meaning of arising due to the condition of birth. In this way, because it follows successively from birth, it is called jātipaccayasamudāgataṭṭha. Whatever birth acts as a condition in whatever way, it means the appearance [of aging and death] in accordance with that. This meaning is profound in the sense of being 'unfathomable' (agādha), as there is no footing for the knowledge of those who have not accumulated the requisites of merit (pāramī). The same method applies to the remaining terms.

The meaning of ignorance being the condition for formations refers to the manner and the state in which ignorance is a condition for formations. Because both the manner of occurrence and the state in which ignorance exists as a condition for various formations are difficult to understand, ignorance [is a condition] for formations by way of nine modes...
85:
The meaning of the condition that ignorance [assists] formations by way of nine modes is profound in the sense of being unfathomable, as there is no footing for the knowledge of those who have not accumulated the requisites of merit. This method is the same for the remaining terms.

In some places, it is taught in forward order (anuloma); in some places, in reverse order (paṭiloma). Here, however, the meaning described as the arising of the conditioned effect due to the arising of the condition is intended as forward order. The meaning described as the cessation of the conditioned effect due to the cessation of the condition is intended as reverse order. Alternatively, proceeding from the beginning to the end is intended as forward order, and proceeding from the end to the beginning is intended as reverse order.

When taught from the beginning in forward order, or from the end in reverse order, there are three links (tisandhi) and four groups (catusaṅkhepa). When taught from the middle in reverse order, such as 'Bhikkhus, what is the source of these four nutriments?' etc., or in forward order, such as 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises,' etc., there are two links and three groups. In texts such as 'Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that lead to fetters, craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging arises,' etc., there is one link and two groups.

Indeed, Dependent Origination consisting of a single factor is also taught. This single-factor Dependent Origination is to be understood by the power of this sutta: 'Therein, bhikkhus, the well-informed noble disciple closely and wisely attends to Dependent Origination itself: "Thus, when this exists, this comes to be... [it] ceases,"' and 'Bhikkhus, dependent on contact to be experienced as pleasant, pleasant feeling arises.'

Thus, because it is taught in various ways due to various reasons, Dependent Origination is profound in terms of teaching (desanā). Therefore, it is said, 'This is the profundity of teaching.' Indeed, in that profound Dependent Origination of the teaching, no knowledge other than Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññutañāṇa) finds a footing.

In the passages beginning with 'But of ignorance' (avijjāya pana), the meaning of non-knowing (aññāṇa) of ignorance, which is the opposite of knowledge (ñāṇa) characterized by knowing, is profound. The meaning of non-seeing (adassana), which is the opposite of knowledge that is like vision by making the object manifest, is profound. The meaning of non-penetration of the truths (saccāsampaṭivedha) of that ignorance is profound, whereby it exists by covering and shrouding the true nature of suffering, etc., according to their actual essence, not allowing them to be penetrated.

Abhisaṅkharaṇa means arranging or planning (saṃvidhāna, pakappana). Āyūhana means combining (sampiṇḍana), the act of gathering associated states in accordance with their respective functions. A portion of the formations of demerit (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) is called 'with lust' (sarāga). Another [portion] is called 'without lust' (virāga). Or, because it is not the opposite of lust, it is that which increases lust...
86:
All unmeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), which are also causes for the arising of lust, are called 'with lust' (sarāga). Other formations are called 'without lust' (virāga) because they are far from that lust. [The Buddha taught:] 'Monks, for a long time the uninstructed worldling has been attached to this consciousness, has cherished it, and has misapprehended it thus: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self."' Because consciousness is specifically taught as the basis for the misapprehension of a self, the meaning of consciousness as being empty of self is profound. Because of the strength of the obsession that 'the self knows, the self wanders through saṃsāra'—implying activity and transmigration—the meanings of the absence of activity, the absence of transmigration, and the manifestation of rebirth-linking are also profound.

The arising together of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) at the moment of rebirth-linking is called 'simultaneous arising' (ekuppāda). During the course of existence (pavatti), however, there is simultaneous arising separately as appropriate. Because name is not conjoined with form, and form is not conjoined with name, their 'separability' (vinibbhoga) should be applied; and because name is not separate from name, and form is not separate from form, or some names from other names and some forms from other forms, their 'inseparability' (avinibbhoga) should be applied. When inseparability is intended by way of simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation, that inseparability is found among the material phenomena arising in a single group (kalāpa). Alternatively, it should be understood that in the one-constituent (ekavokāra) and four-constituent (catuvokāra) realms, there is mutual separability because name and form do not coexist, while in the five-constituent (pañcavokāra) realm, there is inseparability because they coexist.

The 'bending' of name towards an object is the meaning of bending (namanaṭṭha). The arising of difference in form when meeting with opposing conditions is the meaning of being deformed (ruppanaṭṭha). The state of being a condition of faculty (indriya-paccaya) is the meaning of predominance (adhipatiyaṭṭha). The meanings such as 'world,' 'door,' and 'field' as taught should be applied to the five bases (āyatana) such as the eye-base. In the mind-base (manāyatana), these meanings should be understood because it is subject to breaking up and because it serves as a door and a field for mind-contact and so on. The 'shining' (obhāsana), which has the characteristic of being suitable for manifesting visible forms and so on that have come into range, is the state of being the 'subject' (visayibhāva) of the eye and so on. For the mind-base, the act of cognizing is the state of being the 'subject.' The meaning of 'impingement' (saṅghaṭṭanaṭṭha) is specifically applied to the five such as eye-contact; the others (the meaning of touching) are applied to all six kinds of contact. Touching is the individual characteristic of contact (phassa). Impingement is its function (rasa). The remaining aspects are the modes of manifestation (upaṭṭhānākāra). The meaning of experiencing the flavor of the object is taught by way of function (rasa). The meaning of experiencing (vedayitaṭṭha) is taught by way of characteristic. The states of pleasure, pain, and the middle (equanimity) are taught according to the nature of the three feelings respectively. Because of the strength of the obsession that 'the self feels,' the meaning of feeling as being soulless (nijjīvaṭṭha) is very profound. Alternatively, the experiencing by a soulless feeling is 'soulless experiencing' (nijjīvavedayita); because it is that very meaning, it is called the 'meaning of soulless experiencing' (nijjīvavedayitaṭṭha).
87:
The meaning of 'greatly delighting' (abhinandita) of craving accompanied by joy should be understood. The act of swallowing and finishing by means of a more powerful craving is the meaning of 'cleaving' (ajjhosāna). The remaining meanings should be understood by way of being the chief, descending, being like the ocean, being difficult to cross, and being insatiable.

The meanings of firmly holding, grasping with clinging, and excessive obsession are the common meanings of all four types of clinging (upādāna). Just as the meaning of misapprehension belongs only to clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna) and so on, so too does the meaning of being difficult to cross. Because of the teaching 'the wilderness of views' (diṭṭhikantāra), the difficulty of crossing over views is understood. Alternatively, because of the firmness of the grasp, the meaning of being difficult to cross may be applied to all four types of clinging.

In the compound 'yonigatithitinivāsasukhipana,' the non-elision of the locative case ending should be noted. Because of this note, the compounding of that term with the term 'āyūhanābhisaṅkharaṇa' occurs. Arising in an indefinite manner is the meaning of 'birth' (jāti). Arising due to the coincidence [of conditions] is the meaning of 'reproduction' (sañjāti). Arising by way of descending into the mother's womb is the meaning of 'descent' (okkanti). Arising from that birth is the meaning of 'generation' (nibbatti). The mere appearance is the meaning of 'manifestation' (pātubhāva).

Since the factor of aging-and-death (jarāmaraṇa) has death as its primary element, the meanings of death such as 'exhaustion' (khaya) and so on are shown to be profound. Because of the exhaustion of the ever-arising new mental and material phenomena, the worldly usage of 'aging' (jarā) occurs in the process of maturation such as broken teeth and so on. Alternatively, it should be noted that the meaning of exhaustion is said to be the meaning of aging. Since departure from a new state is fit to be called 'exhaustion,' the meaning of 'alteration' (vipariṇāma) should be applied by way of both aging and death. Or, the states of exhaustion and fall of aging should be applied by way of the continuity (santati), and the meanings of breaking up and alteration of death should be applied by way of the conventional (sammuti) and the momentary (khaṇika).

Because the nature of ignorance (avijjā) and so on is penetrated, it is called 'penetration' (paṭivedha). This is stated in the Nidānakathā: 'The non-perverted nature, known as the individual characteristic of those various dhammas taught in those various places, which is to be penetrated, is called penetration.' That nature of ignorance and so on is profound because it is to be penetrated only by the Path-knowledge (maggañāṇa) by way of non-deluded penetration, and because of the meaning of 'unfathomable' (agādha) as being a place where ignorance (non-knowledge) cannot find a footing.

The profundity of that entire Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), which is fourfold in brief and of many varieties in detail, appeared as if it were clear to the Elder [Ānanda] because he was endowed with four factors. [The Buddha said:] 'Do not say so, thinking: "To me, this Dependent Origination appears clear; does it also appear clear to others in this way?" Stand firm in the method of the meditation on the Four Truths as given by Me.'
88:
## Apasādanāvaṇṇanā

'Oḷārika' (gross) means large or coarse in the sense of being capable of transgressing against objects (vatthu-vītikkama). In reality, although sensual lust (kāmarāga) and aversion (paṭigha) are essentially the same as the fetters of sensual lust and aversion (kāmarāga-saṃyojana, paṭigha-saṃyojana) and the latent tendencies of sensual lust and aversion (kāmarāga-anusaya, paṭigha-anusaya), they are considered 'four defilements' by taking the distinct types of defilements based on their specific functions. This is because the sense of 'fetter' (saṃyojana) is one kind due to its binding nature, while the sense of 'latent tendency' (anusaya) is another kind due to its nature of lying dormant with strength in the mental continuum as it has not yet been abandoned. The same method applies to the remaining fetters and latent tendencies. 'Aṇusahagata' means having reached a minute or subtle state. Indeed, this word 'sahagata' has that subtle meaning, as in the Pali passages such as 'nandirāgasahagatā' (accompanied by delight and lust).

Just as the penetration of the Four Noble Truths through the power of attaining the higher paths occurs because of the penetration of the mode of conditions (paccaya-ākāra), so too, the penetration of the Four Noble Truths through the power of attaining Disciple Enlightenment (sāvaka-bodhi), Pacceka Enlightenment (pacceka-bodhi), and Perfect Self-Enlightenment (sammā-sambodhi) occurs only through the penetration of the mode of conditions; to show this, the words beginning with 'kasmā ca' are stated. 'Sabbathā' means in every way, without leaving even a slight remainder. To show the differences in time required for the accumulation of the requisites of enlightenment (bodhi-sambhāra) according to the intensity of effort—low, medium, or high—of the Great Bodhisattas who have made their formal resolution for Great Enlightenment, it is said: 'four, eight, or sixteen incalculable eons (asaṅkheyyas).' This meaning should be taken from the Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā. A disciple, being a trainee (sekkha), stands in partial knowledge (padesa-ñāṇa) even within that state of a trainee. This is contrary to the words of the Buddhas, such as 'The Tathāgata penetrates that [Dhamma].' Indeed, the Lion's Roar (sīhanāda) of the Buddhas occurs through a power that is not shared with others, not through a power shared with others.

By the words 'vāyamantasseva' (only for one who strives), it specifically refers to the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramitā), which is the accumulation of the requisites of knowledge (ñāṇa-sambhāra). For that perfection of wisdom, all merit (puñña) is a strong supporting condition (upanissaya).

As it is said: 'This merit is a treasure for devas and humans that grants all desirable things; whatever they wish for, all that can be obtained by this [merit].' Therefore, the entire accumulation of merit of the Great Bodhisattas is beneficial up to the accumulation of knowledge, as it is capable of achieving Perfect Self-Enlightenment.
89:
Regarding the words 'paccaya-ākāraṃ ...pe... natthī', the Blessed One has preached in the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta: 'This merit performed by oneself is like a buried treasure that grants all desired benefits to devas and humans; whatever happiness and benefit they long for, all that can be obtained because of this merit.' Therefore, the accumulation of merit of all Great Bodhisattas is indeed beneficial up to the accumulation of knowledge, as it is capable of attaining Perfect Self-Enlightenment; thus the teacher has explained the profound distinction. Now, to show the supreme profundity of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) by way of showing the great power of the penetration of the mode of conditions, the words beginning with 'avijjā' (ignorance) are stated.

'By nine aspects' means by the nine aspects beginning with arising (uppāda). Ignorance (avijjā) assists by being the arising (uppāda) of volitional formations (saṅkhāra), and it assists by being the occurrence (pavatta), the sign (nimitta), the striving (āyūhana), the bond (saṃyoga), the impediment (palibodha), the origination (samudaya), the root cause (hetu), and the condition (paccaya). In the same way, volitional formations and so on assist consciousness (viññāṇa) and so on. This is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali: 'How is the wisdom in discerning conditions called the knowledge of the stability of Dhamma (dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa)? Ignorance is the stability of arising (uppāda-ṭṭhiti), the stability of occurrence (pavatta-ṭṭhiti), the stability of the sign (nimitta-ṭṭhiti), the stability of striving (āyūhana-ṭṭhiti), the stability of the bond (saṃyoga-ṭṭhiti), the stability of the impediment (palibodha-ṭṭhiti), the stability of origination (samudaya-ṭṭhiti), the stability of the root cause (hetu-ṭṭhiti), and the stability of the condition (paccaya-ṭṭhiti) for volitional formations; by these nine aspects, volitional formations arise conditioned by ignorance,' and so forth.

In that context, 'by nine aspects' means by the nine aspects of reaching the state of being a condition. It is called 'uppāda' (arising) because the fruit arises from this; it is the state of being the cause for the arising of the fruit. When ignorance exists, volitional formations arise; when it does not exist, they do not arise. Therefore, ignorance assists by being the arising (uppāda) of volitional formations. Likewise, when ignorance exists, volitional formations occur and are led along. Just as they are cast into [new] existence and so on, so ignorance is the condition for them. Likewise, they strive (āyūhanti) or exert for the arising of the fruit, and they are conjoined (saṃyujjanti) with their own fruit. In whichever continuum they themselves have arisen, they impede (palibundhanti) that continuum. They originate (udayanti) or arise when there is a combination of other conditions. Ignorance reaches the state of being the cause of volitional formations. Depending on ignorance, volitional formations come to be or occur; thus the specific ways ignorance reaches the state of being a cause for volitional formations, such as arising and so on, should be understood. The same applies to volitional formations and so on regarding consciousness and so on, in the stability of arising and so forth. It is called 'ṭhiti' (stability) because it stands or is established by this; it is the cause. Arising itself is the stability, thus it is 'uppāda-ṭṭhiti'. This same method applies to the remaining terms.

'Paccayo hoti' (is a condition): these words here show the fact that the Lord of the World at that time undertook the discernment of conditions (paccaya-pariggaha). And that undertaking was established in the right method, just as it was carried out by previous Great Bodhisattas at the foot of the Bodhi tree. To show how the ten-thousandfold world system (dasa-sahassī-lokadhātu) shook and trembled, struck by the force of this wonder, the words beginning with 'diṭṭhamatteva' are stated.

'Etassa dhammassa' means of this Dhamma known as Dependent Origination. That Dhamma, in terms of meaning, is the root cause of the things that arise from causes. Therefore, it is said 'of this conditional Dhamma'; the meaning is because of the conditionality of birth (jāti) and so on for aging and death (jarā-maraṇa) and so on. The discernment of mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) and the discernment of their conditions (paccaya-pariggaha) do not occur by mere initial attention.
90:
...it is so. In truth, it is because of the repeated penetration, known as the repeated arising of knowledge, regarding that delimitation of mentality-materiality. To show the absence of both types, he said: "not knowing through the power of full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā)." Insight (vipassanā), which occurs by abandoning the perception of permanence and so forth, is indeed called penetrating the phenomena because it attains a sharp and clear state by dispelling opposing states. The full understanding by investigation (tīraṇapariññā), which has that insight as its basis, and the Noble Path (ariyamagga), because it occurs through the power of the realization of abandoning and full understanding, are included in full understanding by investigation and full understanding by abandoning. To show the absence of these two kinds of penetration, he said: "tīraṇa...pe... appaṭivijjhanā" (not penetrating by investigation...).

It is called "tanta" (warp/thread) because weavers stretch and attach the skein of thread to a post for the purpose of weaving cloth. That thread is taken as a metaphor for being tangled because of the confusion of the strands. Therefore, he said: "they have become tangled like a weaver's thread (tantākulakajātā)." To explain in detail the meaning stated in brief, he said "yathā nāma" (just as) and so forth. "Samānetuṃ" means to bring the front and back threads together evenly, to make them straight and not uneven. Or, the thread itself is a tangle, thus "tantākula"; having become like a tangled thread, they are "tantākulakajātā." Beings, not approaching the Middle Way (majjhimapaṭipadā) and falling into the two extremes, stumble and become confused in Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Because of falling into those two extremes, they wander about through the grasping of various views and do not know how to practice the straight Dhamma-stability (dhammaṭṭhiti). Therefore, he said: "they are unable to make that Dependent Origination straight."

"Dve bodhisatte" refers to (excluding) the Paccekabodhisatta and the Mahābodhisatta. "Attano dhammatāya" means by one's own nature, without the instruction of others. "Tattha tattha guḷakajātaṃ" means the tangle that arises in various places is also a knot of thread called "gaṇṭhi." Because of being knotted in that way, it is "baddhagaṇṭhika" (bound by knots). "Paccayesu pakkhalitvā" means stumbling through the grasping of permanence and so forth in the conditional phenomena (paccaya-dhamma) which have the nature of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Being unable to abandon that grasping of permanence and so forth, they are unable to straighten their own vision, which is the sign of conditional phenomena, and they become those with knots through the power of the bodily tie of insistence that 'This is the truth' (idaṃsaccābhinivesakāyagantha). Therefore, he said: "dvāsaṭṭhi...pe... gaṇṭhibaddhā" (the sixty-two [views]... bound by knots). Those recluses or brahmins who rely on and cling to views such as the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi).

Because of weaving, the weaver who receives the name "kulā" in the feminine gender has a "gaṇṭhika" (knot), which is a tangled weaver's thread that is difficult to distinguish from the beginning or the end because of its confusion. Therefore, he said: "kulāgaṇṭhikaṃ vuccati pesakārakañjiyasuttaṃ" (a weaver's knot is called a weaver's starched thread). "Sakuṇikā" refers to a female bird that builds a nest. She has a nest hanging from the branches of trees. Bringing blades of grass and such from various places to that nest...
91:
The female bird has a hanging nest. She brings blades of grass and so forth from here and there and weaves that nest in such a way that, like a weaver's starched thread, it is impossible to join or distinguish the end from the end or the beginning from the beginning. Therefore, he said "yathā hi" (just as) and so forth. "Tadubhayampi" refers to both the starched thread called "kulāgaṇṭhika" and the bird's nest. "Purimanayeneva" means in the same manner as previously stated, such as "evameva sattā" (even so, beings).

Indeed, munja and babbaja grasses, even in their natural state, fall down because of their length and, weaving into each other in the forest, remain in a confused and tangled state. However, to show that those grasses are not as difficult to disentangle as grasses that have become ropes, he said "yathā tāni" (just as those) and so forth. The remaining words are in the same manner as stated below.

"Apāya" means a realm devoid of growth, happiness, or the cause of happiness (merit). "Dukkhassa gatibhāvato" means because it is the place of occurrence for the suffering that exists in the planes of misery. "Sukhasamussayato" means [devoid] of the accumulation of happiness or prosperity. "Vinipatitattā" means because it is a state of existence that has fallen ruinously. When one falls in such a way, the accumulation of happiness cannot occur in that state of existence; because of falling in this way, it is called "vinipatita." The other one is "saṃsāra" (the round of rebirths). If one asks, "Are not the four planes of misery mentioned as 'apāya' and so forth also saṃsāra?", it is true; however, "apāya" and so forth are taken separately to show the extreme nature of the suffering in hell and so on. This meaning should be understood by the "cattle and bull" logic (gobalībadda-nyāya). The "succession of aggregates" means the repeated occurrence of the five aggregates as cause and effect. "Abbochinnaṃ vattamānā" refers to the sequence occurring without interruption. "Taṃ sabbampi" refers to all the suffering of the planes of misery and the suffering of the round of rebirths mentioned as "apāya" and so forth. "Mahaasamudde vātukkhittanāvā viya"—this simile is intended to show the vastness of the place of wandering and the instability of the wandering. "Yantesu yuttagoṇo viya"—this simile should be understood as showing the lack of control over one's own will and the difficulty of escape.

## Description of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādavaṇṇanā)

In the phrase "iminā tāva," the word "tāva" expresses the sense of sequence. By that word, it is indicated that the connection of the term "tantākulakajātā" will become clear later. In the phrase "atthi idappaccayā," "this condition" is called "idappaccaya." It means "because of this condition." The intended meaning is: "Is there indeed a condition for aging and death which can be stated as 'aging and death occur because of this specific condition'?"
92:
Therefore, he said, "Atthi nu kho... pe... bhaveyyā." Here, based on the fact that above, in the statement "What is the cause of aging and death? Aging and death are caused by birth," the words jāti and paccaya are shown to have the same referent (samanādhikaraṇa), and because the word kiṃ is shown to have the same referent as the word idaṃ, it is appropriate for the word idappaccaya to be a kammadhāraya (adjectival) compound.

In this context, inquiring whether aging and death arise from "this cause" (idappaccaya)—referring to aging and death or something else—is not appropriate because it is either already known or impossible; rather, it should be an inquiry into the cause of aging and death itself. Since the word idaṃ has the same referent as the word paccaya, the inquiry into the cause as "from this cause" (imasmā paccayā) is fitting.

Although such co-referentiality (samanādhikaraṇatā) can also be found in a bahubbīhi compound with an external referent (aññapadattha), since there is no intention for an external referent here, it should be understood as a kammadhāraya compound. In the case of a genitive determinative compound (sāmivacanasamāsa/saṭṭhī-tappurisa), co-referentiality is impossible. One might ask: "In the phrase 'Idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppādo,' is not the word idappaccaya intended as a genitive compound?" True, it is intended so. Because there the intention is to directly refer to Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), whereas here the intention is merely to inquire about the cause of aging and death. Therefore, just as the word idaṃ functions as an attribute of Dependent Origination there, and here it has the meaning of the cause being inquired about, the formation of the compound in both places should be understood accordingly.

Why is a kammadhāraya compound not desired there? Because the meaning "Dependent Origination is the cause of things produced by causes" is impossible in a kammadhāraya compound, and because the intended meaning is "this cause (idappaccaya) is the cause corresponding to its own conditions." The meaning taken by the word idaṃ here is already captured by the word jarāmaraṇa in the sentence "Atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ"; thus, the word idaṃ abandons the meaning of Dependent Origination and, as no other meaning is possible, it stands only in the sense of "cause." Therefore, it is a kammadhāraya compound here. There, however, since there is no reason for the word idaṃ to abandon that meaning, only the genitive compound is desired.

In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), because this teaching on Dependent Origination begins with an inquiry into the cause of aging and death, etc., and because Dependent Origination is said to be, in essence, the cause of things produced by causes, the explanation is given as "the cause of this aging and death."

"Paṇḍitena" refers to one endowed with wisdom capable of knowing specific types of questions, such as those requiring a categorical answer (ekāṃsabyākaraṇīya). To show his state of being a wise person, [the text says] "Yathā" etc.
93:
A person with wrong view asks whether a certain soul (jīva) is not different from the body (sarīra) but is one and the same, saying, "That soul is that body." That soul is not found (does not exist) in the sense of ultimate reality (paramattha). How could one explain the difference or non-difference from the body of such a non-existent soul, just like [discussing] the tallness or shortness of a barren woman's son? Therefore, the status of that question as one to be set aside (ṭhapanīyata) should be understood. Remaining silent in such a case might seem like a lack of respect or harassment toward the questioner. Therefore, it is said in another way: "This is undeclared (abyākata)."

The reason for not answering in this way should be explained to one who wishes to know. Even after it is explained, a knowledgeable person might still be negligent. The method of explanation is already shown by "Yādisassa" etc. "Evaṃ appaṭipajjitvā" means not falling into silence etc., as in the case of a question to be set aside. The word "appaṭipajjitvā" is merely an illustration.

When asked, "Are all things impermanent?", one should answer after asking a counter-question: "Are you asking with reference to conditioned things (saṅkhata) or with reference to the unconditioned (asaṅkhata, i.e., Nibbāna)?" When asked, "Are the five aggregates entirely to be fully understood (pariññeyya)?", one should answer analytically: "In those five aggregates, there are things to be fully understood, and there are things not to be fully understood." This is the intended meaning here in the Pali "Evaṃ appaṭipajjitvā."

Previously, because only the existence of a certain cause was inquired about, only its existence was answered. Indeed, the answer must correspond to the nature of the question. Now, to indicate that the inquiry is being made into the specific nature of that cause, it is said, "Puna kiṃ" (What again?). Here too, all the words starting with "Yathā" should be brought in and spoken.

By making an effort through the method of application "Esa nayo sabbapadesu" (This is the method in all cases), the effort to state the negation there was begun with the words "Nāmarūpapaccayā" etc. The construction is: "Because he wishes to show, therefore this was said." Because things from consciousness down to feeling are the sequence of results (vipāka), in many Sutta passages and in the Abhidhamma, the taking of only those six resultant contacts (vipāka-phassa) is generally well-established.

"Idha" means in this Sutta. The word "ca" has a contrastive meaning (vyatireka). Therefore, it illuminates the distinction being stated here with the words "Gahitampi" etc. The status of being a cause depends on the result (produced by the cause), for without that result, the cause cannot exist. Therefore, "saḷāyatanapaccayā" is connected with the phrase "saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso." Or, this "saḷāyatanapaccayā" is a designation of the whole by its part; therefore, it means what is said by the phrase "saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso." "Gahitampi" refers to the sixfold resultant contact, and "agahitampi" refers to non-resultant contact, as well as wholesome, unwholesome, and functional contact. The distinction of the result...
94:
The connection is made with the desire to show (a specific condition). In this context, it is not only the resultant clung-to (upādinnaka) aggregates that are intended; rather, the condition is also intended as a clung-to state. Thus, by taking only the internal bases (ajjhattikāyatana) under the name of the sixfold base (saḷāyatana), it is stated: "From the sixfold base... pe... [He] desires to show."

Indeed, the condition for contact (phassa) is not merely the six bases such as the eye; rather, because of the scriptural statement: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact," etc., the material phenomena such as the form base (rūpāyatana) and the mental phenomena such as eye-consciousness are also conditions. Therefore, the Blessed One, desiring to show this general condition—which is not a common condition like adverting (āvajjanā) that exceeds the six bases such as the eye, but is a common condition for each specific contact—expressed it without distinction by the word "pi" (also), and thus the statement "With name-and-form as condition, contact [arises]" (nāmarūpapaccayā phasso) was spoken. This is the connection.

In the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya (Abhidhamma classification) as well, referring to this very condition of name-and-form, it was stated: "With name-and-form as condition, contact [arises]." In its commentary (Atthakathā), the explanation is given: "For the purpose of showing the specific condition and for the purpose of inclusion within the Great Discourse on Causation (Mahānidāna-desanā)."

"Paccayānaṃ" refers to the conditioning states such as birth (jāti). "Nidānaṃ kathitaṃ" means the causal status for effects such as aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) has been stated; the certain (ekaṃsika) state of being a condition has been stated. To show that the state of being a condition is invariable in those phenomena, the subsequent teaching proceeds with the words "Iti kho panetaṃ," etc.

"Nijjaṭe" means without entanglement. "Niggumbe" means without thickets, which implies abandonment (nikkhepa). By both terms, only the absence of confusion is shown. Therefore, because the great causal condition (paccaya-nidāna) which is without confusion is taught in this sutta, and because there is no deviation from this nature, it is called the Mahānidāna Sutta.

"Of those various conditions" refers to those various conditions such as birth. The state of being a condition is "true" (tatha) because those specific effects arise from those specific conditions that are neither deficient nor redundant; or else, it is true because when the conditions have reached harmony, the effects which have the nature of arising do not fail to arise even for a moment. "Not false" (avitatha) means unerring, devoid of the manner of deception, because other effects do not arise from the conditions of different phenomena. It is called "not otherwise" (anaññathā) because there is no state of being otherwise. Therefore, it is said: "To show the state of being a condition which is true, not false, and not otherwise."

It is called "pariyāya" because it occurs by embracing its own effect; since it means "cause," it is said: "'Pariyāyena' means by way of cause."

"Sabbena sabbaṃ" means...
95:
As all birth (*jāti*) by way of the state of all beings such as the state of devas, etc., is called 'in every way as a whole' (*sabbena sabbaṃ*). In those states of devas, etc., all birth in all modes such as the *Cātumahārājika* mode is called 'in every way in all modes' (*sabbathā sabbaṃ*). Both these terms are particles (*nipāta*). A particle is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), and because it remains in one single form across all genders, cases, and numbers, it is stated in the Pali as: "*sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ*."

In the explanation of the meaning, however, to show the occurrence in the feminine sense in reference to the respective word *jāti*, it is stated as: "all (birth) in all modes" (*sabbākarēna sabbā*), etc. "By this very method" means by the method already stated in the section on birth (*jātivāra*). In the word "among devas, etc." (*devādīsu*), the word 'etc.' includes the *Gandhabbas*, *Yakkhas*, etc., mentioned in the Pali, as well as other varieties of beings.

"For the purpose of analyzing the meaning laid down here" refers to a particle used to highlight the pointing out of the meaning stated in brief without specification as "of anyone, in anything" (*kassaci kimhici*); the meaning is a particle that highlights that sense. "Of that" (*tassa*) means of that word. "To you" (*te*) refers to the Elder (Ānanda) who was the recipient of the Dhamma teaching. "As follows" (*seyyathidaṃ*) has the sense of asking, "What are those meanings?" It means: what are those meanings stated indefinitely as "of anyone" and "in anything"? This is a question arising from the desire to speak (*kathetukamyatāpucchā*).

"For the state of a deva" (*devabhāvāya*) means for the sake of the state of a deva. "Birth of aggregates" (*khandhajāti*) is the manifestation of the aggregates. Just as when the aggregates have arisen, the designation "deva" occurs, so the arising of those aggregates is meant by 'birth'. Therefore, it is said: "whichever..." (*yā yā*), etc. This is the same in all words indicating birth such as "for the state of *Gandhabbas* for *Gandhabbas*," etc., and also in words such as 'existence' (*bhava*), etc. If this application of meaning is made for 'birth', then in the words indicating 'existence' such as "existence" (*bhavo*), etc., it should be applied in the same way as in the words indicating birth.

"Devas" refers to the devas by rebirth (*upapattideva*) from the *Cātumahārājika* realm up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*). They are called 'devas' because they sport, play, and dwell with the strands of sensual pleasure, and because they shine. They are called *Gandhabbas* because they consume scents; they are the attendants of the Great King *Dhataraṭṭha*. They are called *Yakkhas* because they worship the Great King *Vessavaṇa*, *Sakka*, etc., or because they are to be worshipped and honored through various aspirations and actions; they are the attendants of the Great King *Vessavaṇa*. In the Commentary, however, they are mentioned generally as "non-humans" (*amanussa*). "Beings" (*bhūta*) refers to the *Kumbhaṇḍas*, who are the attendants of the Great King *Virūḷhaka*. In the Commentary, however, they are mentioned generally as "whatever beings have been reborn."

Bone-winged creatures are those such as large black bees and honeybees. Skin-winged creatures are those such as bats and flying foxes. Feather-winged creatures are those such as swans and peacocks. Creeping things (*sarīsapa*) are those such as snakes, scorpions, and centipedes.
96:
The phrase "tesaṃ tesaṃ" (of those and those) is not a statement made for the purpose of including unstated meanings like the yevāpanaka exposition; rather, it is a statement made for the purpose of including meanings already stated, like a non-yevāpanaka exposition. Since the iterative meaning (repetition) is included by the word ādi (etc.) itself, it is said, "of those various devas, gandhabbas, and so on." "Tadattāya" means for the sake of the state of those devas, gandhabbas, and so on. It means for the sake of the arising of those aggregates of such a nature that, when they are occurring, the worldly designation "devas" or "gandhabbas" arises. Therefore, it is said, "for the sake of the state of devas, gandhabbas, and so on." Although "nirodha" (cessation) and "vigama" (disappearance) usually refer to the state of not obtaining what was previously obtained, here, absolute non-existence (abhāva) is intended. This is because it is not stated as "sabbaso jātiyā asati" (if birth were completely absent), but as "jātinirodhā" (from the cessation of birth). Thus, it is said, "it means non-existence (abhāva)."

Just as a fruit arises from its cause, so it [the cause] occurs to bring about the fruit; it means it reaches the state of being a cause for that result. In saying "Take this [fruit]," it is as if one is handing it over, saying, "This is my fruit, take it." After pointing out the general meaning with "This is the method," the word "apica" (moreover) and so on are stated to show a specific meaning. Since this birth (jāti) is a state of alteration (vikāra), is it not the case that it is neither a produced (parinipphanna) state nor a conditioned (saṅkhata) state? If so, how can that birth be the cause of aging and death? Aiming at this objection, the text says, "Of aging and death..." and so on. The existence of aging and death when birth exists, and their non-existence when birth is absent, is indeed the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya) of birth for aging and death.

"Okāsapariggaha" (delimiting the space) means grasping the place of occurrence. It is appropriate in the rebirth-process (upapattibhava) because the aggregates of rebirth do not arise anywhere other than the stated place. However, in this context of the Mahānidāna Sutta, where terms like "kāmabhava" (sense-sphere existence) appear, it is appropriate in the kamma-process (kammabhava) because the sense-sphere existence and so on are specifically the causes of birth. Therefore, it is said, "That kamma-process is a condition for birth by way of decisive support (upanissaya)." If one asks, "Is not the rebirth-process also a condition for birth by way of decisive support?"—it is true, it is. However, that rebirth-process is not the primary (padhāna) cause in providing support; only the kamma-process is the primary cause because it is the generator (janaka). To show this, it is said, "That kamma-process for birth..." and so on. Kamma that leads to sense-sphere rebirth is called "kāmabhava." This same method applies to fine-material and immaterial existence. Since the grasping of beings has already been done by the word "kimhici" (in anything), only the delimiting of the space (okāsapariggaha) is performed.

[It conditions] the three types of kamma-process such as the sense-sphere kamma-process, and the three types of rebirth-process such as the sense-sphere rebirth-process.
97:
Similarly, the remaining types of clinging, such as clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna), are conditions for the three types of kamma-process and the three types of rebirth-process. By the word "iti" (thus), in the manner stated, the twenty-four types of existence—namely, the twelve types of kamma-process and the twelve types of rebirth-process—should be understood.

Because clinging becomes a condition for the rebirth-process primarily through its role as a condition for the kamma-process, and not otherwise, clinging is a direct (nippariyāya) condition for the kamma-process. Therefore, the teacher says, "In this context, twelve types of kamma-process are obtained without figurative language." The word "tesaṃ" refers to those kamma-processes. "Sahajāta-koṭiyā" (by way of the conascent category) means that for an unwholesome kamma-process, the clinging that arises together with that unwholesome kamma-process conditions it through the conascent group. Other types of clinging condition it through the decisive support group by way of proximity-decisive support (anantarūpanissaya) and so on. For a wholesome kamma-process, however, clinging conditions it only through the decisive support group.

In showing this matter, just as it is said "sahajāta-koṭiyā" to show that conditions such as mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) are included together under the conascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya), so too it should be noted that "upanissaya-koṭiyā" is said by way of taking object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya), proximity-decisive support (anantarūpanissaya), and natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya) together.

Regarding the word "upādānassa" (of clinging), craving conditions clinging to sense-pleasures (kāmupādāna) only through the decisive support group. For the remaining three types of clinging, it should be noted that it conditions them through both the conascent group and the decisive support group. This should be understood as the procedure of resultants (vipāka) starting from consciousness (viññāṇa) and ending with feeling (vedanā).

Regarding the phrase "yadidaṃ vedanā" (that is, feeling), resultant feeling conditions only that resultant feeling through the decisive support group. This is because the conascent category, other than the decisive support category, is impossible. Other feelings—wholesome, unwholesome, and functional (kiriya) feelings—also condition through the conascent group according to the word "aññathāpi" (otherwise also).

"Ettāvatā" (to this extent) refers to this much of the teaching which proceeds by way of showing the succession of conditions for aging and death and so on. "Purima-taṇhaṃ" refers to the craving accomplished in a previous life. Having taught "This feeling is the condition for craving," the extraction of contact (phassa) as the condition for feeling immediately after that teaching—as in "With contact as condition, feeling arises"—is the path of the teaching of dependent origination according to the method found in other suttas. However, without entering that path of teaching, by teaching the states rooted in craving primarily through the manifestation of active craving (samudācāra-taṇhā), it is as if the Buddha is deviating from the habitual path of teaching, and as if He is teaching by forcefully overcoming that [usual] teaching which does not occur here. To show this meaning, it is said "idāni" (now) and so on. The phrase "dve taṇhā" (two cravings) refers to the craving intended in this Pali text, which is spoken of by dividing it into two types.
98:
In this way, [the Buddha] speaks by distinguishing [the craving that is desired] into two types. Esanā-taṇhā is craving that occurs by way of seeking wealth. Esita-taṇhā is craving that arises for wealth that has already been sought. Samudācāra-taṇhā is the name for craving that occurs by way of the obsession of defilements. This craving, which occurs dependent on feeling (vedanā), is of two kinds: seeking to obtain wealth not yet obtained because of the cause of feeling, and the enjoyment, etc., of that wealth once obtained.

It is called pariyesanā (seeking) because one searches by way of longing. Seeking through inclination (āsaya) and effort (payoga) is the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) that occurs in that way. Therefore, He said: "When there is craving, there is [seeking]." Obtaining objects such as forms (rūpa) occurs by way of searching for those forms along with their bases. However, at the time of occurrence, they may be obtained without searching; even such obtaining is essentially called "obtained through seeking" because it is obtained due to having performed such kamma in the past. Therefore, He said: "When there is seeking, there is [obtaining]." Sukhavinicchaya (decision regarding pleasure) is so called because it specifically decides upon pleasure. The knowledge that occurs after knowing pleasure as it really is—by way of its nature, its origin (samudaya), its cessation (atthaṅgama), and the escape from it (nissaraṇa)—is called sukhavinicchaya. Jaññā means "one should know" (or "can know"). Deciding upon or attributing various false aspects to an object, such as "beautiful pleasure," by way of inclination, is called vinicchaya (decision). The nature of decision through craving and view (diṭṭhi) that observes [objects] as enjoyable should be understood in this same way.

In this sutta, however, it should be construed that only thought (vitakka) is mentioned. "In this sutta" refers to the Sakkapañha Sutta. For in that sutta, it is stated: "O Sakka, Lord of Devas, desire (chanda) has thought as its source." "In this" refers to this Mahānidāna Sutta. By the words "one decides only by thought," the instrumental sense (karaṇa-sādhana) of the word vinicchaya is stated: "it is called vinicchaya because one decides by means of this [thought]." The words "this much," etc., show the manner of deciding.

It is called chanda (desire) in the sense of longing; likewise, it is called rāga (lust) in the sense of being enamored. Since that lust occurs weakly because it is not constantly cultivated, it is intended here as "a name for weak lust." Ajjhosāna (attachment) is the firm mental application by way of craving and view. The grasping through craving, "This is mine," is mostly dependent on the grasping of a self (atta). Therefore, He spoke of those graspings reaching a state of firmness as "I, mine" and "strong conviction." Grasping by way of craving and view means...
99:
...the state of taking possession and remaining fixed upon the object of attachment—the self and what belongs to the self—which has been firmly applied with strong conviction as "I" and "mine," as if making it exclusive to others. This is the arising of consciousness associated with greed (lobha) that occurs in such a manner of possession (pariggaha). The mental state of a person who cannot endure the shared ownership of the object they have possessed with others is called stinginess (macchariya). In this way, the ancient teachers state the word-definition (vacanattha) according to the method of linguistics (nirutti). In the science of grammar (sadda-lakkhaṇa), however, a person is called "stingy" (macchara) because of association with the state of stinginess; the state or the action of that person is macchariya. Stinginess is a phenomenon in the ultimate sense (paramattha). Guarding with care due to the strength of stinginess is called ārakkha (protection). Therefore, the teacher said: "Guarding well by means of doors... etc." It is called karaṇa (cause) because it produces its own fruit. Any cause that is an excessive cause is adhikaraṇa (principal cause/occasion), a specific cause. Because it is the specific cause for the occurrence of misfortunes such as guarding wealth and taking up the rod, it is said: "on account of protection" (ārakkha-adhikaraṇa), and so on.

"For the purpose of warding off others" means for the purpose of harming others through killing, etc. It is called ādāna because the rod is taken up by this [act]. Taking up the rod is daṇḍādāna; it is the arising of consciousness with the intent to harm others by overpowering them. The same method applies to taking up weapons (satthādāna). Strife performed with the body, such as grabbing with the hands, is physical strife (kāya-kalaha). Dispute performed with speech, such as speaking painful words, is verbal strife (vāca-kalaha). It is called viggaha (quarrel) because one takes [a position] wrongly in a contradictory manner by this [act]. It is called vivāda (dispute) because one speaks contradictorily by this [act]. Tuvaṃ tuvaṃ (you, you) is the state of speech that occurs along with disrespectful and rude words. All these states that occur in the manner of taking up the rod, etc., should be understood as the arising of consciousness associated with hatred (dosa). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Many evil, unwholesome states arise."

He "turned back the discourse" means that the discourse, which was set forth in the forward order (anuloma) as "dependent on craving, there is seeking," etc., was turned back and taught again in the reverse order (paṭiloma) starting from "on account of protection." "By way of lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure" means: one who has the five cords of sensual pleasure as objects is pañcakāmaguṇika; the lust that occurs there by way of being enamored and delighted is [the cause]. Craving for forms, etc., which arises by way of that [lust] and occurs by way of being enamored and craving, is craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā). The view of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi) that occurs as "it always exists, it remains for all time" is called bhava (existence) by dropping the latter word (uttarapada-lopa); craving associated with that is craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā). The view of non-existence (vibhava-diṭṭhi) that occurs as "it perishes, it is annihilated" is called vibhava by dropping the latter word; craving associated with that is craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). Therefore, He said: "eternalism" (sassata-diṭṭhi), and so on. These two...
100:
"Dhammā" refers to these two states: the craving that is the root of the round (vaṭṭamūla-taṇhā), spoken of as "This craving is the condition for clinging," and the active craving (samudācāra-taṇhā), spoken of as "Dependent on craving, pursuit arises."

"By way of the root of the round and the active [craving]" (means just that). "By two portions" means by two parts. "By two components they converge (samosaranti)" means they occur equally in terms of arising from this [condition]; therefore, the condition is called "convergence" (samosaraṇa). These cravings have a single convergence, thus they are "of a single convergence" (ekasamosaraṇā). If it is asked, "By what are they of a single convergence?", it is said: "By feeling (vedanā)." This is because both types of craving have feeling alone as their condition. Therefore, it is said: "They have a single condition by way of the condition of feeling."

Having descended from various objects, the place of meeting is called "convergence" (samosaraṇa). Feelings that occur by way of descending together with feeling into a single object are "convergent"; thus it is said: "This is called co-nascent convergence (sahajāta-samosaraṇa)."

By the word "sabbe" (all), only the resultant contacts (savipāka-phassa) are spoken of, distinguished by way of the doors of arising, by making a resultant process (vipāka-vīthi) starting from consciousness and ending with feeling. Since the talk on Dependent Origination is a talk on the round of suffering (vaṭṭakathā), it is said: "Excluding the four supramundane resultant contacts."

"Bahudhā" means in many ways. In the five doors, for the five feelings based on the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), etc., contact such as eye-contact is a condition in eight ways: by way of co-nascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), result (vipāka), nutriment (āhāra), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). For the sense-sphere resultant feelings occurring by way of receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigating (santīraṇa), and registration (tadārammaṇa) in each of the remaining doors, contact such as eye-contact is a condition in only one way: by way of decisive support (upanissaya). In the mind-door as well, for the sense-sphere resultant feelings occurring by way of registration, co-nascent mind-contact is a condition in the same eight ways; likewise for the resultant feelings of the three planes occurring by way of rebirth (paṭisandhi), life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti). As for those sense-sphere feelings occurring by way of registration in the mind-door, the mind-contact associated with mind-door adverting is a condition for them in only one way: by way of decisive support. Thus, it should be understood that contact is a condition for feeling in many ways.

"Vedanādīnaṃ" refers to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. They have "dissimilar natures" (asadisa-bhāva) such as the nature of experiencing, perceiving, constructing, and cognizing. These phenomena are known by their mutually distinct modes such as being experienced; therefore, they are called "aspects" (ākāra).
101:
“Teyeva” refers to those very aspects of feeling etc., such as experiencing, which were mentioned. “Sādhukaṃ dassiyamānā” means being clearly manifested as if directly perceived. They are called “signs” (liṅga) because they make known various hidden and unmanifest meanings, such as “the meaning of immateriality is the meaning of inclining towards an object.” They are called “marks” (nimitta) because they are the cause for recognizing each immaterial meaning etc., and because they are repeatedly known through various dissimilar meanings such as experiencing and perceiving. They are called “designations” (uddesa) because they are to be pointed out or spoken of in various ways, such as being immaterial states or having the nature of experiencing. Therefore, He reviews the meaning already stated by the words “because of dissimilar natures” etc., as a cause. Since feeling etc. have mutually dissimilar natures and are called aspects etc. in the sense already mentioned, therefore, this meaning now to be stated is the meaning in this Pāli term.

“Nāmasamūhassa” refers to the collection of immaterial states known as the four aggregates, such as feeling, which receive the name “Nāma” (Name) because of the meaning of inclining towards an object. “Paññatti” refers to various ways of making known, such as “the group of mental states,” “the immaterial cluster,” or “the immaterial aggregates.” Because mental formations (saṅkhāra-kkhandha) have volition (cetanā) as their chief, it is said “the aspect of volition of formations” etc. Indeed, in the Suttanta-bhājanīya of the Vibhaṅga, in the analysis of the aggregate of formations, only volition is described in detail as “that which is volition, purposive volition, the state of having willed.”

“Asatī” means “in the absence of” (asantesu). This is stated thus by way of grammatical substitution (vacana-vipallāsa), changing the plural to the singular. “Cattāro khandhe vatthuṃ katvā” means taking the states that are the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya), recognized as these four aggregates—feeling, perception, consciousness, and volition etc.—as the basis. Although this method is possible in the five doors as well, it is specifically mentioned as “in the mind-door.”

“Adhivacanasamphassa-vevacano” refers to that mind-contact (manosamphassa) which has received the name “designation-contact” (adhivacana-samphassa) because it is to be apprehended through the door of designation (paññatti). In the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra), it is certainly manifest in the physical body (rūpakāya) because it is obtainable depending on the heart-base (hadayavatthu). However, this method is not intended here; because the impossibility [of mind-contact] by way of excluding feeling etc. is being highlighted, the meaning is stated as “it would arise depending on the five sense-bases.” Indeed, without the support of feeling, the occurrence of mind-contact depending on the five sense-bases is not possible. If the place of origin does not exist, the arising of a result from a place where it does not arise never occurs; to show this meaning by way of illustrating the meaning already attained...
102:
He spoke the phrase beginning with "Ambarukkhe" (as an illustration). "Rūpakāyato" means from the aggregate of form alone. "Tassa" refers to (the turn of the non-arising of) mental contact (manosamphassa).

When conflicting causes meet, the very distinct and different arising, or the state of being the cause of such distinct arising existing within one's own continuity, is called the mode of being deformed (ruppanākāra). That very mode of being deformed is called a sign (liṅga) because it makes known hidden meanings such as the base (vatthu) and impingement (sappaṭigha). It is called a sign (nimitta) because it is the cause of recognizing various things. It is called an indication (uddesa) because it is indicated in such and such ways. In this way, the meanings of the terms such as "mode" (ākāra) should be understood here. The mutual striking of the base and the object is called impingement (paṭigha). Contact born from that impingement is called impingement-contact (paṭighasamphassa). Therefore, he said "sappaṭighaṃ," etc. "Nāmakāyato" means from the aggregate of name alone. "Tassa" refers to (the non-arising of) impingement-contact. The remaining meaning is the same as the method stated in the first question.

"Ubhayavasena" means by way of both types of contact: designation-contact (adhivacanasamphassa) and impingement-contact (paṭighasamphassa), which have both the aggregate of name and the aggregate of form as their support.

To show the respective causes means having shown the causes known as the aggregate of name and the aggregate of form individually by way of the negative method (vyatireka). "Tesaṃ" means of those contacts. "Avisesato" means generally, without making a distinction. "To show" means to show by way of the negative method itself. "Eseva hetu" means this cause called name-and-form occurring in the six doors is indeed the cause of the two types of contact as appropriate. Now, to show the occurrence of that cause by classifying it as appropriate, he spoke the phrase beginning with "Cakkhudvārādīsu hi."

Associated aggregates (sampayuttakhandhā) are the aggregates such as feeling (vedanā) associated with contact. Here, by taking the associated aggregates, adverting (āvajjana) should also be understood as taken, because it cannot occur without them. The same method should be understood for the mental contact that follows. "Being of five kinds" means being of five kinds by way of eye-contact, etc. "That contact" refers to impingement-contact. "In many ways" means it assists in many ways. Specifically, resultant name (vipāka-nāma) assists the many-fold resultant mental contact (vipāka-manosamphassa) by way of seven conditions: conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), result (vipāka), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). Here, whatever function of nutriment exists, it assists by way of the nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya). Whatever function of faculty exists, it assists by way of the faculty condition (indriya-paccaya). Non-resultant name assists non-resultant mental contact by way of the other conditions, excluding the result condition. Form, consisting of the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), etc., [assists] the five kinds of contact such as eye-contact...
103:
...by way of six conditions: support (nissaya), pre-nascence (purejāta), faculty (indriya), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). Form such as visible objects (rūpāyatana), etc., assists those five kinds of contact by way of four conditions: object (ārammaṇa), pre-nascence (purejāta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). For mental contact (manosamphassa), however, those visible objects, etc., and mental objects (dhammārammaṇa) assist only by way of the object condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). Heart-base matter (hadayavatthu-rūpa) assists mental contact by way of five conditions: support (nissaya), pre-nascence (purejāta), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). Thus, it should be understood that name-and-form assists that contact in many ways.

To show by way of the negative method the meaning that consciousness is the specific cause of name-and-form in the initial arising, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "If it did not descend into the mother's womb," etc. Although the rebirth of womb-born beings (gabbhaseyyaka) is like someone entering the mother's womb from outside, in reality, it is just the first arising of the aggregates there in the mother's womb according to conditions. Therefore, the commentator said, "Having entered... etc... it would not occur." "Suddhaṃ" means pure, unmixed with consciousness, or devoid of consciousness. This word "avasesaṃ" (remainder) regards "name" (nāma); therefore, "avasesaṃ nāmarūpaṃ" means it would be only the remaining name-and-form, excluding this consciousness.

"Descended by way of rebirth" means either by way of taking rebirth or by way of descending as the first part of the child entering the mother's womb. "Vokkamissatha" means it would come to an interruption of continuity or destruction; to show that such arrival is called death, he said "by way of death (cuti)." "Assa" means of consciousness; that consciousness is spoken of by way of consciousness in general (viññāṇasāmaṇya). Therefore, he said "only by the cessation of that mind," meaning only by the cessation of the rebirth-consciousness. "Tato" means from the rebirth-consciousness. To clarify with a suitable reason the aforementioned meaning that death (cuti) cannot occur due to the cessation of the rebirth-consciousness or the second and third minds following it, he spoke the phrase beginning with "Paṭisandhicittena hi."

"In this interval" means in this period of sixteen thought-moments (cittakkhana). In the phrase "there is no danger," let there be no danger of death for the child first, because at that time rebirth-consciousness [as a cause for death] is impossible. But how can there be no danger of death for the mother at that time? Because a mother who is of a nature to die within that interval, without passing those sixteen thought-moments, cannot possibly conceive a womb (take rebirth). Therefore, he said, "For this is not the occasion," meaning it is not the occasion for death (cuti).

"Matter arisen together with rebirth-consciousness" refers to kamma-born matter (kammajarūpa) produced at the moment of descent (okkanti). Only those are strictly called matter arisen together with rebirth-consciousness; temperature-born matter (utusamuṭṭhāna) is not, because it arises after the arising phase (uppāda) of the rebirth-consciousness.
104:
Materiality produced by consciousness (cittaja-rūpa) and materiality produced by nutriment (āhāraja-rūpa) are simply impossible at that time. The types of materiality that arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) are threefold: those arising at the sub-moment of arising (uppāda), the sub-moment of presence (ṭhiti), and the sub-moment of dissolution (bhaṅga) of that rebirth-linking consciousness. Among these three, the materiality arising at the sub-moment of arising ceases at the sub-moment of arising of the seventeenth life-continuum (bhavaṅga); the materiality arising at the sub-moment of presence ceases at the sub-moment of presence; and the materiality arising at the sub-moment of dissolution ceases at the sub-moment of dissolution. Regarding such cessation, although it cannot be said that 'a phenomenon that is ceasing is a condition for a phenomenon that is ceasing,' it is not that it cannot be said for the sub-moments of arising and presence. Therefore, it is stated: 'Because they exist during the sub-moments of arising and presence of the seventeenth life-continuum, they are unable to provide support to that consciousness.' This is because in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhava), the occurrence of the mental body (nāmakāya) is possible only when supported by the physical body (rūpakāya). Referring to the greater strength of that consciousness over those material phenomena, it is said: 'The occurrence of the seventeenth... occurs.' The phrase 'the series is connected' means that the series of forty-eight kamma-born materialities (kammaja-rūpa) occurs in a connected manner. First, there is the rebirth-linking consciousness, then up to the sixteenth life-continuum consciousness; each of these has three sub-moments: arising, presence, and dissolution. In each of these three sub-moments of every single consciousness, thirty kamma-born materialities arise. Thus, sixteen sets of three make forty-eight. This method applies to subsequent moments as well. With reference to this, it is said: 'The series of forty-eight kamma-born materialities occurs in a connected manner.' If the materialities arising with the rebirth-linking consciousness were unable to provide support to the seventeenth life-continuum (if they were not capable), and if the seventeenth consciousness from the rebirth-linking consciousness were the death consciousness (cuti-citta), then kamma-born materiality would not even arise during the sub-moments of presence and dissolution of the rebirth-linking consciousness, let alone during the sub-moments of the life-continuum consciousness. If that were the case, that consciousness would not obtain any condition, and the process of existence would not proceed; the series would not be connected but would instead be cut off. Therefore, it is said: 'It is called vokkāmati (it departs/descends),' and so on.

'Itthattāya' means the state of being in this manner. This is said in reference to the physical body of a womb-born being as it is. For such a being, the five aggregates are complete without deficiency; therefore, it is explained as 'for the sake of reaching the state of the complete five aggregates.' 'Upacchijjissatha' means to cut off by the interruption of the continuity. 'Suddhaṃ nāmarūpam-eva' refers to name-and-form alone, devoid of consciousness. The fulfillment of the limbs and organs is called 'vuddhi' (growth). Reaching a state of firmness is called 'virūḷhi' (development). Reaching the state of maturity is called 'vepulla' (expansion). It is stated that these—vuddhi, virūḷhi, and vepulla—occur respectively by the power of the first stage of life and so on, hence 'by the power of the first stage of life, etc.' The word 'vā' (or) has an indefinite meaning; therefore, it should be understood that periods such as two thousand years are also included.
105:
The restrictive term 'viññāṇam-eva' (consciousness alone) is a term that excludes the 'Self' (atta) and 'Creator' (issara) etc., imagined by outsiders. Since the word of emphasis (avadhāraṇa) serves to exclude opposing views, it is not a term that excludes ignorance (avijjā), contact (phassa), and so on. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: 'This alone is the cause,' and so forth. This method should be applied appropriately to all other terms as well. Now, to illustrate by way of a simile that consciousness alone is the primary cause of name-and-form, the phrase 'yathā hi' (just as), etc., is stated. To show that name-and-form, whether individually or collectively, is incapable of performing its own function without consciousness, it is taken together as 'this thing called name-and-form.' 'Having a precursor' means being the forerunner. Indeed, consciousness is the forerunner of conascent phenomena. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: 'Phenomena are preceded by the mind' (manopubbaṅgamā dhammā). 'Bahudhā' means it assists as a condition in many ways.

How? At the moment of rebirth-linking, the rebirth-linking consciousness or another resultant consciousness assists the resultant mental factors (vipāka-nāma) through nine conditions: conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), dependence (nissaya), result (vipāka), nutriment (āhāra), faculty (indriya), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). At the moment of rebirth-linking, it assists the base-materiality (vatthu-rūpa) through nine conditions: conascence, mutuality, dependence, result, nutriment, faculty, dissociation (vippayutta), presence, and non-disappearance. Excluding the base-materiality, it assists the remaining materiality through eight conditions, having removed the mutuality condition from these nine. However, the volitional consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa) assists the materiality of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), or the kamma-born materiality in the five-constituent realm, in only one way: by the power of decisive support (upanissaya), according to the Suttanta method. It should be understood that all other consciousnesses, starting from the first life-continuum, also assist that name-and-form as appropriate. This is just a summary; if the method of conditions were to be shown in detail, all the teachings from the Great Book of Relations (Mahāpaṭṭhāna) would have to be brought in, so it is not expanded upon here.

How is it to be believed that 'rebirth-linking name-and-form arises because of consciousness'? It is to be believed both by way of scripture (sutta) and by way of reasoning (yutti). In the Pali texts, the fact that feeling (vedanā) and so on have consciousness as their condition appears in many ways, such as in the method 'phenomena that follow the mind,' etc. By way of reasoning, in this world, based on the visible materiality produced by consciousness (cittaja-rūpa), it is understood that consciousness is also the condition for invisible materiality. It is observed that when the mind is clear or not clear, corresponding types of materiality arise. Based on such visible materiality produced by consciousness, it is to be believed that consciousness is also the condition for the invisible rebirth-linking materiality. This is because the fact that kamma-originated materiality, like consciousness-originated materiality, has consciousness as its condition is mentioned in the Paṭṭhāna.

In the Pali 'dukkhasamudayasambhavo,' the word 'samudaya' carries the same meaning as 'samudāya,' meaning a collection or mass. Therefore, it means the arising of the mass of suffering. The meaning of the Commentary is: 'I wish to see the state of a king who is without an entourage, ministers, or servants, and who has no companion.' Because he gladdens the entourage, he is called a king (rājā). By the word 'vatthu' (base) itself, the dependence (nissaya) is also included. Because of the state of being an immediate (anantara) condition with nothing in between...
106:
In this context, the word *samudaya* (origin) is a synonym for a collection (*samūha*), just like the word *samudāya*; therefore, it is said, "the arising of the mass of suffering." *Ekako* means one who is without companions, devoid of a royal retinue. The intended meaning is: "We wish to see your state of kingship without us." He is called a king (*rājā*) because he pleases (*rañjeti*) his retinue as appropriate. Even if not explicitly stated in terms of the fulfillment of meaning, it is as if it were stated. By this term *hadaya-vatthu* (heart-base), its support should also be understood as included.
