Because of the state of having no interval, the support of the support is also called simply "support" (*nissaya*). As for rebirth-consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*), "let it arise"; the meaning is that there is no possibility for this [to arise without conditions]. Therefore, it is said, "We shall see," and so on.

*Bahudhā* means it assists in many ways. How? In the rebirth-linking moment, mentality (*nāma*) assists consciousness (*viññāṇa*) in seven ways through the conditions of conascence (*sahajāta*), mutuality (*aññamañña*), support (*nissaya*), resultant (*vipāka*), association (*sampayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*). In some instances, it also assists through the root condition (*hetu-paccaya*), and in others through the nutriment condition (*āhāra-paccaya*); thus, it assists in other ways as well. Mentality that is not a resultant (*avipāka-nāma*), excluding the resultant condition from the aforementioned conditions, assists through the remaining six conditions. In some instances, it assists through the root condition, and in others through the nutriment condition; thus, it assists in other ways too, and that occurs only during the course of existence (*pavatti*), not at the moment of rebirth.

On the side of matter (*rūpa*), however, the heart-base (*hadaya-vatthu*) assists consciousness at the moment of rebirth in only six ways through the conditions of conascence, mutuality, support, dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence, and non-disappearance. During the course of existence, excluding the conditions of conascence and mutuality, it assists through the pre-nascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) along with those same conditions. The five types of matter, such as the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*), also assist their respective consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*), through the conditions of support, pre-nascence, faculty (*indriya*), dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance. Thus, it should be understood that mentality-and-materiality (*nāmarūpa*) assists consciousness in many ways.

The fact that mentality-and-materiality assists consciousness in sequence, and consciousness assists rebirth mentality-and-materiality, is sometimes superior on the side of consciousness, sometimes superior on the side of mentality-and-materiality, and sometimes equal in both. To show that these three modes are taken together by the word *ettāvatā* (to this extent), it is said, "In consciousness... (pe)... in those occurring." Furthermore, to show that all the occurrences of the round of rebirth (*saṃsāra-vaṭṭa*) arise only because of this much—the five aggregates called consciousness and mentality-and-materiality occurring through mutual support—it is said, "By this much... (pe)... rebirths." Therein, *ettakena* means only by this much; the meaning is that it is not due to a self (*atta*) that has the nature of a doer or an experiencer, nor due to a creator lord (*issara*), etc. This word is one that contains the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) within it.
107:
"*Vacanamattameva adhikicca*" means focusing only on the mere expression; it refers to designations that arise by giving weight only to the usage of words, which are not true in reality, like the names "Sirivaḍḍhaka" (Increaser of Prosperity) given to slaves and so on. Therefore, it was said, "without looking at the meaning." *Vohārassa* means mere conventional usage. *Patha* (path) refers to the course of occurrence or the objective substance (the five aggregates) which is the object of occurrence.

Because a person is called "mindful" (*sata*) due to the action of remembering (*sati*), and "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāna*) due to the action of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), it is said, "by way of indicating the cause." The utterance made by extracting the cause is called *nirutti* (expression). Because it makes known a single meaning through various modes such as *paṇḍita* (wise), etc., it is called *paññatti* (concept). That same person is made known in various ways as "wise" (*paṇḍita*), "adept" (*vyatta*), or "sagacious" (*medhāvī*). He is made known as *paṇḍita* by way of the mode of having wisdom, and as *vyatta* by way of the mode of being adept; thus, because of making known through various modes, it is called *paññatti*. In this context, the terms *adhivacana*, *nirutti*, and *paññatti* have the same meaning. All words can attain the state of being a designation (*adhivacana*), etc. Therefore, it should be understood that this connection of meaning is made with the intention that all words are spoken of by the terms *adhivacana*, etc., which occur specifically in certain distinct words, through the commonality of manifesting the conceptual meaning.

Alternatively, the word *adhi* expresses the meaning of "above"; speech that is "above" is *adhivacana*. Above what? The meaning is clear: it is spoken above the meaning to be manifested. Or, speech that is dependent (*adhīna*) is *adhivacana*. Dependent on what? Dependent on the meaning. Likewise, speech that is decided or fixed in manifesting various meanings is *nirutti*. Because it makes known through various modes such as the earth element, a man, etc., it is called *paññatti*. In this way, the occurrence of the terms *adhivacana*, etc., in all words should be understood. Otherwise, only words like *Sirivaḍḍhaka* and *Dhanavaḍḍhaka* (Increaser of Wealth) would be *nirutti*, and only words like *paṇḍita* and *vyatta*, which make known a single meaning through various modes, would be *paññatti*. In this way, the course of usage of the designation expressed by the three names should be understood as "mentality-and-materiality together with consciousness" by this much. Therefore, it was said, "*iti*," and so on.

"To be entered into by wisdom" means the meaning that is to be brought about or known by wisdom. Therefore, it is said, "it should be known." The round (*vaṭṭa*) refers to the three types of rounds: the round of defilements (*kilesa-vaṭṭa*), the round of kamma (*kamma-vaṭṭa*), and the round of results (*vipāka-vaṭṭa*). *Vattati* means it occurs or revolves. This statement is made by way of concluding the meaning expressed by the five terms beginning with *jāyetha* (should be born). By the word *ādi* (etc.), the designations such as "woman," "man," etc., should also be understood as included. "For the sake of the designation of name" means to make known names such as aggregates, contact, beings, women, and so on. The objective base (*vatthu*) is also completed by this much. Therefore, it is said, "The five aggregates are also manifested by this much." "By this much" (*ettāvatā*) means by the occurrence of mentality-and-materiality together with consciousness to this extent.
108:
## Description of the Designation of Self

It is called *anusandhi* (connection) because it connects with the teaching that occurs above. The subsequent teaching, which proceeds by way of connection with the preceding teaching, is called *anusandhi*. That connection has already been shown by way of the first phrase (sentence). Now, as it is to be shown by way of the second phrase, the Blessed One said "Iti Bhagavā" and so forth, wishing to show that meaning. "Rūpī" means one who has form (or one who possesses rūpa-kasiṇa jhāna). "Parittaṃ" means a self that is not extensive, but small. This is because, in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a "self." It is merely a concept imagined by those with wrong views. Therefore, wishing to show the place where their perception of self arises and the manner in which they imagine it as having form and so on, He said "Yo" and so forth.

"Rūpiṃ parittaṃ" means that one designates the self as having form by way of the kasiṇa-form that appears to oneself as the self, and as limited because that kasiṇa-form has not been expanded. One who has attained various kasiṇas, such as the blue kasiṇa, designates that self. "Anantaṃ" (infinite) means that one designates it as infinite because the kasiṇa-sign is immeasurable and its boundaries do not appear. "Ugghāṭetvā" means removing or abstracting through meditation. "Nimittaphuṭṭhokāsaṃ" refers to the space touched or pervaded by that kasiṇa-sign. "Tesu" means it occurs in those four mental aggregates (*nāma-kkhandha*). "Viññāṇamattameva" means that one who holds the view "the self consists of consciousness" takes only consciousness.

This word "etarahi" (now) is a term used with emphasis (limitation). Wishing to show that meaning, after explaining it as "idāneva" (only now), the meaning excluded by the emphasis is stated as "na ito paraṃ" (not beyond this). One who holds that beings are cut off right there in their respective existences is called an annihilationist (*ucchedavādī*). Therefore, it was said, "This is spoken by way of annihilation." "Bhāviṃ" refers to the nature of always existing, of not perishing. Therefore, it was said, "This is spoken by way of eternalism." "Atathāsabhāvaṃ" means not having the true nature as spoken by other teachers of wrong views. "Tathabhāvāya" means for the sake of the self's annihilation or for the sake of its permanence. This is a statement made without specification, by way of indicating a general sense. "Sampādessāmi" means "I will fulfill and show the true nature to him," or "I will establish it." Thus, He will say later, "Having made the eternalist view known," and so forth. "Iminā" refers to the statement beginning with "Atathaṃ vā pana," meaning that even if it has a non-annihilation nature, it is the intended meaning according to the view of the eternalist. "Upakappessāmi" means "I will approach and strengthen it."

When this is so, the rūpa-kasiṇa jhāna is called "rūpa" by the method of dropping the latter word. Because of the attainment of that rūpa-kasiṇa jhāna, one is called "rūpī." Therefore, it was said, "Rūpī means one who has attained rūpa-kasiṇa jhāna." In this term "parittattānudiṭṭhi," the word "rūpī" should also be brought in and stated by the method of repetition (*āvutti*). This is because that person with wrong view adheres to the idea of having form just as they adhere to the idea of being limited.
109:
It is as if one stands firmly adhering to one's own view. In the word "arūpī," the same method should be understood. They say: "A wide creeper that is like a thick, tangled thicket with many leaves and branches is called *valli*; a creeper with a long, continuous growth that is the opposite of that is called *latā*." "In the sense of not being abandoned" means because it has not been eradicated by the Path (*magga*). The fitness to arise when an occasion or cause is obtained is the meaning of "underlying tendency" (*anusayana*).

What is called "arūpa-kasiṇa" is the space obtained by removing the kasiṇa (*kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa*), not the limited space-kasiṇa. Some teachers say, "Both are indeed arūpa-kasiṇa." Alternatively, "one whose domain is the mental aggregates" means that since the mental aggregates such as feeling (*vedanā*) are the domain of the adherence to the "self" for one with wrong view, it refers to the person with wrong view whose domain is the mental aggregates. The word "vā" (or) has the sense of providing an alternative to the stated meaning. As for the grammatical connection of the Pali: the mental aggregates (*arūpa*) are the domain of this person, thus he is "arūpī"; it refers to that "arūpī" person.

"The four who have attained" refers to the four types of people with wrong views who, by way of attaining rūpa-kasiṇa and so forth, personally conceive those respective wrong views and, having taken them up, uphold and designate them. "Their disciples" refers to the four who learn the views of those masters either directly or through lineage and, accepting and liking them in the same way, designate them. "The four speculators" (*takkikā*) refers to the four who, without attaining kasiṇa jhāna, personally adhere to and uphold the four aforementioned wrong views through mere reasoning. Their disciples should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

## Description of the Non-Designation of Self

"Even one who has begun insight" refers to one who practices insight for the sake of the future Path-fruit; by this, it shows a person established in strong insight. The meaning is that even if such a person is not very learned (*abahussuta*), they simply do not designate a self. Such is the power of insight. A person within the Dispensation who has attained jhāna and supernormal knowledge (*abhiññā*) should not be said to "not designate," and thus such a person is not mentioned here. Now, the reason for their not designating is shown by the words beginning with "Etesañhi." "Knowledge alone arises" means that the distorted grasp (wrong view) does not occur because the cause for that distorted grasp has been driven far away. The connection is: "Knowledge alone arises regarding the mental aggregates."

## Description of the Contemplation of Self

"Having contemplated by way of view" means contemplating through the power of wrong view, not through the power of knowledge. And that contemplation is, in essence, by way of seeing through wrong view.
110:
The passage "one repeatedly regards feeling as the self" refers to the personality belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) based on the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). By the word "appaṭisaṃvedana" (non-experiencing), meaning "one does not experience various objects such as desirable ones," the state of being an experiencer is rejected, and consequently, the states of perception (saññā) and so forth are also rejected. This is because perception and the others are inseparable from the nature of feeling. Therefore, it is said, "By this statement, the personality belief based on the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) is taught." By the statement "My self experiences," the state of non-experiencing is rejected. Thus, it is said, "It is not that there is no nature of experiencing." However, by the phrase "one who has the nature of feeling" (vedanādhammo), the view "Feeling is my self" is rejected. This is because it acknowledges the state of being endowed with feeling, asserting that the phenomenon called feeling belongs to this self. Therefore, it is said, "For this self, the phenomenon of feeling has an inseparable nature." It should be construed as teaching the personality belief based on the aggregates of perception, mental formations, and consciousness. In saying "one experiences because of being associated with feeling," it means that the function of experiencing is performed due to association with that feeling. It is like saying a man is "volitional" because of association with volition (cetanā). Although all phenomena that arise with an object obtain the experience of that object, they only obtain the experience of the object's flavor partially, merely by contact. Feeling, however, should be understood as experiencing the flavor of the object in the capacity of a master, as is appropriate. By the power of that feeling, perception and so forth are also said to "experience" because they are associated with that feeling. Thus, it is stated in the Atthasālinī Commentary: "Having reached the state of experiencing the flavor of the object, the associated phenomena remaining after feeling experience only a single portion." This meaning is also clearly illustrated in that commentary by the simile of the king and the cook. "Etassa" refers to the three mental aggregates, such as perception and so forth. By the phrase "having an inseparable nature," it points to a certain distinction arising from constant and inseparable association.

Among those three holders of views in those sections who hold: "Feeling is my self," "The self has no nature of experiencing," and "My self has feeling," it is not appropriate for one who regards pleasant feeling as the self to regard painful feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as the self, because the three types of feelings have distinct natures. In the same way, it is said of the remaining two: "Whichever feeling one repeatedly regards as the self." By the phrase "because after having been, it is no more," it shows that they are impermanent because they have arising and passing away. By the words "such and such" and so forth, they are called "conditioned" (saṅkhata) because they are compounded and conditioned by many causes. "Such and such causes" refers to phenomena that arise through appropriate causes, depending on their respective causes such as the sense-faculty, the object, consciousness, and contact (phassa) through which pleasant feeling is experienced. Because there is no permanence or total annihilation, it is a phenomenon that arises through appropriate causes, supporting causes, similar causes, and suitable causes. It is described by these four terms: it is called "subject to exhaustion" (khayadhamma) because it has the nature of being exhausted; "subject to fall" (vayadhamma) because it has the nature of falling away; "subject to fading away" (virāgadhamma) because it has the nature of fading; and "subject to cessation" (nirodhadhamma) because it has the nature of ceasing.
111:
Depending on their respective causes such as contact (phassa) and so forth, they arise through appropriate, supporting, similar, and suitable causes, because there is neither eternalism (sassata) nor annihilationism (uccheda). By these four terms—subject to exhaustion (khayadhamma) because it has the nature of exhaustion, subject to fall (vayadhamma) because it has the nature of falling away, subject to fading away (virāgadhamma) because it has the nature of fading, and subject to cessation (nirodhadhamma) because it has the nature of ceasing—He shows only the nature of the breaking up of feeling. Therefore, it is stated as "khayo... khayadhammā" and so forth.

"Vigata" means disappeared through the disappearance of its nature. "Ekasseva" refers to the view of a single holder of wrong views. "Tīsupi kālesu" refers to the times when the three types of feelings occur. In saying, "This nature of pleasant feeling, or the nature of painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, is my self," He asks with the intention: "How could anyone, unless insane, believe that a single person has such diverse natures?" To show that such a view is impossible for that person, He says, "Why would it not be possible?" and so forth. "Visesena" means by way of distinction, such as pleasantness and so forth. In the phrase "sukhañca dukkhañca," the word "ca" includes neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; or else, it is included within pleasant feeling itself because of its peaceful and subtle nature. "Avisesena" means by way of the generality of feeling without distinction. "Vokiṇṇa" means mixed by way of the divisions of pleasantness and so forth. This holder of wrong views takes those three types of feelings together and repeatedly regards them as the self. If taken merely as the nature of feeling without specific distinction, it would lead to the occurrence of many feelings in a single moment. If that were the case, it would lead to the flaw that all feelings must always be occurring for the self; thus, the holder of wrong views would be forced to admit the occurrence of many feelings in a single moment, which is improper. Therefore, not wishing to allow that possibility, He says, "There is no occurrence of many feelings in a single moment," meaning that this contradicts direct experience. Because it contradicts experience and because there is no self-entity at all, the wise do not delight in it; the meaning is that the wise do not accept this view.

Even in the continuity of form associated with the sense-faculties, a certain movement (action) can be obtained by the power of the diffusion of the air element. Therefore, even in the pure aggregate of form without sense-faculties, whenever the diffusion of the air element can be obtained, He takes that as an example and says, "either in a palm-leaf fan or in a window." "Vedanādhammesu" means in phenomena that have the nature of feeling. By the statement "I am," He teaches the manner in which the "I-conceit" (ahaṃkāra) arises by taking the three aggregates together. However, by the statement "This one am I," He teaches the manner in which the "I-conceit" arises by taking each of those aggregates individually. Therefore, the commentator said.
112:
In the passage beginning with "Ekadhammopi," the word "taṃ" refers to the arising of ahaṃkāra (ego-conceit), the notion that "I am." This ahaṃkāra, because it lacks a basis due to the cessation of the four mental aggregates, cannot exist, just like the sharpness of a rabbit's horn.

"Ettāvatā" refers to this much of the teaching, which has arisen by way of showing the connection (anusandhi) to the phrase "tāntākulakajātā" (they have become like a tangled skein) in the passage beginning with "Ānanda, to this extent."

Although it is true that the discourse on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭakathā) was also spoken below, here, the Buddha spoke the words showing the gravity of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) to illustrate how a person with wrong views is unable to lift their head from the suffering of the round. Thus, it is said, "He spoke the vaṭṭakathā."

Is it not true that the roots of the round are ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā)? Why then is the vaṭṭakathā spoken here in a different way without examining that ignorance and craving? To answer this, it is said, "The Blessed One..." and so on. "With ignorance at the head" means making ignorance the chief and leading factor, or starting with ignorance. "The beginning is not known" means that even with my unimpeded omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa), the beginning or limit of ignorance is not known, such as saying, "Ignorance arose during the time of such-and-such a Buddha or Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), and did not exist before that." This is because such a beginning simply does not exist. "This cause" means because of this cause, such as the taints (āsavas). "Bhavataṇhā" refers to craving that binds one to existence. "Bhavadiṭṭhi" refers to the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi). By the phrase "arising in various existences," he shows the endless arising from this existence to that, and from that existence to this. Therefore, he said, "In the great ocean..." and so on.

"One who is confused about the mode of conditions (paccayākāra)" is a statement of fact and not a specific attribute. This is because everyone with wrong views is indeed confused about the mode of conditions (paṭiccasamuppāda). "He spoke of the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa)" means he spoke of Nibbāna, which is called vivaṭṭa because it is free from the round (vaṭṭa). "Of the one who acts" means of the one who follows and practices the Teacher's advice correctly. Therefore, he said, "Of the one who dwells in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)." Such a person, through correct practice in the contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā) and contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā), deserves to be described by the words "he does not see feeling as self," and so on. Therefore, he said, "One of such a nature..." and so on. "In all things" means in all things belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka). These are the things to be comprehended (through insight). "Not another" means not seeing other things such as perception (saññā) as self, apart from feeling. "The world of aggregates, etc." refers to phenomena such as form (rūpa), and to show that these are a collection of such phenomena, it is said, "In phenomena such as form." One does not cling firmly through the power of the grasp of view and craving. The conceit (māna), craving (taṇhā), and conceiving (maññanā) that arise as "I am superior," etc., also cause one to wander in the round, just like ahaṃkāra, diṭṭhi, and maññanā.
113:
Conceiving (maññanā) through the conceit (māna) that has arisen is also of the nature of agitation (paritassanā), just like conceiving through craving and view; therefore, he said, "also due to agitation through craving, view, and conceit."

If someone were to say that an Arahant has such a kind of view, that statement is improper and incorrect. In the Pali "thus is his view," it should be understood as "such a kind of view exists in the continuity of that Arahant." If someone were to say, "The Tathāgata exists after death," and if that person's words were true, it would imply that "the Arahant knows nothing." This is because such a (wrong) view does not exist in an Arahant who knows the truth. Because it is improper to say that he knows nothing, at the end of all four modes (vāra) beginning with "The Tathāgata exists," he said, "For what reason is that?" and so on. Because it is summarized in the first three modes and detailed in the final mode, it is said, "At the end, he said 'Taṃ kissa hetu', etc."

Some teachers, however, say that the teaching in the first three modes is the same as in the final mode, but the Pali text is merely summarized. "Vohāra" (usage/designation) refers to the conventional designations used as "being, woman, man," or as "aggregates, bases," or as "contact, feeling." He stated that the basis for the occurrence of those designations is, in brief, these very aggregates, bases, and elements (dhātu). Since Nibbāna is made known in the preceding stage only as the cessation of formations (saṅkhāra), it can be said that Nibbāna is also reached through the door of the aggregates; thus, he said, "the five aggregates to be reached by wisdom." Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "In this very fathom-long body, endowed with perception and mind, I declare the world (the truth of suffering), the origin of the world (the truth of the origin), the cessation of the world (the truth of cessation), and the practice leading to the cessation of the world (the truth of the path)."

Alternatively, because this term "paññāvacara" (the range of wisdom) takes up the things belonging to the three planes, he said only "the five aggregates." Therefore, in the phrase "yāvatā paññā" (as far as wisdom), it should be understood that only mundane wisdom (lokiya paññā) is taken. This is a discourse on the round (vaṭṭakathā). Indeed, it was said, "As far as the round revolves." For this reason, he said, "He showed the connection (anusandhi) to the word 'tāntākulaka'." Since the Blessed One, having spoken the discourse on the round in this sutta with view as the head, continued to speak the discourse on the round according to the connection, he said with emphasis (using the word 'eva'), "He showed only the connection to the word 'tāntākulaka'." The discourse on dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) here is expanded only to clarify its depth, and although there is a discourse on the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa), it should be understood that here it is examined only in relation to the round.
114:
## Explanation of the Seven Stations of Consciousness

"Going, going" (gacchanto gacchanto) refers to one who is well-established in the practice of tranquility (samatha) and proceeds through the progress of insight (vipassanā) and the path (magga). One is called "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) because of being liberated from both parts (the form-body and the name-body). That person, described as "one who does not repeatedly contemplate in this way," is a practitioner of the vehicle of insight (vipassanā-yānika); thus it is said, "He who does not repeatedly contemplate, that person, while going, is called one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta)." "Mentioned below" refers to the two worldling monks (puthujjana-bhikkhu) appearing in the lower Pali text, such as in "Ānanda, to what extent does one not designating the self not designate it?" and "Ānanda, a monk does not repeatedly contemplate feeling as the self," etc. "Nigamana" means escape (from the suffering of the round). "Nāma" refers to names such as "liberated by wisdom" (paññāvimutta) and so on.

"Spoken of by way of rebirth" refers to the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) which are distinguished by the specific differences of diverse bodies and diverse perceptions at rebirth. Depending on various groups of beings, the diversity of bodies and so on should be understood as arising from the rebirth-perception (paṭisandhi-saññā) included in those groups. This is because the action-process (kammabhava) that brings about that being was accumulated in such a manner. "Four will come" means that the four stations of consciousness by way of the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and mental formations will come, as in "Friends, consciousness, when standing, stands attached to form," etc. "The station of consciousness" refers to the cause for the station of the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) at the present time. In terms of meaning, the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and mental formations in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhava), and the three aggregates starting with feeling in the four-constituent realm (catuvokāra-bhava), which are distinguished by the aforementioned specific perceptions, should be understood. Based on the state of being an abode for beings, "two bases" (āyatana) refers to two dwelling places. The word āyatana also carries the meaning of a dwelling place, as in "two shrines of devas" (devāyatana-dvaya). "All" refers to all of the stations of consciousness and the two bases. The intention of the commentator is to take all of them without excluding even one. The reason it does not reach the point of taking them without remainder is that the stations of consciousness and the two bases are mutually inclusive within each other.

"Seyyathāpi manussā" is a particle used for illustration, meaning "just like humans." Even though there is no difference in the external physical cause, there is indeed a distinction because the internal [mind] is different. Because there is diversity in the bodies of those beings, or because they have diverse bodies, they are called "those of diverse bodies" (nānattakāya). In this way...
115:
The meaning should also be understood in the remaining terms. "Nesaṃ" refers to humans. Because these beings have rebirth-perceptions of a diverse nature, they are called "those of diverse perceptions" (nānattasaññī). Because they have a falling away from the mass of happiness, they are called "fallen ones" (vinipātikā). Even though they have the state of devas, they are called vinipātikā because they lack divine prosperity, or because they have not fallen into great suffering in the lower realms (apāya). Therefore, it is said, "those liberated from the four lower realms."

"Dhammapada" refers to the groups of Dhamma such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). "Vijāniyā" means having first known through the wisdom consisting of learning (sutamaya-ñāṇa) from the heard teaching, one should develop wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) according to that sequence and also practice the right practice such as the purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi). And that practice would be for our benefit, for all benefits including those of the present life. Now, wishing to show the practice of virtue in that practice by way of division, he spoke the verse beginning with "Pāṇesu ca" (And regarding living beings).

Those born in the assembly of Brahmas or the group of Brahmas produced by the first jhāna are called "devas of the Brahma retinue" (brahmakāyika). Those who stand in the position of attendants to the Great Brahma are "Brahma's retinue" (brahmapārisajja). Those who stand in the position of ministers to the Great Brahma are "Brahma's ministers" (brahmapurohita). Those who are great in terms of lifespan, appearance, and so on are "Great Brahmas" (mahābrahmā). Even though all three types are produced by the first jhāna, the statement "But the Brahmapārisajjas..." etc., is made to show that this distinction exists due to the difference in the occurrence of the jhāna.

"Parittena" means by a limited or inferior jhāna. That inferiority should be understood through the inferiority of desire (chanda) and so on, or it is an inferior jhāna that is merely attained. "Kappassa" refers to an incalculable aeon (asankheyya-kappa). Because they are born in the middle of the inferior and superior ones, they are produced by a medium jhāna. That medium state should be understood through the medium state of desire and so on, or it is a medium jhāna that is not very well developed after being attained. "Upaḍḍhakappo" is half of an incalculable aeon.

"Vipphārikataro" means more extensive in measure than the Brahmapārisajjas and more noble in nature. Indeed, they are more noble by nature, but here that is not the measure. For instance, although there is a difference in nature in the bodies of the Brahmas of Limited Lustre (parittābha) and so on, and the Brahmas of Limited Glory (parittasubha) and so on, they are designated only by way of unity; thus they are called "those of uniform bodies" (ekattakāya).

"Paṇītena" means by an exalted first jhāna. That exalted state should be understood through the excellence of desire and so on, or it is an exalted jhāna that is well-developed and has reached mastery (vasībhāva), having been led to a state of prominence. Here too, "aeon" (kappa) should be understood only by way of an incalculable aeon, because a complete great aeon (mahākappa) is not possible. "Iti" means in the manner stated above. "Te" refers to all three types of Brahmas called "Brahmakāyika." "Unity of perception" (saññāya ekattā) means the rebirth-perception, due to being triple-rooted (tihetuka)...
116:
They are known because of being triple-rooted (tihetu) and because of the nature of the similarity of rebirth-linking perception (paṭisandhisaññā). In truth, there is no other distinction in that resultant of the first jhāna by way of kamma or by nature. By the words 'In this way', He shows those who have diverse bodies but unified perception (nānattakāya ekattasaññī). 'Daṇḍukka' refers to a torch. 'Sarati' means it moves as if running. 'Vissarati' means it moves as if being scattered. 'Dve kappā' refers to two great aeons (mahākappa). In the realms beyond this, the same method should be applied. In this sutta, by taking the Ābhassara Brahmas as the highest limit, all Parittābha and Appamāṇābha Brahmas are also included.

They are called 'Subha' because they have beautiful radiance. In the term 'Subhakiṇṇa', which refers to Brahmas suffused with beautiful radiance, the long 'ā' is shortened and the final 'ṇ' is changed to 'h', thus it is spoken as 'Subhakiṇha'. In the Commentary, however, it is interpreted as 'those who are suffused and scattered with beauty' because they are beautiful with a steady and solid radiance; here too, the change of the final 'ṇ' to 'h' is desired. Because it is a solid radiance, the light does not go out intermittently. Because the body and perception are of a single nature, they belong only to the fourth station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). They are called 'Vehapphala' because they have results such as abundant and peaceful happiness, lifespan, and complexion. In this station of consciousness (it is known).

The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas are established on the side of liberation (vivaṭṭapakkha) because they never return to the lower realms. Having said 'it is not permanent', the phrase 'even for a hundred thousand aeons' is mentioned to clarify that impermanence. Because the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas attain parinibbāna after the passing of sixteen thousand aeons, and others are not reborn there, that place becomes empty in a world void of Buddhas; therefore, the Suddhāvāsa realms are not permanent and are like military camps (temporary quarters). By showing the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas as an abode of beings (sattāvāsa) in this sutta, their status as a station of consciousness is also shown. Therefore, the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas belong to the fourth station of consciousness among the seven stations of consciousness, and to the fourth abode of beings among the nine abodes of beings.

They are called 'Sukhumā' because they have reached the state of subtle remaining formations (saṅkhāra). Because there is no manifest consciousness-function, they are not 'percipient' (viññāṇa), yet because they are not entirely without consciousness, they are not 'non-percipient' (aviññāṇa); therefore, they are not mentioned among the stations of consciousness that have manifest consciousness-functions (but are mentioned among the bases/āyatana).

128. 'That station of consciousness' refers to the first station of consciousness. It is known in various ways: by its individual nature as mentioned below, by the division of humans etc., in brief, and by the distinction of 'mind and matter' (nāma-rūpa).
117:
One also knows it in its various aspects. One knows the twenty-five kinds of origin (samudaya) of that first station of consciousness. The same method as mentioned for origin applies to its passing away (atthaṅgama). It is called gratification (assāda) because it is to be enjoyed and because of the enjoyment itself. This nature of impermanence etc., is the danger (ādīnava). It is called the removal of desire and lust (chandarāgavinaya) because desire and lust are removed by this (the Noble Path), or because desire and lust are removed in this (Nibbāna); it is Nibbāna together with the Path. In the term 'abandoning of desire and lust' (chandarāgappahāna), the same method should be understood.

Delight (abhinandana) as 'I' through the power of conceit (māna) and views (diṭṭhi), or as 'mine' through the power of craving (taṇhā), should be seen like the distress of conceit. 'In all places' (sabbattha) means in all the remaining eight cycles. 'There' (tattha) refers to the three higher stations of consciousness and the second base (the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception). In those realms, there is no form (rūpa). 'There' (tattha) mentioned again refers to the first base (the realm of non-percipient beings). In that non-percipient realm, there is only the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). The word 'here' (ettha) is also said in reference to that same base. In that non-percipient realm, because form arises only from kamma, connection by way of nutriment (āhāra) is not possible.

In the phrase 'Yato kho', the suffix '-to' is a time-designation like the suffix '-dā', thus 'Yadā kho' (when) is what is meant. 'Without grasping' (aggaheတွာ) means living without grasping any formations (saṅkhāra) with (clinging such as) 'this is mine' etc. 'Liberated by wisdom' (paññāvimutta) refers to a person who, because of not attaining the eight liberations (vimokkha) and thus lacking the power of superior concentration, is liberated by the power of wisdom alone. Therefore, it is said, 'without having realized the eight liberations, by the power of wisdom alone' etc. 'Non-occurrence' (appavatti) is made by ensuring no future recurrence. Alternatively, one is 'liberated by wisdom' because of being liberated while knowing in various ways. Knowing the Four Noble Truths through ways such as full understanding (pariññā) etc., without the contact of the first jhāna, and penetrating them, one is 'liberated' (vimutta) because of being specially freed due to having reached the summit of those tasks and having completed the work. That person is a wisdom-liberated (paññāvimutta) individual.

A 'dry-insight practitioner' (sukkhavipassaka) is so called because their insight (vipassanā) is dry, rough, or unmoistened due to the absence of the 'moisture' of serenity meditation (samatha-bhāvanā). 'Having stood' (ṭhatvā) means being established by way of making it a foundation (pādaka-jhāna). 'In one or another' (aññatarasmiṃ) means in any one of the jhānas. In this way, there would be five types of such wisdom-liberated persons. By the words 'he does not dwell having touched the eight liberations with his body', the absence of the power of superior concentration is shown. By the words 'having seen with wisdom' etc., the presence of the power of superior wisdom is shown. In the phrase 'having seen with wisdom, his taints (āsava) are exhausted', it is not that the taints see with wisdom, but rather their exhaustion due to the cause of seeing is called 'exhausted after seeing'. Because exhaustion depends on seeing, seeing is the preceding action for the destruction of the taints.
118:
## Explanation of the Eight Liberations

12. "For one monk" (*ekassa bhikkhuno*) means one of the seven types of noble persons, specifically the monk liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*). It also indicates the escape to Nibbāna through the power of full understanding of the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), etc., and the name "liberated by wisdom." "For the other" (*itarassa*) refers to the monk liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*). Indeed, the previous mention of "for two monks" (*dvinnam bhikkhūnam*) was intended for these two: the one liberated by wisdom and the one liberated in both ways. "In what sense" (*kenaṭṭhena*) means by what nature. In truth, because the nature of things is to be known by knowledge as it really is, it is called *attha*. In this word *attha*, the letter 'tth' is changed to 'ṭṭh' and it is called *aṭṭha*.

"In the sense of being resolved" (*adhimuccanaṭṭhena*) means by the nature of being liberated from hindrances, etc., through a superior and special power. By this phrase "in the sense of being resolved," it is shown that although all fine-material sphere jhānas are liberated from opposing states by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*), this specific jhāna arises by being liberated from opposites with a power superior to ordinary fine-material jhānas due to a special development (*bhāvanāvisesa*). Indeed, even though it is of the same class as ordinary fine-material sphere jhānas, there can be a superior mode of occurrence due to the power of intense preliminary development. For example, the mode of occurrence for one who has attained vision (*diṭṭhippatta*) is superior to that of one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*) due to the excellence of development. Similarly, it is called liberation (*vimokkha*) because of being well-liberated from opposing states, because of being free from doubt as it is not suppressed or restrained, and because of the sense of being well-resolved toward the object through the power of delight. Therefore, it is stated in the Commentary, "In the object, too," and so on. This sense of being resolved toward the object does not exist in the final eighth liberation, the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). In that attainment, only the sense of being liberated (*vimutta*) is obtained. The commentator himself will explain this later.

In the word "possessing form" (*rūpī*), this person is endowed with the material form of a kasina, such as blue or black, which is included within his own continuity. That kasina-form is a distinguished form acting as the cause for that liberation-jhāna. Because of that distinguished form, he should be called "possessing form" (*rūpī*). This is because the word *rūpī* expresses an excellent meaning. That jhāna, obtained by the power of form included within one's own continuity, should be understood here as the thing that truly accomplishes the state of "possessing form." Therefore, it is stated in the Commentary, "internally" (*ajjhattam*), and so on. When the fine-material jhāna is called "form" (*rūpa*), it is called so by dropping the latter word "jhāna." In the word "forms" (*rūpāni*), however, it should be understood that the preceding word "kasina" has been dropped. Therefore, it is said "forms such as the blue kasina" (*nīlakasiṇādirūpāni*). The perception that occurs regarding the kasina-form is called "perception of form" (*rūpasaññā*). One who has that perception of form is called "one perceiving form" (*rūpasañညီ*). Here, the jhāna is spoken of by highlighting the perception. By rejecting that perception of form, one is called "one not perceiving form" (*arūpasañညီ*). Therefore, it is stated, "internally he does not perceive form" (*ajjhattam na rūpasañညီ*), and so on.

By the words "within the absorption, there is no advertence that 'it is beautiful'," it is shown that such a resolution can occur through the power of prior advertence (*pubbābhoga*). Thus, the objection raised in this context is resolved. Because, in the very pure color kasinas such as blue, the sense of being well-resolved through the power of delight of those who have performed the preliminary tasks (*adhikāra*) in those kasinas...
119:
...can occur; therefore, the third liberation is explained in that way in the Commentary. Because the development occurring through the power of loving-kindness (*mettā*) views beings as non-repulsive, it occurs only by being resolved in those beings. Therefore, it is stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: "The development of the divine abidings is the beautiful liberation." It should be understood that both of these are not contradictory as they are taught through their respective methods (*pariyāya*).

"Wholly" (*sabbaso*) means without any remainder. Indeed, in that eighth liberation, not even a single part of the four immaterial aggregates remains. "Because of being purified" (*visuddhattā*) means because it is ceased at the determined time. What is called the "supreme liberation" is so called because it is to be attained only by the Nobles (*Ariyas*), because it ends in the fruit of Arahantship, and because it is the attainment of Nibbāna in this very life.

"Starting from the beginning" (*ādito paṭṭhāya*) means starting from the first attainment. It continues until the final attainment. "Without stopping" (*aṭṭhatvā*) means without staying in any single attainment, but entering them continuously, either in order or out of order. Therefore, it is said, "It is taught by way of wandering here and there." "He wishes to attain" means he enters and attains. Here, "he attains, he enters" is said because the person endowed with the attainment is as if he has entered into those respective attainments.

"Liberated in two ways" (*dvīhi bhāgehi vimutto*) means one who is liberated by these two parts of liberation: by the liberation of suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimokkha*) which is the immaterial jhāna, and by the liberation of eradication (*samuccheda-vimokkha*) which is the Path; and also liberated from these two parts that are to be liberated from: from the material body (*rūpakāya*) by the immaterial attainment, and from the mental body (*nāmakāya*) by the Path. Therefore, it is said, "by the immaterial attainment" (*arūpasamāpattiyā*), and so on. "Liberated" (*vimutto*) means one who is liberated from the defilements; the meaning here is that when one is being liberated, one is liberated from the two bodies by the suppression and eradication of the defilements. Also, in the verse, the Buddha declared the sage Upasīva, who had attained the sphere of nothingness, as a sage liberated in both ways, saying "liberated from the mental body" (*nāmakāyā vimutto*). In that context, "goes to rest" (*attham paleti*) means he reaches cessation. "Does not come to be reckoned" (*na upeti sankham*) means he does not come to be described as "having gone to such and such a direction." Thus, the Arahant is liberated from the mental body. In this way, the trainee sage (*sekhamuni*) born in the immaterial realm is naturally already liberated from the material body, and in that immaterial realm, having produced the fourth path and having fully understood the mental body, he is again liberated from the mental body. Having become an Arahant liberated in both ways, without clinging...
120:
It means reaching the cessation called Parinibbāna; one no longer comes to designations such as "Khattiya" (warrior-noble), "Brāhmaṇa" (brahmin), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "Aññatarato vuṭṭhāya" (having emerged from a certain [attainment]), is this spoken in terms of a person who has attained any one of the four formless jhānas (arūpajhāna) such as the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), or is it spoken in terms of a person who has attained all the formless jhānas? Let it be as you wish. If it is spoken in terms of one who has attained all formless jhānas, there is no contradiction. However, if it is spoken in terms of one who has attained any one of them, would it not contradict the statement: "Ānanda, when a bhikkhu enters these eight liberations (vimokkha) in forward order..."? This is because even one who has attained only one of the four formless jhānas is called "one who has attained the eight liberations," since there is the capacity to give that name even to a part [of the set]. This designation of "eight liberations" is established for a part just as it is for the whole. Therefore, it is said, "having emerged from any one of the jhānas such as the base of infinite space."

After stating "there are five types," some teachers also conceive of six types of the person liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta). That conception is merely their opinion. To show that this problem has already been decided by the former teachers, the phrase "Keci pana" (But some...) is mentioned. Here, "some" refers to the monks residing at Uttaravihāra and the teachers of the Sārasamāsa. These teachers say that "ubhatobhāgavimutta" means one liberated by both concentration (samādhi) and insight (vipassanā), and they consider one to be liberated from dangers such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) even by means of fine-material sphere concentration (rūpāvacarasamādhi). Thus, while striving as one liberated in both ways—by the part of fine-material jhāna and the part of formless jhāna—they explain the meaning of the word "Tādisameva" (just like that) as: just as the formless jhāna has the power to suppress the defilements, the fourth fine-material jhāna also has that same power. Therefore, the phrase "Tasmā" (Therefore...) is mentioned.

"Ubhatobhāgavimuttapañho" refers to the problem arising based on the six types of the one liberated in both ways. "Vaṇṇanaṃ nissāya" means based on the explanation of the meaning of that word. "Cirena" means after a long time in the latter part of the Elder's life. "Viniccayaṃ" means reaching a conclusion that cuts off doubt. "Taṃ pañhaṃ" refers to that meaning. Indeed, a meaning desired to be known is called a "problem" (pañha). "Na kenaci sutapubbaṃ" means that no one has ever heard even a little of this matter. The word "kiñcāpi" should be applied to each: "kiñcāpi upekkhāsahagataṃ" (although accompanied by equanimity) and "kiñcāpi kilese vikkhambheti" (although it suppresses the defilements). "Samudācarati" means it occurs. The reason for this is stated with "Ime hi," etc. By that statement, it is shown that formless cultivation (arūpabhāvanā) suppresses defilements more exceptionally than fine-material sphere cultivation (rūpāvacarabhāvanā).
121:
He shows this because formless cultivation is a cultivation for the revulsion of form, and because it is a higher cultivation. In this way, in the section on formless cultivation in the Visuddhimagga Commentary, it is said: "For him who repeatedly directs his mind to that sign (nimitta), the hindrances are suppressed and mindfulness is established," etc. (Visuddhimagga 1.281). This statement becomes firm.

By the Pali "This sutta," he refers to the Puggalapaññatti text. The meaning that all the Buddha's words are called "sutta" because they indicate the meaning, etc., is indeed correct. Whatever needs to be explained regarding the word "sutta" has already been stated in the introductory section (Nidānakathā) below.

It should be understood that this liberation in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutti) is the most excellent of all, because the mental continuity is exceedingly refined by entering the eight liberations in forward order, etc., and because one is liberated in both ways by attaining the highest path (arahattamagga) after developing insight with the eighth sublime liberation as the proximate cause.

## The Līnatthappakāsanā Ṭīkā, which clarifies the hidden meanings of the Commentary on the Mahānidāna Sutta, is concluded.
122:
## 3. Commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta

It is called Mahāparinibbāna because it is worthy of worship, and because it is the great final passing away that occurs after setting aside the Buddha’s physical perfection. It is also called Mahāparinibbāna because it is the final passing away based on the great destruction of defilements (the Noble Path) through the abandonment of defilements along with latent tendencies (vāsanā). It is also called Mahāparinibbāna because it is the final passing away accomplished through a great mass of virtues over a long period of time. It is also called Mahāparinibbāna because of its greatness and the abundance of relics (dhātu). It is also called Mahāparinibbāna because it is the final passing away that has emerged from the great world of Saṃsāra. It is also called Mahāparinibbāna because it is the final passing away of the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is great through virtues such as morality (sīla), which are not common to the whole world. It is also called Mahāparinibbāna because the final passing away of the Blessed One occurs while the great Dispensation (Sāsana) is firmly established. The sutta related to this Mahāparinibbāna is called the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta.

"Vultures (gijjha) live here," thus it is called Gijjha. Because it has a peak (kūṭa) where vultures rest, it is called "Gijjhakūṭa." Alternatively, it is called "Gijjhakūṭa" mountain because it has a peak shaped like a vulture. (He stayed) at that Gijjhakūṭa mountain. Therefore, it was said, "Gijjha," and so on. In the word "Abhiyātukāmo," the word "abhi" expresses the meaning of overcoming, as in the words "abhivijānātu," etc. Therefore, it was said, "desiring to go to overcome and subdue."

"Vajjirājāno" refers to the kings named "Vajjī" based on the earlier saying, "These are people to be avoided (vajjitabbā)," or it refers to the kings of the Vajji country. The name "Vajji" for the Vajji country should be understood in relation to the princes who resided in that country.

"Rājiddhiyā" means by the nature following kingship. That nature was famous in the world and long-lasting due to the mutual unity (sāmaggi) of those republican kings (gaṇarājā); thus it was said, "He spoke of the state of unity."

"Anubhāva" is that which increases the state of one who possesses it repeatedly. "Anubhāva" itself is "ānubhāva" (majesty/power). That majesty of theirs became famous in the world due to the excellence of vehicles such as elephants and horses, and because they were well-trained in those vehicles; thus it was said, "He spoke of such majesty."

"Tāḷacchiggaleṇa" means through a keyhole. "Asanaṃ" refers to an arrow. "Atipātayissanti" means they surpass or overshoot. "Poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ" means arrow-notch after arrow-notch; the meaning is making each subsequent arrow follow the notch of the preceding arrow. "Avirādhitaṃ" means without missing or unerringly. "Ucchindissāmi" means "I will cut off the lineage by way of uprooting." Since rejecting growth (aya) is "anaya" (misfortune), it was said, "this name called non-growth." "Vikkhipati" means throwing far away or removing.
123:
"Gaṅgāyaṃ" means near the Ganges river. "Paṭṭanagāmaṃ" refers to a port town the size of a league (yojana). "Āṇā" means that authority is spreading. "Aḍḍhayojanaṃ" is said in reference to the inhabitants of the district living within half a league of that port. "Tatra" means in that port. "Balavāghātajāto" means that strong anger has arisen. "Me" means mine. "Gatena" means by going.

## Commentary on the Conditions for Non-decline of Kings

At that time (while Venerable Ānanda was fanning the Buddha), there was neither cold nor heat. Due to the power of their merit, Buddhas always have a climate that is evenly cold and hot (temperate); it was said, "there is no cold or heat," in reference to that. "Abhiṇhaṃ sannipātā" means assembling constantly. To show that constant assembly, "daily," etc., was said. "Sannipātabahulā" means assembling many times. "Vosānaṃ" means shrinking back or slackening. Although the word "yāvakīvaṃ" is a term indicating measure, here the time of assembly is intended; thus it means "for as long a time." To show the meaning of the words "vuddhiyeva," etc., by way of the opposite, it was said, "if they do not assemble constantly," and so on. "Ākulā" means agitated and disturbed, not peaceful. "Bhijjitvā" means breaking away from the group and becoming separate.

"Sannipātabheri" is the drum for announcing the assembly. "Aḍḍhabhuttā vā" means even if the owners have half-eaten (or finished eating). "Osīdamāne" means being in a state of decline.

"Pubbe akataṃ" means not previously established (or collected). "Suṅka" (tolls/customs) is the portion to be given to the king's men at mountain passes, river crossings, village gates, etc., by those carrying goods. "Bali" (tax) is the tax obtained as one-sixth, one-seventh, etc., from harvested crops and the like. "Daṇḍa" (fine) is the monetary fine of ten, twenty kahāpaṇas, etc., to be taken according to the offense. "Vajjidhammaṃ" refers to the laws of the Vajji kings. Now, to show in detail the faults and benefits in matters such as enacting what was not yet enacted, it was said, "tethaṃ apanyattaṃ," and so on. "Pāricariyakkhamā" means being able to endure or tolerate attendance and service.

Those who have a great measure by way of lineage, wealth, and power are called "Mahāmattā" (great ministers). The great ministers appointed for judgment according to the treatises on law (nīti) are called "Vinicchayamahāmattā." (The thief) is handed over to those great ministers. If they think, "he is a thief," because of their fear of wrongdoing, they do not say anything themselves but hand him over to the "Vohārikā" (magistrates) appointed for judgment according to the science of punishment (daṇḍanīti). They are also called "Dhammaṭṭha" (those established in justice). "Suttadharā" refers to those who bear the legal treatises (nīti-sutta) and are appointed for such judgments.
124:
Those known as Nītisuttadhara are those who bear the Nītisutta text and are appointed in such legal decisions. The eight elderly men born into the eight families brought by successive kings, who refrain from following the wrong paths (agati), are called the Aṭṭhakulika.

Sakkāra refers to the worshipful honor and hospitality provided. 'Garubhāvaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā' means establishing the state of being worthy of respect in that honor, thinking, "These are our respected ones." 'Mānenti' means they greatly revere them. To show that such reverence is preceded by their own natural state of affection for those elders, it is said, "They cherish them with their hearts." 'Nipaccakāra' refers to the act of humble prostration. 'Dassenti' means they show the attitude of a respectful mind, being humble and thinking, "These elders are our grandfathers and grandmothers," and so on. 'Sandhāretuṃ' means to connect or join without interruption.

'Pasayhākāra' is a name for the act of force (balakkāra). Although growth (vuddhi) is worthy of worship and thus the term 'vuddhihāniya' (growth and decline) is mentioned in the commentary in that order, the meaning should be applied according to the sequence explained in the commentary, placing decline first and growth later. Alternatively, because it is stated in the Pali text that "only growth is to be expected, not decline," the term 'vuddhihāniya' is used following that Pali sequence.

As long as an unwholesome kamma has not yet found an opportunity to ripen, or there is no opening for the result (vipāka) of that kamma, the affliction by deities (devatopasagga) has no opportunity to occur. To show that the opportunity for affliction by deities arises only when that unwholesome kamma and its result find an opening, it is said, "Those not yet arisen... they increase." In this same way, the meaning of "happiness not yet arisen" should also be understood. The assistance of deities on the battlefield should be understood through such acts as making the army appear double or triple in size, or displaying terrifying forms.

'Anicchita' refers to undesired dangers. 'Āvaraṇato' means because of prohibition or prevention. Protection that is not devoid of wholesome Dhamma is called 'dhammiya'; here it is spoken of as 'dhammika'. Wandering in the forest with dogs and such to kill animals like deer and pigs is called 'vāja' or 'migavā'. Those engaged in that 'vāja', or because they lead and bring the animals, are called 'vājikā'; they are hunters who wander about killing animals. The Blessed One asks about the occurrence of the mind (cittappavatti). This is because the occurrence of the mind is made manifest and clear in the world through physical and vocal efforts.

It is called a 'cetiya' (shrine) because it is piled up (citattā) as a residence for deities, and because it is a place of honor (cittīkāra) for the world.

They are called 'akaraṇīyā' (not to be done/taken) because nothing can be done to them by way of one's own will (kāmaṃkāra). Since 'kāmaṃkāra' here refers to capturing them into one's own hands, it means "they should not be captured." 'Abhimukhayuddhena' means by way of direct, face-to-face combat.
125:
To show the strategies of persuasion (upalāpana) and giving (dāna), the word "alaṃ" and so forth is spoken. Here, dissension (bheda) is also considered a strategy for victory, thus it is said, "except by sowing mutual dissension." That war is not a means for victory was already shown earlier. This statement, "except by persuasion, except by sowing mutual dissension," was spoken by the Brahmin Vassakāra. "Having obtained the method from the discourse..." means having obtained the strategy for victory from the Blessed One's words, "As long as... no decline."

'Anukampāya' means with the favor of wishing to support the Vajjī kings. 'Assa' refers to the Blessed One's (will).

'Kathaṃ' refers to the talk concerning the war to be waged with the Vajjīs. 'Ujuṃ karissāmi' means, "I will make them straight by bringing the rival kings and causing the city walls and moats to be altered in some way."

'Patiṭṭhitaguṇo' means one who possesses the established qualities of a teacher. The meaning should be applied as follows: the Licchavī kings no longer assembled, saying, "Let the rulers assemble; we are not the rulers. What is the use of us going to that assembly?" The same method applies to the phrase, "Let the heroes assemble."

'Balabheri' refers to the war drum used to rouse the army for battle.

## Commentary on the Conditions for Non-decline for Monks (Bhikkhu-aparihāniyadhamma-vaṇṇanā)

They are called 'aparihāniya' because they are beneficial for non-decline. Alternatively, they are called 'aparihāniya' because one does not decline because of these qualities. Since these qualities are the makers of non-decline, they are called 'aparihānikara' (causing non-decline). Because they are the direct opposites of the causes of decline, they are called 'vuddhihetu' (causes of growth). Because the Blessed One's teaching clarifies the light of wisdom higher and higher, destroying the darkness in the hearts of beings, and makes the meanings to be revealed very clear like an emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) in the palm of the hand, it is said, "A thousand moons... I shall preach."

The Blessed One thought: "While preaching the practice of the Vajjīs, such as their frequent assemblies, in the presence of that Brahmin, this talk on the conditions for non-decline is mundane (vaṭṭanissita) and does not lead out of suffering. In my Dispensation (Sāsana), however, such a talk on the conditions for non-decline should be preached that leads out of suffering (niyyānika), is oriented towards Nibbāna (vivaṭṭanissita), and will cause the Dispensation to endure for a long time even after my Parinibbāna." Therefore, he had the monks assemble and preached the conditions for non-decline to them in that same manner. Thus it is said, "This is just like what was preached in the Vajjisattaka Sutta." Thus, in brief:
126:
Wishing to show in detail the meaning already stated in brief, he said the words beginning with "Idhāpi ca". In that passage, the word "Tato" etc. refers to the news arriving from various directions. Because the boundary (sīmā) of the monastery is unclear, the performance of Uposatha and Pavāraṇā has ceased.

"Olīyamānako" means deteriorating both in terms of the Pali text and its meaning. "Ukkhipāpentā" means supporting by making one proficient and by explaining the meaning.

It is like the monks in Sāvatthī being made to confess a Pācittiya offence (for what the Buddha did not prescribe), or like the Vajjiputtaka monks abolishing (what the Buddha prescribed) by presenting ten points. "Gihigatāni" is said to be the training rules related to laypeople. Training rules that occur among laypeople or are known by laypeople are called "gihigatāni". The period when the smoke of such a training rule arises is called "dhūmakālika". This is because after the smoke from the funeral pyre has subsided, that training rule no longer exists.

"Thirabhāvappattā" refers to those who have reached a state of firmness and non-regression in the Dispensation. "Therakārakehi" refers to the qualities such as virtue that make one an Elder, and the dhammas of the Asekha (Arhats). "Bahu rattiyo" refers to those who have known many nights since their ordination. To show that establishing others in qualities such as virtue is indeed leadership in the Dispensation, he said, "They engage them in the three trainings."

They do not give advice (ovāda) because there is no capacity to receive it. "Paveṇīkathā" is Dhamma talk that explains the correct practice, handed down through the lineage of teachers. "Sārabhūtaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ" refers to the scriptural tradition (dhammatanti) of the Dhamma such as the Bojjhaṅga Sutta, Kosalla Sutta, Anuttarasītībhāva Sutta, and Adhicitta Sutta, which are essential because they lead to the attainment of serenity, insight, the Path, and the Fruit.

In the word "Punabbhavadāna", it becomes "Punabbhava" due to the dropping of the subsequent term. "Itare" refers to those monks who do not follow the desire for requisites and gains, and do not have eyes only for material things; those monks do not fall under the power of craving.

"Āraññakesu" refers to dwellings located in or belonging to forest areas. Aiming at the objection, "Is not craving blameworthy in any case?", he said the words beginning with "Gāmantasenāsanesu hi". By this, he shows that just as the attachment (pihā) mentioned in the Pali "Anuttaresu vimokkhesu pihaṃ upaṭṭhāpayato" belongs to the group of things to be cultivated, so too, attachment (sālayatā) to forest dwellings belongs to the group of things to be cultivated.

"Attanāva" means by oneself. By this, he shows that they hope for the arrival of virtuous monks who come of their own accord without being urged by others, and for the comfortable living of those who have already arrived. "Iminā nīhārena" means because of such conduct and virtue.

"Abhikkantaṃ" means learning the Pariyatti Pali that has not yet been learned. In "Abhipathayanti", the word "saṃ" has the meaning of contemplating the Pariyatti Dhamma already learned. "Upaganti" means they arrive. They sit (nisīdanti) after seats have been prepared (sayana-paññāpanā). It is called "Ārāma" because of the sense of being delightful. Delighting in work (kamma) is called "Kammarāmatā". It is delighting only in work, not in the duty of study (ganthadhura) or the duty of insight (vipassanādhura). "Anuyuttā" means being excessively devoted to those tasks.
127:
Learning the Pariyatti Pali that has not yet been learned is "Aggahitadhammaggaahaṇa". Contemplating well the meaning of the Pariyatti Dhamma already learned is "Gahitasajjhāyakaraṇa", for the word "sajjhāya" has the meaning of contemplation.

"Enti" means they approach. They sit down through the preparation of seats and so on.

Work is called "Ārāma" in the sense of being something to delight in. Those who delight in work, not in the duty of study (ganthadhura) or the duty of meditation (vāsadhura), are called "Kammarata". They are repeatedly engaged in that work with devotion. Such "work to be done" refers to various major and minor duties of monks, such as managing robes. Therefore, he said "Seyyathidaṃ" and so on. "Upatthambhana" refers to the supporting and stitching of double or triple layers. It is so called because it is the cause for supporting the first layer and so on. If such work as managing robes is called "kamma", one might ask why the Buddha rejected "delight in work" (kammarāmatā); therefore, he said "Ekacco hi" and so on.

"Karontoyeva" means while speaking the aforementioned "animal talk" (tiracchānakathā). Even if it is not animal talk but general conversation, the emphatic word "yeva" is used to show that one is excessively devoted to that talk. "Pariyantakārī" is one who speaks making limits and boundaries. Has it not been said, "He speaks words that are bounded"? "Appabhasso" means one who has limited speech, because he speaks only what is definitely to be spoken. Attaining meditative absorption is called "Noble Silence" (ariya-tuṇhībhāva).

"Niddāyatiyeva" means just sleeping without seeing the danger in falling asleep. He does not dispel that sleep by changing postures and so on.

"Evaṃ saṃsaṭṭho" means he lives only in a state of mingling through association with a group in the manner described.

"Dussīlā pāpicchā" means they are immoral themselves and, because they possess the desire to be praised for qualities they do not have, their desires are evil and base; thus they are called "pāpicchā". Because they make friendship with evil persons, they are "pāpamitta". Because they always exist together with them, they are "pāpasahāya". Because they are inclined toward those evil deeds, they are "pāpasampavaṅka".

To say that they have faith, he said "Saddhāsampannā". Faith that arises through the practice leading to the Knowledge of the Arahat Path and Omniscience is called "Āgamanīyasaddhā". That "Āgamanīyasaddhā" is of superior power, and for the Great Bodhisattas, without the instruction of others, it perceives the object of faith without distortion...
128:
Because of entering into and making a decision, it is said, "It occurs to the Omniscient Bodhisattas." Faith arising from the penetration of the Four Noble Truths is called "faith of attainment" (adhigama-saddhā), like the faith of the Noble Ones such as King Suddhodana. The clarity that arises regarding the Buddha and others, such as "The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One," is called "faith of devotion" (pasāda-saddhā), like that of King Mahākappina and others. The decision made by entering into and plunging into faith, thinking "This matter is just so," is called "faith of conviction" (okappaṇa-saddhā). Between those two types (pasāda-saddhā and okappaṇa-saddhā), pasāda-saddhā has the nature of being led by others because it is clarity based on mere hearing. Okappaṇa-saddhā occurs as if making a personal realization, entering into and following the object of faith, thinking "This matter is just so." Therefore, it is said, "The person resolved through faith (saddhādhimutta) is like the Elder Vakkali."

For one endowed with that faith of conviction, there is moral shame (hiri), which is the nature of loathing evil; it means their mind has the quality of loathing evil, and thus it is said, "They have minds that loathe evil." Because they are terrified and afraid of evil, they are called "possessing moral dread" (ottappī). One is called "of great learning" (bahussuta) because of having heard many scriptures such as Sutta and Geyya. Here, the mention of "hearing" (suta) is merely an illustration for memorization, constant practice, inquiry, repeated reflection, and investigation with wisdom. Alternatively, since all those things are rooted in hearing, they should be understood as included by the term "hearing" itself. It is called "scriptural learning" (pariyatti) because it should be mastered by those desiring their own benefit, and because it is mastered for the accomplishment of welfare in the present and future lives; it consists of the Three Pitakas. The penetration of the Four Noble Truths is called "penetration of the truths" (sacca-paṭivedha). That penetration of the truths is also "great learning" (bāhusacca) because it is the fulfillment of the function of the aforementioned great learning. In this context, pariyatti is intended because being of great learning through the bāhusacca that leads to the penetration of the truths is desired. That scriptural great learning is of only four types because there is no fifth kind.

"One of great learning in all aspects" (sabbattha-kabahussuta) means not being partial like "one of great learning released from dependence" (nissayamuccanaka-bahussuta), but being one of great learning in all aspects because of being able to explain the entire meaning in all Three Pitakas. These are desired here because of being well-established in the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-saddhamma), which is the foundation of the Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti) and the Dhamma of penetration (paṭivedha).

"Aroused" (āraddha) means exerted. To show those two types of effort by way of the division of the arousal of energy, the text beginning with "tattha" is stated. There, "solitary" (ekakā) means alone, dwelling in seclusion.
129:
"Having asked" (puccitvā) means asking after having the people go outside the city. "To make them accept" (sampaṭicchāpetum) means asking, "Are you not the one with this name?" and making them acknowledge it by saying, "Yes, Bhante."

To show that those with mature wisdom who are capable of recollecting deeds done long ago and so forth reach the fulfillment of the development of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness without difficulty, it is said, "Referring to such monks." For that very reason, the commentator said the passage beginning with "apica."

It is called a "factor of enlightenment" (bojjhaṅga) because it is a part of the collection of dhammas such as Right View, which is named "Bodhi" because it penetrates the Four Noble Truths or awakens one from delusion. An excellent or beautiful bojjhaṅga is called a "factor of supreme enlightenment" (sambojjhaṅga). It is called the "characteristic of establishment" (upaṭṭhāna-lakkhaṇa, i.e., mindfulness) because it has the characteristic of being established on the object, which is the marking of the body, feelings, mind, and dhammas as foul, suffering, impermanent, and non-self. It is called the "characteristic of investigation" (pavicaya-lakkhaṇa, i.e., investigation of dhammas) because it has the characteristic of investigating and examining the Four Noble Truths by way of oppression and so forth. It is called the "characteristic of exertion" (paggaha-lakkhaṇa, i.e., energy) because it has the characteristic of uplifting and raising the mind by way of preventing unarisen unwholesome states and so forth. It is called the "characteristic of pervasion" (pharaṇa-lakkhaṇa, i.e., joy) because it has the characteristic of pervading the entire body with sublime material qualities. It is called the "characteristic of calming" (upasama-lakkhaṇa, i.e., tranquility) because it has the characteristic of calming the fevers of body and mind. It is called the "characteristic of non-distraction" (avikkhepa-lakkhaṇa, i.e., concentration) because it has the characteristic of non-distraction on the object by destroying mental wandering. It is called the "characteristic of reflection" (paṭisaṅkhāna-lakkhaṇa, i.e., equanimity) because it has the characteristic of reflecting and looking on with indifference, without concern for uplifting, suppressing, or gladdening, while the mind of the path and fruit of insight is occurring, free from sluggishness and restlessness.

"By four causes" refers to: having mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and inclination towards that mindfulness. "By six causes" refers to: being inquisitive, cleaning objects, balancing the faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, and inclination towards that investigation of dhammas. In the commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, however, it will be said "by seven causes"; those seven should be understood by adding this cause: reflecting on things to be known with deep wisdom. "By nine causes" refers to: reflecting on the fear of the states of deprivation, reflecting on the path to be traveled, respecting the alms-food, reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, reflecting on the greatness of fellow celibates, avoiding lazy persons, associating with energetic persons, and inclination towards that energy. In the commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta...
130:
Specifically, it will be stated (in the commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna) as eleven factors, together with the habit of seeing the benefits of cultivation and the reflection on the greatness of one's birth. The 'ten factors' are: recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), recollection of the Dhamma (dhammānussati), recollection of the Saṅgha (saṅghānussati), recollection of virtue (sīlānussati), recollection of generosity (cāgānussati), recollection of deities (devatānussati), recollection of peace (upasamānussati), avoiding persons with coarse minds, associating with persons with gentle minds, and inclination towards the arousal of that energy.

In the commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna, however, it will be stated as eleven factors, together with the reflection on the inspiring discourses (pasādanīya-suttanta). The 'seven factors' are: consuming fine food, enjoying a comfortable climate, enjoying comfortable postures, moderate application of effort, avoiding persons with agitated bodies, associating with persons with tranquil bodies, and inclination towards the development of that bodily tranquility.

The 'ten factors' are: cleaning the physical basis (vatthu-visada-kiriyā), balancing the faculties (indriya-samatta-paṭipādanā), skill in the sign (nimitta-kusalatā), uplifting the mind when it should be uplifted, restraining the mind when it should be restrained, gladdening the mind when it should be gladdened, observing the mind with equanimity when it should be observed with equanimity, avoiding unconcentrated persons, associating with concentrated persons, and inclination towards the development of that concentration. In the commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna, however, it will be stated as eleven factors, together with the reflection on the jhānas and liberations (vimokkha).

The 'five factors' are: equanimity towards beings, equanimity towards formations (saṅkhāra), avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations, associating with persons who are equanimous towards beings and formations, and inclination towards the development of that factor of enlightenment of equanimity. Whatever else needs to be said here will appear in the commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna.

Indeed, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) are, in the direct sense, associated with the Noble Path because they lead out of suffering (niyyānika). Since the Suttanta teaching is a figurative discourse (pariyāyakathā), it is said, "Through this insight... He taught."

Repeatedly contemplating the formations belonging to the three realms as 'impermanent' is the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā).
