Insight (vipassanā) that proceeds in such a way is called 'perception arisen together with the contemplation of impermanence' because it is developed and manifested by the perception that accompanies it. Alternatively, this is a designation for insight itself, using 'perception' as the primary term. The same method applies to the perception of non-self (anattasaññā) and so on. These are also mundane insights because they proceed by way of 'impermanence' and so forth. In the phrase 'also mundane insight,' the word 'also' implies that there are also mixed mundane and supramundane insights here. To establish this implied meaning and to show it in its specific form, the words 'dispassion' (virāga) and so forth are stated. According to the Pāli text mentioned there, 'dispassion and cessation' refer to Nibbāna.
131:
Among those (seven perceptions), because Nibbāna is taught as 'dispassion' and 'cessation,' the perceptions taught in this Dispensation as 'perception of dispassion' and 'perception of cessation' can also have Nibbāna as their object. Therefore, it is said (in the commentary), "The two perceptions are also supramundane."

A mind is called 'loving-kindness' (metta-citta) because loving-kindness exists in it. Bodily action originating from that mind of loving-kindness is 'bodily action of loving-kindness' (metta-kāyakamma). The same method applies to the remaining two (verbal and mental actions). These bodily actions of loving-kindness and so forth are mentioned in terms of monks because they are the noble assembly. To show that just as they are found among monks, they are also found among laypeople because they are common to the fourfold assembly, the phrase "to monks as well" and so forth is stated. Indeed, bodily actions of loving-kindness can be obtained even by listening to the Dhamma related to the initial holy life (ādibrahmacariya). However, to show that this meaning is intended through listening to the Dhamma of conduct (cāritta-dhamma) in a non-figurative sense, it is said, "fulfilling the Abhisamācārika-dhamma." Even the Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana), the Tipitaka, when it is carried out by way of questioning and explaining the meaning, should be carried out with an intention for welfare (and thus it is verbal action of loving-kindness).

'Āvī' means openly or manifestly. The state of being manifest here is because it is done in the presence of the person for whom that bodily action is intended; thus it is said, "in the presence" (sammukhā). 'Raho' means secretly or non-manifestly. The state of being non-manifest is because it is done in the absence of the person for whom that bodily action is intended; thus it is said, "in the absence" (parammukhā). Entering into a state of companionship is (done) in their presence. "By both" means with both the juniors and the elders.

'Paggayha' means uplifting or exalting (in speech).

Indeed, opening the eyes moistened with the lubricant of loving-kindness and looking with a clear face is certainly bodily action of loving-kindness. However, with reference to the mind by whose power the eyes are moistened with the lubricant of loving-kindness and the face is clear, it is said, "it is called mental action of loving-kindness."

The word 'lābha' (gain) has the sense of 'that which is acquired' (kamma-sādhana), as in the phrases "What a gain!" and "A gain has been acquired." Here, because it is stated as "acquired through Dhamma," it refers to the past tense; thus it is said, "acquired requisites such as robes." They are called 'dhammika' because they come through righteous means. Therefore, it is said, "acquired through Dhamma." To show this very meaning, the words "scheming (kuhanā) and so forth" are stated. To show the root cause, which is sharing with the body preceded by sharing with the mind, it is said, "thus sharing with the mind." By this, it shows that one should not make a distinction (for oneself) even by a mere thought. 'Appaṭivibhattaṃ' (undivided) is either an exposition of the state (bhāva-napumsaka) or an exposition of the object (kamma-niddesa) meaning 'one enjoys gains that are not divided' (i.e., shared).
132:
He does not give those acquired requisites to laypeople for the sake of purifying his own livelihood. Thinking, 'May I not be one who enjoys gains alone,' he does not consume them by himself. By the words, 'While receiving... [pe]... he looks,' it is shown that the acquired gain is placed as common property during all three times. By the words, 'While receiving, may it be common to the Saṅgha,' the time of receiving is shown. By the words, 'Having received... [pe]... he looks,' the time after receiving is shown. Since both these times cannot occur without such prior reflection (pubbābhoga), the preceding time (before receiving) is also established by implication. That reflection occurs before receiving as: 'I will receive with the thought: May it be common to the Saṅgha.' While receiving, it occurs as: 'I receive with the thought: May it be common to the Saṅgha.' After receiving, it occurs as: 'It has been received by me with the thought: May it be common to the Saṅgha.' Thus, a monk who acts in accordance with these three characteristics and consumes the acquired gains without violating the final characteristic is one who shares gains (sādhāraṇabhogī) and one who shares without discrimination (appaṭivibhattabhogī).

This 'sāraṇīyadhamma' refers to this fourth quality that should be remembered. Indeed, the virtuous do not accept the requisites of the immoral (dussīla); therefore, for an immoral person, sharing gains does not even exist. If the beginning cannot even occur, how could it be fulfilled? This is the meaning. By the word 'parisuddhasīlo' (one of pure virtue), the lawfulness of the gain is shown. By the words 'vattaṃ akhaṇḍento' (not breaking the duty), sharing without discrimination and sharing gains are shown. When both are present, the sāraṇīyadhamma is fulfilled; thus he says, 'he fulfills' (pūreti). By the words 'making it specific' (odissakaṃ katvā), it is shown that for a monk who gives to his father, or to teachers and preceptors, etc., starting from the seat of the elders without making it specific, it is indeed sāraṇīyadhamma. However, because it is given by making it specific to a person who should be looked after, it is not sāraṇīyadhamma for that monk. Therefore, it is said, 'It is called looking after an impediment (palibodha),' and so on. If so, is specific giving (odissaka-dāna) always improper for one who fulfills the sāraṇīyadhamma? No, it is not improper; to show that it is proper in the appropriate place, he said 'But by that' (tena pana), etc. Giving specifically to the sick (gilāna), etc., is included in the category of non-discrimination (appaṭivibhāga) because there is no rejection such as 'I will not give to such a person.' Indeed, discrimination (paṭivibhāga) is the opposite of non-discrimination. Therefore, he said 'the remainder' (avasesaṃ), etc. By the word 'pi' in 'even for not giving,' he shows that giving is also proper. However, such giving is by the power of compassion (karuṇā), not by the power of fulfilling the duty (vattapūraṇa).

'Susikkhitāya' means well-trained in the method of fulfilling the sāraṇīyadhamma, meaning well-skilled (sukusalā). Now, to show the skill of that assembly, he said 'susikkhitāya'.
133:
He said 'hī' and so on. By the words, 'It is fulfilled in twelve years, not less than that,' he shows the difficulty of fulfilling that sāraṇīyadhamma. Indeed, that sāraṇīyadhamma has great fruit and great benefit; even in the present life, very weighty results and benefits follow. A person endowed with that quality becomes one possessed of wonderful and marvelous qualities in the world, like a noble person (ariya) who has attained a distinction.

How so? That person, having pushed far away the opposing states of the merit of giving and the merit of virtue which are difficult to abandon, dwells well-known and recognized in the world with an extremely pure mind. To clarify this meaning of that monk through both the negative and positive aspects, he said 'sace hi' and so on; that statement is easy to understand.

Now, to show the benefits in the future life and the present life, he said 'evaṃ' and so on. Because unwholesome states have been shaken off by long-term cultivation, envy (issā) and stinginess (macchariya) do not occur at all. Because the habit of generosity is pure, he is dear to humans. Therefore, it was said: 'The giver is dear; many people associate with him,' and so on. Because obtaining requisites is a present benefit of giving for those with noble intentions through the power of giving, he easily obtains the four requisites. Because he fulfilled the duty of sāraṇīyadhamma continuously for twelve years, the offerings that have entered his bowl do not run out. Because he gave daily to those worthy of offerings starting from the best, he receives the best of goods. Because he fulfilled the merit of giving for a long time with a mind free from attachment to himself and without making distinctions between the gift and the recipient, thus purifying his mind, when danger or famine arrives, the deities take care of the matter of his alms-food.

'Tatra' means among those described benefits. These matters are the reasons that illustrate those benefits. 'Alabhantāpi' means even if they do not receive alms-food due to not having great merit, they know the path similar to the path of wandering for alms.

Because this quality is not a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), and for the sake of dispelling the doubts of the elders, he said, 'Venerable Sir, the sāraṇīyadhamma has been fulfilled by me.' Likewise, in the second story, the elder revealed himself. This story is also a testimony to being dear to humans and having easily obtainable requisites. However, to specifically clarify the distinction of the alms in the bowl not running out, he said, 'This story is a testimony here,' and so on.
134:
Giribhaṇḍamahāpūjā refers to the great offering ceremony performed with lamps, flowers, and incense, involving boats, rafts, and such, placed in the ocean for the distance of one yojana, at Cetiyagiri Monastery and throughout the entire island of Sīhaḷa. "Pariyāyenapi" means even by a mere hint (implying a desire not to speak). "Anucchavikaṃ" means that speaking the truth in this way, due to fulfilling the sāraṇīyadhamma (virtues of friendliness), is suitable for you, Venerable Sirs.

The townspeople fled without informing (the Elder) because of the danger from rebels. Some also say, "because of the difficulty of their own livelihood."

"Vaṭṭissati" means it will be allowable (to consume). The Elder Nun was one who fulfilled the sāraṇīyadhamma. However, it was solely due to the power of the Elder’s virtue that the deity took concern for the alms-food matter.

Because there is no breaking or fragmenting of the training rules in those virtues, they are called "akhaṇḍa" (unbroken virtues). To show the breaking and fragmenting of those virtues, the words beginning with "yassa" are spoken. In that context, the beginning and end of the virtues of a monk should be understood according to the order of the recitation of the Pāḷi text. Therefore, it is said starting with "sattasu". For the virtues of those who are not ordained, however, the beginning and end are obtained according to the order of the training rules undertaken. "Like a cloth torn at the edge" means like a cloth that is torn at its border. This is a dissimilar illustration (visadisūdāharaṇa) because it excessively fulfills the meaning of "akhaṇḍa" (unbroken). The remaining illustrations follow this same method.

Having a break or fragment is called "khaṇḍa". This is the same for virtue. In terms like "chidda" (holed) and so on, the same method should be understood. It relates to being like a cow that is pierced in the middle or has a variegated color. Virtues that are free from brindled spots are called "asabala" (unspotted). Likewise, virtues without spots or blemishes are called "akammāsa" (unblemished).

Liberating virtue from being a slave to craving means bringing it to the state of being a strong support for the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭūpanissaya). Because the person endowed with that virtue can act according to their own will, it is called "bhujissa" (free/liberated). Therefore, those virtues are called "bhujissa". For that reason, it is said, "They are called bhujissa because they are the cause of being free." Because they are well-purified and worthy of praise by the wise, they are called "viññuppasattha" (praised by the wise). Because they are not misapprehended by craving and wrong view, such as "By this virtue, I wish to become a deity," or "It is permanent, stable, and eternal in the state of a deity," or "Purification is through virtue," they are called "aparāmaṭṭha" (unmisapprehended). It means being unable to be accused or destroyed by any of the four failures (vipatti) by saying, "This is a fault in your virtue." Because they have the benefit of producing concentration, they are called "samādhisamvattanika" (conducive to concentration).

"Samānabhāvūpagatasīlā" refers to those with virtue who have reached a state of equality through the perfection of virtue, those with a similar way of living. Indeed, there might be no difference in the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) among worldlings,
135:
but that is not absolute. This virtue of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) is absolute because of its fixed nature (niyama); therefore, it is said, "There is no difference in path-virtue (maggasīla)." Referring to that path-virtue, the words beginning with "Yāni tāni sīလာနိ" were spoken.

"Yāyaṃ" refers to this view which is evident to both Me and you. "Diṭṭhi" refers to the Right View (sammādiṭṭhi) included in the Path. "Niddosā" means having faults removed, meaning having evil states such as greed etc. cut off. "Niyyāti" means it leads out from the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha). Indeed, Right View itself leads out from the suffering of the round, and thus it is said that it causes the person endowed with that Path to lead out from the suffering of the round. Whatever instruction of the Teacher there is, because one follows and practices that instruction, one is called "takkaro" (one who acts accordingly). It means of that person who practices according to what has been taught. "Samānadiṭṭhibhāvaṃ" means the state of having the same view, the state of having an undivided view through the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. "Vuddhiyeva" means only growth through qualities such as virtue in the Dispensation of the Noble One, the Buddha, and not decline. This teaching on the conditions for non-decline (aparihāniyadhamma) was taught here in this Mahāparinibbāna Sutta by the Blessed One, who desired the long-lasting endurance of Himself and the Dispensation.

"Āsannaparinibbānattā" is explained with the thought that Parinibbāna would occur in about a year and a few months. "Etaṃyeva" refers only to "Iti sīlaṃ" and so on. In this context of "Iti sīlaṃ," the word "iti" is taken by combining the meaning of "manner" (pabheda) and the meaning of "measure" (parimāṇa); thus it is said, "Such virtue, this much virtue." "Such virtue" refers to virtue having the various types such as the fourfold purification virtue. "This much" means only this fourfold purification virtue is the measure; there is nothing more than this. "Catupārisuddhisīla" should be understood as the mundane fourfold purification virtue which is a prerequisite for the Path. The same method applies to "concentration which is one-pointedness of mind." "Standing in which virtue" means standing in the virtue described as, "Even before the Path, that monk's bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are well-purified," which is the proximate cause for supramundane wholesome states. "This concentration" refers to the concentration of the Path and Fruit. "Paribhāvito" means fully saturated and well-developed by that virtue. In the phrase "has great fruit, has great benefit," Path-concentration first has great fruit through the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) and has great benefit by the stilling of the suffering of the round. The other, Fruit-concentration, has great fruit by the abandonment through subsiding (paṭippassaddhippahāna) and has great benefit by the arising of the bliss of Nibbāna. "Standing in which concentration" means standing in the concentration of the base jhāna (pādakajjhāna) and the concentration of emergence-leading insight (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā), which are the proximate causes for supramundane wholesome states. "That wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the Path and Fruit. "Saturated by that concentration" means fully saturated and developed by the aforementioned concentration. Having great fruit and great benefit should be understood by the method stated for concentration. Furthermore, those types of wisdom have great fruit because they are the cause for the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), path factors (maggaṅga), and jhāna factors (jhānaṅga).
136:
It should be understood that there are great benefits because it is the cause for distinguishing the seven types of persons worthy of offerings. Standing in that insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā), or insight wisdom associated with concentration (samādhi), [the path and fruit arise]. For a practitioner of serenity (samatha-yānika), wisdom accompanied by concentration is indeed a special condition for attaining the Path. The phrase "perfectly indeed" (sammā-deva) means being liberated from all taints (āsavas) so that not even a trace remains. This was said with reference to the moment of the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga).

The accomplishment of the word "abhiranta" should be noted like the accomplishment of words expressing well-known meanings in the world. Abhiranta, abhirata, and abhirati are identical in meaning. This word "abhiranta" is a synonym for desire (abhiruci), not for sensual enjoyment (assāda). One who stays in a place out of sensual enjoyment might experience discontent (anabhirati) when the object of enjoyment is gone; however, this does not occur in Arahants, let alone in the Buddhas. Therefore, it is said, "For the Buddhas... there is no [discontent]." The Buddhas do not move elsewhere because of a lack of delight after staying in a place through delight. Rather, they stay in a place for the purpose of training those who are to be trained (veneyya), and when that task is accomplished, they go elsewhere solely for the purpose of training others; this is the manner according to their wish.

In the word "āyāma", the syllable "ā" has the same meaning as "āgaccha" (come), thus it means "Come, let us go." In the reading "ayāma", the letter "a" is merely a particle (nipāta). He addresses Venerable Ānanda because he was nearby, not because there were no other monks staying with the Teacher at that time. At that time, the Saṅgha of monks with the Blessed One was beyond counting. Therefore, it is said, "together with a great Saṅgha of monks." "Ambalaṭṭhikāgamana" refers to the Pali text concerning the journey to the Ambalaṭṭhikā garden. The same method applies to the journey to Pāṭali village. This matter is very clear as it has been explained before and after.

## Description of Sāriputta’s Lion’s Roar (Sāriputtasīhanādavaṇṇanā)
The collection of Pali starting with "Venerable Sāriputta" has been explained in detail in the old commentary on the Sampasādanīya Sutta (DN 28); therefore, we intend to explain it in detail according to the meaning in that sutta as well.

## Description of the Danger of Immorality (Dussīla-ādīnavavaṇṇanā)
It is called "āvasatha" because guests (āgantuka) come and stay there. Since that place is also called a house (agāra), "āvasathāgāra" means a rest house for guests.
137:
"To the two kings" refers to the Licchavī king and the Magadha king. "Companions" means attendants or servants. "Families" refers to householders (kuṭumbika). "Spread out" (santhata) is called "sabba-santharī" because everything is spread out; it refers to the fully furnished rest house. This word "sabba-santharī" is a neuter term used as an adverb. Therefore, it was said, "as if everything were spread out, so [it was spread]."

In the word "dussīla", the prefix "du" denotes absence, as in "duppañña" (unwise) and so on; it does not denote blame. Therefore, it means one without virtue or one devoid of virtue. In the word "bhinnasaṃvara", one who has undertaken the precepts but reaches a state of broken virtue for some reason is first called "bhinnasaṃvara" (one of broken restraint). But how can one who has not undertaken precepts at all and is devoid of good conduct be called "bhinnasaṃvara"? Such a person is also called "bhinnasaṃvara" because of the breaking or decline of good conduct (sādhusamacāra). It means one who has abandoned restraint or is devoid of restraint.

It refers to the basis of various crafts (livelihood). "Māghātakāla" (time of non-killing) occurs on the day when the command "Do not kill living beings" is proclaimed.

An evil reputation spreads upwards.

Because of frequent remorse, one becomes dejected in disposition.

"Tassa" refers to that immoral person. "The place where it occurs upon undertaking" means that the actions performed with exertion and effort appear in the mind. "Opening the eyes to this world" means seeing this visible world by seeing one's children, wife, and so on when the eyes are open. "Closing the eyes to the next world" means seeing the world of the next life by the appearance of the sign of destiny (gati-nimitta) when the eyes are closed (at the time of death). Therefore, [the Buddha] spoke of the four woeful states and so on. "The fifth point" refers to the fifth group of dangers spoken of as "with the breaking up of the body" and so on.

## Description of the Benefits of the Virtuous (Sīlavanta-ānisaṃsavaṇṇanā)

"By the opposite of what was spoken" means by the opposite of the discourse on dangers already mentioned. Such explanations as "A diligent person is able to complete various tasks like farming, trade, etc., at the proper time," and "One is called 'sīlavā' because of having praiseworthy virtue; one is called 'sīlasampanna' because of being endowed with virtue," are not dealt with here because they are easy to understand.

"Pāḷimuttakā" refers to words associated with a Dhamma talk that were not included in the Council (Saṅgīti). "Tattheva" means only in that very rest house for guests.

## Explanation of the Founding of Pāṭaliputta City

"Issariyamattāya" should be understood as either by the measure of sovereignty, or by both sovereignty and wealth and possessions. In the world, the wealth and possessions used for enjoyment are also called "mattā". "Pāṭaligāmaṃ nagaraṃ katvā" means making the place formerly known as Pāṭaligāma into a city now. "Māpenti" means they establish or build. "Āyamukhapacchindanatthaṃ" is for the purpose of cutting off the channels of revenue. There is also the reading "sahassasevā", which means only by thousands. Therefore, it is said, "becoming a thousand for each group." "Gharavatthūni" means the sites for establishing houses. "Cittāni namanti" means that by the power of various deities, the minds of the experts in the science of sites (vatthuvijjā) incline toward those very places occupied by the deities. "Sippānubhāvena" means by the power of the science (mantra) associated with the craft. "Nāgaggāho" means the occupation of a place as a dwelling for Nagas. The same method applies to the other two terms (Yakkhas and Asuras). "Pāsāṇo" means an indistinct stone or pebble. "Khāṇuko" means some kind of stump. The experts recite mantras, avoid such dangerous places, and build those various houses by giving instructions as if consulting with the deities who occupy those plots of land. "Nesaṃ" refers to the experts in the science of sites and to all the deities. "Maṅgalaṃ vaḍḍhāpessanti" means they will increase blessings. Since seeing the wise and so on are supreme blessings, it is said, "Then we," and so forth.

Fame spreads because the whole is indicated by a part, just as it is said, "Devadatta is adorned (Devadatto alaṅkato)."

"Ariyakamanussānaṃ" means of the people living in the Ariyan region. "Rāsivaseneva" means only in the form of heaps or masses, such as by thousands or hundreds of thousands; because the buying and selling of small amounts of goods can be found elsewhere, it is said "only in the form of heaps." "Vaṇippatho" means the place where trade occurs, according to the first method. According to the second method, it means the place where merchants reside; desiring to show this meaning, it is said, "the place where merchants reside." "Bhaṇḍapuṭe bhindanti" means they open the bundles of goods here, thus it is called "Puṭabhedana"; desiring to show this meaning, it is said, "they... the bundles of goods."

## Explanation of the Discourse on the Noble Truths

The village established at the place where the pinnacle of King Mahāpanāda's palace fell is called 'Pāsādakoṭiyaṃ katagāma'. Because they cause those who penetrate the Four Noble Truths to become Noble Ones (Ariyas), these truths are called 'Ariyabhāvakara' (factors that make one a Noble One), using the cause metaphorically as the agent. They are called 'Sacca' (Truths) because they are true and non-distorted in nature. 'Anubodha' refers to the preliminary insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), while 'paṭivedha' refers to the penetration (abhisamaya) through Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). Between these two, penetration which is preceded by preliminary knowledge cannot occur without that preliminary knowledge. Some preliminary knowledge is also connected with penetration. It is precisely because of the absence of both that one wanders in the round of suffering (vaṭṭa-dukkha). Therefore, it was taught in the Pāli as 'Ananubodhā... tumhākañca', etc. Transitioning from one existence to another by way of taking rebirth is called 'sandhāvana' (running on), and wandering by way of repeated death and rebirth is called 'saṃsaraṇa' (wandering). This meaning is shown by the words beginning with 'bhavato'. In the first method (vikappa), the terms 'sandhāvita' and 'saṃsarita' in the phrase 'mayā ca tumhehi ca' are intended in the sense of the object of action (kammasādhana). In the second method, the phrase 'mamañceva tumhākañca' is stated according to the Pāli text, keeping in mind the sense of the action itself (bhāvasādhana). 'Nayanasamatthā' means having the power to lead from one existence to another. Just as a man holding a rope in his hand leads a bird tied with a long rope to another place, the volitional formations (kamma) that produce new existence lead the continuum of beings, who are tied by the rope of craving (taṇhā), to another new existence. Therefore, that craving is called 'bhavanetti' (the guide to existence). Because that guide to existence, craving, has been well-severed by the sword of the Noble Path, it is called 'bhavanettisamūhatā'.

## Explanation of the State of Non-Return and Enlightenment as the Destination

There are two villages named 'Nātikā'. Here, the use of 'Nātikā' by changing the letter 'ñ' to 'n' is similar to that in Pāli passages such as 'animittā na nāyare'. Therefore, it is explained as 'Ñātigāmaka'. 'Giñjakā' refers to bricks. Because it is a dwelling made only of bricks, it is called 'Giñjakāvasatha' (Brick Hall). It is said that this dwelling was built by laying and covering with bricks alone, without the need for plastering. Therefore, it is explained as 'iṭṭhakāmaye āvasathe'. However, the beams, rafters, door-leaves, and planks were made of wood only.

'Ora' refers to the sensual realm (kāmadhātu). Because they lead to that lower sensual realm as a cause for rebirth, they are called 'orambhāgiya' (lower-fettering). Alternatively, they are called 'orambhāgiya' because they are fetters that are beneficial to (or associated with) the lower part. Therefore, it is stated as 'heṭṭhābhāgiyānaṃ', etc. 'Tīhi maggehi' refers to the three lower paths. Because they are abandoned by these three lower paths, the fetters are called 'orambhāgiya'. Now, after explaining the meaning of 'orambhāgiya', the statement beginning with 'tatthā' is made to clarify the nature of these fetters as 'orambhāgiya' through the method of contrast (vyatireka).
141:
Because they are to be abandoned by those three lower paths, these fetters are called 'orambhāgiya' (lower-fettering). Alternatively, according to the method of linguistics (nirutti), they are called 'orambhāgiya'. Now, to clarify their nature as 'orambhāgiya' through the method of contrast, the statement beginning with 'tattha' is made. Although worldlings (puthujjanas) may have suppressed them through mundane jhāna, they are not able to prevent rebirth in the fine-material or immaterial realms. Noble Ones (ariyas), however, have eradicated them completely, so they do not take rebirth in those realms. Therefore, it is said, 'not suppressed, not completely eradicated'.

'By way of occurrence' means by way of taking rebirth (paṭisandhi). They do not allow one to go because they obstruct the accumulation of kamma that leads to the sublime realms (mahaggata). Although the three fetters such as personality belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) are not direct obstacles to rebirth in the sublime realms like sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and ill-will (byāpāda), they are special causes for rebirth in the sensual realm (kāmabhava). Thus, even if one is born in a sublime realm, when the kamma that caused that birth is exhausted, they lead one back to be reborn in the sensual realm. Therefore, all five fetters are indeed 'orambhāgiya'. 'By way of rebirth, they have the nature of not returning' means they do not return from that Pure Abode (Suddhāvāsa) to this sensual realm by way of taking rebirth. However, their coming for the purpose of seeing the Buddha, seeing the elders, and hearing the Dhamma is not prohibited.

Thinness (tanubhāva) is described in two ways: being sparse due to occurring only occasionally, and being non-thick due to the weakness of their outbursts (pariyuṭṭhāna). 'Abhiṇhaṃ' means occurring many times. Defilements are very intense. In the continuum of worldlings, defilements arise by crushing, spreading, and creating darkness. However, because they have been abandoned by two paths, they arise only very thinly and weakly. The statement 'they have sons and daughters' is not a counter-argument. This is because children can be born even by the mere touching of major and minor limbs. The statement 'due to the thinning of greed, hatred, and delusion' was refuted when taken by Elder Mahāsīva to mean 'by way of fewness of lives'. The lives obtained by Noble Ones are only those with complete characteristics. In the lives that are not obtained, there is no such thing as 'thinning of lives'. Therefore, to show the impossibility of 'thinning of lives' in both ways, the statement beginning with 'for a Stream-enterer' (sotāpannassa) was made. In the eighth life, there is no thinning of life because the eighth life itself does not exist at all. The same method applies to the remaining cases.

This was taught with reference to the sensual world (kāmāvacara-loka), as it is impossible to speak in that way with reference to other worlds. Even a Once-returner (sakadāgāmī) who is reborn alternately in the deva and human worlds must be defined within the scope of sensual existence (kāmabhava). The Blessed One, while staying in the sensual world, taught: 'Returns to this world only once...'
142:
By the words 'having come to this world' (imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā), among the five types of Once-returners (sakadāgāmī), four are excluded and only one is taken. Some Once-returners reach the fruit of Once-returning in this human existence and attain Parinibbāna right here. Some reach it here and attain Parinibbāna in the deva world. Some reach it in the deva world and attain Parinibbāna right there. Some reach it in the deva world, and after being reborn in this human existence, attain Parinibbāna. These four types of persons are not included in the Pāḷi phrase 'having come to this world.' Indeed, the person intended here is the one who reaches [the path and fruit] in this human existence, lives in the deva world until the end of their lifespan, and then is reborn once more in this human existence to attain Parinibbāna. However, in the Commentary, it is stated that 'this world' (imaṃ lokaṃ) refers to the sensual realm (kāmabhava); to clarify this meaning, another group of four is shown starting with 'If indeed' (sace hi).

'No nature of falling ruinously into the four states of deprivation' means that the evil unwholesome states that lead to the states of deprivation have been entirely abandoned. 'By the law of Dhamma' (dhammaniyāmena) means by the fixed law of the Path (magga). One is 'fixed' (niyata) because the attainment of the higher paths will certainly occur. Therefore, it is said: 'Destined for enlightenment' (sambodhiparāyaṇa), meaning one who has the higher path as their future destination.

## Commentary on the Mirror of Dhamma Discourse (Dhammādāsadhammapariyāyavaṇṇanā)

'The destination of knowledge of various beings' (tesaṃ tesaṃ ñāṇagatiṃ) refers to the attainment of specific knowledge by various beings, such as 'this person is a Stream-enterer, this person is a Once-returner,' and so on. 'The arising of knowledge, the future state of knowledge' (ñāṇūpappattiṃ ñāṇābhisamparāyaṃ) refers to the future existence as a result of rebirth accompanied by knowledge, such as 'he is fixed, destined for enlightenment, and having come to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering.' For the Buddha who looks with the eye of knowledge, such looking is merely a physical fatigue for Him. It means that there is no particular benefit for the beings to be tamed (veneyya) through such looking. 'Mental weariness' (cittavihesā) means mental exhaustion; such mental weariness does not exist for the Buddhas because it is associated with defilements. It is called a 'mirror' (ādāsa) because one looks at oneself directly through it. The mirror that is the Dhamma is the 'Mirror of Dhamma' (dhammādāsa); this is a designation for the Knowledge of the Noble Path (ariyamaggañāṇa). By that mirror of the Noble Path, the noble disciple, having destroyed delusion regarding the Four Noble Truths, knows himself truly and can declare himself truly. Because it reveals that meaning, this sutta teaching should be known as the 'Mirror of Dhamma.' In this context, 'by which Mirror of Dhamma' (yena dhammādāsena) refers specifically to the Path Dhamma (maggadhamma).

The clarity of faith that arises from knowing truly is called 'unshakable faith' (aveccappasāda). It is the clarity of faith produced by the attainment of the Noble Path. Because that faith is as steady as a stone mountain and cannot be destroyed by any cause, it is said to be 'unshakable and immovable' (acalena accutena). The words 'five precepts' (pañcasīlāni) are spoken in terms of householders.
143:
The words 'five precepts' (pañcasīlāni) are spoken in terms of householders, because they must certainly be observed by them. For noble ones (ariya), however, all virtues are truly dear. Therefore, it is said: 'In this Dispensation, all forms of restraint (saṃvara) are indeed obtained.' 'Of all' (sabbesaṃ) means of all noble ones. 'Without conflicting with the training rules' (sikkhāpadāvirodhena) means in such a way that no offense arises from speaking the truth. 'In the appropriate place' (yuttaṭṭhāne) means in a place where it is suitable to act.

## Commentary on the Story of Ambapālī the Courtesan (Ambapālīgaṇikāvatthuvaṇṇanā)

At that time, it is said that Vesālī was prosperous, wealthy, populous, endowed with all features, and had reached greatness. Referring to that prosperity of Vesālī, it is said: 'The prosperity of Vesālī should be understood in the manner stated in the Khandhaka.' In that assembly of monks, about five hundred monks were newly ordained and had waning energy. Therefore, it will be said: 'Among those monks, some were waning in energy,' and so on. 'For the purpose of establishing mindfulness' (satipaccupaṭṭhānatthaṃ) means for the purpose of making mindfulness present to those monks. 'He remembers' (sarati) means he repeatedly recollects and firmly bears in mind the objects such as the body according to their true nature with mindfulness associated with knowledge. 'He clearly comprehends' (sampajānāti) means he knows equally in various ways; he understands through penetration. This is the summary here; the detail will come later in the commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

'All-inclusive' (sabbasaṅgāhakaṃ) is a term that encompasses all instances of the color blue/dark, whether in the body or in clothes and ornaments. 'Of that very thing' (tasseva) refers to the meaning spoken by way of the all-inclusive term 'blue' (nīlā). 'Showing the divisions' (vibhāgadassanaṃ) means showing the varieties. Just as those Licchavī kings, though not naturally yellow, appeared yellow in some cases due to the power of ointments, so too, though not naturally blue, some appeared blue due to the power of ointments; referring to this, it is said: 'Their natural color was not blue,' and so on. Because there are blue gems in those ornaments, they are called 'blue gems' (nīlamaṇi); these are ornaments inlaid with blue jewels such as indanīla and mahānīla. It is said that those ornaments, with the radiance of gems set in gold, appeared entirely blue. 'Inlaid with blue gems' (nīlamaṇikhacitā) means surrounded by blue jewels. 'Enveloped in blue cloth' (nīlavatthaparikkhittā) means surrounded by blue cloth or blue blankets. 'With blue armor' (nīlavammikehi) means covered with blue coats of mail. 'In all phrases' (sabbapadesu) means in all phrases such as 'they are yellow,' and so on. 'Collided' (parivaṭṭesi) means struck against. 'Revenue' (āhāra) is that which royal officers bring from this place as tax; referring to the district from which that tax is obtained, it is said: 'Sāhāraṃ means together with the district.' The snapping of fingers also [refers to] the finger...
144:
"Snapping the fingers" means by the power of moving the fingers; thus it is said, "they moved their fingers." "Ambakā" refers to women. Among women, these three terms—"Ambakā, mātugāma, jananikā"—are merely conventional designations (upacāra).

"Avaloketha" means to look without turning the face elsewhere. Intending such repeated looking, He said, "Look again and again." "Upanetha" means to make a comparison, thinking, "Just as this assembly of Licchavī princes is endowed with supreme beauty, so too is the assembly of Tāvatiṃsa gods." Therefore, He said, "Look at them, making them equal to the Tāvatiṃsa gods."

The words, "O bhikkhus, compare the assembly of Licchavī princes to the assembly of Tāvatiṃsa gods," are not an injunction to grasp at a sign (nimittaggāha). Rather, it should be understood as a discourse on the bliss of heaven in the gradual instruction (anupubbikathā), simply stating that the sovereign prosperity of these kings is like divine prosperity. However, for some of those bhikkhus, grasping at a sign in that assembly of kings might occur; with reference to that, it is said, "He urges them to grasp at a sign." Just as He showed the bliss of heaven to the Venerable Nanda out of a desire for his welfare, so too He urged them out of a desire for the welfare of those bhikkhus. Therefore, it is said beginning with "Tatra kira." "Osannavīriyā" means one whose energy has slackened or one who has abandoned energy in the right practice (sammāpaṭipatti). It was spoken for the purpose of making the mark of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) clear to the bhikkhus by means of the kings' condition.

## Description of Entering the Rains Retreat at Veḷuvagāma

"Veḷuvagāma" is a satellite village of Vesālī situated nearby, such that one could go and return in either the morning or the evening. "Saṅgamma" means having properly arrived and met. "Assa" means to the Blessed One (this thought occurred).

"Pharuso" means harsh, meaning very severe. "Visabhāgarogo" is a very strong illness arisen due to the discordance of the elements, not just a mere ailment. "Ñāṇena paricchinditvā" means having accurately delimited and weighed with knowledge the momentary nature, the suffering, and the selflessness of the feelings. "Adhivāsesi" means He dwelt having taken those feelings upon Himself by way of the manner of overcoming and suppressing them, not being overcome by them. Therefore, He said, "without being distressed" (avihanyamāno) and so on. "Adukkhīyamāno" means by way of mental suffering...
145:
For the Blessed One who was enduring, it cannot be said that there was no bodily suffering. For if that bodily suffering were absent, the very act of endurance would be impossible. "Anāmantetvā" means without informing (those who attend). "Anapaloketvā" means without asking leave (of the Saṅgha). Therefore, it is said that it means "without giving advice and instruction." "Pubbabhāgavīriyena" means with the preparatory energy (parikammavīriya) performed in the stage prior to the attainment of fruition. "Phalasamāpattivīriyena" means with the energy associated with the attainment of fruition. "Vikkhambhetvā" means having removed or suppressed.

For example, if a wedge is driven into a campaka tree or the like at the time of flowering, as long as that wedge is not removed, the tree's ability to flower is suppressed and removed. In the same way, by driving in the wedge of energy mentioned above, those feelings were suppressed and removed in the Blessed One's body for the determined period. Therefore, it is said, "Vikkhambhetvā means vinodetvā (having removed)." The life-faculty is also called life-formation (jīvitasaṅkhāra) because it is conditioned by kamma. Life, which is on the verge of being cut off due to the encounter with opposing causes, is connected and maintained by the perfection of effort (payogasampatti) which is the attainment of fruition. "Adhiṭṭhāya" means having made a resolution. Therefore, it is said, "He entered the attainment having resolved, 'Let (the pain) not arise for ten months.'" Since that resolution can also be called "bringing about" (pavattana), it is said, "having resolved and brought about."

"Khaṇikasamāpatti" is an attainment that is to be entered immediately without making such a preliminary preparation (pubbābhisaṅkhāra). Because no special preliminary preparation is made, the feelings again overwhelm the body. The sevenfold groups of materiality and the sevenfold groups of non-materiality (rūpasattaka, arūpasattaka) should be understood according to the detailed method explained in the Visuddhimagga commentaries. Because the preliminary preparation has superior power, it can well suppress the feelings. Now, to clarify that meaning with a simile, it is said beginning with "Yathā nāma." "Apabyūḷho" means removed. By means of those sevenfold groups of materiality and non-materiality, in fourteen ways, the insight-consciousness (or the whole body) is lubricated to prevent the harshness and dryness produced by the discordant disease; because it was well suppressed by the Buddha with the force of the superior attainment, the feelings no longer arise.

"Gilāno hutvā puna vuṭṭhito" means having previously been ill and then recovering from that illness. "Madhurakabhāva" refers to the stiffness of the body. Since that stiffness is preceded by heaviness, it is said, "heaviness and stiffness arose." By the words, "they do not appear in various ways," my disorientation of the directions...
146:
He shows that Venerable Ānanda became confused about the directions due to the power of grief. The teachings of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), such as the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā), which had appeared clearly before, do not appear clearly to me now.

It is called 'making internal' because of keeping it secret only within oneself. It is called making a person an 'internal person' because of having previously supported that person with the Dhamma by treating them as an equal. 'In the time of youth' means in one's own youth. He shows that he did not keep any secret text without telling it to any of his resident pupils (antevāsika) by the words 'without telling anyone'. 'Making a fist' means making something secret as if it were held within a fist. Alternatively, if a certain Dhamma disappears, all other Dhammas rooted in it are destroyed; that initial, fundamental Dhamma can be lost or destroyed. Because all Dhammas can be destroyed by the loss of this, it is called 'muṭṭhi' (fist). He shows that there is nothing at all that is kept secret by always carrying it like such a fist.

The limitation 'only I' is intended to show the desire for others to be involved in the matter of leading the Saṅgha of monks. However, it should be understood that without such a limitation, words like 'I (shall lead) the Saṅgha of monks' show the absence of 'I-making' (ahaṃkāra) and 'mine-making' (mamaṃkāra) in leading the Saṅgha of monks. 'Because of the sense of being pointed out as the Teacher' means because of the sense of being designated as 'the Teacher'. It means, 'When I have passed away, may the monks not (be those who look to others besides me)'. Or there is a reading 'mā vā ahosi'. 'It does not happen thus' means that the occurrence of thought in the manner of 'I shall lead the Saṅgha of monks' etc., does not exist. By the words 'said to show the state of having reached the final stage of life', he shows that just as his age has reached its end, the Buddha's duties to be performed are also a completed task. Binding the axle-pole of a cart to make it firm is called 'bāhabandha'. Binding the joints of the wheel and the rim to make them firm is called 'cakkabandha'.

That meaning is as already stated: 'it should be understood as being mixed with bindings'. Because the Dhammas such as form (rūpa) appear as if they have a physical body, they are called 'rūpanimitta' and so on. Because of the cessation of those mundane feelings (vedanā), the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) should be entered; because of their cessation, there is comfort (in phalasamāpatti). Likewise, there is comfort for the body afflicted by severe pains (due to the cessation of feelings). 'For that purpose' means for the purpose of dwelling in the attainment of fruition. In this context, it is called 'dīpa' (island) because the water flows away on two sides. A piece of land that is surrounded by a flood but not submerged is called an island. But here, one's own self, which is not submerged by the four floods (ogha) or by the great flood of saṃsāra, is intended as the 'island'. Therefore, he said, '(Like an island) in the great ocean' and so on. 'Having self as refuge' means having oneself as a support (and so dwell). Or 'having self as a place of rest' means...
147:
Be those who have yourselves as a place of rest. In saying 'do not seek another refuge', it means do not think of or seek any other refuge or place of rest besides yourself. Why? Because in this Dispensation, what is called 'atta' (self) is, in the ultimate sense, the Dhamma residing within. Having practiced this Dhamma to completion is for you an island, a protection, a resort, and a refuge. Therefore, he said 'having the Dhamma as an island' and so on.

And so he said: 'Self is indeed the refuge of self; for who else could be the refuge?' (Dhp. 160, 380). Indeed, what depends on another is merely the instruction and guidance; all other achievements depend on the person himself. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'You yourselves must make the effort; the Tathāgatas are only teachers' (Dhp. 276). 'Tamagge' means because of the absence of association with darkness (tamas) (or because there is no one superior to them). Therefore, he said 'these are the highest' and so on. 'Mama' means in my Dispensation. Only those monks who dwell having developed and increased the four foundations of mindfulness, making that very foundation of mindfulness their domain and their place of occurrence, will be the highest.

## The Explanation of the Second Recital Section (Bhāṇavāra) is finished.

## Explanation of the Discourse on the Hint and the Sign

The Blessed One dwelt in Vesālī many times. Therefore, to specify this entry into Vesālī for alms, he asked 'When did he enter?' and, wishing to show it from the time of his arrival, he said 'Bhagavā kira' and so on. 'By the same path he had come' means turning back by the same path he had previously come from Veḷuva village. 'By the determined time' means by the specified time. 'From that' means from the attainment of fruition. 'This' refers to the manner that will now be described. Looking at the place of the day-dwelling and so on is a demonstration of the certainty of his Parinibbāna. 'Relinquished' means the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra) was given up, thinking 'I shall live for only three months more'.

By the words 'to the elder and younger brothers', he speaks referring to all fellow monks (sabrahmacārī). 'I shall make them practice' means I shall urge them to practice the path. 'Maṇiphalake' means on a wooden slab laid out at the entrance decorated with gems. 'That first seeing' refers to the seeing that occurred when he came to the Veḷuvanarāma in the form of a wanderer (paribbājaka). Or, it is the first seeing of the Buddha, just as one saw him face-to-face at the time of making the initial aspiration (abhinīhāra) while believing the words of the Blessed One Anomadassī.
148:
Seeing the venerable ones is accomplished as if seeing them in person; that seeing is the first seeing. *Paccāgamanacārika* means wandering for the purpose of returning.

*Sattāha* is a word in the accusative case used in the sense of continuous duration (*accantasaṃyoga*). The house containing the birth chamber of the Elder Sāriputta was, it is said, more secluded than other houses and had an open courtyard; therefore, being suitable for the approach of devas and Brahmas, he said, "Clean the birth chamber." *So* refers to Uparevata. *Taṃ pavattiṃ* refers to that matter spoken because of the desire to reside there.

"Tathāgatas ask even though they know." By this method, the Elder asked, "Who are you?" When asked, "Are you greater than the four Great Kings?" he, wishing to attribute his own greatness to the Teacher, said, "These are like the *ārāmikas* (monastery attendants) of our Teacher." Indeed, praising the accomplishment of the disciples clarifies, in meaning, the accomplishment of the Teacher himself.

*Sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya* means having become established in the fruit of stream-entry due to the power of the Elder's teaching and the maturity of his own supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) and wisdom.

*Ayaṃ* is the word already mentioned. *Ettha* refers to this entry into Vesālī: "He entered Vesālī for alms." *Anupubbīkathā* is a talk that explains things in order.

*Udenayakkhassa cetiyaṭṭhāne* means in a place honored by the public, constructed with bricks as the residence of the yakkha named Udena. *Katavihāro* means a monastery built dedicated to the Blessed One. *Vuccati* means it is called "Udena Cetiya" by former usage. *Gotamakādīsupi* means the same applies to terms like "Gotamaka Cetiya." *Eseva nayo* indicates the fact of building a monastery at the site of a shrine (*cetiya*). *Vaḍḍhitā* means developed by the power of the fulfillment of meditation (*bhāvanā*). *Punappunaṃ katā* means made to occur repeatedly by frequent practice of meditation. *Yuttayānaṃ viya katā* means just as a vehicle drawn by noble steeds, managed by a skilled charioteer, proceeds as desired, so too these have been brought to a state of being manageable as desired. *Patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena* is because of the sense of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*). *Vatthu viya katā* means made like a well-cleared site because, by completely purifying defilements, it becomes the basis for the occurrence of psychic power. *Adhiṭṭhitā* means well-developed by removing opposing states, thus becoming suitable for various resolutions...
149:
(The bases of power) have been established. They have been brought to the stage of accumulation of meditation in every part. Therefore, it is said, "well-developed." "Well-exerted" means well-cultivated until reaching the peak of the meditation on psychic power.

By the indefinite statement, "Whosoever." By defining with the specific term, "The Tathāgata." *Āyuppamāṇa* refers to the maximum lifespan; the reason for taking it thus should be understood according to the method stated in the Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta. But the Elder Mahāsiva said: "Keeping in mind the capacity of the kamma that gives rebirth in the final existence of Great Bodhisattas to bring about an incalculable lifespan, the ability of the life-constituent (*āyusaṅkhāra*) of the Buddhas to ward off danger is indeed mentioned in the Pali; thus, he could remain for this entire Bhadda-kappa." By the words "afflicted by broken teeth, etc.," it is implied that just as old age cannot be prevented by psychic power, so too death cannot be prevented. Just as one cannot know exactly where an arrow is shot and where it falls, the statement of Elder Mahāsiva, though differing from the Commentary, should be seen as supporting the words of the Commentary itself. Therefore, it says, "That [view] is not liked... it is defined."

*Pariyuṭṭhitacitta* means one whose mind is so overwhelmed that they cannot notice what is beneficial or harmful. That overwhelming is like a great flood of water covering a small amount of water; thus it is said, *ajjhotthaṭacitta*. *Aññopi* means someone other than the Elder [Ānanda], or any worldling (*puthujjana*) other than the Noble Ones (*ariya*). The inclusion of the worldling here is to show that just as a worldling whose perversions (*vipallāsa*) are not at all abandoned cannot notice any benefit when overwhelmed by Māra, so too the Elder [Ānanda] did not notice at all the sign and suggestion made by the Blessed One. Therefore, it says, "For Māra..." etc.

The four perversions are: the perversion of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*) and the perversion of mind (*citta-vipallāsa*) that perceives the foul as beautiful, and the perversion of perception and the perversion of mind that perceives suffering as happiness. Although the Elder Ānanda had abandoned the other eight perversions, because these four mentioned perversions were not yet abandoned, Māra could oppress him. "Oppresses" means it is as if he oppresses just by touching; otherwise, if oppressed by him in another way, the death of beings would occur. The meaning is: "How could Māra not be able to put his hand into the mouth of the Elder Ānanda? (He certainly could)."
150:
Why would he not be able to do so? Did not this Māra once enter the belly of the Chief Disciple (Venerable Mahāmoggallāna)? It is true that he entered; however, that entry was merely to demonstrate his own power and not with the intention of causing harm. But here, in the episode where Māra overwhelmed the mind of Venerable Ānanda, it is said, "Why would he be able to?" because it relates to the intention to cause harm, as Māra had obtained the opportunity to act as if he were squeezing the heart.

In the term "nimittobhāsa" (hint and sign), "nimitta" (hint) refers to creating a mental impression of the Buddha's ability to remain for an entire aeon (kappa) due to the power of his development of the four bases of power (iddhipāda). This was done through indirect speech, such as, "Ānanda, whoever has developed the four bases of power..." in order to prompt a request for the Blessed One to remain for the full duration of the aeon. On the other hand, "obhāsa" (sign) refers to speech that directly clarifies one's intention, setting aside such indirect hints.

"Even while knowing" means even while knowing that Ānanda was possessed by Māra. The Buddha said, "to lessen grief by laying blame," meaning that the sorrow of beings is diminished and not as intense when it is attributed to one's own fault or shortcoming. Did the Elder Ānanda know what happened during the time his mind was possessed by Māra only later? He did not know by his own nature, but he came to know through the power of the Buddha.

## Description of the Request of Māra (Mārayācanakathāvaṇṇanā)

Māra is called "Māra" because he kills by inciting one toward what is harmful and by destroying virtues (guṇa), or because he acts as if killing beings born in various existences by being the cause of rebirth through the obstruction of passionless states (virāga). He is called "Pāpimant" because of his extreme wickedness. He is called "Kaṇha" because he is endowed with dark, unwholesome states. He is called "Antaka" because he brings an end to virtues such as passionlessness. He is called "Namuci" because he does not release beings from the practice that leads to harm. He is called "Pamattabandhu" (Friend of the Negligent) either because he binds the negligent with his snare of Māra, or because negligent beings are his kinsmen.

"In the eighth week" refers to the seven days following the seventh week; it is not because there is a specifically designated eighth week with a fixed duty like the week at the throne (pallaṅka-sattāha). This is because, after the seventh week, while at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, Māra became aware that the Blessed One had consented to the Great Brahmā and Sakka, the King of Devas, to teach the Dhamma. He became dejected, thinking, "Now, by teaching the Dhamma to beings, the Blessed One will make them transcend my realm." He then thought, "Well now, I shall use a stratagem to make him attain Parinibbāna; thus his wish will be altered, and my own wish will be fulfilled." Having thought thus, he approached the Blessed One, stood to one side, and requested Parinibbāna, saying, "May the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna, Bhante." It is in reference to this request that it is said, "In the eighth week," and so on. In that passage, "today" refers to the day the Buddha relinquished the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra). The Blessed One, [knowing] his intention...
151:
Although the Blessed One knew Māra's intention, he did not reveal it, but instead rejected the request by declaring that it was not yet the time for Parinibbāna. Therefore, he said, "Not until..." and so forth.

They are "accomplished" (viyatta/byatta) because of their proficiency in penetrating the Four Noble Truths through the power of the Path. They are "disciplined" (vinīta) because they have been trained through the total eradication of defilements by the power of the Path. They are "confident" (visārada) because they have attained boldness in the Teacher's Dispensation through the attainment of the Noble Path; this means they have reached a state of confidence due to the departure of evil, unwholesome states such as wrong view and doubt, which cause timidity. In this context, "learned" (suta) refers to the learning of the Three Baskets (Tipiṭaka) which enables escape from the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha), as indicated by the phrase "by way of the Tepeṭaka" (the Three Baskets). The collection of the three baskets is called Tepeṭaka or Tipiṭaka. They bear that very scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma) in their hearts, having mastered it thoroughly so that it does not perish, like lion's fat placed in a golden bowl. Having thus shown the state of being very learned and a bearer of the Dhamma through scriptural Dhamma, the text now says "or else" (atha vā) to show this through the Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha-dhamma) as well. This refers to the ninefold Supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma) or the Dhamma of the Noble Path and Fruit. "In accordance with the Dhamma" (anudhamma-bhūta) refers to the practice of Insight (vipassanā) or the six purifications (visuddhi), which are appropriate for the realization of that Dhamma. They are in the habit of practicing (caraṇa-sīla) virtues such as fewness of wishes (appicchatā), which scrape away defilements and are suitable for that aforementioned practice. Alternatively, the Path and Fruit are the "anudhamma" of this Insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā), and they are in the habit of practicing that Insight. They will teach the doctrine of their own Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, which is the teaching of the Four Noble Truths. The Blessed One is the "Teacher" (Ācariya) because he teaches the conduct and training to the world including the devas. His doctrine (vāda) is the teaching of the Four Noble Truths.

"They will announce" (ācikkhisanti) means they will speak from the beginning; it means they will make others learn according to the method they themselves have learned. "They will teach" (desessanti) means they will recite; it means they will properly make known the Pali text. "They will make known" (paññāpessanti) means they will cause others to understand or perceive. "They will establish" (paṭṭhapessanti) means they will set forth in various ways or manifest. "They will reveal" (vivarissanti) means they will make open. "They will analyze" (vibhajissanti) means they will make divided/classified. "They will make plain" (uttāniṃ karissanti) means they will make what is obscure and deep plain and evident. In the phrase "with the Dhamma" (saha dhammena), the word "Dhamma" is a synonym for cause (kāraṇa), just as in the passage, "Knowledge of causes is the discrimination of Dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā)."
152:
The teacher says, "With speech that is accompanied by reasons and causes," as in the Vibhaṅga beginning with "Dhamma-paṭisambhidā." "Sappāṭihāriyaṃ" means being accompanied by emancipation (from false views); just as one establishes one's own doctrine by crushing the doctrines of others, so they will teach the Dhamma by fulfilling the intended meaning with reasons and examples. Therefore, it is said, "They will teach the Dhamma by making it emancipating (niyyānika)." This means they will make known the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. Here, by the six terms beginning with "paññāpessanti," the six groups of meaning (atthapada) are shown. By the first two terms, the six groups of phrasing (byañjanapada) are shown. By this much, the Word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka is shown as being comprised by the method of commentary. For it is said in the Netti: "The twelve terms are the Sutta; all of that is both phrasing and meaning."

"Sikkhattaya-saṅgahitaṃ" means that which is comprised of the three trainings, such as the training in higher virtue. "Sakalaṃ sāsana-brahmacariyaṃ" means the noble conduct that is the Teacher's entire dispensation without remainder. "Samiddhaṃ" means that which is well-developed or prosperous. "Jhānassāda-vasena" means by way of the bliss of jhāna well-attained by various monks. "Vuddhippattaṃ" means that which has reached complete growth by attaining a state of being grand and sublime. Because it has reached the pinnacle of the dispensation's growth by way of the attainment of direct knowledge (abhiññā), it is like all the pāliphualla flowers in bloom. "Paṭiṭṭhita-vasena" means by way of being established, meaning by way of reaching a state of establishment. "Bāhujaññaṃ" refers to the welfare of many people through the power of penetration. Therefore, it is said, "By way of the realization of many people." "Puthubhūtaṃ" means having become widespread or having reached a state of extensiveness. Therefore, it is said, "Reached in every aspect... [pe]..." "Suṭṭhu pakāsitaṃ" means that which is well-proclaimed by being well-known through its goodness in the beginning, etc.

## Explanation of the Relinquishment of the Life-Principle
"Satiṃ supaṭṭhitaṃ katvā" means: "I have carried this burden of suffering, known as the individual existence (attabhāva), divided into the body and so on, for this long. Now, it should no longer be carried. For the sake of not carrying this burden, I have accumulated the requisites of the Noble Path for a very long time. That Noble Path has been penetrated. Because of that penetration, I have fully understood these things, such as the body, as being foul (asubha), etc., having well-established the fourfold right mindfulness on its object as it truly is." (This is the meaning). "Ñāṇena paricchinditvā" means: "The benefit for oneself (attahita), which was the purpose of carrying this burden of suffering known as the individual existence, was completed at the foot of the Great Bodhi tree. However, the benefit for others (parahita), which is the discipline of those who are teachable by a Buddha, must be completed." (Reflecting thus).
153:
That task (of disciplining those to be taught) will reach completion in only three months from now. Therefore, he said, "I will attain Parinibbāna on the full moon day of Vesākha." Having thus delimited with Buddha-knowledge and made a decision in every respect, he relinquished the life-principle (āyusaṅkhāra). "Relinquished the life-principle" means he relinquished the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), which specially conditions life, saying, "I will no longer enter it." By relinquishing that fruition, he relinquished the life-formation (jīvita-saṅkhāra) conditioned by that attainment, saying, "I will no longer let it proceed." Therefore, the commentator said "tattha," etc. The earthquake was great both because of the greatness of its location and the greatness of the manner in which it occurred. There, to show the greatness of the earth's shaking due to the greatness of the location, it is said, "At that time... it shook." That place of the earthquake was only the ten thousand world systems that constitute the birth-field (jāti-khetta), not any other. Those ten thousand world systems also shook at the time of the Great Resolve, the Great Birth, and so on. What is the reason for only that many (ten thousand) world systems shaking at that time? It is because only that world system was delimited from the beginning as the birth-field. Such delimitation should be understood as a natural law (dhammatā). For previous Buddhas, too, the birth-field was only that much. Thus it is said: "The ten thousand world systems become silent and undisturbed... the great ocean stirs, the ten thousand world systems shake," and so on. Because it causes those who are not yet free from lust to fear by shaking in six ways up to the edge of the water, it is called "bhimsana" (terrifying). That same "bhimsana" is called "bhayajanaka" (causing fear). "Celestial drums" is just a synonymous term for the sound of the devas' dundubhi drums. Here, no actual drum is intended by "devadundubhi"; rather, it is the thundering sound in the sky that occurs as a portent. Therefore, it is said "deva," etc. "Deva" means a cloud. When a sound known as "dry thunder" is emitted from a clear sky without rain, it is designated as "devadundubhi." Therefore, it is said, "The sky-deva thundered with dry thunder."

"Released by the force of joy" means that the Blessed One, having felt joy thinking, "This great burden of suffering called individual existence, which I have carried for so long, will now be laid down before long," naturally uttered an inspired utterance (udāna) released by the force of joy. To show that by uttering this inspired utterance, this meaning is also accomplished, it is said in the commentary "kasmā," etc. "Tulīyati" means "tulaṃ" (it is measured/delimited). To show that the word "tula" is a passive derivative (kamma-sādhana), it is said "tulitaṃ." It is a kamma that is delimited because of its small power. Thus, because it is fragmented all around, it is called "paritta" (limited kamma). Because it suppresses the opposites (hindrances), because it has a long continuity, and because it has widespread results, it is called "atula" (immeasurable kamma). In the first method, the sublime (mahaggata) kamma is called "atula" because it is unparalleled. For what reason? Because of reasons such as the kamma of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) being superior to the kamma of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
154:
Because the results are extensive and abundant, they cannot be compared or delimited. For certain reasons, the mahaggata (great) states were previously called "atula" (incomparable) without making a distinction. These reasons exist more preeminently in the arūpāvacara (formless sphere) than in the rūpāvacara (fine-material sphere). Therefore, the arūpāvacara is called "atula," while the remaining (kāmāvacara and rūpāvacara) states are called "tula." Among the three types of kamma, that which has little result and is inferior is called "tula." That which has great result and is noble, the mahāvipāka kamma, is called "atula." As for the middle kamma, it should be divided into two—inferior and noble—and included in the appropriate category. Just as explained in the Hīnattikavaṇṇanā, one should determine the state of having little or much result and, by that means, understand the nature of being tula or atula.

It is called "sambhava" because results arise from this kamma. Thus, it means "the cause of sambhava." One who delights in the phenomena within one's own continuity through the power of vipassanā (insight) or through the cultivation of the object is called "niyakajjhattara." Kamma that occurs with its result and gives only pavatti-vipāka (resultant during the course of existence) is called "sambhava" in the sense of giving results. That kamma does not produce a new existence such as kāmabhava. Therefore, to distinguish it from kamma that gives pavatti results, it is first called "sambhava" and then "bhava-saṅkhāra." "Ossajjī" means abandoning by means of the ariyamagga (noble path). He also destroyed the defilements (kilesa) that arose within himself, which remained enveloping the personality like armor. To show the abandonment of kamma along with the destruction of defilements, the cause of both was stated as "ajjhattara samāhita" (one who is delighted within and concentrated).

"Tīrento" refers to contemplating as "Arising is danger, non-arising is safety," and so forth. To explain in detail the meaning briefly stated as "tulento tīrento," etc., the Buddha spoke of the "pañcakkhandhā" (five aggregates) and showed the manner of abandoning the bhava-saṅkhāra in its true form. With the words beginning with "evaṃ," the meaning previously stated at the beginning of the Udāna commentary is shown by way of conclusion.

## Mahābhūmicālavaṇṇanā

The word "yaṃ" is intended as a nominative case in the sense of instrument (karaṇa) or location (adhikaraṇa), thus it is said as "at which time." "Ukkhepaka-vāta" refers to the winds that toss up, cutting off the wind that supports the water from its place. The statement "sixty... [pe]... thick" refers only to the height of that air mass. In terms of length and breadth, it can indeed cut off the water-supporting wind that is ten thousand cakkavāḷa (world-systems) in size. "Ākāse" refers to the space previously occupied by the wind. Again, "wind" means that when the ukkhepaka wind has acted thus and disappeared, the water-supporting wind again...
155:
The wind that supports the water binds and holds it so that the water does not fall away. Thus, supporting the water, it binds and holds it by the power of a constructed canopy. "From there the water rises" means that because it is bound and held in that way, the water supported by that wind rises upwards. "It just happens" means it happens from time to time. "Because of its thickness" refers to the greatness of the mahāpathavī (great earth). Indeed, when the entire mahāpathavī sinks or rises at that time, the shaking is not apparent because of the earth's immense momentum.

"Of the accomplishment" means the accomplishment of the desired benefit. It refers to the accomplishment of the experienced mastery, prosperity, and so forth. "Limited" means it is merely obtained and not yet very well developed. Since such bhāvanā (meditation) lacks strength, it is called "weak." The Buddha taught bhāvanā by taking saññā (perception) as the head. "Measureless" means the state of being proficient and well-developed. Since that bhāvanā is firm and stable, it is called "strong." The teaching "limited perception of earth, measureless perception of water" is merely a conventional discourse. In truth, when the perception of water (āpo-saññā) is well-developed, the shaking of the earth is easily accomplished; this is the meaning to be understood here. This was done either to cause trepidation in Sakka, the king of gods, who was negligent in celestial splendor, or to test his own psychic power (iddhi) attained at that moment. The shaking of the palace by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna is well-known, so without discussing that, the shaking of the palace by the novice Saṅgharakkhita is shown with the words beginning "That venerable one, as it is heard." Because there is a smell mixed with a foul odor in this head, it is called "pūtigandha" (foul-smelling head). With that foul-smelling head, just like the smell that arises in the mother's womb (he shook it). The meaning is that you are just a very young child.

"Teacher" refers to the teacher's instruction. What is called the "formation of psychic power" (iddhābhisaṅkhāra) is desired by way of being the opposite of various psychic powers. Since he himself had not properly mastered the skill in the means of that psychic formation, it was not yet learned; thus it was said, "You have entered the battle without being trained." With the word "floating," it is shown that by turning the entire site of the palace into water, the determined palace floats on that water. To show the procedure of determination (adhiṭṭhāna) by way of a simile, the words beginning "Dear son... know" were spoken. In that context, "pan-cake" (kapallaka-pūva) refers to a cake poured into a pan. When cooking that cake, they first place a little flour-water in the pan, gradually increase it, and then trim it with the edges. They place the cake having trimmed it all around. In the same way, when determining by the power of the water kasiṇa, "Let the place where the palace stands be water," one should determine so that it becomes water all around the palace up to its boundaries; this is instructed by the simile.
156:
In the Mahāpadāna Sutta, it is said: "Monks, it is the nature of things (dhammatā) that when the Bodhisatta, passing away from the Tusita heaven, descends into his mother's womb..." and "this ten-thousandfold world system shakes, quakes, and trembles." Similarly, it is said: "Monks, it is the nature of things that when the Bodhisatta comes forth from his mother's womb..." and "this ten-thousandfold world system shakes, quakes, and trembles." Since the earthquake at the conception and birth of the Great Bodhisatta is stated in the Mahāpadāna Sutta as occurring by the power of nature (dhammatā), it is implied that in the other four instances as well, the earthquake occurs solely by the power of nature; this is the intended meaning in the Mahāpadāna Sutta.

Now, to show the distinction between these earthquakes by way of cause and manner of occurrence, the passage beginning with "iti imesu" is stated. "Dhātukopena" means due to the disturbance of the air element (vāyodhātu), which is characterized by upward displacement after cutting through the water element. "Iddhānubhāvena" means by the power of psychic potency (iddhi), whether arising from the power of knowledge (ñāṇa) or the power of the ripening of kamma (kammavipāka). "Puññatejena" means by the power of merit, the merit-power of the Great Bodhisatta. "Ñāṇatejena" means by the power of the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa). "Sādhukāradānavasena" means: just as the great earth was struck and shaken at the time of the Great Enlightenment by the power of the knowledge of penetration, which is unique to him, so too the great earth was struck and shaken by the power of the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa), which is unique to him. That shaking is like the earth's giving of applause (sādhukāra); hence it is said, "by way of giving applause."

The Blessed One—whose physical body was adorned with the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa), whose Dhamma-body was perfected with the jewels of virtues such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) purified in every way, who reached the highest excellence in greatness of merit, strength, fame, psychic power, and wisdom, who is peerless, the equal of the unequalled, the incomparable person, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—though capable of maintaining the five aggregates known as his individual existence (attabhāva) for an aeon (kappa) or the remainder of an aeon, he relinquished the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) without attachment. He did so by way of a special knowledge that regards conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma) with revulsion, considering them as not even worth a blade of grass. Struck by the power of that relinquishment, the great earth shook at the moment he gave up the life-force. It is said that this shaking was as if the earth were established in a state of compassion (kāruñña).
157:
"By way of compassion" (kāruñña-sabhāvena) means that at the time of his Parinibbāna, the Blessed One entered into two million four hundred thousand (2,400,000) meditative attainments, interspersed with the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). Prior to those attainments, he aroused an exceedingly sharp and courageous insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). Thinking, "For so long a time, I have accumulated this unique and supreme store of knowledge, and I have attained the unsurpassed liberation; today, the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu), which is the ultimate goal and the fruit of my highest achievement, will be fulfilled," the Blessed One reached a state of extreme joy. There arose in him an extraordinary and unique knowledge of immense power, characterized by the pervading of rapture (pīti) and other virtues. It is in reference to the power of this extraordinary knowledge, bolstered by the strength of meditative attainments, that it was said: "These two alms-offerings are of equal fruit and equal result," and so on. Therefore, struck by the power of that knowledge, the great earth shook. At that time, the shaking of the earth was as if it had reached a state of weeping; thus it is said, "the eighth is by way of weeping" (ārodanena).

Now, to explain in detail the meaning stated in brief, he said: "When descending into the mother's womb," and so on. "This meaning" refers to the meaning stated by "by way of giving applause," etc. "By the power of the earth-deity" (pathavī-devatāya vasena) means that just as there is a deity of the ocean, there is indeed a presiding deity (adhidevatā) who governs the great earth. When such a cause exists, this great earth shakes, quakes, and trembles by the will of that deity, just as winds blow by the will of the deities of the wind-clouds, or as cold, heat, and rain occur by the will of the deities of the cold, heat, and rain-clouds.

Indeed, on the full moon day of Visākha, to defeat the host of Māra that had arrived to create obstacles for the Lord of the World seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree for the sake of Enlightenment—

"This earth is unconscious; it knows neither pleasure nor pain.
Yet, by the power of my generosity (dāna), it shook seven times."

Immediately upon these words, the great earth split and overturned Māra along with his followers.
