"This" refers to the giving of applause, etc. Although the earth, being unconscious (acetana), does not possess such a nature, it can be said to occur by the power of nature (dhammatā) in the manner described. Nature (dhammatā), in its true sense, is the nature of Dhamma (dhamma-sabhāva), which is the natural power of the Dhamma of merit or the Dhamma of knowledge. All this has been investigated, and by doing so—

The statement "These perfections (pāramī) cause me to shake" is confirmed. While the Bodhisatta was reflecting on these perfections through their natural characteristics, the ten-thousandfold world system shook by the power of nature. The phrase "niddiṭṭha-nidassanaṃ" is a concluding remark for the detailed explanation. By these words, through the appearance of signs such as the earthquake and because the Blessed One showed the causes of the earthquake, the Venerable Ānanda was able to know by the remaining method: "Today, the Blessed One has relinquished the life-force."
158:
“While contemplating these Dhamma qualities of perfections with their natural and individual characteristics, by the power of the Dhamma, the earth, ten thousand world-systems in extent, trembled.” This initial sentence found in the Buddhavaṃsa is completed.

Niddiṭṭhanidassanaṃ means the conclusion or summary of the meaning that has been pointed out in detail. By this statement, [it can be known] through the event of the terrifying earthquake and through the Blessed One's words explaining the cause of the earthquake. “Indeed, today the Blessed One has relinquished the life-principle (āyusaṅkhāra),” he [Ānanda] noted by the method of elimination (pārisesa-naya). Thus, at that time, the Venerable Ānanda investigated the matter: “This earthquake is not caused by the disturbance of elements, for such a nature of elemental disturbance is not apparent. Outside the Buddha's Dispensation, there is no ascetic of such great power in this era of the Buddha. Even within the Dispensation, there is no monk who would cause the earth to tremble without informing the Teacher. The remaining five causes are also impossible at this time. This earthquake is extremely terrifying and hair-raising. Therefore, by elimination, he noted: ‘Today the Blessed One has relinquished the life-principle.’”

## Description of the Eight Assemblies (Aṭṭhaparisavaṇṇanā)

Okāsaṃ adatvā means without giving the Venerable Ānanda the opportunity to make a request, such as “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One remain for an aeon,” and so forth. Wishing to show other groups of eight (aṭṭhaka) collectively, besides the eight causes of earthquakes, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with “There are these eight,” intending to include the three groups of eight regarding assemblies (parisā), bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana), and liberations (vimokkha). Some teachers say this was spoken to avert the arising of sorrow in Venerable Ānanda and to distract his mind. For if spoken suddenly, powerful sorrow might arise.

It is called samāgama (assembly) because they should come together or because they come together as one. The assembly headed by King Bimbisāra is the Bimbisāra-samāgama. The same method applies to the other two terms. Because it is similar to the assembly of King Bimbisāra and others, it is connected as the “Assembly of Nobles” (khattiya-parisā). Even in other world-systems, the Teacher's approaching of the assembly of nobles and so on is indeed obtained. The Teacher's initial speaking with them is called ālāpa. Mutual conversation is called sallāpa. Questioning and counter-questioning connected with the Dhamma is called dhamma-sākacchā. Speaking based on appearance...

The word tesaṃ relates to both the preceding and following words. Just like the signs and appearance of those nobles, the appearance of the Teacher's body was also entirely manifest to them. The Blessed One does not have jeweled earrings adorned. This is the sequence of the teaching. Bhāsantaraṃ means they have two types of voices. The voices are cracked yet clear. From the speech of those beings...
159:
Because it expresses the meaning of appearance or form, the word vaṇṇa is used as in Pali sentences such as “having created the great form of an elephant king,” and so forth. The word tesaṃ relates to both the preceding and following words. It means, “Just like the signs and appearance of those [nobles], the appearance of the Teacher's body was also entirely manifest to them.” It should be connected as: “The Blessed One does not have jeweled earrings adorned.” Chinnassara refers to those with a divided voice. Gaggarassara refers to those with a cracked yet clear voice. Bhāsantara refers to a language other than the language of those beings. Vīmaṃsā means reflection or investigation.

“For what purpose... does he teach?” This question is asked with the meaning: “Is it not that if he teaches the Dhamma after making himself known as the Buddha, their devotion would be even greater?” For those who develop devotion only when the Dhamma is taught without knowing he is the Buddha, and not when he is known, the Teacher acts accordingly, intending such individuals, by teaching without making himself known. The benefit of doing so is stated as “for the sake of latent tendencies” (vāsanā). Even if the preacher is not known and his arrival is not known, the Dhamma heard, by its own excellent nature, becomes a condition for the listener in the future.

The Pali Dhamma beginning with “Ānanda,” which was not included in the [First] Council, is shown in the same way. This method should be understood in other similar instances hereafter.

## Description of the Eight Bases of Mastery (Aṭṭha-abhibhāyatana-vaṇṇanā)

Because of mastering, the preliminary work (parikamma) or knowledge (ñāṇa) is called abhibhū (master). The base for this mastery is the jhāna, thus it is called abhibhāyatana. Or, the object which is to be mastered is the base, thus it is abhibhāyatana. Because of mastering objects, it is abhibhū; and it is āyatana (base) because it is the ground for the yogi's special happiness, or because of its nature as the mind-base (manāyatana) and mental-object-base (dhammāyatana). Thus, the jhāna together with its associated states is called abhibhāyatana. Therefore, it is said, “the causes of mastery,” and so on. These are indeed the jhānas known as the bases of mastery. “Due to the person's excellence of knowledge” should be applied in both places. How? Due to the person's excellence of knowledge, they master opposing states by way of being an antidote, and they master objects. For just as mastering objects occurs through the power of knowledge, so too does the mastering of opposing states.

One is “percipient of forms internally” (ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī) by the power of preliminary work, not by the power of absorption (appanā). For absorption jhāna having a counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) as its object cannot occur with an internal object; therefore, other than that, by the power of internal preliminary work...
160:
The acquired kasiṇa sign is indeed still impure; it is not pure like the sign acquired through the power of external preliminary work (parikamma).

'Parittāni' (limited) refers to forms that are as they are acquired, having the size of a small bowl or a pot. Therefore, it is said, 'avaḍḍhitāni' (unexpanded). 'Parittavasena' (by way of the limited) means that although there is attention to the color, this base of overcoming (abhibhāyatana) is taught only by way of the limited. Here, being limited is the cause for overcoming. Whether there is attention to color or not, the development of the bases of overcoming is possible only for a person of sharp wisdom, not for others; thus, it is said, 'a person of superior wisdom' (ñāṇuttarika puggala). In the phrase 'having overcome, he enters and dwells' (abhibhavitvā samāpajjati), because the overcoming and the attainment occur immediately after the acquisition of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) to produce absorption (appanā-jhāna), it is said, 'simultaneously with the arising of the sign, he reaches absorption.' The phrase 'saha nimittuppādena' (simultaneously with the arising of the sign) is a term indicating the absence of repeated habituation (parivāsa) for reaching absorption. The development of the bases of overcoming occurs only for one whose wisdom is even more superior than the person called 'one of swift direct knowledge' (khippābhiñña). 'Ettha' (herein) means in this sign. 'Appanaṃ pāpeti' means leading the meditation to absorption.

In this regard, some teachers say: "When access concentration arises, taking it as the object, at least two or three impulsion turns (javana-vāra) occur; those impulsions belong only to the side of access concentration. Thereafter, absorption occurs without habituation by the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) or repetition of access. Simultaneously with the arising of the sign, he reaches absorption." This statement is merely their opinion. This is because absorption-sequence through repeatedly habituated preliminary work is not desired, nor is the definite reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) in access concentration desired, as it is in the sublime (mahaggata) and immeasurable (appamāṇa) jhānas. Therefore, for one who reaches absorption at the end of a few life-continuum thoughts after acquiring access concentration, it is said, 'simultaneously with the arising of the sign, he reaches absorption.'

The phrase 'saha nimittuppādena' is a statement made by way of intention; it is not to be taken literally (nītattha). The intention should be understood in the manner already stated. This is because such attention (ābhoga) is impossible within the meditative attainment itself. It should be understood that the attention of one who has emerged from the attainment occurs by taking the manner of overcoming that occurred at the moment of jhāna through the power of the preceding stage of development. In the Abhidhamma Commentary, however, it is said: "By this, his preceding attention is spoken of." If there is no such attention within the attainment, why is it said 'even in the perception of jhāna'? To answer this, it is said, 'abhibhavana... pe... atthi' (there is overcoming... etc.).
161:
"Vaḍḍhitappamāṇāni" means having a vast or extensive measure. It does not mean increasing by an inch or two, as such an increase is impossible in this context. Therefore, it is said to be "great." "Bhattavaḍḍhitakaṃ" refers to rice served by increasing the portion in the bowl, meaning about half the amount of rice a man can eat in one sitting.

Perception of form is called "rūpasaññā." One who has that perception is "rūpasaññī." One who does not have perception of form is "arūpasaññī." In this context, the teaching refers to jhāna based on perception. The term "arūpasaññī" here specifically means not giving rise to the perception of internal kasiṇa forms.

"Bahiddhāva uppannaṃ" means arising only in external objects. In the Abhidhamma, however, the four bases of mastery (abhibhāyatanas) are mentioned: "Not perceiving form internally, one sees external forms, small, beautiful, or ugly... immeasurable, beautiful, or ugly." The Abhidhamma Commentary raises a question: "Why does the Abhidhamma only teach 'not perceiving form internally' for all four bases of mastery, whereas the Suttanta says 'perceiving form internally, one sees external forms, small...'?" The reason given is "because internal forms cannot be mastered (overcome)." Whether in Suttanta or Abhidhamma, only external forms are to be mastered; thus, they must always be taught consistently. The phrase "perceiving form internally" is merely a stylistic variation (desanā-vilāsa) of the Buddha's teaching.

In this context, all small forms, whether attended to by color or not, are called "small, beautiful, or ugly forms." Immeasurable forms are described in the same way. There is a method (pariyāya) where, when mastering small forms and entering jhāna, if one occasionally attends to them by way of color, it can be said that one "masters beautiful or ugly forms." Suttanta teaching is taught by way of pariyāya (figurative method).

In the Abhidhamma, however, because it is a direct teaching (nippariyāya), forms without attention to color and those with it are taught separately. This is because there is a distinction in the way they are mastered in both cases. Similarly, in this Sutta, because it is a pariyāya teaching, there is also a method of mastery in the liberations (vimokkhas). Thus, the first vimokkha is included in the first and second abhibhāyatanas starting with "perceiving form internally," the second vimokkha in the third and fourth abhibhāyatanas, and the third vimokkha in the abhibhāyatanas of color, according to the occurrence of mastery. In the Abhidhamma, to show the liberations and bases of mastery without confusion, the abhibhāyatanas are taught excluding the vimokkhas. All jhānas that perform the function of vimokkha are taught in the teaching on vimokkhas.
162:
It should be understood that the two stages of mastery (abhibhāyatana) mentioned as 'perceiving forms internally' are distinguished separately without being mixed with the stages of mastery in the Abhidhamma, because they are not mentioned among the abhibhāyatanas there, and because passages such as 'possessing form, he sees forms' are general statements pertaining to all functions of deliverance (vimokkha).

The statement 'because internal forms cannot be mastered' (ajjhattarūpānaṃ anabhibhavanīyato) is the reason why it is never said 'he sees forms internally' but always 'he sees forms externally' in all places. Therefore, that statement, which has another cause (overpowering), is spoken by way of that cause. It is shown that no other reason should be sought for the Abhidhamma's mention of 'perceiving formlessness internally' (ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññitā) other than the elegance of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa). The inability to master internal kasiṇa forms is because those forms are not as distinct as external forms. The elegance of teaching should be understood according to the aforementioned definition, as it is a discourse using conventional terms (pariyāya-kathā) existing according to the inclinations of those to be taught (veneyyajjhāsaya).

If it is argued that the abhibhāyatanas such as blue (nīla) should not be mentioned because they are already covered by the words 'beautiful and ugly' (suvaṇṇa-dubbaṇṇa), that is not so. For those who have made efforts in kasiṇas like blue, the very nature of being blue is the cause for mastery. The cause of mastery is not the smallness or greatness of those pure or impure colors, but rather the nature of being blue, etc. To show for which temperament these abhibhāyatanas are accomplished among these small and other kasiṇa forms, the passage beginning with 'But in these' (imesu pana) is spoken.

'By way of all-inclusive' (sabba-saṅgāhaka-vasena) means in common with all that is blue-colored, blue-showing, and blue-shining. 'By way of color' (vaṇṇa-vasena) means by way of its natural color. 'By way of appearance' (nidassana-vasena) means by way of being visible, being graspable by the cognitive process of eye-consciousness, etc. 'By way of radiance' (obhāsa-vasena) means by way of shining with light. Umapupphaṃ means the flax flower. It is pure blue because it is not mixed with other colors. Vārāṇasī-sambhavan means cloth produced in the city of Vārāṇasī.

A person outside the Dispensation, while looking at an excessively expanded kasiṇa sign, might feel fear, thinking, 'Does this sign overwhelm and cover the entire world?' These abhibhāyatanas are brought forth to show that the Tathāgata has no such fear or trepidation, demonstrating his state of fearlessness.
163:
## Explanation of the Eight Deliverances (Aṭṭha-vimokkha-vaṇṇanā)
Since the meaning has been extensively analyzed and explained below in the Mahānidāna Sutta, these deliverances have a clear and obvious meaning. Even the sound of the word 'deliverance' (vimokkha) brings fear to some individuals who delight in the round of suffering (vaṭṭa). However, for the Blessed One who dwells having attained deliverance, there is no such fear; these abhibhāyatana-jhanas are brought forth and taught solely to demonstrate his state of fearlessness.

## Explanation of the Account of Ānanda's Request (Ānanda-yācana-kathā-vaṇṇanā)
'Bodhi' refers to Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Since the penetration of Omniscience is rooted in the penetration of the four Path Knowledges (magga-ñāṇa), it is stated simply as 'penetration of the four Path Knowledges'. 'Ananda, if the Tathāgata so desires, he could remain for an aeon (kappa) or more than an aeon'—this refers to the fact of having spoken thus.

Although the Blessed One made such a clear and gross hint, Māra had overwhelmed the mind of the Venerable Ānanda, so he could not understand or notice that hint.

'Beginning with' (ādikehi) means with friends, ministers, and well-wishers. They are called 'dear' (piya) because they are loved, and 'agreeable' (manāpa) because they increase the mind's pleasure. 'By birth' (jātiyā) means becoming separate and disconnected through the course of birth. 'Separation by death' (maraṇena vinābhāva) is the parting by death from which there is no returning to that same state of existence (attabhāva). 'Change of state through becoming' (bhavena aññathābhāva) means changing from a previous form to another form by taking a new existence. This should be applied to cases such as a being of the sense sphere becoming a Brahma of the fine-material sphere, or a human becoming a deva, etc. 'How can it be obtained here?' (kuta-ettha labbhā) means in what place, in this continuity of the aggregates, can it be obtained that 'what is born... may it not decay'? It is not possible because the cause for such a thing does not exist; thus he said, 'This is not possible' (netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati). The intention is: if even the body of the Tathāgata, which is of such wonderful and marvelous nature, must reach destruction, what need is there to mention the bodies of others? Because he had firmly established mindfulness, delimited with knowledge, and relinquished the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra), and because the Buddha's duties were completed, there is no possibility of taking back the relinquished life-force, like swallowing back what has been vomited. Indeed, after these three months, there are no more beings to be guided (veneyya) by the Buddha himself.

The long endurance of the Sasana is due to all the factors of the Noble Path along with their requisites. Thus it is said, 'It is spoken with reference to all mundane and supramundane states.' This is because the supramundane cannot exist solely by itself without mundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
164:
This is because it is impossible to attain the supramundane Dhamma without mundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

## The Explanation of the Third Recitation Section (Bhāṇavāra) is finished.

## Explanation of Nāgāpalokita

Nāgāpalokita means a look like that of a great elephant, a look similar to the looking of a noble elephant. Āhacca means having touched. Aṅkusakalaggāni viya means they are established by being linked and connected to one another, like hooks joined together. Ekābaddhāni means being connected together as one. Tasmā means because the neck bones are connected as a single solid mass. It is not only the neck bones that are connected as one; in fact, except for the twelve great joints such as the shoulder joints and the finger joints, all the bones of the Buddhas are established as being connected to the other joints as one. Because the bones are thus connected as one, the physical strength of the Buddhas is equal to the strength of a thousand ordinary elephants.

To make him face the city of Vesālī, the earth turned like a potter's wheel, just as it had turned to face the city of Kapilavatthu at the turning point of the horse Kaṇṭhaka. If the earth turned in this way, why is it called the "elephant look" (nāgāpalokita)? It is so called in reference to the Buddha's intention. Although the Buddha had the intention to look like a great elephant, due to the power of his merit, the place where he stood (the earth) turned; therefore, it is still called "nāgāpalokita."

"Ānanda, this is the Tathāgata's last look at Vesālī." This statement is not the reason for looking at Vesālī, because it is not the sole reason. In truth, it is merely a statement of what happened. After showing that statement by way of clarifying the journey, the teacher said "Nanu ca" etc., wishing to show another reason for this looking. All such looks at various cities were the last looks, because he was leaving those cities with the desire to go to Kusinārā in due order and attain Parinibbāna. By the word "Anacchariyattā," he removes the aforementioned uncertain reason; this is merely a clarification of the journey. To show that this is the unerring reason in this context, he said "Api ca" etc. The Blessed One did not look at Vesālī with lingering attachment; he looked out of compassion for the world, for the benefit and happiness of many beings, by way of showing, "This journey of mine is a journey from which there is no return." Therefore, he said "Api ca Vesālīrājāno" etc.
165:
Antakara means one who makes an end, one who destroys, one who brings to non-existence the entirety of the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha) within one's own continuity and the continuity of others. He is called Cakkhumā (The One with Vision) because he is endowed with the five eyes: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the divine-eye, the flesh-eye, and the universal-eye. Because he has completely cut off the defilements along with their latent tendencies (anusaya), he is extinguished through the supreme Parinibbāna of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna).

## Explanation of the Four Great Authorities (Catu-mahāpadesa)

Mahāokāse means in a vast place. It refers to vast places for establishing the Dhamma. In which places is the Dhamma established so that it can be determined without doubt? They are the descents into the Suttas (suttotaraṇa) etc., which are distinguished by their source from the Buddha, the Saṅgha, and so on. In the second alternative, apadesā means the reasons pointed out. It is the reason for deciding "This is the true Dhamma" when someone brings a teaching, saying, "Friend, I heard this directly from the Blessed One," and so on. What is that reason? It is the checking of that brought teaching through the descent into the Suttas and so forth.

If that is so, why is it said there are four? Since there are two types of teachers who bring the Dhamma to completion—the Teacher (the Buddha) and the disciples—and among those disciples, there are three types: the Saṅgha, a group (gaṇa), and an individual (puggala); thus, there are four according to the distinction of teachers who are pointed out, saying, "I received this Dhamma from you." Therefore, he said, "Friend, I heard this directly from the Blessed One," and so on. Likewise, it is said in the Netti: "There are four great authorities: the authority of the Buddha (buddhāpadesa), the authority of the Saṅgha (saṅghāpadesa), the authority of many elders (sambahulatherāpadesa), and the authority of a single elder (ekatherāpadesa). These are the four great authorities." Buddhāpadesa means the Buddha is the authority (teacher pointed out) for this. This method applies to the rest as well. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary, "The Buddha and so on... are the great reasons (mahākāraṇāni)."

Neva abhinanditabbaṃ means it should not be (immediately) accepted. Since accepting a text is indeed hearing it, he said, "It should not be listened to." Padabyañjanāni means words and phrasing, referring to the words of meaning (atthapada) and the words of phrasing (byañjanapada). They are called "pada" (words) because the meaning is reached (pajjati) through these phrasing-words such as syllables. They are called "pada" because they are to be reached; these are the meaning-words such as the explanations (saṅkāsanā). In the Commentary, some say that "byañjanas called padas" refers only to phrasing-words (byañjanapada), but that is not correct. Phrasing-words are called "byañjana" because they reveal (byañjenti) the meaning, and meaning-words are also called "byañjana" because they are to be revealed by those phrasing-words; thus, both are included. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne means in this place of the Sutta brought by that person. Pāḷi vuttā means the Pāḷi text alone, without the meaning, has arisen. Attho vutto means the meaning of the Pāḷi has been stated and pointed out. Anusandhi kathito means the connection (sambandha) between the discourse already begun and the subsequent discourse has been stated.
166:
The connection (of the discourse) has been stated. 'Stating the preceding and the succeeding' means stating and clarifying the lack of contradiction between earlier and later statements and the conveyance of special meanings. Thus, the proper noting and upholding of the Pali teachings and so forth is called 'good learning' (sādhukaṃ ugghahaṇaṃ); hence it is said, 'having grasped well.' 'They should be entered into the Sutta' means they should be merged and compared with the Sutta (the Pali text) through wisdom. Such entering through wisdom constitutes being included (anuppavesana) within that Pali text; therefore, it is said, 'they should be entered into the Sutta.' Showing by comparing and contrasting is called sandassana; hence it is said, 'they should be compared with the Vinaya.'

In investigating what that Sutta is and what that Vinaya is, the following is stated starting with 'And herein' to show the meaning through the different views of the teachers. 'Vinaya' refers to the text of the Vibhaṅga. Since that Vibhaṅga text indicates the meaning of the Sutta known as the Mātikā, it deserves to be called 'Sutta.' Because it contains various methods and distinguished methods, the Khandhaka text is called 'Vinaya.' In this way, even when the Sutta and Vinaya are grasped, the Vinaya Piṭaka is not yet fully exhausted because the Parivāra text is not included. Alternatively, the Suttanta Piṭaka and Abhidhamma Piṭaka are called 'Sutta' because they are the source of meanings such as indicating welfare. Thus, even when the division of Sutta and Vinaya is stated as 'The Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are Sutta, and the Vinaya Piṭaka is Vinaya,' they are not yet fully grasped without remainder. Why? It is stated starting with 'For there is that which is not named Sutta.' This is because there are words of the Buddha, such as the Jātaka, which were chanted at the Councils but do not bear the name 'Sutta'; therefore, by the aforementioned method, the three Piṭakas are not entirely exhausted. With the intention that the Suttanipāta, Udāna, Itivuttaka, etc., were not chanted at the Councils by assigning the name 'Sutta' like the Dīgha Nikāya, etc., those texts are also taken here along with the Jātaka. The reason for not taking the Buddhavaṃsa and Cariyāpiṭaka here should be sought. Or what is the use of such seeking? This entire method of explanation is already rejected by way of showing the Theravāda view.

'There is'—what is there? It shows that there is indeed no word of the Buddha that is not named Sutta. Indeed, in the commentary on the Introduction (Nidāna), we have said: 'Sutta is a general rule, while the other eight factors are specific rules.' Having rejected all that, and having corrected the explanation stated as 'Sutta is Vinaya' etc. by saying 'This meaning is not intended here,' (it is explained): It is called Vinaya because it removes defilements by this means. It is the means for removing defilements, and because it performs that removal, it is the cause; hence it is said, 'But Vinaya is the cause (kāraṇa).'
167:
'Dhamme' refers to the Pariyatti-dhamma (the scriptural Dhamma). 'Sarāgāya' means for the increase of sensual passion and passion for existence (for the sake of being with passion). 'Saṃyogāya' means for binding with the fetters of existence. 'Ācayāya' means for the increase of the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). 'Mahicchatāya' means for the state of great desire. 'Asantuṭṭhiyā' means for the state of lack of contentment. 'Saṅgaṇikāya' means for living in entanglement with defilements and social groups. 'Kosajjāya' means for the state of laziness. 'Dubbharatāya' means for the state of being difficult to support. 'Virāgāya' means for the sake of detachment from the entire round of rebirth. 'Visaṃyogāya' means for the sake of being dissociated from sensual existence and so forth. 'Apacayāya' means for the reduction of the entire round of rebirth, meaning for the sake of Nibbāna. 'Appicchatāya' means for the total disappearance of desire through fewness of wishes regarding the four requisites. 'Santuṭṭhiyā' means for the state of the twelve kinds of contentment. 'Pavivekāya' means for the sake of seclusion, for the accomplishment of bodily seclusion and so forth. 'Vīriyārambhāya' means for the sake of upholding both bodily and mental energy. 'Subharatāya' means for the sake of being easy to support.

In this way, whatever Pariyatti-dhamma exists which, for a person practicing according to the truth through learning, upholding, questioning, and wise attention, becomes the cause for avoiding the states of passion and so forth and leads to the states of dispassion and so forth—that is truly 'Dhamma.' That same teaching is called 'Dhamma' because it upholds one from falling into the four woeful states and so forth; it is called 'Vinaya' because it removes defilements; and it is called 'Satthusāsana' (the Teacher's Instruction) because it is the advice and instruction of the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened Buddha. Thus you should remember, thus you should know, thus you should understand. It is called Suttanta because it indicates the Four Noble Truths; therefore, it is said, 'Sutte means in the word of the Buddha, the Tipitaka.' Indeed, in the word of the Buddha, the Tipitaka, there is no teaching devoid of the Four Noble Truths. Because the Buddha showed the cause for removing passion and so forth through the Sutta passages, it is said, 'Vinaye means in this cause for removing passion and so forth.'

In this context, 'entering into the Sutta' (osaraṇa) should also be understood only by way of being included in the word of the Buddha, the Tipitaka, and not otherwise; therefore, it is said, 'without coming anywhere in the sequence of the Suttas.' 'Having raised the bark' means just as one might peel off a layer or chip of bark from a large, healthy tree through effort, so one might present flaws such as contradictions between earlier and later statements, which are like bark, by making them appear as if they were included in the flawless Dispensation (Sāsana) merely through the phrasing. Such words, however, certainly belong to texts like the Guḷhavessantara; therefore, it is said, 'Guḷhavessantara... paññāyantīti attho.' 'Rāgādivinaye' means for the purpose of removing passion and so forth. Those words that are not evident or seen as being for the purpose of removing passion and so forth should be discarded, avoided, and not accepted. 'Sabbattha' means in all instances.
168:
Regarding the section explaining these Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa), it refers to the place where these Great Authorities are pointed out. By the words beginning with 'There are four Great Authorities in the Sutta,' [the author] points out the table of contents (mātikā) through miscellaneous discourse (pakiṇṇakakathā), taking together both the Great Authorities explicitly taught and those not explicitly taught. The meaning that needs to be known is called a question (pañhā). The answers to those questions are called explanations of questions (pañhābyākaraṇa). Because of the meaning such as indicating the welfare [of beings], the Pāḷi text is called Sutta. Because it makes one conform to that Sutta Pāḷi, the Great Authority is called 'Conformity to the Sutta' (suttānuloma). Because teachers explain the Pāḷi in detail through this work, the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) is called 'Teacher's Tradition' (ācariyavāda). Because it is the personal opinion and preference of various elder monks, it is called 'One's Own Opinion' (attanomati).

'When reaching the judgment of the Dhamma' means when a matter to be decided upon arises. 'These' refers to the four Great Authorities mentioned hereafter. By these Great Authorities, the Dhamma is weighed, delimited, and decided; therefore, they are called the standard (pamāṇa). Therefore, [the Buddha] said, 'Whatever here conforms,' and so on. 'The other' refers to what does not conform to the Great Authorities. Furthermore, the word 'the other' is spoken with reference to making what is unallowable seem allowable and rejecting what is allowable.

Because it must be answered categorically, it is called 'to be answered categorically' (ekaṃsabyākaraṇīya). 'Vibhajja' (analytical) means answering by analyzing the questioned meaning through distinctions such as limitation. 'Paṭipucchā' (counter-questioning) means answering by questioning the person who asked the question. 'Ṭhapanīya' (to be set aside) is a question that should be set aside without giving an answer because it cannot be answered by the three [previous] methods. Regarding the question 'Is the eye impermanent?', it is said 'It should be answered categorically,' referring to the limitation in the latter term, because there is not even a trace of permanence in that eye. However, in the limitation of the former term, it should be answered analytically, because the specific and general meanings of the eye and the ear are not mutually applicable. The objection regarding the similarity of those two, the eye and the ear, should be answered only by counter-questioning; since it must be answered by way of rejection or by way of acceptance, it is said: 'Is the ear the same as the eye? ... This is a question to be answered by counter-questioning.'

'Is the soul (jīva) the same as the body (sarīra)?' is a question asking about the identity of the soul and the body. Since that soul and body, whose identity is questioned, are not found in the ultimate sense, it is like speaking of a barren woman's son as a mother; therefore, because it should not be answered, it is taught as 'to be set aside' (ṭhapanīya). These four ways of answering questions are standards (pamāṇa), because those questions should be answered only by those methods.

The Great Authority of the Vinaya is called 'conformity to what is allowable' (anulomakappiya) in a non-figurative sense because it is arranged in accordance with what is allowable. Because they are Great Authorities and thus similar to the Great Authority of the Vinaya, this commentarial term 'anulomakappiya' also exists in the Great Authorities of the Sutta. Even if the miscellaneous teachings delivered by the Blessed One in various Pāḷi texts are themselves the Commentary, the Elders who were the Recorders of the Dhamma (dhamma-saṅgāhaka), having first chanted the three Piṭakas, then that...
169:
It is called "Ācariyavāda" (Teacher's Tradition) because it is established in the course of instruction in accordance with the detailed explanation of the meaning. Teachers explain and clarify the Pali Canon (Pāḷi) through this discourse. Therefore, it is said, "What is known as Ācariyavāda is the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā)."

The course of discourse, which is the explanation of the meaning of the Buddha's words that had been recited in the three Councils, was brought to the island of Tambapaṇṇi by the Elder Mahinda. Later, the Great Elders of Tambapaṇṇi maintained it in the Sinhala language to avoid confusion with the views of other sects. "Attanomati" (one's own opinion) refers to the interpretation that is the view of the Elders. By "Nayaggahaṇa" (grasping the method), it means taking the method obtained from the Suttas and other scriptures. By "Anubuddhi" (following knowledge), it means the intellect that follows only the Suttas and other scriptures. "Appearance in one's own knowledge" means that various meanings appear in one's own intellect according to the methods mentioned. They spoke the meanings exactly as they appeared.

By the phrase "Only that which is consistent should be accepted," it is shown that when extracting meanings, one should extract meanings from the Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa) so that they are consistent and in harmony with the Suttas. Due to a lapse in reading or recitation, the Ācariyavāda may sometimes not be in harmony with the Pali Canon. To show that such Ācariyavāda should not be accepted, it is said, "Even the Ācariyavāda should be accepted only if it is consistent with the Suttas." "Attanomati" is the weakest of all because it is an opinion that appears in the knowledge of a single individual. Although it is weak, that Attanomati should still be accepted. As to what kind of Attanomati should be accepted, it should be connected as: "Only the Attanomati that is consistent with the Suttas should be accepted."

"In those" refers to the three Councils. By the phrase "Only what has come down is the authority," it is shown that only the Pali Canon recited by the Elders such as the Venerable Mahākassapa is intended here as "Sutta," thereby rejecting the status of "Sutta" for any other Pali. This is because the purpose of the three Councils was indeed such rejection. "Therein" refers to the group of blameworthy Pali. It should be understood that they do not descend into the Suttas nor are they seen in the Vinaya, because that Pali is not a Sutta. Therefore, the meaning already stated as "Only the Anulomakappiya (allowable according to what is suitable) that is consistent with the Sutta should be accepted" is shown by way of conclusion. In all places, the phrase "not the other" should be understood as showing the benefit of limiting the meaning to be taken in those respective places.

## Kammāraputtacundavatthuvaṇṇanā
"Sūkaramaddava" refers to the tender meat of a wild boar. Since Cunda was a noble disciple (Ariyasāvaka) who was a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), and since he and others, when preparing food for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, prepare only that which is blameless, it is called "Pavattamamsa" (meat already available). That is true; it is meat with special qualities described as "neither too young nor too old," and so on. Indeed, it is described as "both tender and oily." It is called "Maddava" because of its nature as tender meat and because of the special way it was prepared.

Thinking, "This is the final meal of the Blessed One," and desiring a special merit, the devas infused it with divine essence (dibba-ojā). However, because of the divine essence thus infused, that food became heavier (difficult to digest).
170:
Others, not knowing that the food was difficult to digest, might criticize and accuse, saying, "He destroyed it without giving it to anyone." To free Himself from such criticism by others, the Blessed One let out a Lion's Roar (Sīhanāda), starting with "I do not..." and so on.

How is this Lion's Roar possible? One might ask, "Did that food not reach proper digestion even for the Blessed One?" This should not be viewed in that way. Because it can be said that "it reached proper digestion for the Blessed One," since there was no disorder (illness) arising from that Sūkaramaddava, and because it even mitigated the pain arising from other causes (past kamma). Therefore, it is stated in the Commentary, "But not because of what was eaten," and so on. Indeed, neither the Blessed One nor other Arahants (Khīṇāsava) consume food for the purpose of producing new feelings, but they consume food only after making it endowed with the eight factors. If so, why is it said in the Pali, "After eating the meal, a sharp illness arose"? That was said because it arose in the period after eating. The meaning intended as "But not because of what was eaten" is explained in the Commentary.

Due to the power of kamma that had been performed and accumulated and had found an opportunity to ripen, even though a strong disease arose, the suppression of the pain occurred because of consuming the heavy and oily food. Therefore, it is said, "If indeed..." and so on. "In the desired place" means in the place where He wished to go, and His wish should be understood as a concern for the beings to be tamed (veneyya) who were to be guided there. In the verse as well, by the word "heard," it is shown that this is merely the talk of others, and that the Steadfast One (Dhīra) was not touched by illness because of the food.

## Pānīယာharaṇavaṇṇanā
It should be understood that the clarity of the water is due to its pure state; thus it is said, "Acchodaka means having clear water." Because it has a good taste, it is said, "Madhurodaka means having sweet water." Only thin water is particularly cool, while thick water is not; thus it is said, "Tanusītalasalila means having thin and cool water." By the word "mudless" (Nikkaddama), the cause of its white appearance is stated. Although the appearance of water is discolored due to mud, slush, and so on, by nature, that water is indeed white in color.

## Pukkusamallaputtavatthuvaṇṇanā
"Dhuravāte" means in a headwind blowing from the opposite direction. "Dīghapiṅgala" means one who is tall and has tawny eyes. He was known as "Āḷāra" because he had tawny eyes. "Of such a nature" refers to the construction of future verbs such as "will see," "will do," or "will be." "In such places" refers to places associated with indeclinable particles (nipāta) such as yatra, yañca, and so on.
171:
The flashes of lightning appear as if they are issuing forth from the clouds; therefore, 'niccharantīsu' means 'vicarantīsu' (while wandering or moving about). 'Navavidhāya' means of nine kinds. In fact, even a single thunderbolt among the nine types is called 'ninefold' because it is included within those nine categories. This kind of naming is a conventional designation (ruḷhī), similar to the term 'attainment of the eight deliverances' (vimokkha). It makes a being who is overwhelmed by its sound and power (teja) unconscious (asanna). 'Ekaṃ cakkaṃ' refers to a single circle (maṇḍala). It is called 'saterā' because it appears to cut and destroy rubbish and debris. 'Gaggarāyamānā' means falling while making a 'gaggara' sound; this is an onomatopoeic word (anurava) representing the sound of thunder. 'Kapisīsā' is a thunderbolt shaped like a monkey's head. 'Macchavilolikā' is a thunderbolt that moves like a fish tossing about in water. 'Kukkuṭasadisā' is a thunderbolt shaped like a cock with spread wings. When plowing, there is often a knob (maṇikā) at the place where farmers hold with their hands. Based on that knob, the plow is called 'daṇḍamaṇikā'; therefore, a thunderbolt shaped like the knob of a plow-handle is called 'daṇḍamaṇikā.' For this reason, it is said to be 'naṅgalasadisā' (like a plow). A great thunderbolt is called 'sukkhāsanī' (dry thunderbolt) because it remains luminous even while it rains and cannot be dampened by water. For this reason, it is said, 'It digs up and destroys the place where it falls.'

'Bhusāgārake' means in a small house made of chaff. In that place, it is said that a large pile of straw was hollowed out from the inside to create a hall-like dwelling suitable for monks; at that time, the Blessed One stayed in that straw hut. Because that straw hut was circular like a threshing floor and resembled a hall, it is called 'khalasālāyaṃ' (in the threshing-floor hall). The word 'ettha' uses the locative case in the sense of cause (hetu), meaning 'because of this reason.' It means because of the cause of the six people being killed by the lightning strike. 'So tvaṃ bhante' is also the original Pali text.

Siṅgī gold is said to be an excellent and extremely radiant gold from the deva world, which shines like the complexion of the Buddhas. For this reason, it is said, 'having a color like the color of Siṅgī gold.' Raising the question himself, 'Why did the Elder Ānanda accept that cloth?' and wishing to show the reason for such acceptance, he said the words beginning with 'kiñcāpi.' 'For that very reason' refers to the four aforementioned reasons: (1) reaching the peak of the attendant's position, (2) cutting off the opportunity for others to criticize, (3) honoring the Teacher with that cloth, and (4) following the Teacher's wish.

The Elder Ānanda, at that very moment, offered that smooth cloth of Siṅgī-gold color to the Blessed One, saying, 'Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept this smooth cloth of mine; may that acceptance be for my long-term welfare and happiness.' The Blessed One accepted it, and having accepted it...
172:
...He wore it. Therefore, it is said, 'The Blessed One also wore one of those pairs of garments as an undergarment and one as an upper robe.' At that very moment, it is said that the monks finished the sewing work by merely hemming the edges and presented it to the Elder, and the Elder presented it to the Blessed One. 'Hataccikaṃ viya' means having its radiance eclipsed; the word 'viya' is merely a particle. Because it was overwhelmed by the bodily radiance of the Blessed One, the brilliance of that pair of garments did not appear. 'Antanteneva' means only within; it means it shines only from the inside. Therefore, it is said, 'But on the outside, there is no radiance from that cloth.'

By the words 'it produces a clear appearance,' the meaning is shown that after consuming this food offered by Cunda, that disease of dysentery did not recur. Because it is the time of the attainment of the two Nibbāna elements, the bodily radiance becomes clear in this way at these two times. The words to be spoken regarding 'in the Upavattana, between the twin Sāla trees' will come later.

Everything became golden in color because it was constantly overwhelmed by the extremely pure, radiant, and solid bodily aura of the Blessed One.

'Dhamme' means in the Pariyatti Dhamma. 'Pavattā' means taught as the principal word (pāvacana). He sat right in front because he was one who followed the Blessed One's advice.

'Gains known as the benefits of giving' refers to the desirable gains occurring in this life and the future life, known as the benefits of giving, such as the gift of beauty, the gift of strength, and so on. 'Te alābhā' means all those benefits are not gains for you; they are no longer gains. Benefits occurring in this very selfhood, clearly seen in this life, are called 'diṭṭhadhammika.' Benefits occurring in the future world, which is named 'samparāya' because it is to be gone to after passing away, are called 'samparāyika.' Those occurring in both this life and the future life are called 'diṭṭhadhammika-samparāyika.' They are gains that are the benefits of giving. Because they are equal in every way and have equal results, not just in part, they are called 'samasamaphalā' (of exactly equal fruit). By the word 'piṇḍapātā,' he speaks of the merit consisting in giving (dānamaya) with that alms-food as the object.

If the equality of the fruit of these two offerings is intended by way of the 'field' (the recipient), he said the words beginning with 'nanu ca' to show: 'Even though it is the same continuity of aggregates, is it not that the fields are distinct, being established by the state of a worldling and the state of an Arahant?' 'Parinibbānasamatāya' means because of the equality of Nibbāna through the extinction of defilements and the extinction of the aggregates. By the words 'having consumed, He attained Parinibbāna,' it means that the group of Supramundane Path factors (ariya-magga) based on the material body (rūpakāya) that received the excellent alms-food easily abandoned the defilements.
173:
In this way, just as the Dhamma-body, supported by the physical body sustained by the enjoyment of excellent alms-food, abandoned the defilements with ease, so too did he relinquish the aggregates with ease through the accomplishment of suitable food. Thus, because the abandonment of defilements and the relinquishing of the aggregates were both accomplished with ease, the equality of the fruits of both alms-offerings is illustrated. By the heading "alms-food," the merit of offering alms-food is illustrated. Just as Sujātā had the noble aspiration, "Depending on this food, may my deity be fully endowed with the qualities of beauty, happiness, strength, and so on," so too did Cunda the smith's son have the noble aspiration, "Depending on this food, may the Blessed One be fully endowed with the qualities of beauty, happiness, strength, and so on." Because of this equality in the nobility of their aspirations, the equality of the fruits of those two offerings should be understood.

Although he was accustomed to entering into two trillion four hundred billion attainments (samāpatti) daily, on the day of his Enlightenment, he initiated new insight (vipassanā) and, by means of the fourteen modes such as the seven groups of materiality (as described in detail in the Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā, Volume II, page 707), he saturated the element of insight and entered those attainments through the gateway of Great Insight. Similarly, on the day of his Parinibbāna, he entered all those attainments. Because of this equality in the entry into attainments, the equality of the fruits of those alms-offerings should be understood. Cunda's recollection is even more noble because it was a direct offering to the Blessed One without any deviation. As for Sujātā, although she perceived it as an offering to a deity, why is it so noble? It is because she had the perception, "The one receiving my alms-food is not a deity, but a Bodhisatta; by consuming this food, he will attain Buddhahood," and so on, as stated in the passage beginning with "Sujātā ca."

"Aparabhāge" refers to the period after attaining Buddhahood. "Puna aparabhāge" refers to the period after the Parinibbāna. "Dhammasīsaṃ" refers to Nibbāna, which is the pinnacle of all dhammas. "It was taken by my own will" is the meaning. Therefore, it is said, "My..." and so on.

The state of being a leader or predominance is called "ādhipateyya." Therefore, it is said, "conducive to the state of being a leader."

"Saṃvare" refers to the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara). "Veraṃ" refers to the five kinds of enmity, such as killing living beings. This is called "vera" (enmity/danger) because it is the nature of those who have enemies and because it is the cause of enmity. Wisdom is called "kosalla"; one endowed with that wisdom is called "kusala." Therefore, it is said, "Kusala is one endowed with wisdom." The perfection of wisdom is called "ñāṇasampadā," which should be understood through the Path of Arahatship. Since the Path of Arahatship abandons defilements without remainder, it is said, "He abandons... by the Noble Path." In the phrase "having abandoned this evil," it means having abandoned evil such as greed and stinginess through generosity (dāna), and evil such as killing through virtue (sīla); having abandoned them by the power of substitution (tadaṅga-pahāna), then by the power of suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna) through the qualities of tranquility and insight, and finally abandoning all evil without remainder by the power of eradication (samuccheda-pahāna) through the sequence of the Paths.
174:
Because they have been thus abandoned, through the destruction of lust and so on, and through the complete subsiding of defilements in the Nibbāna of defilements, the Blessed One, who has attained peace and Parinibbāna, reaching the pinnacle of the teaching on the Nibbāna element with residue (sa-upādisesa nibbānadhātu), uttered the inspired utterance: "Thus for Cunda... [pe]... seeing this, he uttered the inspired utterance."

## The Explanation of the Fourth Recitation Section is Finished.

## Explanation of the Twin Sal Trees
"Thus it was in Kusinārā" means that just as the Thūpārāma is to the southwest of the city of Anurādhapura, so too that grove is to the southwest of the city of Kusinārā. "Therefore" means that those wishing to enter the city approach from the grove and turn towards the city; hence it is called "Upavattana." That grove is a sal forest where sal trees stand in rows. "Between" means in the middle. "Of that couch" means of that small couch spread there. Between those two rows of sal trees, one tree was at the head and one tree was at the feet; therefore, it is said, "between the twin sal trees." "Intertwined" means as if they were stitched together because their branches and twigs were clinging to each other. In the Commentary, it is also said, "with standing branches." In the Pali, the instruction "Prepare the couch with the head to the north" was given according to the suitability for the deities and Brahmas who came to have their final sight. Some teachers, however, say, "It means prepare the couch with the head to the east so that the face is looking towards the north"; this is merely their opinion.

"These are the noblest of elephants" means that these elephants, named Gocari and so on by lineage, are the most excellent in strength among bull elephants. In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, some elephants appear with different names, but that difference should be understood as a matter of name only.

"From the time of consumption... [pe]... reached exhaustion" means that the meaning should be understood as previously stated, that it reached exhaustion not because of the alms-food consumed. "Caṅgavāre" means in a wave of water. Considering that a disease arising from the power of an opportunistic unwholesome kamma oppresses health, the word "like" (viya) is used to show this meaning. Although the Blessed One was capable of remaining for an aeon (kappa) or the remainder of an aeon as stated before, because there was no benefit in remaining for such a long time, he relinquished the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra). To show the meaning of not giving an opportunity to such kamma, it is said, "like water put into a wave." This statement is very appropriate. The Blessed One saw this so that people would know and remember, "One should perform merit that has such great power and benefit."
175:
The Blessed One, because there was no longer any benefit in remaining for a long duration, relinquished the life-principle (āyusaṅkhāra) and gave opportunity to that kind of karma (which could cause affliction). Therefore, for the commentator wishing to show this meaning, it is appropriate to say "like water that has been poured out."

"This merit is of such great fruit, such great advantage, and of such great power"—knowing this, they will note that merit should be performed.

Because the cessation of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) for even a single being is extremely rare, it appears as something to be specially cared for by the Buddhas. Therefore, it is said, "He sees another benefit as well," and so on. This meaning should be understood through the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta.

The third reason is the avoidance of harm that would arise for beings. To show this reason, he said again, "He sees another benefit as well," and so on.

## Sīhaseyyanti.
In this context, reclining is called seyyā. Reclining like a lion is the Lion’s Posture (sīhaseyya). Alternatively, sīhaseyya means the noble posture (seṭṭhaseyya). Both these meanings will appear later.

The reclining described as "they sleep on the left side" is the sleep of those who indulge in sensual pleasures (kāmabhogī). There is no one who sleeps [habitually] on the right side [in that context], because the right hand is capable and fit for tasks such as supporting the body. This is spoken in terms of the capacity of a man.

Beings are unable to sleep on only one side because of the arising of pain.

That this is the Lion’s Posture means that reclining on the right side as described is called sīhaseyya because it resembles the lion’s sleep. By the word "tejussadattā," the lion’s fearlessness is shown. Other animals, being fearful, enter their dens and sleep haphazardly, preceded by terror. The lion, however, being fearless, sleeps having well-established mindfulness, like a monk who acts with mindfulness. Therefore, it is said, "on the front paw," and so on. By placing the left front paw on the right front paw, it should be understood that the two front paws are placed in one position, and the two hind paws are also placed in one position as previously mentioned. The marking of the place where the paws rest is only due to fearlessness. The lion’s behavior described as "raising the head," and so on, should be understood as occurring by way of natural habit, accomplished through fearlessness, like waking up without alarm. The lion’s stretching (vijambhita) is for the purpose of making the body parts, which have been kept in one position for a long time, fit for movements such as walking. The lion’s roaring three times is for the purpose of warding off animals of little majesty. ... movement.
176:
It is called 'seyyā' (sleep/posture) because it is a state that occurs in a manner free from anxiety. The Fourth Jhana itself is the sleep, thus it is called the 'Fourth Jhana Posture' (catutthajjhānaseyyā). What is that Fourth Jhana? It is the Fourth Jhana of Mindfulness of Breathing (ānāpāna). For the Blessed One, having emerged from that Fourth Jhana of Mindfulness of Breathing and having developed insight (vipassanā), attained the Supreme Path in due order and became the 'Tathāgata'.

'This Fourth Jhana of Mindfulness of Breathing is only the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) [for the Path], not the sleep,' some teachers say. Furthermore, because it will be said [in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta], 'The Blessed One attained Parinibbāna immediately after emerging from the Fourth Jhana,' some say that only the mundane attainment of the Fourth Jhana is the 'Tathāgata’s Posture' (tathāgataseyya). If that were so, the Tathāgata’s Posture would be a state occurring only at the time of Parinibbāna. Moreover, the Blessed One did not frequently dwell in the attainment of the mundane Fourth Jhana. However, in this context, the Fourth Jhana occurring by the power of the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) should be understood [as the Tathāgata’s Posture]. In that sleep, just as the sleep characterized by falling asleep for beings occurs by the power of the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta) and is the common behavior throughout their lives, so the Fourth Jhana, which is the Fruit of Arahantship and the common behavior in the Blessed One’s Ariya lineage, should be understood as the 'Tathāgata’s Posture'. Because the Lion’s Posture is the most noble sleep, he said 'the supreme posture' (uttamaseyya).

Because there is no rising again from this reclining, it is called the 'posture of no-rising' (anuṭṭhānaseyya). Because there is no reflection such as 'I shall rise from here,' it is not said [in the Pali] 'having attended to the perception of rising.' Here, the non-rising is only by way of the body, not by way of the mind. Non-rising by way of the mind means falling asleep; to show the absence of that, it is said 'by way of sleep' (niddāvasena), and so on. 'Bhavaṅgassa' refers to the life-continuum mind characterized by falling asleep.

'Sabbapāliphullā' means blooming extensively in all places, not just blooming in one part. Therefore, it is said, 'they bloomed all around in every direction.' 'Ekacchannā' means being covered everywhere in a uniform manner with well-bloomed flowers. 'Ullokapadumāni' are lotus flowers that stand as if looking downwards. Because they are covered with flowers of five colors, they appear like a bundle of peacock feathers.

'Nandapokkhoraṇīsambhavāni' are flowers born on the banks of the Nanda pond. 'Mahātumbamattaṃ' means [branches] the size of a large vessel (tumba/āḷhaka). 'Paviṭṭhāni' means flowers that have been cast down. 'Sarīrameva okiranti' means they shower down and scatter all over the Blessed One’s body.
177:
Sandalwood powder offered to the deities refers to white sandalwood powder that wafts for sixty or fifty yojanas. Divine scented powders refers to celestial scents and celestial powders. Divine substances such as yellow orpiment and eye-salve should also be understood as being extremely fragrant. For this reason, it is said, "all varieties of divine scents."

Gathering in a single world-system, they played musical instruments in the sky, just as they did at the time of the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana).

"Those goddesses" refers to the devatās. "Weaving" means they were indeed weaving garlands. "Though not yet finished" means before they had finished making offerings as they desired. "Hand by hand" means holding another's hand with one's own hand. "Neck by neck" means embracing another's neck with one's own neck. "Holding" means touching or grasping. "The Great Famous One, the Great Famous One" is a repetitive form of address to one another.

"Great effort" means [the Buddha] spoke upon seeing the great effort being made through the performance of offerings and honor to the Tathāgata.

"That very practice" refers to the preliminary stage of practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā). "Because of suitability" means because it is appropriate for the ninefold supramundane Dhamma to be attained.

"Virtue" (sīla) refers to virtue of conduct (cāritta-sīla). "Ācārapaññatti" is also virtue of conduct. "Until Gotrabhū" refers to the Right Practice (sammā-paṭipadā) of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā) that should be maintained until the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). Now, to clarify that Right Practice through both negative and positive aspects, the passage beginning with "Tasmā" is stated. "The Jinakālasutta" refers to the disciplinary rules (sikkhāpada) which are like a black plumb line (kālasutta) set by the Great Architect, the Conqueror (Jina), showing the dhammas to be avoided and the dhammas to be adopted. In the section concerning laymen and laywomen, the statement "performing offerings of scents and garlands" is said with reference to placing such actions within the category of virtue of conduct. Therefore, it should be understood that such actions are also permitted for monks and nuns.

"This person" is said with reference to the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhamma-paṭipadā).

## Description of the Elder Upavāṇa

"Removed" means he acted so that [the Elder] moved away from where he was standing; it was not a rebuke. Therefore, the passage beginning with "Ānanda" is stated. "Similar to what was said" means they are just like what was said in the Samacittapariyāya Discourse. "Covering" means obscuring.
179:
The word 'bhāvanīya' is a 'kamma-sādhana' (objective derivative) in the sense of 'worthy' and has the meaning of 'sambhāvana' (praise); therefore, it is said to mean 'that which should be developed by the mind' or 'that which is to be praised.' In the second method, to show the meaning of causing the arising and development of wholesome states by abandoning opposing states, it is said, 'those who also,' and so forth.

One must be a person of clear mind regarding the Three Jewels, such as the Buddha, and not merely possess faith in kamma and its results. To show that the possession of faith (saddhā-sampadā) of that clansman is the cause, through the effect of being endowed with proper conduct, it is said, 'of one who is endowed with conduct.' What is called 'saṃvega' is knowledge accompanied by dread (ottappa). Since places such as the Buddha's birthplace are the causes for the arising of that 'saṃvega', they are called 'places that cause spiritual urgency (saṃvega).'

Wandering for the purpose of worshipping a stupa is called 'cetiyacārikā.' Because the wholesome intention (kusala-cetanā) that takes the Buddha's qualities as its object has the nature of leading to the heavenly realms, those who wander to worship stupas will certainly be established in heaven.

## Ananda-pucchā-kathā-vaṇṇanā

In this context, 'ettha' (herein) refers to 'mātugāma' (women). Not seeing or looking at women is the supreme practice. This is because all forms of ruin and misfortune have their root cause in seeing and looking. 'Lobha' (greed) refers to sensual desire (kāma-rāga). 'Citta-calanā' (mental agitation) is the shaking and disturbance of the mind that creates obstacles to the practice. 'Murumurāpetvā' is an onomatopoeic expression for the sound produced when crunching something along with the bones. Experiencing suffering for an immeasurable period is called 'apariccinna-dukkhānubhavana' (uninterrupted experience of suffering). 'Vissāsa' (intimacy) refers to an intimacy that does not yet involve clinging or physical contact. 'Otāra' (access/entry) is the repeated entry of the mind into that woman. It is oppressive, like encountering an enemy with a sword in hand or an ogre (pisāca) wishing to devour one, through such acts as trampling. Regarding that woman, if there is work to be done by monks, such as receiving offerings, one should firmly establish mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) by focusing on the collection of parts such as hair and body hair.

'Atantibaddha' means not carrying a burden. 'Pesitacitta' means having a mind directed towards Nibbāna.

It refers to something made of cotton that has been beaten, just as tangles are cleared by a bow used for carding cotton. Therefore, it is said, 'well-beaten.' It means cotton that has been well-beaten without being mixed. By mentioning places that are worthy of being seen and that cause spiritual urgency, the place of residence is described.

## Ananda-acchariya-dhamma-vaṇṇanā

Not seeing the Venerable Ānanda, the Buddha reflected and, knowing the place where the Elder was standing and the circumstances, he addressed him.
180:
The bodily action (kāyakamma) of the Venerable Ānanda, being performed with an intention for welfare, is said to be a bodily action that brings about the increase of welfare; thus it is said, 'performed with the increase of welfare (hitavuddhi).' Its nature of happiness is due to the absence of physical pain and its arising from mental happiness; thus it is said, 'performed with happiness and joy (sukhasomanassa).' To show the meaning of non-duality, without distinction between presence and absence, the word 'yathā' (as) and so forth are used. Because of the perfection of the Buddha's field of merit and the perfection of the Elder's intention, this merit cannot be measured as 'this much'; thus, to show the immeasurable nature of that kamma, it is said, 'even the world-system (cakkavāḷa),' and so forth.

One who has performed merit that is a powerful support for Nibbāna, performed through the power of such specific loving-kindness meditation (mettā-bhāvanā), is called 'katapuñña' (one who has performed merit). Therefore, it shows that the Venerable Ānanda is one who is endowed with extraordinary merit (abhinīhāra) performed to attain the fruit of Arahantship.

These five similes—like spreading out the earth that is shriveled in some places, like expanding the sky that is contracted, like lowering the Cakkavāḷa mountain which is one hundred and sixty-four thousand yojanas high, like lifting Mount Sineru which is one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas high, and like taking the great Jambū tree, which is one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, by its trunk and shaking it—have appeared to demonstrate the greatness of the Elder's virtues and the difficulty for others to perform such deeds. By the word 'ca' (and) in 'eteneva ca', one should include such scriptural passages as: 'I am now the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One' and 'In the world with its devas, there is no person equal to me.' 'Byatta' means being endowed with skill, such as proficiency regarding the aggregates (khandha). 'Medhāvī' means being endowed with wisdom that has been well-developed.

'Paṭisanthāra-dhamma' (the nature of friendly greeting) is spoken of by way of natural habit. He teaches the Dhamma to the monks and nuns who come to him by answering their questions and according to their mental inclinations at the appropriate time. To the lay disciples (upāsaka and upāsikā), however, he teaches the Dhamma through conversation while they are sitting nearby.

## Commentary on the Teaching of the Mahāsudassana Sutta

The word 'khuddaka' denotes an imitation; the suffix '-ka' has the meaning of 'small' or 'insignificant.' Therefore, 'khuddakanagarake' means in a small, cramped city that is a mere imitation of a city. Because that city has an uneven shape, it is called 'ujjaṅgalanagaraka' (a rough city), which is explained as 'visamanagarake' (in an uneven city). Since it is only the size of a portion of other great cities, it is like a branch. Here, the word 'khuddakanagarake' expresses the smallness of that city; the word 'ujjaṅgalanagaraka' expresses the poor and ruined state of the ground; and the word 'sākhānagaraka' expresses its status as merely an insignificant branch-city. 'Sārappattā' refers to those many people who have attained great essence through wealth, substance, and so forth.

In the phrase 'kahāpaṇasakaṭaṃ,' it is said that one cart carries two 'kumbhas.' One 'kumbha' consists of ten 'ambaṇas.' 'Dve pavisanti' means that two cartloads of coins enter daily as income.

'Subhikkhā' means that food is easy to obtain and that there is excellent food. Therefore, it is said, 'khajjabhojjasampannā' (endowed with edible and soft food). 'Saddaṃ karonte' means making sounds like the trumpeting of elephants in a state of joy, projecting their voices. 'Avivittā' means not secluded or not quiet. Sometimes one chariot goes first and another follows it; sometimes the second chariot goes first and the other follows it; in this way, they follow one another in succession. In this city of Kusāvatī, because of its greatness and prosperity, musical instruments such as the great drum are always in use. The sound of calling one another affectionately as 'samma samma' is the 'samma-sadda.' The sound of all percussion instruments such as gongs and bronze bells is the 'tāḷa-sadda.' The sound of the pot-drum is the 'kūṭabheri-sadda.'

In other cities, such sounds occur respectively due to streets being strewn with rubbish, or due to shouting while gathering roots, tubers, and leaves in the forest, and due to speaking about the hardships of living in such forests. In this city of Kusāvatī, however, such sounds do not occur because it is fully endowed with all forms of prosperity, like the celestial realm.

'Mahantaṃ kolāhalaṃ' refers to the great shouting that arises in front of the Blessed One through the power of the deities and lay followers who are endowed with faith. Because there was no monastery built for the Blessed One in that city of Kusinārā, and because the community of bhikkhus was large, the Blessed One sent the Venerable Ānanda, intending that those Mallas would come and arrange seating and accommodation for the Saṅgha. In sending him, the Blessed One thought, 'Let there be no distress in the hearts of these Mallas, thinking, "Why did the Blessed One not inform us of his circumstances in his final hour?"' Thus, he sent the message beginning with, 'Vāseṭṭhas, today...'

## Commentary on the Homage of the Mallas

Those who manifest or reveal suffering (dukkha) are called 'aghāvin' (those showing distress). The commentator says 'uppannadukkhā' (those in whom suffering has arisen) because they have manifest suffering. 'Kulaparivatta' (family circle) refers to the way lineages revolve within this group through the nature of being kinsmen and blood relations. The assembly of beings stationed according to their respective family portions is called 'kulaparivattaso,' which is explained as 'kulaparivatta.' It is said that those Malla kings, partitioned by their respective family lineages, lived in common areas such as main streets, etc., in that city; this is expressed as 'by way of common main streets and by way of common alleys.'

## Commentary on the Story of the Wanderer Subhadda

Doubt itself is the 'nature of doubt' (kaṅkhādhamma). 'Ekato vā' means without dividing the field, but as joint owners. Taking the first-fruits from the seeds, preparing food, and giving it is 'bījagga' (the first-fruit of seeds). 'Gabbhakāle' refers to the time when the milk-sap forms after the grain has been conceived. Therefore, it is said, 'having split the grain and extracted the milk-sap,' and so forth. 'Puthukakāle' refers to the time when the crops are not yet fully ripe and the fruit is suitable for making flattened rice. 'Lāyanagga' is the gift given at the time of reaping the ripe crops. Binding the reaped crops into sheaves is called 'veṇikaraṇa.' The gift given at the start of that process is 'veṇagga.'

Bringing the sheaves together into a heap is called 'kalāpa' (a bundle). The first-fruit gift from that bundle is 'kalāpagga.' The first-fruit gift given when taking from the bundle and threshing is 'khalagga.' The first-fruit gift given when winnowing the threshed grain and making a heap is 'khalabhaṇḍagga.' The first-fruit gift given when moving the grain from the threshing floor into the granary is 'koṭṭhagga.' 'Uddharitvā' means having taken it out from the granary.

By the statement 'he gave nine kinds of first-fruit offerings,' it is shown that he (Subhadda) was a suitable vessel for the foremost Dhamma teaching. This is because he had accumulated the merit that serves as a powerful support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) through the power of these foremost offerings, with the thought, 'How may I be the very first to be liberated from the round of suffering in the presence of the Teacher?' and because his wisdom had thus reached maturity. Therefore, it is said, 'I shall preach this foremost Dhamma to him,' and so forth. 'Ohīyitvā' means having reached a state of decline or regression.

Subhadda, having only the desire to know, did not wrongly cling to his own view (sandiṭṭhiṃ parāmasī). 'Abbhanyiṃsu' is interpreted as the answer to the question of the doubting Subhadda, meaning 'did they know?' Therefore, it is said in the Pali, 'all of them did not know.' 'Nesaṃ' refers to the great teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa. That claim is the one acknowledged in the passage beginning with, 'O Great King, to one who acts, to one who causes to act...'
183:
Whether it be the claim of omniscience itself, or because it is accompanied by the power to preach in a way that establishes one's own doctrine while refuting opposing views, it is called *niyyānika* (leading out of the round of suffering). Or, the claim known as the doctrine of those teachers is called *niyyānika* because of its sense of leading out from the suffering of the round of rebirth. It should be understood that due to the perfection of the teaching (Sāsana), they attain the state of omniscience, and conversely, due to the imperfection of the teaching, they reach the state of non-omniscience. Therefore, He said "Tasmā" and so forth. "Atthābhāvatō" means because there is no benefit to be achieved for the wanderer Subhadda. "Okāsābhāvatō" means because there is no opportunity or time to preach the Dhamma in such detail. Now, to show that very lack of opportunity, He said "Paṭhamayāmasmiṃ" and so forth.

Because of the fulfillment of those qualities that make one a recluse (samaṇa) who has stilled the defilements, one is called a *samaṇa*; these qualities, by way of indicating the highest, are the qualities of the Noble Path. Thus, because of the completion of the four paths, four types of *samaṇas* are taught in the Pāḷi text. Wishing to show that these *samaṇas* are entirely non-existent in external sects, He taught "Paṭhamo sotāpannasamaṇo" and so forth. "Purimadesanāyā" refers to the discourse taught starting with "Yasmiñca kho, Subhadda, dhammavinaye". It clarifies the intended meaning both by way of exclusion and by way of inclusion. Therefore, it should be noted that the first method is also included by the term "Purimadesanāyā". Wishing to define His own teaching, He taught "Imasmiṃ kho", which should be construed accordingly. "Āraddhavipassakehi" refers to those practicing insight (vipassanā) associated with the work of concentration (samādhi), meaning those who have reached the peak of insight, not those who have just begun practicing insight. Other teachers, however, say that since there is no path for practicing insight in external sects, this statement is not specific but refers to all who practice insight.

"Adhigataṭṭhānaṃ" means the practice which is the cause of the path already attained, the preliminary path for the sake of that path. One who has attained the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) through a certain practice, but has not yet attained the higher paths, is called one established in the path of stream-entry because there is no danger of falling away due to defilements. Or, because of the completion in that path, by way of what has occurred before, he is a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) known as one established in the path of stream-entry. The remaining noble ones are not called those established in the path of stream-entry because they have reached other stages. A stream-enterer can make another person established in the path of stream-entry by preaching the path of stream-entry he has attained. The eighth person (the one on the path to stream-entry) cannot do so because it is impossible. In the case of "sesamaggaṭṭhesū" (those established in the remaining paths), the meaning should be understood in this same way. "Paguṇaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ" means one's own well-mastered meditation subject of insight. By this statement, it should be noted that the view of "avisesavacanaṃ" (non-specific statement) is refuted.

The knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is intended. That omniscience is called "skilful, clever, and subtle" in understanding all knowable things. This is because it proceeds therein without attachment or obstruction.
184:
There are more than one year (fifty years). By this [Dhamma], they penetrate the Four Noble Truths as they really are; therefore, it is called *ñāya*. Intending that this *ñāya* is the supramundane path, He said "Ariyamaggadhammassa". By this [Dhamma], the Noble Path is seen directly and clearly; therefore, it is called *padesa*. That *padesa* is insight (vipassanā), as it is said "Padese vipassanāmagge". In the term "samaṇopi", the word "pi" should also be brought to and connected with the term "padesavatti"; therefore, He said "Padesavatti... natthi" (it is said that it does not exist).

"So" refers to the close disciple (*antevāsī*) mentioned. "Tena" refers to the teacher (*ācariya*). He is one placed in one's own position because he is appointed to tasks such as ordaining others.

"Sakkhisāvaka" means a direct disciple, an eyewitness disciple. "Bhagavati dharamāne" means in the presence of the Blessed One while He was still living. In the remaining two terms, the method should be understood in this same way. All three types of such persons are called "sabbopi so". This person, having reached Arahantship and thus attained perfection and the summit, is the final "sakkhisāvaka".
