## Commentary on the Last Words of the Tathāgata

"Taṃ" (that) is the word uttered by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhakas) to show the factor for giving advice to the Saṅgha of monks. Making known the Dhamma contained in the Sutta and Abhidhamma is called "desanā" (teaching). Establishing that very Dhamma in various ways within the continuities of beings to be tamed is called "paññattā" (making known). Therefore, it is said "The Dhamma has been taught (desitō) and made known (paññattō)". Similarly, making known the meaning of what is contained in the Vinaya Pāḷi, which is called "Vinaya" because it disciplines the body and speech, is called "desanā". Establishing that very meaning well without confusion is called "paññattā". Therefore, it is said "The Vinaya has been taught and made known".

Since it is the detailed explanation of the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) and thus the root of the Dispensation (Sāsana), the Vinaya should be learned first. Wishing to show the nature of that Vinaya, He said "Mayā hi vo" and so forth. Therein, "sattāpattikkhandhavasena" means (taught) by way of not transgressing the seven groups of offenses. It will perform the duty of the Teacher because it advises by distinguishing what should be done and what should not be done, saying "This should be done by you, this should not be done by you".
185:
"In various ways" means in various modes that are in accordance with the inclinations of the tractable beings (veneyya). "These dhammas" refers to these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhammā). Because these factors of enlightenment are primary in the Suttanta discourses, it is said, "The Suttanta Piṭaka has been taught." The Teacher's duty will be accomplished by instructing with right practice according to the respective temperaments. There are nine roots (hetu) by way of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. The statement beginning with "seven contacts" (satta phassā) is spoken by way of association with the seven consciousness elements (viññāṇa-dhātu). In the Dhamma-anuloma, there are six Paṭṭhānas such as the Tika-paṭṭhāna; likewise, there are six each in the Dhamma-paccanīya, Dhamma-anuloma-paccanīya, and Dhamma-paccanīya-anuloma. Thus, because there are twenty-four Universal Paṭṭhānas (Samanta-paṭṭhāna) in this Great Book of Paṭṭhāna, it is called "Catuvisati-samanta-paṭṭhāna." When this Great Book of Paṭṭhāna is analyzed by way of the conditional correlations (paccaya-anuloma), etc., it has infinite methods; therefore, it is said to be "adorned with the Great Paṭṭhāna of infinite methods" (anantanaya-mahāpaṭṭhāna-paṭimaṇဍita). "Will accomplish the Teacher's duty" means that when known through the classification of aggregates (khandha), etc., it can bring about the penetration of the Four Noble Truths; thus, it will fulfill the duty to be performed by the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha).

"They will exhort, they will instruct" is said because it fulfills the task of exhortation and instruction. "Conduct" (cāritta) refers to the modes of address and behavior. It means speaking affectionately to juniors and speaking respectfully to seniors. Therefore, it is said, "either as 'Bhante' or as 'Āyasmā'." This term "Bhante" or "Āyasmā" is a respectful form of address. In the world, however, the terms "Tatra bhavaṃ" and "Devānaṃ piya" are indeed respectful forms of address.

When it was said, "If it wishes, let [the Saṅgha] abolish [the minor rules]," it also implies "If it does not wish, let it not abolish them." Therefore, it is said, "He left it only with a discretionary statement (vikappa-vacana)." "Power" (bala) refers to the power of knowledge (ñāṇa-bala). If He foresaw the non-abolition and desired only that non-abolition, then why did the Blessed One say, "If it wishes, let it abolish"? It was spoken according to the inclinations of such persons. For there are some who do not wish to undertake and practice the minor and lesser training rules (khuddānukhuddaka sikkhāpada). If the Blessed One had not spoken thus (granting permission to abolish), distress would arise in them. That distress would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. But when spoken thus, distress would not arise in them, as they would reflect, "This is only our fault, because even among us, some do not wish to abolish them." Some teachers say, "It was spoken thus to make the entire Dispensation (Sāsana) dependent on the Saṅgha." The monks, who are the sons of the Sakyan (Sakyaputtiya), respectfully accept whatever training rule was prescribed by the Teacher and protect it like their own lives. Because they protect them like their lives, even though it was said, "If the Saṅgha wishes, let it abolish the minor and lesser training rules," they did not abolish them. Just as the sons of the Sakyan protected them in His presence, they also protected them after His passing. Thus, it should be understood that it was spoken in this way to demonstrate the greatness of the Buddha's Dispensation and the Saṅgha.
187:
This account of entering the sixty-five meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti) as mentioned is also just a summary. Why? Because the Blessed One, at that time, entered all the daily attainments without any omission, and to show this, it is said, "When entering the city of Nibbāna," and so forth.

Both of these (the sequence of jhāna and the sequence of reviewing) are mostly immediate (anantara) states because they occur immediately after reflection and belong to the side of jhāna. Since the bhavaṅga-citta, which is the very last of all consciousnesses, shifts from the present life, it is called "cuti" (death). Therefore, to show that not only the Blessed One but all beings pass away with the bhavaṅga-citta, it is said, "Whosoever," and so forth.

"Paṭibhāgapuggalavirahito" means the Blessed One who is without a peer because there is no one equal to him in qualities such as virtue (sīla).

In this (Nibbāna), formations (saṅkhāra) are stilled; therefore, it refers to Nibbāna, which is known and spoken of as "vūpasama" (appeasement).

The word "yaṃ" is a second case ending (accusative) used in the sense of the first case (nominative), meaning "the Blessed One who has passed away."

"Suvikasiteneva" means with a mind that is very open and joyful due to being associated with rapture and happiness. He endured the feeling because the arising of phenomena was well understood. Unobstructed liberation (anāvaraṇa-vimokkha) occurs because of total extinguishment.

Because they produce their own results in a similar manner, "ākāra" refers to causes. "Sabbākāravariūpete" means endowed with all excellent causes, such as the qualities of virtue and so on.

"Kathaṃbhūtā" means "of what nature are they?"

"Cullakaddhānaṃ" means a short period of time, about half an hour or two to three hours.

## Description of the Worship of the Buddha's Body

Since instruments such as gongs and bronze drums are included here, "tāḷāvacara" refers to all musical instruments like the ātata and so on. Therefore, it is said, "all musical instruments."
189:
"Bhāveti" etc. (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1, 251) and the one or two bhūmantara (intermediate planes) also occur. "If the root is destroyed, we will be like ghosts" means, for example, a ghost living in a tree stays by the trunk when the branches and foliage are destroyed; when the trunk is destroyed, it stays by the root; but when the root is also destroyed, it becomes truly supportless. In the same way, we shall become.

Alternatively, "if the root is destroyed" refers to a tradition that a ghost cuts a certain root of a tree or shrub and gives it to its child. As long as it does not leave the child's hand, the ghost wanders in that place invisibly. When that root is lost, either because someone snatched it or through forgetfulness, the ghost must wander visibly to humans. Referring to such a ghost whose root is lost, the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera said, "If the root is destroyed, we will be like ghosts."

"Making me a bodily witness (kāyasakkhi)" means, because I am one who has personally realized that Candūpama-paṭipadā (moon-like practice), making me a witness to that teaching. "He made me accept it"—this entrustment should be illustrated by the Kassapa Sutta.

It is called sandanacitaka (sandalwood pyre) because of the abundance of sandalwood logs. "Hearing those words" means the people heard the desire of the devas as spoken by the Venerable Anuruddha Thera. "Even a fringe" means not even a single thread from the fringe of the wrapped, brand-new Kāsika cloths moved. "Even a piece of wood" means even a piece of wood from the sandalwood pyre moved.

Because terms used for a whole are also seen applied to parts, the bone relics, which are parts of the Blessed One's body, are called "sarīrāni (bodies)."

"Did not scatter" means they remained in their original form. After saying, "The remaining relics scattered," the phrase beginning with "tattha" is spoken to show how those relics scattered.

"Streams of water appeared and extinguished [the fire]" means that by the supernatural power of the devas, streams of water appeared and extinguished the Blessed One's pyre. To answer the question of why such large and numerous streams of water appeared, it is said, "The Blessed One's pyre was large." Indeed, that sandalwood pyre was very large, being one hundred and twenty cubits high. "With aṭṭhadantaka" means with plows; because those plows have eight tooth-like pointed wooden stakes, they are called "aṭṭhadantaka (eight-toothed)."
190:
It is said that "the Dhamma talk alone is the measure (pamāṇa)." This is because the event was exceedingly wonderful and marvelous, because it brought extraordinary inspiration to those who saw and heard it, and because it specifically demonstrated the supernatural power of the Buddha. For the Dhamma-preachers who recount the events of the Blessed Buddha who has attained Parinibbāna, saying, "Such is the power of the Blessed One," the Dhamma talk proceeding according to the strength of their own wisdom is the only measure here, because the subject matter to be praised is of a vast scope. Therefore, the meaning is that this is a "ground for praise (vaṇṇanābhūmi)."

"Having caused an application of the four types of scents to be made" means having caused a smooth and fine application to be made with scents produced by grinding tagara, saffron (kuṅkuma), cloves (yavanapuppha), and tamāla leaves (tamālapattāni). "Khacitvā" means decorating by hanging here and there. Flowers taken and strung together with scented materials are called scent-garlands (gandhadāma). Jewel ornaments are called jewel-garlands (ratanadāma). "Having caused an enclosure of curtains and bamboo mats to be made" means by making an enclosure of bamboo mats on the outside and an enclosure of curtains on the inside. Banners that catch the wind are called wind-banners (vātapaṭākā). A couch with legs carved in the form of a sarabha beast is a sarabhamaya-pallaṅka; "on that sarabhamaya-pallaṅka," and so on.

Men with spears in their hands are called "spears (satti)" because they go about with those spears, just as it is said, "The lances proceed." "Having them surrounded by men with spears in their hands" refers to the fivefold protection (pañcakaraṇa). The same method applies to the bowmen. "Making it like a lattice-work (gavacchijāla)" means by arranging a continuous, gapless guard.

"Sādhukīḷita" means the play of the virtuous (sādhu), because it accomplishes the welfare of oneself and others. It is so called because it generates noble merit and because it is a playful dwelling that is not contrary to the welfare of the future life.

## Description of the Distribution of the Bodily Relics (Sarīradhātuvibhajana-vaṇṇanā)

"In this manner alone" means according to the custom of sitting on the noble floor of the palace, sitting alone in that manner without any guards or protection. "Supinaka" means a bad dream. "Wearing double white garments" means wearing two white cloths together as one. By wearing them thus, even for one overwhelmed by grief, those clothes remain in place without slipping off.

"The anointer (abhiseka-siñcaka)" means the one who preaches and sprinkles the auspicious Dhamma of consecration, because it is a supreme blessing in the royal consecration. "He became unconscious (visaññī)"—just as King Ajātasattu became unconscious due to his unwavering love born from knowing the nectar-like essence of the Buddha's special qualities, his settled devotion based on the faith of a worldling, and the tenderness of heart produced by the gratitude for the favors received.
191:
A chest like a golden image refers to a chest resembling a well-crafted backrest.

Why are the Mallas of Pāvā mentioned last in the Pali text? Did they depart last despite being closer to Kusinārā? Yes, to show that they departed last, the passage beginning with "Tattha pāveyyakā" is stated.

'Dhātupāsanatthaṃ' means for the purpose of worshipping and attending to the relics of the Teacher. The deities became their partisans, considering that "the relics rightfully belong to those Mallas."

'Doṇagajjitaṃ' refers to the thunderous speech of the Brahmin Doṇa, which was associated with three moments of the Teacher and consisted of two recitation sections (bhāṇavāras). Indeed, for the purpose of delivering this speech, the Buddha, while traveling, sat at the foot of a certain tree after making a resolution: "As long as the Brahmin Doṇa, who is following behind, sees my footprint, let it not disappear." The Brahmin Doṇa, observing that "these are the footprints of the Supreme Person in the world including the devas," followed the tracks and approached the Teacher. The Teacher then taught him the Dhamma, and he became established in faith in the Blessed One. Regarding what speech was uttered, it says: "Suṇantu... pe... avoca."

Be united, gathering together in body and having consistent, non-conflicting speech. To show the cause of that unity, it says "sammodamānā." Therefore, it means "be mutually joyful in mind as well."

To the assembly of kings who had gathered from their respective places of residence; likewise, to the groups that had arrived, acknowledging them by accepting their words.

## Explanation of the Worship of the Relic Stupa

Possession by a deity is called 'yakkhaggāho' (seizure by a yakkha). 'Khipitaka' refers to a coughing illness caused by the disturbance of the elements. 'Arocaka' refers to the illness of having no appetite for food.

'On the seventh day' means on the seventh day after seven years and seven months. 'According to strength' means according to the strength of one's wealth and resources.

'The Elders who performed the Recital later' refers to the Elders of the Second and Third Councils. 'Seeing the danger to the relics' means seeing that danger would arise from heretics to the relics as they were established in various stupas; and seeing that in the future, King Dhammāsoka would extract them from the great relic deposit and distribute them widely, thereby bringing welfare and happiness to the world including the devas. Placing only enough relics for worship in the hands of the king, and not in the stupas... in later times, King Asoka would not find the relics in the stupas. Due to previous meritorious deeds...
192:
Seeing the danger that would come to the relics residing in various stupas through the power of heretics, and seeing that in the future, King Dhammāsoka would extract those relics from the great relic deposit where they were well-protected and distribute them, bringing welfare and happiness to the world including the devas—this is the meaning. Only the relics intended for personal worship were placed in the hands of the kings, and not in the stupas. For this reason, in later times, King Asoka did not find the relics in the stupas.

To make it suitable and easy to take the previously made relic casket, he had subsequent caskets made, including eight caskets and eight stupas made of yellow sandalwood and so on. The same method applies to caskets made of red sandalwood and others. Excluding caskets made of ruby, pearl, cat's eye, and crystal, the relics were placed in caskets adorned with other various gems. The crystal stupa was the size of the stupa built by King Devānampiyatissa (Thūpārāma).

He had golden inscriptions made, resolving: "Until King Dhammāsoka extracts these relics from here to build stupas outside, let these flowers not wither." He also placed door-pulls, keys, and locks for opening the doors. He installed a mechanical device (yanta) like a pack of predators, made of interconnected figures that could move and appear terrifying. Therefore, it was said in the Commentary, "wooden figures," and so on. Vissakamma, the celestial architect, after binding that intricate machine made of many wooden figures with a single pin through his divine power, returned to the deva realm. The passage beginning with "from all around" describes the manifestation of King Ajātasattu's special and persistent effort in the work of that relic deposit.

When the King asked, "In which place is the relic deposit?" some say that in that assembly, there were no recipients of special attainment who knew the location. Others say they did not speak, thinking that by remaining hidden and relying on the words of the senior Elder, the King would investigate and find out. He employed those possessed by deities and those who could control spirits through offerings and rituals. The Elders of the Second Council placed this passage: "Thus it was in the past." The Elders of the Third Council also included the account of the Great Relic Deposit as part of the meaning.
